C1.justification: The first channel-wise influence claim and the anomaly-detection/channel-pruning contributions remain. v2 adds the explicit conclusion that channel pruning removes more redundant data than sample-wise pruning, and foregrounds dataset redundancy and insufficient data utilization by current models. These extend the conclusions within the existing research scope.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's general limitation about unexplored tasks, v2 specifically discusses strengths on localized channel faults and possible weakness on globally synchronized anomalies. It adds a temporal-dependence explanation for MoSo's performance, physical interpretations of selected ETTh1 channels, and explanations of differences from LIME and SHAP. These substantially expand mechanism discussions and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies a code-repository link and clarifies that anomaly-detection metrics on SMD, MSL and SMAP are computed per trace and then averaged. It also documents the units of work used for timing measurements. The existing PyTorch, RTX 3090, optimizer, loss and window-length disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: All original anomaly-detection and forecasting datasets remain. v2 adds ETTh1 and ETTm1, extending pruning evaluation to seven-channel transformer datasets, including an ETTh1 interpretability case study. The underlying anomaly-detection and forecasting tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds TimeInf to the anomaly-detection comparison and LIME, SHAP and NFS to the main channel-pruning comparison. Random channel selection is removed from that corresponding 96-step comparison, although retained in other experiments. Figure 3 additionally compares channel pruning against MoSo and random sample pruning, substantially expanding the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 5.2.3 introduces a substantive evaluation design comparing sample and channel pruning at matched retained-data proportions. Additional protocols include 192-step forecasting, DLinear as a forecasting backbone, retaining two or three ETT channels, and per-instance or per-timestamp timing measurements. Existing main experiments retain their stated metrics, optimizers and input windows.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ETTh1 case study examining whether selected channels represent distinct physical variables, sample-versus-channel pruning analysis, and runtime/scaling analyses. Appendix D.4 also extends generalization checks to DLinear and longer forecasts. The original gradient-parameter ablation, architecture-generalization results and equidistant-versus-most-influential selection study are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experiments. Mean/standard-deviation and median/IQR calculations concern the unchanged anomaly-score normalization procedure, not experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Most matched original scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial baseline, pruning, ETT, 192-step, DLinear and runtime results. New comparisons reveal exceptions to ChInf's lead: in Table 3, iTransformer on Solar at 20% retention scores 0.214 with LIME versus 0.219 with ChInf. PatchTST full-channel reference MSE also changes from 0.224 to 0.223 on Solar and 0.454 to 0.452 on Traffic between v1 Table 5 and v2 Table 3, without an explanation.

M1.justification: The gradient-based influence score, maximum channel self-influence anomaly score and equidistant pruning strategy remain. Algorithm 2 corrects its selection condition from i == t to i mod t == 0, making the pseudocode implement the periodic selection already described in v1. This is a limited algorithm correction; the PDFs do not establish a changed experimental implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten, and the method is consistently presented as ChInf. Section 4.2 is reorganized around dataset pruning, the pruning experiments gain a subsection structure, and broader impact and dataset descriptions move into the appendices. The title, author block and section terminology also change.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a conference layout and places the algorithms side by side. It removes the original framework diagram, moves and enlarges the anomaly-score visualization, relocates dataset tables and condenses the main architecture-generalization table while retaining full appendix results. New displays include ETTh1 traces, sample-pruning curves, a summary of existing retention ratios, and additional forecasting and runtime tables.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning by acknowledging TimeInf and distinguishing temporal influence from channel-wise influence. It expands connections to dataset pruning, including language-model data pruning, and contrasts ChInf with LIME, SHAP and NFS. Additional anomaly-detection references support the new applicability discussion; these changes go beyond citation-format updates.

T1.justification: v2 reverses the loss difference defining TracIn in Equation 1 and the appendix proof, and explicitly describes the reference model as trained without the studied example. Appendix D.6 adds an O(nd) computational-complexity argument. The channel-wise decomposition remains; the proof's intermediate Taylor-expansion sign is still inconsistent with the revised loss difference.

improvement.justification: v1's main pruning validation relied on naive channel selectors. v2 addresses this important evidence gap through LIME/SHAP/NFS comparisons and direct sample-pruning comparisons, while TimeInf supplies a relevant time-series influence baseline. Runtime measurements and specific anomaly-type limitations further improve practical assessment. Some new table highlighting overstates ChInf's wins, the proof retains a sign inconsistency, and uncertainty remains unreported, but the comparative evidence is substantially stronger overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same channel-wise influence method and its anomaly-detection and channel-pruning applications. The text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite renaming and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, an ETTh1 case study, sample-pruning comparisons and additional forecasting and runtime results.

before.justification: v1 reports original anomaly-detection, forecasting and channel-pruning experiments, including architecture generalization and selection-strategy analyses in Appendix C.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Using a long-standing conjecture from combinatorial group theory, we explore,
from multiple perspectives, the challenges of finding rare instances carrying
disproportionately high rewards. Based on lessons learned in the context
defined by the Andrews-Curtis conjecture, we propose algorithmic enhancements
and a topological hardness measure with implications for a broad class of
search problems. As part of our study, we also address several open
mathematical questions. Notably, we demonstrate the length reducibility of all
but two presentations in the Akbulut-Kirby series (1981), and resolve various
potential counterexamples in the Miller-Schupp series (1991), including three
infinite subfamilies.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the claimed resolution of stable AC-triviality for AK(3) with length reduction for AK(n), n at least 5, and triviality results for three infinite Miller–Schupp subfamilies. They also foreground a global topological hardness measure and PPO successes on cases missed by greedy search.

C2.justification: The retained 53-move connection to AK(3) is explicitly reinterpreted as insufficient to establish stable AC-triviality. v2 adds explanations of the horizon curriculum, interprets barcode ratios as suggesting comparable complexity under different move sets, and distinguishes proven knot-presentation subclasses from broader unresolved conjectures.

D1.justification: v2 supplies additional explicit AC paths, identifies XGBoost and SHAP, and directs readers to a verification notebook. Existing hyperparameters and dataset-generation pseudocode are retained, while the giotto-TDA version and old AK(3) search-budget details are omitted. New printed paths use undefined h0 despite definitions running from h1 to h12, limiting reproducibility.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds a tested presentation from the Meier–Zupan family, P(5, 2; 4/5), beyond the earlier Miller–Schupp and Akbulut–Kirby examples. The main 1,190-presentation dataset and approximately 1.8-million-presentation Transformer corpus remain unchanged; the newly solved Miller–Schupp cases belong to retained coverage.

E2.justification: The main BFS, greedy-search, and PPO comparisons remain. Section 8.2 adds explicit XGBoost comparisons using length-only and neighborhood-size baselines against barcode and combined features. The separate GS-versus-BFS comparison for the length-25 presentation in v1 Section 3.5 is omitted.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include PPO training for 100 million interactions with horizons increasing from 200 to 400, 800, and 1200, a 20-million-node greedy search on AK(5), and a 4:1 train/test split evaluated with F1 for the barcode-feature study. The original benchmark settings and Appendix A hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v1 mainly reports neighborhood-size distributions and brief observations about centrality and spectral features. v2 adds barcode-vector sensitivity analysis, exhaustive feature-subset comparisons, and SHAP feature attribution in Section 8.2 and Figures 21–22. Section 7 also adds analysis of ratios between the retained AC and AC-prime graph statistics.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same five-seed experiment, individual solution counts, and mean of 334.4. v2 introduces no additional quantified uncertainty, confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run counts for its added experiments.

E6.justification: Under the new horizon schedule, v2 reports two additional Miller–Schupp solutions with shortened paths of 195 and 381 moves, plus a 49-move solution for P(5, 2; 4/5). New classifier F1 scores are 0.885 for length, 0.930 for neighborhood size, 0.943 for barcode features, and 0.962 for selected combined features. The principal fixed-setting search/PPO totals and Transformer validation loss remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 adds staged-horizon PPO training and barcode features for hardness prediction. The underlying greedy-search rule, PPO objectives, reward function and networks, Transformer architecture, and adaptive-supermove Algorithm 3 remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, and outline are substantially rewritten. Language modeling moves ahead of topology; the former combined topology section becomes separate global-hardness and local-analysis sections; stable AC material is extensively rewritten in Section 9 and appendices. PPO discussion is reorganized into fixed- and variable-horizon subsections.

P2.justification: v2 adds RL and adaptive-action diagrams, feature-analysis plots, crossing and unknot diagrams, and Reidemeister illustrations. Existing comparison plots are relocated and rearranged. The graph-statistics tables are shortened to lengths 11–16 and supplemented by a ratio table; many retained plots preserve their underlying data.

R1.justification: The relationship to Myasnikov–Myasnikov–Shpilrain changes fundamentally: a result previously used to justify the central theorem is scrutinized and its misprint shown to invalidate that application. v2 also positions its infinite-family results against Lisitsa's finite cases and adds connections to theorem-proving, learned optimization, and Meier–Zupan presentations.

T1.justification: v1's Theorem 1 asserting stable AC-triviality of AK(3) is withdrawn after identifying its faulty premise. v2 adds proofs for infinite Miller–Schupp subfamilies, Akbulut–Kirby length reductions, and unknot-derived presentations, together with new conjectures and the Reidemeister-move proof in Appendix E. It also substantially expands the persistent-homology formalization.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves a central correctness problem by withdrawing v1's unsupported stable AC-triviality theorem for AK(3) and explaining the faulty premise in Appendix F. New mathematical proofs and quantitative hardness analyses substantially strengthen the paper. Undefined h0 entries in the new certificates remain a reproducibility defect, but the correction of the centerpiece claim and added supporting evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Andrews–Curtis case study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated during the substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and reports additional variable-horizon PPO outcomes, computational trivializations, and quantitative feature-prediction experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original search and PPO experiments, Transformer training and embedding results, and computations of presentation neighborhoods and persistent homology.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly
important. However, due to the quadratic time complexity of attention
computation, scaling LLMs to longer contexts incurs extremely slow inference
speed and high GPU memory consumption for caching key-value (KV) vectors. This
paper proposes RetrievalAttention, a training-free approach to both accelerate
attention computation and reduce GPU memory consumption. By leveraging the
dynamic sparsity of attention mechanism, RetrievalAttention proposes to build
approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) indexes for KV vectors in CPU memory
and retrieve the most relevant ones through vector search during generation.
Unfortunately, we observe that the off-the-shelf ANNS indexes are often
ineffective for such retrieval tasks due to the out-of-distribution (OOD)
between query vectors and key vectors in the attention mechanism.
RetrievalAttention addresses the OOD challenge by designing an attention-aware
vector search algorithm that can adapt to the distribution of query vectors.
Our evaluation demonstrates that RetrievalAttention achieves near full
attention accuracy while only requiring access to 1--3% of the data. This leads
to a significant reduction in the inference cost of long-context LLMs, with a
much lower GPU memory footprint. In particular, RetrievalAttention only needs a
single NVIDIA RTX4090 (24GB) to serve 128K tokens for LLMs with 8B parameters,
which is capable of generating one token in 0.188 seconds.

metadata.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly important. However, scaling LLMs to longer contexts incurs slow inference speed and high GPU memory consumption for caching key-value (KV) vectors. This paper presents RetrievalAttention, a training-free approach to both accelerate the decoding phase and reduce GPU memory consumption by pre-building KV vector indexes for fixed contexts and maintaining them in CPU memory for efficient retrieval. Unlike conventional KV cache methods, RetrievalAttention integrate approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) indexes into attention computation. We observe that off-the-shelf ANNS techniques often fail due to the out-of-distribution (OOD) nature of query and key vectors in attention mechanisms. RetrievalAttention overcomes this with an attention-aware vector index. Our evaluation shows RetrievalAttention achieves near full attention accuracy while accessing only 1-3\% of the data, significantly reducing inference costs. Remarkably, RetrievalAttention enables LLMs with 8B parameters to handle 128K tokens on a single NVIDIA RTX4090 (24GB), achieving a decoding speed of 0.107 seconds per token.

C1.justification: The central training-free, OOD-aware retrieval contribution and the 4.9×/1.98× decoding-speedup claims remain. The abstract drops the specific claim that serving an 8B model with 128K tokens requires only 16GB of GPU memory, retaining the less specific claim that it fits on a single 24GB RTX4090. This narrows the quantitative memory claim without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explanation attributing InfiniGen's accuracy loss to inaccurate speculation from previous layers. Appendix F interprets the budget-allocation results as task dependent, explicitly noting improved KV retrieval but reduced English QA performance. The million-token and 70B experiments extend the applicability discussion, while the central explanation based on dynamic sparsity and query–key distribution mismatch remains.

D1.justification: v3 distinguishes the RTX4090 server's 10 physical CPU cores from its 20 logical cores and newly specifies the A100 testbed's EPYC 7V13 processor and 220GB DRAM. It documents the new 70B experiment's eight 40GB A100 GPUs and layer partitioning. Appendix C revises the stated original KV format from FP32 to FP16 without explaining whether this corrects documentation or reflects an implementation change. Most implementation optimizations were already documented in v1.

E1.justification: The three benchmark suites and their existing tasks remain. Appendix A.3 extends Needle-in-a-haystack accuracy evaluation from the earlier 4K–128K range to 250K–1M tokens, adding an extreme-length retrieval scenario. v1 already measured million-token latency, but did not report retrieval accuracy at those lengths.

E2.justification: v1 explicitly excludes Quest and discusses InfiniGen without evaluating it. v3 adds Quest to the three-model ∞-Bench comparison, InfiniGen to its Llama-3 comparison, and both methods to the appendix RULER comparison in Table 9. Figure 6 also introduces RobustVamana as an OOD-aware index comparator. These substantially expand the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: StreamingLLM's budget changes from 640 to 2K tokens in Tables 2–3. Section 2.3 replaces a 64K-token, single-query Llama-2 sparsity examination with a 100K-token Llama-3 experiment profiling 20 generated tokens and comparing static versus dynamic top-1000 selection. New settings include uniform versus layer-dependent retrieval budgets and Llama-3-70B on eight A100 GPUs. Table 1 changes its named model, and Appendix C changes the stated KV precision from FP32 to FP16; these reporting revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 replaces the original attention-score/MSE illustration with a controlled static-versus-dynamic selection analysis across heads and layers. Section 4.4 adds direct recall-versus-scanning analysis of RetrievalAttention and competing indexes across three models. Appendix F adds a layer-budget allocation ablation, and Appendix A.3 adds extreme-context retrieval stress tests. The latency breakdown moved from v1 Appendix A.3 to v3 Section 4.3 is retained evidence, not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed schedules, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new profiling of 20 consecutive generated tokens is an evaluation-design detail, not a report of independent repetitions or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main RetrievalAttention benchmark scores and 0.188-second decoding latency are retained, but substantial results are added or replaced. The new sparsity analysis reports 89% dynamic versus 71% static attention recovery; new results cover additional baselines, million-token retrieval, and budget allocation. Table 11 reports 70B-model accuracy/latency of 23.5%/1.62 seconds for RetrievalAttention versus 24.0%/5.68 seconds for Flat. StreamingLLM's Llama-3 RULER average changes from 15.80 to 25.01 under its larger token budget, so this is not a same-setting gain.

M1.justification: The core attention-aware index, CPU–GPU execution, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix F adds a tested PyramidKV-based variant that changes retrieval-budget allocation across layers, assigning more tokens to lower layers instead of using a uniform budget. This is a limited procedural adaptation, not a replacement of the main method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and background receive substantial rewriting and expanded explanations of ANNS operation, distribution mismatch, and resource requirements. The evaluation narrative incorporates the former appendix latency breakdown, adds a dedicated index-analysis subsection, and gains appendices E–G. Citations and references also change from numbered to author–year organization.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a different document template and substantially reorganizes displays. Figure 1 and Table 1 are placed together; the original composite Figure 2 is reworked into separate sparsity and OOD displays; new recall curves and a million-token heatmap appear. Table 2 gains comparator rows, the latency breakdown moves into the main text, and Tables 9–11 add new appendix comparisons. These changes go well beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 adds references covering ANNS applications and algorithms, OOD-DiskANN, PyramidKV, and PQCache. Section 5 extends the comparison with concurrent work to PQCache, while Appendix D narrows the earlier blanket assertion that related sparse-transformer approaches require retraining to acknowledge approaches targeting CPU-only scenarios. The overall research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 2.3 introduces a mathematical definition of recovery ratio as the cumulative attention weight of the top-k critical tokens, replacing the earlier MSE-based characterization. This is a limited metric definition: the attention approximation and CPU–GPU combination equations (1)–(5) remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central efficiency argument: Figure 6 directly tests the proposed index's recall versus scanning cost, whereas v1's corresponding plots only examined conventional indexes. Quest, InfiniGen, and RobustVamana comparisons address important comparator gaps, and the controlled sparsity and budget analyses improve explanatory support. Million-token accuracy and 70B tests broaden validation. Limits remain: Table 11 shows 23.5% accuracy versus 35.0% for full attention, and the precision/model-reporting revisions are unexplained. Nevertheless, the added evidence resolves substantial weaknesses in v1's experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RetrievalAttention, with matching core methods, equations, experiments, and appendices. Their complete text, tables, figures, and algorithms are readable and support comparison, including the additional appendices in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, controlled sparsity analysis, retrieval-budget experiments, million-token retrieval accuracy, and a 70B-model evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy experiments on ∞-Bench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-haystack, attention and vector-search analyses, and decoding latency measurements on RTX4090 and A100 hardware.

arxiv_record.abstract: Machine learning models are often brittle under distribution shift, i.e., when data distributions at test time differ from those during training. Understanding this failure mode is central to identifying and mitigating safety risks of mass adoption of machine learning. Here we analyze ridge regression under concept shift -- a form of distribution shift in which the input-label relationship changes at test time. We derive an exact expression for prediction risk in the thermodynamic limit. Our results reveal nontrivial effects of concept shift on generalization performance, including a phase transition between weak and strong concept shift regimes and nonmonotonic data dependence of test performance even when double descent is absent. Our theoretical results are in good agreement with experiments based on transformers pretrained to solve linear regression; under concept shift, too long context length can be detrimental to generalization performance of next token prediction. Finally, our experiments on MNIST and FashionMNIST suggest that this intriguing behavior is present also in classification problems.
arxiv_record.authors: Alex Nguyen, David J. Schwab, Vudtiwat Ngampruetikorn
arxiv_record.title: Generalization vs. Specialization under Concept Shift

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add explicit claims about a weak/strong concept-shift phase transition and quantitative agreement with transformer experiments, including degradation with longer contexts. These extend the central contribution beyond v1's ridge-regression findings and qualitative classification illustration.

C2.justification: v2 interprets anisotropic-pretrained transformers as learning structured regularization equivalent to feature whitening, and attributes contrasting risk curves to pretraining priors. It also distinguishes concept-shift effects from model misspecification and discusses implications for principal component regression. These substantive interpretations are absent from v1.

D1.justification: Section 4 documents the new task-generation process, eight-layer nanoGPT architecture, embedding dimension 128, causal masking and Adam learning rate 0.0001. Classification settings are relocated without substantive revision. However, Figure 5's SNR=128 is not reconciled with the stated 32-dimensional standard-normal coefficients and noise variance 0.5.

E1.justification: v2 adds empirical coverage of synthetic in-context regression: transformers predict query labels from examples, with coefficient shifts between context and query. It also evaluates anisotropic inputs following isotropic or anisotropic pretraining. MNIST and FashionMNIST coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Figures 5–6 introduce comparisons between pretrained transformers and theoretical ridge predictions. Figure 6 specifically compares isotropic and anisotropic pretraining with isotropic ridge penalties, Λ=λI, and structured penalties, Λ=λΣ. These transformer comparisons and the structured-ridge comparator are absent from v1.

E3.justification: The new transformer experiments introduce a context-length/MSE evaluation protocol, reporting 32-dimensional inputs, 2^20 training tasks and 10,000 new test tasks, alongside coefficient-shrinkage, rotation and pretraining-distribution controls. The existing classification sampling, optimizer and training-budget settings are retained.

E4.justification: Figure 6 adds a controlled analysis of how pretraining covariance affects robustness to concept shift on high-variance features, using κ+² values of 1.0, 0.6 and 0.3. This tests the influence of learned priors beyond v1's analytical feature-anisotropy and shift-strength sweeps.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix C states that variability from stochastic training and training-data selection is smaller than the plotted markers. This statement is omitted when the classification details move to v2 Section 5. Neither version supplies explicit repetition counts or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The original risk and classification curves are retained as Figures 2, 4 and 7. New Figures 5–6 report transformer agreement with isotropic theory, harmful effects of long contexts under strong shift, and contrasting anisotropic-test behavior across pretraining distributions. Figure 3 additionally reports the phase diagram.

M1.justification: The proposed Gaussian regression model and ridge objective and estimator in Equation (3) remain unchanged, as does the classification learner. The transformers and structured-ridge curves added in Section 4 serve as experimental validation and comparison methods.

P1.justification: v2 substantially expands the introduction with an explicit contribution list, develops the isotropic and anisotropic explanations into longer discussions, and adds dedicated transformer and related-work sections. Classification implementation details move from Appendix C into the main narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds a distribution-shift schematic, a phase-diagram heatmap and two multipanel transformer-comparison figures. arxiv_record.abstract: We derive and investigate two DPO variants that explicitly model the possibility of declaring a tie in pair-wise comparisons. We replace the Bradley-Terry model in DPO with two well-known modeling extensions, by Rao and Kupper and by Davidson, that assign probability to ties as alternatives to clear preferences. Our experiments in neural machine translation and summarization show that explicitly labeled ties can be added to the datasets for these DPO variants without the degradation in task performance that is observed when the same tied pairs are presented to DPO. We find empirically that the inclusion of ties leads to stronger regularization with respect to the reference policy as measured by KL divergence, and we see this even for DPO in its original form. We provide a theoretical explanation for this regularization effect using ideal DPO policy theory. We further show performance improvements over DPO in translation and mathematical reasoning using our DPO variants. We find it can be beneficial to include ties in preference optimization rather than simply discard them, as is done in common practice.

arxiv_record.abstract:
There is a well known intrinsic trade-off between the fairness of a representation and the performance of classifiers derived from the representation. Due to the complexity of optimisation algorithms in most modern representation learning approaches, for a given method it may be non-trivial to decide whether the obtained fairness-performance curve of the method is optimal, i.e., whether it is close to the true Pareto front for these quantities for the underlying data distribution.
  In this paper we propose a new method to compute the optimal Pareto front, which does not require the training of complex representation models. We show that optimal fair representations possess several useful structural properties, and that these properties enable a reduction of the computation of the Pareto Front to a compact discrete problem. We then also show that these compact approximating problems can be efficiently solved via off-the shelf concave-convex programming methods.
  Since our approach is independent of the specific model of representations, it may be used as the benchmark to which representation learning algorithms may be compared. We experimentally evaluate the approach on a number of real world benchmark datasets.

metadata.abstract: There is a well known intrinsic trade-off between the fairness of a representation and the performance of classifiers derived from the representation. In this paper we propose a new method to compute the optimal Pareto front of this trade off. In contrast to the existing methods, this approach does not require the training of complex fair representation models.    Our approach is derived through three main steps: We analyze fair representations theoretically, and derive several structural properties of optimal representations. We then show that these properties enable a reduction of the computation of the Pareto Front to a compact discrete problem. Finally, we show that these compact approximating problems can be efficiently solved via off-the shelf concave-convex programming methods.    In addition to representations, we show that the new methods may also be used to directly compute the Pareto front of fair classification problems. Moreover, the proposed methods may be used with any concave performance measure. This is in contrast to the existing reduction approaches, developed recently in fair classification, which rely explicitly on the structure of the non-differentiable accuracy measure, and are thus unlikely to be extendable.   The approach was evaluated on several real world benchmark datasets and compares favorably to a number of recent state of the art fair representation and classification methods.

arxiv_record.abstract: Low-rank training has emerged as a promising approach for reducing memory usage in training Large Language Models (LLMs). Previous methods either rely on decomposing weight matrices (e.g., LoRA), or seek to decompose gradient matrices (e.g., GaLore) to ensure reduced memory consumption. However, both of them constrain the training in a low-rank subspace, thus inevitably leading to sub-optimal performance. This raises a question: whether it is possible to consistently preserve the low-rank constraint for memory efficiency, while achieving full-rank training (i.e., training with full-rank gradients of full-rank weights) to avoid inferior outcomes? In this paper, we propose a new plug-and-play training framework for LLMs called Fira, as the first attempt to achieve this goal. First, we observe an interesting phenomenon during LLM training: the scaling impact of adaptive optimizers (e.g., Adam) on the gradient norm remains similar from low-rank to full-rank training. Based on this observation, we propose a norm-based scaling method, which utilizes the scaling impact of low-rank optimizers as substitutes for that of original full-rank optimizers to enable full-rank training. In this way, we can preserve the low-rank constraint in the optimizer while achieving full-rank training for better performance. Moreover, we find that there are sudden gradient rises during the optimization process, potentially causing loss spikes. To address this, we further put forward a norm-growth limiter to smooth the gradient via regulating the relative increase of gradient norms. Extensive experiments on the pre-training and fine-tuning of LLMs show that Fira outperforms both LoRA and GaLore, achieving performance that is comparable to or even better than full-rank training.
arxiv_record.authors: Xi Chen, Kaituo Feng, Changsheng Li, Xunhao Lai, Xiangyu Yue, Ye Yuan, Guoren Wang
arxiv_record.title: Fira: Can We Achieve Full-rank Training of LLMs Under Low-rank Constraint?

E1.justification: v3 retains C4 pre-training and the eight commonsense datasets, and adds MMLU evaluation covering STEM, social sciences, humanities and other subjects (Appendix J, Table 16). This substantially extends task coverage into multidisciplinary knowledge evaluation.

E2.justification: The commonsense comparison replaces Prefix, Series Adapter and Parallel Adapter with ReLoRA, Flora and full-rank training. E4.justification: Beyond retained ablations, v3 tests alternative stabilization methods, limiter-threshold sensitivity, and the effects of scaling granularity, SVD and rank in Fira-only-scaling. M1.justification: The main Fira update, column-wise scaling, norm-growth limiter and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. v3 introduces the diagnostic Fira-only-scaling variant, which removes the separate projected Adam update and applies low-rank-derived scaling directly to the full gradient (Appendices E.1 and F). P1.justification: v3 revises the abstract and scaling-factor narrative, moves the main algorithm into a dedicated implementation appendix, and reorganizes v1's Appendix A.1–A.7 into separate implementation, settings, overhead, similarity and theory sections. The expanded appendix structure and rewritten explanations substantially change document organization beyond citation-style edits.

P2.justification: v1's scaling-factor heatmaps are replaced by similarity tables and new trend plots. Figure 2 gains an Adam curve, and the method-comparison table gains a full-rank column and gradient-memory row. R1.justification: Appendix I adds substantive positioning against Adam-mini, SlimAdam, MicroAdam, AdaLomo, FRUGAL and GaRare. APOLLO and alternative stabilization research also enter the discussion. arxiv_record.abstract: While language models have shown remarkable performance across diverse tasks, they still encounter challenges in complex reasoning scenarios. Recent research suggests that language models trained on linearized search traces toward solutions, rather than solely on the final solutions, exhibit improved generalization, despite the search traces being potentially noisy or suboptimal. However, relying on such imperfect traces can result in inefficient use of test-time compute. To address this, we propose guided reinforced self-training (Guided-ReST), a fine-tuning algorithm designed to improve the model's capability for effective search during inference. The key insight behind Guided-ReST is that optimal solutions can serve as valuable step-by-step landmarks to guide the model's search process. Based on this insight, we introduce a novel data generation method that seamlessly incorporates optimal solutions into the model's search procedure, enabling the generation of high-quality search traces. By fine-tuning the model on these search traces, we effectively distill improved search strategies into the model. Our method significantly enhances the search capabilities of language models on arithmetic reasoning and code self-repair tasks, including Countdown, CodeContests, and CodeForces. We release the source code at https://github.com/snu-mllab/guided-rest.
arxiv_record.authors: Seungyong Moon, Bumsoo Park, Hyun Oh Song
arxiv_record.title: Learning to Better Search with Language Models via Guided Reinforced Self-Training

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand from Countdown accuracy and guided-training/PPO synergy to inference-time search efficiency and applicability to code self-repair. v2 makes a new central claim of comparable accuracy using roughly half PPO's token budget. The underlying claim that optimal-solution guidance improves learned search is retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains PPO synergy through broader coverage of correct candidates measured by pass@k, replacing the earlier emphasis on training stability and contextual likelihood tradeoffs. It adds substantive limitations concerning access to optimal solutions and an oracle capable of locating errors and backtracking. It also discusses the modest code-repair gains and acknowledges that RL fine-tuning on code was not tested.

D1.justification: v2 adds code-generation, repair, reference-guidance, and reference-masking prompts, together with code sampling settings. Appendix E replaces the TRIL-based implementation description with verl, Liger Kernel, and vLLM, and revises training and hardware details. Earlier GPT-2 configuration and implementation-bug disclosures are omitted. The repository address changes, and v2's release statement mentions source code without v1's explicit trained-model availability statement.

E1.justification: Countdown with seen and unseen targets remains. v2 adds multi-turn code self-repair, training on 16K SYNTHETIC-1 problems curated from APPS, CodeContests, and TACO, and evaluating on CodeContests and CodeForces. This substantially broadens the domain and task requirements beyond arithmetic tree search.

E2.justification: The Countdown comparison adds a reported behavior-cloning result below 40% accuracy in v2 Section 5.2 and omits v1's evaluated Symbolic baseline from Figure 4. SoS and PPO remain; the earlier STaR self-training baseline corresponds to ReST rather than constituting a newly added comparator.

E3.justification: Countdown switches from GPT-2 250M to Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, with revised training budgets and hyperparameters. PPO changes from 25,600 sampled training problems to 200K examples over two epochs. Evaluation adds token-budget sweeps and pass@k; Table 1 uses 10K rather than 200K problems. New code experiments use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, four-turn episodes, 16K-token responses, and private-test execution, without RL fine-tuning.

E4.justification: v2 adds pass@k candidate-coverage analysis and evaluates operation-level PPO and dense rewards across token budgets. It removes v1's First/Rand/Last node-selection sensitivity study, trajectory likelihood/length distributions, value-learning and KL-stability diagnostics, and numerical GPT-Neo/GPT-2 and APA appendix comparisons. These are substantial changes to the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports three training seeds, means, standard deviations, and error bars in Section 4.1, Figure 4, and Table 2. v2 provides point estimates without corresponding seed counts or uncertainty intervals. Its 32 or 128 sampled responses per problem do not establish repeated training runs; the change is a removal of uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The Countdown results are replaced under changed conditions: v1 Table 2 reports GSoS+PPO at 74.77%/73.30% for seen/unseen targets, while v2 reports approximately 87% for both. This is not a same-setting performance gain. New pass@k results include Guided-ReST versus ReST pass@32 of 33.9% versus 30.4% on CodeContests and 37.6% versus 35.9% on CodeForces in v2 Table 3. Multiple earlier diagnostic result sets disappear.

M1.justification: Guided-ReST retains GSoS's subgoal replacement and trajectory truncation mechanism. However, v2 changes PPO from GAE with KL regularization to Monte Carlo returns without a KL penalty, and replaces the correctness/efficiency reward with a binary outcome reward. Section 4 and Algorithm 3 add an episode-level code-repair adaptation using reference-solution feedback, masking reference code during training and supervising only the final response.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methods narrative, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. GSoS becomes Guided-ReST, preliminary fine-tuning sections are consolidated, a separate code-repair section is introduced, and the experiments and appendices are reorganized. These changes substantially alter the document's narrative beyond adding experimental content.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn, and the empirical presentation shifts from fixed-budget bar charts to accuracy-versus-token-budget curves. v2 introduces pass@k tables and four code-prompt panels while removing several diagnostic plots. Retained appendix search-trace examples are restyled and renumbered, rather than being new evidence.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around test-time compute, jump-start RL, and episode-level self-correction. It introduces JSRL as methodological inspiration and identifies Chang et al.'s guided-generation work as the closest predecessor, distinguishing multiple guide–base interactions. The earlier related-work discussion claiming an on-policy extension of higher-level MDP methods is removed.

T1.justification: The formal value-training target changes from GAE-based returns in v1 Appendix D to Monte Carlo returns in v2 Section 3.3, and Section 4 defines episode-level solution/feedback sequences. The operation-level probability factorization already exists in v1; expressing it as a log importance ratio is equivalent mathematics. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens applicability and evaluation beyond v1's synthetic Countdown setting: code-repair experiments test a practical adaptation, while token-budget curves and pass@k analyses directly examine efficiency and candidate coverage. These address important gaps in the earlier evidence. The gains outweigh the loss of seed-based uncertainty reporting and several diagnostic ablations, although those losses weaken confidence. Code RL benefits remain untested, and the higher Countdown scores cannot establish improvement under unchanged conditions because models and training settings changed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same guided-search research, despite the changed title and method name. All 20 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including appendices A–F, support comparison. Changed models and protocols limit direct numerical performance comparisons, not document comparability.

after.justification: v2 reports original Countdown experiments and code self-repair results on CodeContests and CodeForces, including token-budget curves and pass@k tables.

before.justification: v1 reports original Countdown experiments, including accuracy comparisons, node-selection ablations, and operation-level PPO analyses, with additional experiments in the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: While latent diffusion models (LDMs), such as Stable Diffusion, are designed for high-resolution (HR) image generation, they often struggle with significant structural distortions when generating images at resolutions higher than their training one. Instead of relying on extensive retraining, a more resource-efficient approach is to reprogram the pretrained model for HR image generation; however, existing methods often result in poor image quality and long inference time. We introduce RepLDM, a novel reprogramming framework for pretrained LDMs that enables high-quality, high-efficiency, high-resolution image generation; see Fig. 1. RepLDM consists of two stages: (i) an attention guidance stage, which generates a latent representation of a higher-quality training-resolution image using a novel training-free self-attention mechanism to enhance the structural consistency; and (ii) a progressive upsampling stage, which progressively performs upsampling in pixel space to mitigate the severe artifacts caused by latent space upsampling. The effective initialization from the first stage allows for denoising at higher resolutions with significantly fewer steps, improving the efficiency. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that RepLDM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quality and efficiency for HR image generation, underscoring its advantages for real-world applications. Codes: https://github.com/kmittle/RepLDM.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains training-free high-resolution generation through attention guidance and progressive pixel-space upsampling, improving quality and efficiency. The reprogramming terminology reframes the same contribution. Although the abstract drops the explicit speedup number, the introduction and conclusion retain the 5× speedup claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive mechanism arguments about token clustering, earlier structural emergence, frequency modulation, and the residual term as a statistical anchor. It also discusses discrepancies between perceptual quality and distributional metrics, super-resolution tradeoffs, and implementation-dependent memory comparisons. The original limitations concerning text generation and extreme-resolution inference time remain.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the pytorch-fid implementation, discloses tiled VAE encoding/decoding and optimization choices for memory comparisons, and adds component-time and memory information. Section 4.1 changes the reported inference hardware from two 4090 GPUs to one; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. The core pseudocode and principal hyperparameters were already documented in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds a benchmark drawn from the high-resolution subset of LAION-5B alongside the retained SAM benchmark and ImageNet pilot. It also evaluates canny- and depth-conditioned generation with ControlNet at 2048×2048 and 4096×4096, introducing materially different input conditions.

E2.justification: HiDiffusion joins the main quantitative and timing comparisons in Tables 1–2. Appendix J adds SDXL+BSRGAN as a super-resolution comparator. SDXL also joins the corresponding qualitative comparison grids in Figures 5 and 18, where v1 compared only MultiDiffusion, DemoFusion, AccDiffusion, and the proposed method.

E3.justification: New protocols include LAION evaluation using 20k reference images, 2k generated samples at 4096×4096, and KID/KIDc instead of IS/ISc. Appendix H evaluates an SD2.1 backbone with progressive scheduler [0.2, 0.2, 0.3]. Appendices E and K introduce component timing, NFE, FLOPs, and minimum-memory measurements. These extend evaluation rather than replace the retained main SAM protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds token-clustering, denoising-SSIM, Fourier, and attention-map analyses in Appendix A; decay-strategy and pooled-attention ablations in Appendix D; and guidance ablations with ControlNet, SD2.1, HiDiffusion, and DemoFusion. Robustness and component-cost analyses are also new. The original guidance-scale, delay-rate, and progressive-scheduler ablations are retained in Appendix C.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repeated-seed uncertainty reporting. Appendix G in v2 explicitly reports three repetitions with varying random seeds and presents means and standard deviations for four methods on SAM and LAION-5B in Tables 14–15. This substantially strengthens uncertainty reporting for the central comparisons; v1 does not specify an earlier run count.

E6.justification: Shared numerical entries in Tables 1–7 are retained, but substantial new results appear in the added comparisons and Tables 8–20. For example, HiDiffusion takes 3.4 minutes versus RepLDM's 5.7 at 4096×4096 in Table 2. On the new LAION benchmark, Table 15 reports FID 34.01±0.26 for RepLDM versus 37.03±0.27 for DemoFusion at that resolution. These are added comparisons, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The default two-stage method, Equations 1–4, and Algorithm 1 remain substantively unchanged despite AP-LDM/PFSA becoming RepLDM/TFSA. Appendix D.2 adds an explicit alternative variant, TFSA-A, which pools keys and values using 2×2 pooling before attention. This limited procedural addition is tested as an ablation, not adopted as the default method.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten around RepLDM, with widespread terminology changes from attentive guidance/PFSA to attention guidance/TFSA. The appendix is substantially reorganized into sections A–K with a contents list: existing comparisons and ablations move to B/C, and the algorithm moves to F. Expanded explanations, acknowledgments, and a conference checklist further change the document structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds numerous mechanism visualizations, comparison grids, ablation tables, and robustness/resource tables. Existing displays also change substantially: Figure 4 is reordered and its plot redrawn, qualitative grids gain an SDXL column and revised annotations, and several main-text figures are reduced and placed beside wrapped text. Existing appendix image grids are rearranged and condensed.

R1.justification: The literature is updated with FouriScale, HiDiffusion, AccDiffusion v2, FreeScale, and references supporting evaluation and implementation discussions. Appendix J elaborates the relationship to super-resolution research. The existing three-category taxonomy and central novelty argument relative to prior high-resolution generation methods remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the token-mean deviation diagnostic mathematically in Equation 5 and derives TFSA's O((hw)^2c) computational complexity and approximate FLOPs in Appendix E. These are limited mathematical additions. The main method equations remain equivalent, and no theorem or proof framework is added.

improvement.justification: v1's main evidence relies on SDXL/SAM comparisons with point estimates. v2 substantially strengthens reliability and generalization evidence through repeated-seed uncertainty reporting, LAION evaluation, additional backbones and conditioning scenarios, and targeted mechanism and resource analyses. The added comparisons reveal tradeoffs that the broad superiority language does not fully qualify: HiDiffusion is faster at larger resolutions, and SDXL+BSRGAN wins several metrics. Nevertheless, the stronger validation and more transparent comparisons provide a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, renamed from AP-LDM to RepLDM. Matching equations, pseudocode, experiments, and retained results establish continuity. The complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds LAION-5B evaluations, repeated-seed results, ControlNet and SD2.1 experiments, and mechanism and efficiency analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet upsampling experiments, SAM generation benchmarks, a 16-volunteer user study, and quantitative and qualitative ablations, including Appendix A.

arxiv_record.abstract: Time series forecasting, which aims to predict future values based on historical data, has garnered significant attention due to its broad range of applications. However, real-world time series often exhibit complex non-uniform distribution with varying patterns across segments, such as season, operating condition, or semantic meaning, making accurate forecasting challenging. Existing approaches, which typically train a single model to capture all these diverse patterns, often struggle with the pattern drifts between patches and may lead to poor generalization. To address these challenges, we propose TFPS, a novel architecture that leverages pattern-specific experts for more accurate and adaptable time series forecasting. TFPS employs a dual-domain encoder to capture both time-domain and frequency-domain features, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of temporal dynamics. It then uses subspace clustering to dynamically identify distinct patterns across data patches. Finally, pattern-specific experts model these unique patterns, delivering tailored predictions for each patch. By explicitly learning and adapting to evolving patterns, TFPS achieves significantly improved forecasting accuracy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that TFPS outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in long-term forecasting, through its dynamic and pattern-aware learning approach. The data and codes are available: https://github.com/syrGitHub/TFPS.
arxiv_record.authors: Yanru Sun, Zongxia Xie, Emadeldeen Eldele, Dongyue Chen, Qinghua Hu, Min Wu
arxiv_record.title: Learning Pattern-Specific Experts for Time Series Forecasting Under Patch-level Distribution Shift

Existing approaches, which typically train a single model to capture all these diverse patterns, often struggle with the pattern drifts between patches and may lead to poor generalization. C1.justification: The central contribution remains forecasting through dual-domain representations, subspace clustering, and pattern-specific experts. The abstract changes its highlighted performance claim from particular strength in long-term forecasting to particular strength on datasets exhibiting significant distribution shifts, a limited refocusing of the advertised advantage.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for weaker foundation-model comparisons on Traffic, reduced advantages after input-length tuning, regularization sensitivity, real-only Fourier processing, and expert-allocation behavior. It revises the expert-count interpretation around Weather and Wasserstein distances and introduces efficiency tradeoff claims. The existing limitations concerning heuristic patch lengths and emerging patterns are retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies eta = d, Gaussian initialization of subspace bases, q = C × D, d = q/K, and a recommended beta near 0.1. It adds implementation provenance for foundation-model comparisons and a Traffic data-source link. These extend documentation; the repository link, optimizer, GPU, embedding dimension, and encoder depth were already disclosed.

E1.justification: v2 adds Traffic, containing hourly road occupancy from 862 sensors, to the original eight datasets (Table 1 and Appendix A). This adds a transportation domain while retaining the same multivariate forecasting task and all previous dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with AutoTimes, Moment, Timer, MoLE, MoU, KAN4TSF, Koopa, SOLID, and OneNet. It also adds DLinear combined with SIN, SAN, Dish-TS, and RevIN. Within the retained FEDformer normalization comparison, NST is removed from v1 Table 6 to v2 Table 8; the other four normalization methods remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds separate evaluations searching input lengths over 96, 192, 336, and 512, plus systematic regularization-weight sweeps and controlled component replacements (Appendices F, J, and K). Shift diagnostics in Figures 1 and 8 and Table 5 change from MMD to Wasserstein distance. The original benchmark splits, forecasting horizons, and fixed input lengths remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablation, v2 tests imaginary Fourier components, branch-specific PI removal, R1/R2 removal, and alternatives to MoPE. It adds alpha/beta sensitivity, t-SNE representations, expert-allocation distributions, and efficiency analysis. The expert-count analysis changes its second dataset from ETTh2 to Weather, and clustering diagnostics are revised using Wasserstein distance.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, uncertainty intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its experiments. The added checklist marks statistical significance as NA but supplies no new statistical reporting.

E6.justification: The main-table forecasting values for the original eight datasets are unchanged. v2 adds Traffic results, including TFPS MSE values 0.427, 0.445, 0.459, and 0.496 across the four horizons, and extensive tuned, additional-baseline, ablation, and efficiency results. Wasserstein measurements replace MMD diagnostics. Results obtained through input-length search are additional settings, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the dual-domain encoders, subspace clustering, expert routing, aggregation, and training objective. Newly specified initialization and parameter values clarify implementation without establishing a changed procedure. Alternative architectures are evaluated as ablations, while Wasserstein distance replaces a diagnostic metric.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites portions of the abstract and motivation, condenses the PI explanation, moves time-frequency related work into the appendix, and reorganizes existing supplementary material into dedicated comparison and analysis sections. It also adds a conference checklist and funding section. This constitutes substantial document restructuring despite considerable retained method prose.

P2.justification: v2 expands and reorganizes the comparison tables, adds numerous ablation and efficiency tables, and introduces t-SNE, expert-allocation, and sensitivity plots in Figures 9–11. Shift heatmaps and expert-count charts are revised, alongside conference formatting changes. Figure 6(b) retains an ETTh2 label despite the accompanying Weather discussion.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning around foundation models, specialized expert models, and distribution shifts, adding references such as AutoTimes, Moment, Timer, MoLE, OneNet, DUET, and Mixmamba. The earlier Time-LLM/MOIRAI discussion explaining exclusion of pretrained models disappears. Existing time-frequency and general MoE discussions are largely retained or relocated.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix B's MMD definition, RKHS derivation, and empirical estimator are replaced by the Wasserstein transport definition and CDF equivalence in v2 Appendix C. This changes the mathematical basis of the diagnostics. The principal TFPS equations remain unchanged, and no new original theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct comparisons with specialized MoE and distribution-shift competitors and isolated tests of several central design choices. v2 addresses these gaps through Tables 10–11 and 13–16, supported by input-length-search comparisons and additional implementation details. This substantially strengthens validation of the contribution. Reporting defects temper the gain: Appendix I claims a speed advantage over PatchTST, whereas Table 12 reports 6.114 versus 4.861 ms, and uncertainty remains unreported. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TFPS research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial supplementary expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds Traffic evaluation, additional baseline comparisons, parameter searches, targeted ablations, and efficiency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on eight datasets, component ablations, and expert analyses, including Tables 2–3 and Figures 4–8.

arxiv_record.abstract: A key challenge in automated formal reasoning is the intractable search space, which grows exponentially with the depth of the proof. This branching is caused by the large number of candidate proof tactics which can be applied to a given goal. Nonetheless, many of these tactics are semantically similar or lead to an execution error, wasting valuable resources in both cases. We address the problem of effectively pruning this search, using only synthetic data generated from previous proof attempts. We first demonstrate that it is possible to generate semantically aware tactic representations which capture the effect on the proving environment, likelihood of success, and execution time. We then propose a novel filtering mechanism which leverages these representations to select semantically diverse and high quality tactics, using Determinantal Point Processes. Our approach, 3D- Prover, is designed to be general, and to augment any underlying tactic generator. We demonstrate the effectiveness of 3D-Prover on the miniF2F and LeanDojo benchmarks by augmenting popular open source proving LLMs. We show that our approach leads to an increase in the overall proof rate, as well as a significant improvement in the tactic success rate, execution time and diversity. We make our code available at https://github.com/sean-lamont/3D-Prover.
arxiv_record.authors: Sean Lamont, Christian Walder, Amir Dezfouli, Paul Montague, Michael Norrish
arxiv_record.title: 3D-Prover: Diversity Driven Theorem Proving With Determinantal Point Processes

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden the claimed demonstrated applicability from ReProver on miniF2F to multiple proving LLMs and the LeanDojo benchmark. The central contributions—learning transition-aware representations and using DPP filtering to improve proof search—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the costly, unbatchable-overhead account with an efficiency interpretation based on the new InternLM setup. It adds interpretations of proof-length and subgoal-diversity evidence, frames same-dataset adaptation as online improvement, and explicitly discusses restricted evaluation scale, including single-run LeanDojo results. Conversely, it removes v1's warning that transition-training and test splits can contain the same goals.

D1.justification: v2 provides an explicit code-repository link and substantially expands reproducibility information. Appendices G–I document sampling and deduplication, filtering time and VRAM usage, evaluation GPUs and CPUs, concurrent provers, training and evaluation durations, run totals and compute estimates. These are largely new disclosures; the original optimizer, learning rate, batch size and epoch settings remain.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix D adds training and evaluation on LeanDojo Novel Premises, comprising 2,000 evaluation goals, alongside the retained miniF2F benchmarks. This introduces a separate proof population; v1 used LeanDojo tooling but did not report this benchmark evaluation.

E2.justification: The principal comparator addition is No Filtering, newly reported for the existing ReProver experiments and additional evaluations. Table 3 compares InternLM-based 3D-Prover against Top-K under best-first search and No Filtering under critic-guided search. The earlier Top-K, Random, Autoencoder and transition-model controls remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 7B InternLM setup using temperature-0.7 sampling, 128 initial samples deduplicated to at most 64 candidates, K=8 filtering, and best-first or critic-guided search. Its transition model trains on miniF2F-test transitions, unlike the retained ReProver valid-to-test setup. New analyses introduce shortest-observed-proof-length normalization and subgoal similarity measured with all-MiniLM-L6-v2.

E4.justification: v2 adds the compact-goal architectural comparison, proof-length analysis on LeanDojo, similarity analysis of resulting subgoal text, and InternLM candidate-count analysis. It also replaces the rough overhead discussion with measured timing and memory comparisons. The original tactic-embedding analyses and hyperparameter sweep are retained; v1 Table 5 is relocated to v2 Table 12.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes from mean plus standard error to mean with minimum and maximum. Both versions specify four ReProver runs, without stating an increase. v2 additionally documents two- and six-attempt InternLM evaluations and standard deviations for computational measurements; existing tactic-level standard-error reporting remains.

arxiv_record.abstract: Open-Vocabulary Segmentation (OVS) aims to segment classes that are not present in the training dataset. However, most existing studies assume that the training data is fixed in advance, overlooking more practical scenarios where new datasets are continuously collected over time. To address this, we first analyze how existing OVS models perform under such conditions. In this context, we explore several approaches such as retraining, fine-tuning, and continual learning but find that each of them has clear limitations. To address these issues, we propose ConOVS, a novel continual learning method based on a Mixture-of-Experts framework. ConOVS dynamically combines expert decoders based on the probability that an input sample belongs to the distribution of each incremental dataset. Through extensive experiments, we show that ConOVS consistently outperforms existing methods across pre-training, incremental, and zero-shot test datasets, effectively expanding the recognition capabilities of OVS models when data is collected sequentially.

arxiv_record.abstract: Generating realistic time series samples is crucial for stress-testing models and protecting user privacy by using synthetic data. In engineering and safety-critical applications, these samples must meet certain hard constraints that are domain-specific or naturally imposed by physics or nature. Consider, for example, generating electricity demand patterns with constraints on peak demand times. This can be used to stress-test the functioning of power grids during adverse weather conditions. Existing approaches for generating constrained time series are either not scalable or degrade sample quality. To address these challenges, we introduce Constrained Posterior Sampling (CPS), a diffusion-based sampling algorithm that aims to project the posterior mean estimate into the constraint set after each denoising update. Notably, CPS scales to a large number of constraints ($\sim100$) without requiring additional training. We provide theoretical justifications highlighting the impact of our projection step on sampling. Empirically, CPS outperforms state-of-the-art methods in sample quality and similarity to real time series by around 70\% and 22\%, respectively, on real-world stocks, traffic, and air quality datasets.
arxiv_record.authors: Sai Shankar Narasimhan, Shubhankar Agarwal, Litu Rout, Sanjay Shakkottai, Sandeep P. Chinchali
arxiv_record.title: Constrained Posterior Sampling: Time Series Generation with Hard Constraints

It replaces the evaluation's emphasis on a unique matching test sample with distributional and per-sample comparisons, and explicitly discusses the Gaussian and unique-solution restrictions of its convergence results.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility information: GPU hardware, training-epoch limits, checkpoint selection, conditional metadata fields, four-process projection parallelism, the DS classifier, and new baseline settings are documented. V2 substantially extends task requirements through non-convex autocorrelation constraints combined with OHLC constraints on stocks and direct time-series imputation using observed-value constraints. The latter differs from v1's downstream imputation evaluation of synthetic training data.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons with Diffusion-TS, PDM, PRODIGY, and Loss-DiffTime (Tables 1–3); v1 explicitly excluded Loss-DiffTime. Figure 5 also changes comparator membership: PDM and PRODIGY replace Guided DiffTime alongside the retained COP-FT comparison.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained increasing-constraint analysis, v2 adds penalty-schedule comparisons, individual-constraint analyses, guidance-weight sensitivity results, and the noise-correction ablation (Appendix B). It also adds latency scaling and multiple generated samples for identical constraints (Appendices D and E), substantially expanding evidence about design choices, efficiency, and diversity.

E5.justification: Three-seed TSTR reporting is retained. V2 adds five-seed Discriminative Score results, timing summaries averaged over ten runs, and generated-sample mean and standard-deviation bands. E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results in Tables 2–9 and Figures 7–11, adds DS entries, and removes SSIM and violation-rate entries. Table 8's Traffic CPS DTW conflicts with Table 1 and cannot establish a performance improvement.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning around training-based versus training-free constrained generation, adding discussion of PDM, PRODIGY, Mirror Diffusion Models, and constrained-domain diffusion. arxiv_record.abstract: Time series data is prevalent across numerous fields, necessitating the development of robust and accurate forecasting models. Capturing patterns both within and between temporal and multivariate components is crucial for reliable predictions. We introduce xLSTM-Mixer, a model designed to effectively integrate temporal sequences, joint time-variate information, and multiple perspectives for robust forecasting. Our approach begins with a linear forecast shared across variates, which is then refined by xLSTM blocks. They serve as key elements for modeling the complex dynamics of challenging time series data. xLSTM-Mixer ultimately reconciles two distinct views to produce the final forecast. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate its superior long-term forecasting performance compared to recent state-of-the-art methods while requiring very little memory. A thorough model analysis provides further insights into its key components and confirms its robustness and effectiveness. This work contributes to the resurgence of recurrent models in forecasting by combining them, for the first time, with mixing architectures.
arxiv_record.authors: Maurice Kraus, Felix Divo, Devendra Singh Dhami, Kristian Kersting
arxiv_record.title: xLSTM-Mixer: Multivariate Time Series Forecasting by Mixing via Scalar Memories

metadata.abstract: Time series data is prevalent across numerous fields, necessitating the development of robust and accurate forecasting models.  Capturing patterns both within and between temporal and multivariate components is crucial for reliable predictions.   We introduce xLSTM-Mixer, a model designed to effectively integrate temporal sequences, joint time-variate information, and multiple perspectives for robust forecasting.     Our approach begins with a linear forecast shared across variates, which is then refined by xLSTM blocks.     They serve as key elements for modeling the complex dynamics of challenging time series data.    xLSTM-Mixer ultimately reconciles two distinct views to produce the final forecast.     Our extensive evaluations demonstrate its superior long-term forecasting performance compared to recent state-of-the-art methods while requiring very little memory.     A thorough model analysis provides further insights into its key components and confirms its robustness and effectiveness.     This work contributes to the resurgence of recurrent models in forecasting by combining them, for the first time, with mixing architectures.
