arxiv_record.abstract: Most ML datasets today contain biases. When we train models on these datasets, they often not only learn these biases but can worsen them -- a phenomenon known as bias amplification. Several co-occurrence-based metrics have been proposed to measure bias amplification in classification datasets. They measure bias amplification between a protected attribute (e.g., gender) and a task (e.g., cooking). These metrics also support fine-grained bias analysis by identifying the direction in which a model amplifies biases. However, co-occurrence-based metrics have limitations -- some fail to measure bias amplification in balanced datasets, while others fail to measure negative bias amplification. To solve these issues, recent work proposed a predictability-based metric called leakage amplification (LA). However, LA cannot identify the direction in which a model amplifies biases. We propose Directional Predictability Amplification (DPA), a predictability-based metric that is (1) directional, (2) works with balanced and unbalanced datasets, and (3) correctly identifies positive and negative bias amplification. DPA eliminates the need to evaluate models on multiple metrics to verify these three aspects. DPA also improves over prior predictability-based metrics like LA: it is less sensitive to the choice of attacker function (a hyperparameter in predictability-based metrics), reports scores within a bounded range, and accounts for dataset bias by measuring relative changes in predictability. Our experiments on well-known datasets like COMPAS (a tabular dataset), COCO, and ImSitu (image datasets) show that DPA is the most reliable metric to measure bias amplification in classification problems. To compare DPA with existing bias amplification metrics, we released a one-stop library of major bias amplification metrics at https://github.com/kerner-lab/Bias-Amplification.
arxiv_record.authors: Bhanu Tokas, Rahul Nair, Hannah Kerner
arxiv_record.title: DPA: A one-stop metric to measure bias amplification in classification datasets

C1.justification: V2 explicitly frames DPA as a single metric for classification and model selection, claiming it removes the need for multiple metrics to check directionality, sign, and balanced-data behavior. The underlying contribution claims about these capabilities, normalization, and attacker robustness are retained.

C2.justification: New Section 5.2 explains that aggregation can hide opposing effects for individual attribute–task pairs. The hiring example is revised to equal acceptance rates with unequal counts and adds an explicit warning about under-reporting amplification. V2 also develops model-selection applications and interpretations involving unlabeled background cues and shortcuts.

D1.justification: Appendix I newly documents the inverse-cross-entropy quality function and attacker optimizers, learning rates, epochs, batch sizes, and depths. Appendices D.2 and F add robustness-network and shortcut construction/training details. These substantially expand reproducibility information. V1's forthcoming-code statement disappears; neither PDF supplies a code link.

E1.justification: ImSitu changes from a motivating example to an evaluated gender/activity dataset covering 205 activities in balanced and unbalanced subsets. Appendix F also introduces a COCO sink/not-sink task with controlled one-pixel shortcuts and tests with and without those shortcuts. Existing COMPAS and COCO masking coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V1's benchmark comparisons evaluate BA→ and Multi→ against DPA. V2 adds leakage amplification to the retained VGG COCO comparison (Table 9), and evaluates BAMALS alongside these metrics in the ViT COCO comparison (Table 2). These substantially expand the competing metric families tested. COMPAS comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: COCO adds ViT_b_16 alongside VGG16, and the reported unbalanced sampling constraint changes from 1/2–2 to 1/3–3; unchanged sample counts do not establish whether sampling was rerun. New protocols rank nine ImSitu models against concept sensitivity scores and evaluate shortcut-controlled COCO training and test conditions.

E4.justification: V2 adds attacker-width sensitivity experiments on ImSitu (Appendix D.2), a controlled hidden-bias intervention using shortcuts (Appendix F), and additional attribution case studies (Figure 5). The earlier synthetic robustness experiment and simulated heatmaps are retained in Appendices D.1 and J, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 displays uncertainty using unlabeled ± entries in its result tables. V2 explicitly identifies corresponding uncertainties as confidence intervals and links DPA uncertainty estimation to repeated label-flipping iterations. Neither version specifies iteration counts, seeds, or confidence levels, so an increase in repeated runs is not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds ImSitu rankings, ViT masking scores, shortcut results, and real-data robustness findings. Retained VGG COCO DPA values also change: unbalanced/original increases from 0.0006 in v1 Table 4 to 0.0034 in v2 Table 9, alongside revised protocol reporting. COMPAS counts and scores remain unchanged in Tables 6–7.

M1.justification: The direction-specific attackers and normalized predictability difference remain equivalent: v1 Equations 9–14 correspond to v2 Equations 1–6. Label-flipping quality equalization was already used in v1's COMPAS analysis. V2 expands its explanation and discloses experimental choices without establishing a changed DPA procedure.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and method explanation. It folds the standalone leakage discussion into the motivation, combines experimental setup and results, moves COMPAS and several analyses into appendices, and introduces a dedicated limitations section. This substantially reorganizes the narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one. V2 adds a directional-method diagram, model-ranking tables with colored discrepancies, a real-data robustness plot, and an attribution grid. COCO tables gain comparator rows, existing displays move to appendices, and uncertainty values are reformatted as subscripts.

R1.justification: The related-work taxonomy and central positioning against BA→, Multi→, and leakage amplification remain largely unchanged. V2 adds references on bias-amplification theory, language models, attacker sensitivity, shortcuts, concept sensitivity, model architectures, and the Rashomon effect to support its expanded experiments and applications.

T1.justification: The stated DPA range changes from (-1,1) in v1 Section 4.2 to [-1,1] in v2 Section 3.2. Appendix B recasts the conditional-probability directionality argument explicitly around DPA. The core metric definitions and the Multi→ absolute-difference derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially closes v1's validation gap by directly comparing against leakage amplification, checking model rankings against ImSitu concept sensitivity, and testing attacker robustness on real data. Explicit aggregation limitations and implementation details improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh new reporting errors: Appendix F claims only DPA increases although Multi→ also increases in Table 8, and Table 11's exact-ranking caption contradicts its entries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DPA research despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds ImSitu evaluations, ViT masking results, controlled shortcut experiments, and real-data attacker robustness results.

before.justification: V1 reports original COMPAS and COCO experiments, simulated metric heatmaps, and attacker robustness results in Appendix B.

arxiv_record.abstract: Predicting future dynamics is crucial for applications like autonomous driving and robotics, where understanding the environment is key. Existing pixel-level methods are computationally expensive and often focus on irrelevant details. To address these challenges, we introduce DINO-Foresight, a novel framework that operates in the semantic feature space of pretrained Vision Foundation Models (VFMs). Our approach trains a masked feature transformer in a self-supervised manner to predict the evolution of VFM features over time. By forecasting these features, we can apply off-the-shelf, task-specific heads for various scene understanding tasks. In this framework, VFM features are treated as a latent space, to which different heads attach to perform specific tasks for future-frame analysis. Extensive experiments show the very strong performance, robustness and scalability of our framework. Project page and code at https://dino-foresight.github.io/ .
arxiv_record.authors: Efstathios Karypidis, Ioannis Kakogeorgiou, Spyros Gidaris, Nikos Komodakis
arxiv_record.title: DINO-Foresight: Looking into the Future with DINO

C1.justification: The central contribution of unified, modular VFM-feature forecasting remains unchanged. V2 narrows the abstract's blanket claim of outperforming existing methods to strong performance and emphasizes one model handling four tasks. The intermediate-feature benefit remains claimed in the introduction and appendix despite losing its separate headline contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations favoring continuous semantic representations, full future masking, cross-dataset transfer and scaling. Appendix B specifies diffusion/Gaussian-mixture extensions and newer encoders while dropping earlier PCA-replacement and action-conditioning directions. Some new interpretations overreach: Tables 11–12 contain small regressions despite claims of consistently improved performance.

D1.justification: The detailed DPT/Mask2Former recipes and hardware information are largely retained. V2 adds tokenizer specifications, model widths and attention-head counts, VISTA fine-tuning sequence lengths, nuScenes frame-selection details and an inference-runtime comparison. The abstract replaces the direct repository link with a project-page/code link. These extend the existing reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates Cityscapes. V2 adds nuScenes training and evaluation for depth and surface normals at 0.75-second and 1.5-second horizons, Cityscapes-to-nuScenes zero-shot transfer, and joint-dataset training. This substantially broadens represented driving environments and transfer scenarios while retaining the original task types.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated comparators including Futurist, FeatReproj3D, Bayesian S2S, IndRNN-Stack and DiffAttn-Fuse. Tables 2–3 add VAE-latent and 4M-tokenized comparisons. V1's Mask H2F and separate Segmenter Oracle/Copy-Last comparisons disappear. The original 3Dconv-F2F row is retained as 3Dconv-F2F-RGB, rather than being a new comparator.

E3.justification: VISTA changes from the original 22-future-frame setup with separate task models to dataset-specific fine-tuning, shorter sequences and shared DINOv2/DPT evaluation. The reported predictor learning rate changes from 1.6e-4 to 6.4e-4, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include nuScenes rollouts, matched single-layer/no-register quantization controls, fixed-duration model scaling and equal-probability dataset mixing.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of VAE versus VFM representations, discrete versus continuous features, cross-dataset transfer, single versus multiple encoder layers, masking strategies, loss functions, model capacity and training-data scale. These test substantially more design and robustness questions. The original PCA and intermediate-transformer-feature analyses are retained; the latter moves from Section 4.4 to Appendix A.2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The expanded discussion of stochastic future prediction concerns possible model extensions, not uncertainty reporting for the experiments.

E6.justification: Instance forecasting scores change: short-term AP50/AP rises from 44.8/23.0 to 50.5/26.6, while the corresponding oracle changes from 56.1/32.1 to 66.2/40.4; the cause is not specified. Original semantic, depth and normal scores largely remain unchanged. V2 adds extensive nuScenes and ablation results and replaces VISTA scores and qualitative outputs under changed settings, so these are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The default PCA-based continuous feature predictor, factorized transformer and SmoothL1 objective remain intact. V2 Section 4.2 adds a quantized DINO-Foresight variant that predicts 8192 discrete codes with cross-entropy and decodes them into DINO features. This introduces a limited procedural variant.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list, related-work discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the distinction between VFM features and generative latents. P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column conference format, consolidates separate comparisons into a broad multi-task table, and adds several comparison and ablation tables. arxiv_record.abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have advanced photorealistic novel view synthesis, but their reliance on photometric reconstruction introduces artifacts, commonly known as "floaters". These artifacts degrade novel view quality, especially in areas unseen by the training cameras. We present a fast, post-hoc NeRF cleanup method that eliminates such artifacts by enforcing our Free Space Prior, effectively minimizing floaters without disrupting the NeRF's representation of observed regions. Unlike existing approaches that rely on either Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation to fit the data or a complex, local data-driven prior, our method adopts a Maximum-a-Posteriori (MAP) approach, selecting the optimal model parameters under a simple global prior assumption that unseen regions should remain empty. This enables our method to clean artifacts in both seen and unseen areas, enhancing novel view quality even in challenging scene regions. Our method is comparable with existing NeRF cleanup models while being 2.5x faster in inference time, requires no additional memory beyond the original NeRF, and achieves cleanup training in less than 30 seconds. Our code will be made publically available.

arxiv_record.abstract: Marked temporal point processes (MTPPs) model sequences of events occurring at irregular time intervals, with wide-ranging applications in fields such as healthcare, finance and social networks. We propose the state-space point process (S2P2) model, a novel and performant model that leverages techniques derived for modern deep state-space models (SSMs) to overcome limitations of existing MTPP models, while simultaneously imbuing strong inductive biases for continuous-time event sequences that other discrete sequence models (i.e., RNNs, transformers) do not capture. Inspired by the classical linear Hawkes processes, we propose an architecture that interleaves stochastic jump differential equations with nonlinearities to create a highly expressive intensity-based MTPP model, without the need for restrictive parametric assumptions for the intensity. Our approach enables efficient training and inference with a parallel scan, bringing linear complexity and sublinear scaling while retaining expressivity to MTPPs. Empirically, S2P2 achieves state-of-the-art predictive likelihoods across eight real-world datasets, delivering an average improvement of 33% over the best existing approaches.
arxiv_record.authors: Yuxin Chang, Alex Boyd, Cao Xiao, Taha Kass-Hout, Parminder Bhatia, Padhraic Smyth, Andrew Warrington
arxiv_record.title: Deep Continuous-Time State-Space Models for Marked Event Sequences

arxiv_record.abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that exhibit transferability across various models. Numerous approaches are proposed to enhance the transferability of adversarial examples, including advanced optimization, data augmentation, and model modifications. However, these methods still show limited transferability, particularly in cross-architecture scenarios, such as from CNN to ViT. To achieve high transferability, we propose a technique termed Spatial Adversarial Alignment (SAA), which employs an alignment loss and leverages a witness model to fine-tune the surrogate model. Specifically, SAA consists of two key parts: spatial-aware alignment and adversarial-aware alignment. First, we minimize the divergences of features between the two models in both global and local regions, facilitating spatial alignment. Second, we introduce a self-adversarial strategy that leverages adversarial examples to impose further constraints, aligning features from an adversarial perspective. Through this alignment, the surrogate model is trained to concentrate on the common features extracted by the witness model. This facilitates adversarial attacks on these shared features, thereby yielding perturbations that exhibit enhanced transferability. Extensive experiments on various architectures on ImageNet show that aligned surrogate models based on SAA can provide higher transferable adversarial examples, especially in cross-architecture attacks.

Numerous approaches are proposed to enhance the transferability of adversarial examples, including advanced optimization, data augmentation, and model modifications. However, these methods still show limited transferability, partiovovocularly in cross-architecture scenarios, such as from CNN to ViT. To achieve high transferability, we propose a technique termed Spatial Adversarial Alignment (SAA), which employs an alignment loss and leverages a witness model to fine-tune the surrogate model. Specifically, SAA consists of two key parts: spatial-aware alignment and adversarial-aware alignment. First, we minimize the divergences of features between the two models in both global and local regions, facilitating spatial alignment. Second, we introduce a self-adversarial strategy that leverages adversarial examples to impose further constraints, aligning features from an adversarial perspective. Through this alignment, the surrogate model is trained to concentrate on the common features extracted by the witness model. This facilitates adversarial attacks on these shared features, thereby yielding perturbations that exhibit enhanced transferability. Extensive experiments on various architectures on ImageNet show that aligned surrogate models based on SAA can provide higher transferable adversarial examples, especially in cross-architecture attacks.

arxiv_record.abstract: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) is a powerful specification language for describing complex temporal behaviors of continuous signals, making it well-suited for high-level robotic task descriptions. However, generating executable plans for STL tasks is challenging, as it requires consideration of the coupling between the task specification and the system dynamics. Existing approaches either follow a model-based setting that explicitly requires knowledge of the system dynamics or adopt a task-oriented data-driven approach to learn plans for specific tasks. In this work, we address the problem of generating executable STL plans for systems with unknown dynamics. We propose a hierarchical planning framework that enables zero-shot generalization to new STL tasks by leveraging only task-agnostic trajectory data during offline training. The framework consists of three key components: (i) decomposing the STL specification into several progresses and time constraints, (ii) searching for timed waypoints that satisfy all progresses under time constraints, and (iii) generating trajectory segments using a pre-trained diffusion model and stitching them into complete trajectories. We formally prove that our method guarantees STL satisfaction, and simulation results demonstrate its effectiveness in generating dynamically feasible trajectories across diverse long-horizon STL tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: Ruijia Liu, Ancheng Hou, Xiao Yu, Xiang Yin
arxiv_record.title: Zero-Shot Trajectory Planning for Signal Temporal Logic Tasks

arxiv_record.abstract:
Modern machine learning algorithms, especially deep learning based
techniques, typically involve careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve the best
performance. Despite the surge of intense interest in practical techniques like
Bayesian optimization and random search based approaches to automating this
laborious and compute intensive task, the fundamental learning theoretic
complexity of tuning hyperparameters for deep neural networks is poorly
understood. Inspired by this glaring gap, we initiate the formal study of
hyperparameter tuning complexity in deep learning through a recently introduced
data driven setting. We assume that we have a series of deep learning tasks,
and we have to tune hyperparameters to do well on average over the distribution
of tasks. A major difficulty is that the utility function as a function of the
hyperparameter is very volatile and furthermore, it is given implicitly by an
optimization problem over the model parameters. To tackle this challenge, we
introduce a new technique to characterize the discontinuities and oscillations
of the utility function on any fixed problem instance as we vary the
hyperparameter; our analysis relies on subtle concepts including tools from
differential/algebraic geometry and constrained optimization. This can be used
to show that the learning theoretic complexity of the corresponding family of
utility functions is bounded. We instantiate our results and provide sample
complexity bounds for concrete applications tuning a hyperparameter that
interpolates neural activation functions and setting the kernel parameter in
graph neural networks.

arxiv_record.title:
Sample complexity of data-driven tuning of model hyperparameters in
  neural networks with structured parameter-dependent dual function

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important weaknesses in the theoretical foundation: Lemma 5.1's problematic finite-local-maxima treatment of constant branches is replaced by B-monotonicity, supported by Proposition C.22. arxiv_record.abstract: In online inverse linear optimization, a learner observes time-varying sets of feasible actions and an agent's optimal actions, selected by solving linear optimization over the feasible actions. The learner sequentially makes predictions of the agent's true linear objective function, and their quality is measured by the regret, the cumulative gap between optimal objective values and those achieved by following the learner's predictions. A seminal work by B\"armann et al. (2017) obtained a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the time horizon. Subsequently, the regret bound has been improved to $O(n^4 \ln T)$ by Besbes et al. (2021, 2025) and to $O(n \ln T)$ by Gollapudi et al. (2021), where $n$ is the dimension of the ambient space of objective vectors. However, these logarithmic-regret methods are highly inefficient when $T$ is large, as they need to maintain regions specified by $O(T)$ constraints, which represent possible locations of the true objective vector. In this paper, we present the first logarithmic-regret method whose per-round complexity is independent of $T$; indeed, it achieves the best-known bound of $O(n \ln T)$. Our method is strikingly simple: it applies the online Newton step (ONS) to appropriate exp-concave loss functions. Moreover, for the case where the agent's actions are possibly suboptimal, we establish a regret bound of $O(n\ln T + \sqrt{\Delta_T n\ln T})$, where $\Delta_T$ is the cumulative suboptimality of the agent's actions. This bound is achieved by using MetaGrad, which runs ONS with $\Theta(\ln T)$ different learning rates in parallel. We also present a lower bound of $\Omega(n)$, showing that the $O(n\ln T)$ bound is tight up to an $O(\ln T)$ factor.

V6 acknowledges Gollapudi et al.'s existing O(n ln T) bound and instead claims the first logarithmic-regret method with T-independent per-round complexity. The two-dimensional finite-regret result also ceases to be a headline contribution.

C2.justification: V6 explains that previously known finite regret with exponential dimension dependence makes its two-dimensional result an illustrative analysis. The new conclusion discusses possible gradient-norm tradeoffs and finite polynomial regret when line-segment feasible sets are revealed before prediction. Existing explanations of suboptimal feedback and higher-dimensional geometric obstacles remain.

D1.justification: V6's MetaGrad pseudocode explicitly sends both the aggregate prediction w_t and gradient g_t to each expert, whereas v1 sends only g_t. This clarifies implementation of the surrogate loss, which already depended on both quantities in v1.

E1.justification: Neither version trains on or evaluates datasets. The inverse optimization settings and constructed instances are studied theoretically.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. The newly included Gollapudi comparison in Table 1 and Appendix A concerns theoretical guarantees and complexity.

E3.justification: Neither version reports empirical evaluation protocols, training budgets or testing procedures. The revised feasible-set normalization in Appendix C is a theorem assumption, not an experimental setting.

E4.justification: Robustness to suboptimal feedback remains a theoretical guarantee in Section 4. Neither version contains ablations, empirical robustness tests or experimental case studies; the geometric discussion is retained in Appendix C.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run statistics, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical tests. Expectations in the regret bounds concern theoretical randomness.

E6.justification: Neither version reports empirical performance values, measured runtimes or experimental findings. The new Table 1 summarizes theoretical bounds rather than experimental results.

M1.justification: The ONS and MetaGrad designs are retained, but Appendix B.3 changes MetaGrad's dyadic learning-rate grid endpoint from ceil((ln T)/2) to ceil((log_2 T)/2). This changes the number and range of experts and is a limited algorithmic correction. The two-dimensional algorithm is retained in Appendix C.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around computational efficiency. Related work expands, a conclusion is added, and the former Section 6 becomes Appendix C. Together these changes substantially reorganize the paper's narrative.

P2.justification: V6 adds Table 1 comparing theoretical regret and computational complexity. Figures 1–2 and the two-dimensional pseudocode move to Appendix C, preserving the diagrams. Typography, captions and algorithm numbering are also revised.

R1.justification: Adding Gollapudi et al. (2021) substantially changes the nearest-prior-work account and novelty positioning. V6 also expands contextual-search, corruption-robustness and online-portfolio literature, and Appendix A develops a detailed comparison of centroid-based computation. These changes go substantially beyond citation or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: The principal regret bounds are retained. However, v6 tightens the two-dimensional result's feasible-set radius from 1 to 1/2, supporting the proof's unit-diameter bound; Theorem 6.2 becomes Theorem C.2. It also corrects the lower-bound proof's quantifier order and strengthens the MetaGrad grid argument. Appendix A adds a computational-cost derivation for the prior centroid method. These are local corrections and extensions rather than new main theorems.

improvement.justification: V6 resolves a central novelty overstatement by acknowledging Gollapudi et al.'s existing O(n ln T) bound and identifying computational efficiency as its contribution, supported by Table 1 and Appendix A. The corrected MetaGrad grid and feasible-set assumption also strengthen mathematical reliability. These changes substantially improve the paper's accuracy and positioning while retaining its principal guarantees.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same online inverse linear optimization work. Their complete text, equations, algorithms, figures and appendices support comparison despite retitling and reorganization.

after.justification: V6 remains theoretical throughout its main text and appendices. Its new Table 1 compares asymptotic guarantees and computational complexity, not empirical measurements.

before.justification: V1 contains theoretical algorithms, regret bounds, proofs and geometric illustrations, but no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes, including in its appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Harmful fine-tuning attack introduces significant security risks to the fine-tuning services. Main-stream defenses aim to vaccinate the model such that the later harmful fine-tuning attack is less effective. However, our evaluation results show that such defenses are fragile--with a few fine-tuning steps, the model still can learn the harmful knowledge. To this end, we do further experiment and find that an embarrassingly simple solution--adding purely random perturbations to the fine-tuned model, can recover the model from harmful behaviors, though it leads to a degradation in the model's fine-tuning performance. To address the degradation of fine-tuning performance, we further propose Panacea, which optimizes an adaptive perturbation that will be applied to the model after fine-tuning. Panacea maintains model's safety alignment performance without compromising downstream fine-tuning performance. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on different harmful ratios, fine-tuning tasks and mainstream LLMs, where the average harmful scores are reduced by up-to 21.2%, while maintaining fine-tuning performance. As a by-product, we analyze the adaptive perturbation and show that different layers in various LLMs have distinct safety affinity, which coincide with finding from several previous study. Source code available at https://github.com/w-yibo/Panacea.

arxiv_record.abstract: Graphons offer a powerful framework for modeling large-scale networks, yet estimation remains challenging. We propose a novel approach that leverages a low-rank additive representation, yielding both a low-rank connection probability matrix and a low-rank graphon--two goals rarely achieved jointly. Our method resolves identification issues and enables an efficient sequential algorithm based on subgraph counts and interpolation. We establish consistency and demonstrate strong empirical performance in terms of computational efficiency and estimation accuracy through simulations and data analysis.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a unified framework for jointly recovering a low-rank connection matrix and graphon through subgraph moments and interpolation, with consistency and computational advantages. C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of graphon estimation's generative utility, behavior outside smoothness assumptions, and consequences of rank misspecification. It also acknowledges that rank-1 spectral estimation can achieve quadratic complexity. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix H describes overestimation effects as minimal despite substantial deterioration for setting 2 in Table 9.

D1.justification: Section 4 adds a code-repository link, and Appendix H explicitly discloses that main simulations assume known rank and that the simulation threshold 0.2 is heuristic. The previously reported hardware, R version, baseline defaults and power-iteration stopping settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The seven original graphons and school dataset are retained. v2 adds the 1,490-node political-blog dataset, a non-Lipschitz graphon scenario, sparse counterparts of graphons 1, 6 and 7, and tasks assessing motif/transitivity preservation after node subsampling and network regeneration.

E2.justification: Corresponding dense and sparse benchmark comparisons retain USVT, SAS, Nethist, neighborhood smoothing and power iteration. New sparsity-sensitivity and political-blog motif comparisons reuse four existing baselines, omitting power iteration only from those additional comparisons; no existing matched comparison loses a baseline.

E3.justification: Added protocols vary network size, sparsity and assumed rank, measure graphon sup-norm error, and evaluate normalized structural errors after removing 10% of nodes. The school-data rank-selection threshold also changes from 0.2 to 0.25, although retained rank and eigenvalue results do not establish that this experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's limited rank-selection analysis, v2 tests scalability, varying sparsity, violation of Lipschitz assumptions, rank overestimation and underestimation, and estimation after selecting rank. Appendix A additionally examines structural preservation under node subsampling, substantially expanding robustness and diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v1 reports means for its main accuracy comparisons, with standard deviations confined to power-iteration counts. v2 adds standard deviations for MSE and maximum error throughout the main comparisons and uncertainty for additional analyses. Both versions already specify 100 independent trials for the main simulations; an increased run count is not established.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark means are mostly preserved at greater precision, while substantial new results appear. Examples include graphon sup-norm errors of 0.12053 and 0.15539 for settings 3 and 4 (Table 3), correct rank selection in 89/100 trials for setting 7 (Table 8), and political-blog motif errors and runtimes (Table 13).

M1.justification: The core moment estimation, normalization, interpolation, computational corrections and rank-selection algorithms remain unchanged. Remark 3.8 adds an optional procedure that tries different reference components and selects the estimated graphon whose motif densities best match observed densities.

P1.justification: The title changes, much of the introduction and methodological exposition is rewritten, and the rank-r explanation is reorganized around cycle and path expectations. References move before the appendices, the school example moves into a dedicated applications appendix, and the original appendix subsections become a broader A–L structure.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a substantially different page design, restructures the main comparison tables into paired blocks with uncertainty columns and highlighted best values, and adds multiple result tables and scalability, robustness and political-blog figures. arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models show remarkable image generation performance following text prompts, but risk generating sexual contents. Existing approaches, such as prompt filtering, concept removal, and even sexual contents mitigation methods, struggle to defend against adversarial attacks while maintaining benign image quality. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Distorting Embedding Space (DES), a text encoder-based defense mechanism that effectively tackles these issues through innovative embedding space control. DES transforms unsafe embeddings, extracted from a text encoder using unsafe prompts, toward carefully calculated safe embedding regions to prevent unsafe contents generation, while reproducing the original safe embeddings. DES also neutralizes the ``nudity'' embedding, by aligning it with neutral embedding to enhance robustness against adversarial attacks. As a result, extensive experiments on explicit content mitigation and adaptive attack defense show that DES achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) defense, with attack success rate (ASR) of 9.47% on FLUX.1, a recent popular model, and 0.52% on the widely adopted Stable Diffusion v1.5. These correspond to ASR reductions of 76.5% and 63.9% compared to previous SOTA methods, EraseAnything and AdvUnlearn, respectively. Furthermore, DES maintains benign image quality, achieving Frechet Inception Distance and CLIP score comparable to those of the original FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion v1.5.
arxiv_record.authors: Jaesin Ahn, Heechul Jung
arxiv_record.title: Mitigating Sexual Content Generation via Embedding Distortion in Text-conditioned Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central claim of robust defense with preserved benign quality and zero inference overhead remains. v2 narrows the headline objective from general NSFW defense to sexual-content mitigation and replaces the prominent plug-and-play contribution framing with explicit compatibility with recent diffusion models.

C2.justification: v2 explains why fixed original nudity vectors and the evolving neutralized vector do not conflict, explicitly acknowledges semantic distortion of benign prompts, and adds cultural-sensitivity discussion. Its I2I interpretation changes from lowest ASR across all scenarios to lowest average ASR. The earlier limitations concerning image-based attacks and closed-source models remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds encoder-specific memory and training times, including T5-XXL CPU offloading with DeepSpeed, batch size 16, and 160 minutes per epoch. Existing software versions and basic training settings remain. v1's explicit DES repository link disappears; v2 instead states that code and data accompany supplementary material, whose availability cannot be verified from these PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds training with 8,931 violence/illegal CoPro prompt pairs and 1,600 generated Van Gogh prompts. Section 4.4 evaluates six nonsexual I2P categories and Van Gogh concept erasure, substantially extending the represented content and tasks. I2P sexual-content evaluation and inpainting already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds GLoCE and Microsoft/OpenAI filters to SDv1.5 comparisons, EraseAnything to FLUX.1 comparisons, and string-filtering and negative-prompt baselines. FMN and SLD-medium disappear from corresponding sexual-content quantitative comparisons, although FMN remains in the new Van Gogh experiment.

E3.justification: v2 adds FLUX.1, SDXL, SDv3, and SDv3.5 configurations, CCE adaptive attacks, body-part detection counts, and PickScore, ImageReward, and BLIPScore evaluations. Its main black-box ASR average excludes I2P and therefore covers four attacks instead of five. Appendix E.1 additionally evaluates COCO subsets defined by their proximity to the nudity embedding.

E4.justification: Existing loss-component, loss-adjustment, coefficient, target-selection, embedding, and failure-case analyses largely survive under new locations or names. New analyses test whether basic defenses complement DES (Appendix B.7), scaling-factor sensitivity for other concepts (C.3.1), and semantic damage to benign prompts near and far from nudity, including individual cases (E.1). These substantially broaden the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard deviations across attack sets rather than uncertainty across repeated runs. Neither supplies seed counts, repeated-run estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's checklist explicitly acknowledges absent error bars but introduces no uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New results include DES's 5.76% CCE ASR (Table 3), 1.88% mean ASR across six other NSFW categories (Table 5), and 9.47% five-set FLUX.1 ASR (Table 7). The four shared SDv1.5 DES attack scores remain unchanged; the average changes from 0.64% to 0.52% because I2P is excluded. Other reported values change, including the SDv1.5 Ring-A-Bell baseline from 71.96% to 98.13% and several ablation ASRs. SDv1.4 sexual-content result columns and Q16 inpainting scores are omitted.

M1.justification: The core target-generation procedure, three losses, and Algorithms 1–2 remain equivalent after notation changes. Limited extensions include concept-specific neutralization targets, independently training multiple text encoders, and optional DES combinations with filtering or negative prompts (Sections 4.1 and 4.4; Appendix B.7).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, terminology, and experimental narrative are substantially revised. UEN, SEP, and PALA terminology becomes simpler loss descriptions. Inpainting results move into the main text, principal ablations move into Appendix D, and the earlier appendices are extensively consolidated and reorganized.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column main-text layout to a single-column layout with wrapped tables and figures. v1 Figures 1–2 become v2 Figure 1, and Figures 8–9 become Figure 6. The overview schematic is simplified, the main qualitative grid is reduced, tables are restructured with colored rankings, and numerous new result displays are added.

R1.justification: v2 introduces a dedicated sexual-content-mitigation subsection discussing SafeGen and ShieldDiff, adds positioning against GLoCE and EraseAnything, and motivates encoder modification through knowledge localization and continual learning. Additional architecture and image-assessment references further expand the research context beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The target-selection construction and Equations (1)–(7) retain their mathematical content under notation changes. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs. The added explanation of loss compatibility introduces no new formal result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for generalization and benign semantic preservation through newer-model evaluations, another adaptive attack, additional concepts, and direct analysis of semantic damage (Table 7, Section 4.4, Appendix E.1). These gains strengthen the scientific assessment beyond the changed headline averages. They outweigh localized reporting defects: Table 9 gives a negative-prompt average of 78.04% although its entries average 32.78%, and the broad 90-second training claim remains insufficiently qualified despite the much slower T5 training disclosed in Appendix A.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DES framework by the same authors, despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added content to be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on newer diffusion models, additional concepts, adaptive attacks, and benign-prompt semantic preservation.

before.justification: v1 reports original diffusion-model defense experiments, image-quality measurements, inpainting evaluations, ablations, and embedding analyses in the main text and appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Learning the solution operators of PDEs on arbitrary domains is challenging due to the diversity of possible domain shapes, in addition to the often intricate underlying physics. We propose an end-to-end graph neural network (GNN) based neural operator to learn PDE solution operators from data on point clouds in arbitrary domains. Our multi-scale model maps data between input/output point clouds by passing it through a downsampled regional mesh. The approach includes novel elements aimed at ensuring spatio-temporal resolution invariance. Our model, termed RIGNO, is tested on a challenging suite of benchmarks composed of various time-dependent and steady PDEs defined on a diverse set of domains. We demonstrate that RIGNO is significantly more accurate than neural operator baselines and robustly generalizes to unseen resolutions both in space and in time. Our code is publicly available at github.com/camlab-ethz/rigno.
arxiv_record.authors: Sepehr Mousavi, Shizheng Wen, Levi Lingsch, Maximilian Herde, Bogdan Raoni\'c, Siddhartha Mishra
arxiv_record.title: RIGNO: A Graph-based framework for robust and accurate operator learning for PDEs on arbitrary domains

C1.justification: The central claims of accurate, resolution-flexible graph-based operator learning remain. v2 additionally claims that edge masking improves optimization and accuracy, whereas v1 discusses an accuracy tradeoff. Cartesian benchmark dominance is qualified from winning every tested dataset to winning eight of nine.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving weaker spatial correlations, local versus global interactions, weaker advantages on elliptic problems, OOD failure mechanisms, and computational tradeoffs. It interprets Smooth Transport's deterioration as sensitivity to non-local shifts. Conversely, v1 Appendix B.2's explicit limitation concerning more general boundary conditions is removed, and the 3D limitation no longer mentions computational cost.

D1.justification: v2 documents the MeshGraphNet implementation, UPT configurations and training settings, and Transolver size constraints. It newly discloses tuning on one internal dataset, RTX 3090 hardware, and an estimated 9,000 GPU hours for RIGNO experiments. Existing RIGNO defaults and the code link remain, but the direct dataset DOI link in v1's bibliography disappears.

E1.justification: The original benchmark datasets are retained, and Poisson-Gauss adds an elliptic task on point clouds and Cartesian grids. Appendix F.8 additionally evaluates Darcy Flow, Smooth Transport, and Compressible Euler under shifts in characteristic length scales, perturbation locations, and airfoil geometry complexity, substantially broadening task and test-condition coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MeshGraphNet and UPT to the point-cloud comparisons that previously contained Geo-FNO, FNO DSE, and GINO. Appendix G.8 adds Transolver comparisons on five datasets, while Appendix F.10 compares additional GINO configurations. The Cartesian-grid comparator set remains CNO, scOT, and FNO.

E3.justification: Figure 3b changes from training at 2Δt intervals through t14 with Δt rollouts to training at 4Δt intervals through t16 with AR-4 inference. The spatial ablation changes from 92² training resolution, although v2 inconsistently reports 42² in the text and plot versus 64² in the caption. New OOD, transfer, and computational experiments introduce additional sampling, normalization, training, and benchmarking protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds regional-node-count ablations, MeshGraphNet resolution tests, OOD robustness tests, transfer-learning analyses, and accuracy–cost comparisons in Appendix F. It also revises the main spatial and fractional-pairing ablations. Existing model-size, noise-robustness, and uncertainty analyses are largely retained after relocation.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed mean and standard deviation results for NS-PwC and NS-SVS, single-seed training elsewhere, and uncertainty visualizations from 20 stochastic rollouts. No new statistical reporting procedure is introduced. The reassignment of the two seed-result entries changes results, not the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Matched scores from v1 Table 1 remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial benchmark, OOD, transfer, and resource results. For example, Cartesian Poisson-Gauss gives scOT 0.68% versus RIGNO-18's 1.80%. The seed table changes NS-PwC from 1.05 ± 0.040% to 2.50 ± 0.157%, with NS-SVS changing conversely. Figures 3a–b report replacement results under changed settings, and the 10Δt curve is removed from the lead-time analysis.

M1.justification: The regional graph construction, encoder–processor–decoder architecture, edge masking, time conditioning, all2all loss, and fractional pairing remain unchanged. Detailed architecture equations move to Appendix B; new model configurations and transfer-learning experiments do not establish a revision to the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the introduction and edge-masking explanation, adds an explicit contribution list, and condenses the main architecture description by moving equations to Appendix B. Boundary-condition material is reorganized into Appendix A, experimental analyses and baseline appendices exchange order, and related work and limitations receive separate headings.

P2.justification: The original combined benchmark table becomes Tables 1 and 2, with additional rows and comparator columns. Scaling and ablation plots are substantially reformatted, and new regional-node, OOD, computational, Transolver, transfer, and Poisson displays are added. Existing architecture and most solution visualizations are retained but resized or relocated within the revised conference layout.

R1.justification: The introduction and new related-work discussion substantially expand comparisons with MeshGraphNet, multiscale graph methods, GINO, UPT, and neural-field approaches. New citations include Multiscale MeshGraphNets, two neural-field works, and Transolver. v2 also more explicitly credits prior time conditioning and distinguishes fractional pairing from earlier fixed-step output recycling.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds the formal Poisson problem and its Gaussian-source distribution. The existing solution-operator definitions, architecture equations, and loss mathematics are retained or relocated. Neither version provides a RIGNO approximation theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support for the unchanged method: direct graph and attention comparisons address important omissions in v1, while OOD tests expose failure conditions and transfer and resource studies clarify practical usefulness. Expanded implementation details improve assessability. These gains outweigh localized reporting defects, notably Figure 3a's conflicting training resolutions and Appendix F.10's claim of consistently superior accuracy despite GINO outperforming RIGNO on Elasticity in Table F.4. Removal of the boundary-condition caveat and dataset link remains a drawback.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RIGNO and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–H. Relocated sections and retained visualizations can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, distribution-shift tests, transfer-learning experiments, and computational benchmarks.

before.justification: v1 reports original RIGNO benchmark results, scaling experiments, ablations, repeated-seed results, and noise-robustness analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Discrete diffusion models have emerged as a powerful generative modeling framework for discrete data with successful applications spanning from text generation to image synthesis. However, their deployment faces challenges due to the high dimensionality of the state space, necessitating the development of efficient inference algorithms. Current inference approaches mainly fall into two categories: exact simulation and approximate methods such as $\tau$-leaping. While exact methods suffer from unpredictable inference time and redundant function evaluations, $\tau$-leaping is limited by its first-order accuracy. In this work, we advance the latter category by tailoring the first extension of high-order numerical inference schemes to discrete diffusion models, enabling larger step sizes while reducing error. We rigorously analyze the proposed schemes and establish the second-order accuracy of the $\theta$-Trapezoidal method in KL divergence. Empirical evaluations on GSM8K-level math-reasoning, GPT-2-level text, and ImageNet-level image generation tasks demonstrate that our method achieves superior sample quality compared to existing approaches under equivalent computational constraints, with consistent performance gains across models ranging from 200M to 8B. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuchen-zhu-zyc/DiscreteFastSolver.

C1.justification: The central claims of introducing high-order discrete-diffusion solvers and establishing second-order KL convergence remain. The abstract broadens empirical applicability to GSM8K reasoning and claims gains across models ranging from 200M to 8B parameters, extending the practical contribution without redefining the main algorithmic contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly identifies the unresolved positivity issue and explains periodicity versus rejection qualifications, extending v1's existing positivity discussion. It also interprets blockwise gains through LLaDA's preference for left-to-right generation and qualifies the reasoning advantage as primarily occurring at low NFE (Section 6.4 and Appendix D.4).

D1.justification: V2 adds a project code-repository link, identifies GPT-2 Large and LLaMA 3 evaluator checkpoints, and documents the LLaDA checkpoint, noise schedule, early stopping, temperature, block lengths, hardware, and evaluation harness. V1 already supplied RADD/MaskGIT checkpoint information and implementation settings; v2 substantially expands this reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V2 adds GSM8K mathematical reasoning with LLaDA-Instruct, substantially extending task coverage beyond text and image generation. The RADD/OpenWebText, MaskGIT/ImageNet, and toy experiments remain. Renaming the toy experiment from 15-dimensional to 15-state does not introduce different data; v1 Appendix D.2 already specifies 15 states.

E2.justification: V2 adds FHS to the reported text and image comparisons and Semi-AR to RADD text generation. Its new GSM8K comparison evaluates confidence-based and random-remasking Semi-AR variants. FHS was discussed in v1 but was absent from these benchmark comparisons; existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds LLaMA 3 perplexity and unigram-entropy evaluation. The new GSM8K protocol uses an 8B model, zero-shot 256-token responses, 64–256 NFEs, temperature 0.5, and full-sequence versus blocksize-8 conditions. Existing toy, RADD, and MaskGIT sampling budgets are retained; these additions do not establish reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds positivity measurements across NFE budgets, directly probing a convergence-theory assumption (Table 6), and a blockwise versus full-sequence reasoning comparison probing generation order (Table 7). Existing convergence and theta-sensitivity studies remain; their relocation and renumbering do not constitute new analyses.

E5.justification: V2 Table 6 newly reports plus/minus quantities alongside positivity percentages, but does not define their statistical meaning or associated repetition counts. The toy experiment retains 1,000 bootstrap resamples and 95% confidence intervals. An increase in repeated runs is not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds baseline, LLaMA 3, entropy, positivity, and GSM8K results. On GSM8K, Trapezoidal scores 38.4% versus random Semi-AR's 34.3% at NFE 128, but 39.7% versus 40.3% at NFE 256. Shared GPT-2 perplexities remain unchanged in v2 Table 3; however, v2 Table 1 inconsistently reports RK-2 as 36.330 instead of 33.971 at NFE 1024.

M1.justification: The two principal solvers remain. V2 adds a current-state jump-validity indicator to RK-2 Algorithm 1, absent from both v1 Algorithm 1 and its practical Algorithm 4, and introduces a blockwise Trapezoidal variant in Appendix D.4. Positive-part clipping and the wider theta range already existed in v1 Appendix D.1.

P1.justification: V2 edits and condenses prose while retaining the basic narrative. It merges v1 Section 3.3 into Section 4, moves stochastic formulations into Appendix C.1, integrates the practical RK-2 presentation into Algorithm 1, and converts the hyperparameter section into a remark. Most existing exposition and proof text remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column format with wrapped algorithms and tables. Figure 1 gains a solver schematic, comparison plots gain FHS curves and legends, and tables are added or expanded. Existing sensitivity plots and the identical Figure 7 image samples are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands references and positioning toward diffusion-LLM reasoning, discrete neural sampling, and inference-time scaling, including LLaDA, Dream, and d1. Section 1.1 and Appendix A also add numerical CTMC and diffusion-solver literature. These are substantive literature additions beyond the switch to numbered citations.

T1.justification: V2 introduces periodic boundary conditions in Section 5.1 and an O(kappa) rejection argument in Remark C.4. Remark C.6 adds an expected-positivity derivation. Proposition C.20 revises v1 Proposition C.16's local error bound from O(Delta_n^3 epsilon_II + Delta_n^4) to O(Delta_n^3), with altered reasoning. The final second-order KL convergence rate is retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens practical validation through previously missing sampler comparisons, additional text-quality and diversity measurements, and an 8B reasoning evaluation. Positivity diagnostics, more explicit theoretical conditions, and expanded code and implementation information improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the localized RK-2 table inconsistency and undefined plus/minus reporting. The empirical positivity checks nevertheless do not remove the theorem's positivity assumption.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. Algorithms, proofs, and experiments can be matched across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds GSM8K reasoning results, additional sampler comparisons and text-quality measurements, and empirical intensity-positivity diagnostics.

before.justification: V1 reports original toy-model convergence experiments, RADD text-generation perplexities, MaskGIT image-generation FIDs, and parameter sensitivity studies in Section 6 and Appendix D.

arxiv_record.abstract: World models represent a promising approach for training reinforcement learning agents with significantly improved sample efficiency. While most world model methods primarily rely on sequences of discrete latent variables to model environment dynamics, this compression often neglects critical visual details essential for reinforcement learning. Recent diffusion-based world models condition generation on a fixed context length of frames to predict the next observation, using separate recurrent neural networks to model rewards and termination signals. Although this architecture effectively enhances visual fidelity, the fixed context length approach inherently limits memory capacity. In this paper, we introduce EDELINE, a unified world model architecture that integrates state space models with diffusion models. Our approach outperforms existing baselines across visually challenging Atari 100k tasks, memory-demanding Crafter benchmark, and 3D first-person ViZDoom environments, demonstrating superior performance in all these diverse challenges.
arxiv_record.authors: Jia-Hua Lee and Bor-Jiun Lin and Wei-Fang Sun and Chun-Yi Lee
arxiv_record.title: EDELINE: Enhancing Memory in Diffusion-based World Models via Linear-Time Sequence Modeling

C1.justification: V2 withdraws the introductory contribution claiming provably greater information retention with a linearly growing advantage, replacing it with an empirical memory-enhancement contribution. It extends the headline experimental claims to Crafter and explicitly restricts the introductory Atari superiority claim to methods without look-ahead search.

C2.justification: V2 explains the offsetting world-model and actor-critic timing costs, explicitly acknowledges diffusion's computational overhead, and distinguishes acceptable Crafter prediction discrepancies from memory failures (Appendices A, D.8 and D.11). These add qualifications and mechanism explanations while retaining the central memory-based interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly documents parallel-scan execution and the probe inputs, prediction heads and feature source. Core hyperparameters and RTX 4090 profiling information remain. Conversely, v1's explicit 4:1 ViZDoom frame-skipping disclosure disappears; this omission does not establish an actual setting change.

E1.justification: V2 adds Crafter's procedurally generated survival, resource collection and crafting tasks, including remembering previously explored terrain (Section 6.2 and Appendix D.11). Atari, MiniGrid and the five ViZDoom scenarios remain. The new probing and MSE analyses reuse existing environments.

E2.justification: V2 adds a Transformer-based REM comparator in Table 8 and the Crafter qualitative comparison, extending v1's architectural comparisons against GRU and LSTM. The retained Atari baseline roster is unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include Crafter evaluation with a 1M-step budget, probes using 50 training and 10 validation trajectories with 50/100 training epochs, and pixel-MSE evaluation over specified imagination horizons (Appendices D.6-D.7). The existing Atari budget and default hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds representation probing, quantitative generation-quality analysis, a Transformer-versus-Mamba ablation and Crafter memory/error case studies. Existing GRU/LSTM, cross-attention and harmonizer analyses are largely relocated, not newly introduced. V1's PredictPosition qualitative case figure is omitted.

E5.justification: Appendix D.6 specifies five independent seeds for the new probing experiments. Existing benchmark and ablation reporting retains three-run averages, standard-deviation curves and bootstrap intervals. This does not establish increased run counts for retained experiments; probe uncertainty intervals are not supplied.

E6.justification: Retained Atari tables are numerically unchanged, including EDELINE's 1.866 mean HNS. New Crafter results report 11.5 ± 0.9 versus DIAMOND's 2.8 ± 0.5 (Table 2). Tables 3, 4 and 8 add probing, normalized pixel-MSE of 0.918, and Transformer comparison results. Figure 4 adds ViZDoom learning curves.

M1.justification: The proposed Mamba REM, diffusion predictor, shared prediction heads, harmonized losses and actor-critic procedure remain. V2 clarifies parallel execution and timestep sampling; v1's Algorithm 1 already includes burn-in and random target selection. The Transformer variant is an ablation comparator.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are revised, the training explanation is substantially rewritten, and related work is divided into four subsections. Main-text ablations move into Appendix D, which consolidates many previously separate appendices. Background, algorithm and objective sections are also reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive figure resizing, repositioning and pseudocode reformatting. V2 adds four result tables, ViZDoom learning curves and a Crafter image sequence; it removes the PredictPosition image sequence and harmonizer summary bar chart while relocating other displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Crafter, Transformers, GAIA-1, GAIA-2 and Pandora, with limited expansion of generative-game-engine discussion. arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often concentrate their attention on a few specific tokens referred to as attention sinks. Common examples include the first token, a prompt-independent sink, and punctuation tokens, which are prompt-dependent. While the tokens causing the sinks often lack direct semantic meaning, the presence of the sinks is critical for model performance, particularly under model compression and KV-caching. Despite their ubiquity, the function, semantic role, and origin of attention sinks -- especially those beyond the first token -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation demonstrating that attention sinks: catch a sequence of tokens, tag them using a common direction in embedding space, and release them back into the residual stream, where tokens are later retrieved based on the tags they have acquired. Probing experiments reveal these tags carry semantically meaningful information, such as the truth of a statement. These findings extend to reasoning models, where the mechanism spans more heads and explains greater variance in embeddings, or recent models with query-key normalization, where sinks remain just as prevalent. To encourage future theoretical analysis, we introduce a minimal problem which can be solved through the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, and where it emerges through training.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations involving semantic denoising, reasoning-related segmentation, tag orthogonality, activation steering, and MLP reinforcement of shared tags. Appendix K explicitly acknowledges that the mechanism is not proved necessary, optimization can fail, reasoning correlations are not causal evidence, and threshold-based detection is incomplete. These substantially qualify v1's stronger explanations.

D1.justification: v2 adds synthetic-data generation and optimization details, initialization and scheduling information, probe extraction layers/heads, a model inventory, and GPU/runtime estimates (Appendices G, J, L–M). It removes v1's pruning calibration/hyperparameter recipe and project-page link. These substantially revise the available reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v2 removes MMLU evaluation and C4 pruning calibration. It adds city/country truth classification, SST-2 sentiment classification, QuALITY text analysis, and empirical synthetic averaging tasks, including a two-separator task. Several original qualitative prompting scenarios remain in the reorganized visualization appendix.

E2.justification: The evaluated OATS, Wanda, and SparseGPT comparisons in v1 disappear, along with their dense and low-rank-removal controls. v2 introduces comparisons between tag-only, non-tag, and full-activation mass-mean probes in Tables 1, 5, and 7. OATS remains cited but is no longer experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The removed pruning evaluation used 50% sparsity and 0–5-shot MMLU testing. New protocols include aggregation over 170 prompts truncated to 150 tokens, a sink threshold of 0.2, a tag-subspace projection metric, balanced 400/200 probe construction/validation splits, and synthetic-model training for 50 epochs. Model configurations also expand substantially.

E4.justification: v2 removes the low-rank deletion and pruning interventions. It adds sink-token taxonomies, tag-separability measurements, twelve-threshold sensitivity analysis, initialization sensitivity, and a multihead synthetic experiment (Appendices B–D, F, K). Comparisons across reasoning and QK-normalized models add further analyses; these are comparisons between checkpoints, not controlled architectural ablations.

E5.justification: v1 reports no repeated-run analysis. v2 Table 8 reports success frequencies across ten runs for each initialization. P1.justification: The title, abstract, research questions, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around semantic and quantitative analysis. The pruning-centered narrative is replaced, the main proof moves into Appendix E, and the appendix structure is extensively reorganized. This is substantial narrative revision beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, redesigns the retained mechanism/PCA displays, and removes pruning plots and activation-outlier panels. Numerous new violin plots, box plots, heatmaps, histograms, prompt diagrams, and result tables substantially change the visual presentation. Several original appendix examples are retained in compact, rearranged panels.

R1.justification: The compression-focused literature discussion is substantially reduced. v2 adds or expands positioning around over-mixing, positional encodings, QK normalization, semantic probing, and activation steering (Sections 1.3 and 8; Appendix I). arxiv_record.abstract: Aligning visual features with language embeddings is a key challenge in vision-language models (VLMs). The performance of such models hinges on having a good connector that maps visual features generated by a vision encoder to a shared embedding space with the LLM while preserving semantic similarity. Existing connectors, such as multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), lack inductive bias to constrain visual features within the linguistic structure of the LLM's embedding space, making them data-hungry and prone to cross-modal misalignment. In this work, we propose a novel vision-text alignment method, AlignVLM, that maps visual features to a weighted average of LLM text embeddings. Our approach leverages the linguistic priors encoded by the LLM to ensure that visual features are mapped to regions of the space that the LLM can effectively interpret. AlignVLM is particularly effective for document understanding tasks, where visual and textual modalities are highly correlated. Our extensive experiments show that AlignVLM achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior alignment methods, with larger gains on document understanding tasks and under low-resource setups. We provide further analysis demonstrating its efficiency and robustness to noise.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models have been widely applied, but can inadvertently encode sensitive or harmful information, raising significant safety concerns. Machine unlearning has emerged to alleviate this concern; however, existing training-time unlearning approaches, relying on coarse-grained loss combinations, have limitations in precisely separating knowledge and balancing removal effectiveness with model utility. In contrast, we propose Fine-grained Activation manipuLation by Contrastive Orthogonal uNalignment (FALCON), a novel representation-guided unlearning approach that leverages information-theoretic guidance for efficient parameter selection, employs contrastive mechanisms to enhance representation separation, and projects conflict gradients onto orthogonal subspaces to resolve conflicts between forgetting and retention objectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FALCON achieves superior unlearning effectiveness while maintaining model utility, exhibiting robust resistance against knowledge recovery attempts.

In contrast, we propose $\textbf{F}$ine-grained $\textbf{A}$ctivation manipu$\textbf{L}$ation by $\textbf{C}$ontrastive $\textbf{O}$rthogonal u$\textbf{N}$alignment (FALCON), a novel representation-guided unlearning approach that leverages information-theoretic guidance for efficient parameter selection, employs contrastive mechanisms to enhance representation separation, and projects conflict gradients onto orthogonal subspaces to resolve conflicts between forgetting and retention objectives. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FALCON achieves superior unlearning effectiveness while maintaining model utility, exhibiting robust resistance against knowledge recovery attempts.

C1.justification: The central claims about selective unlearning, utility preservation and recovery resistance remain. The introduction changes the claimed contribution from theoretical insights to empirical insights and frames MI as an auxiliary signal. The conclusion now explicitly extends the effectiveness claim across diverse tasks.

C2.justification: New discussion explains why MI-selected layers can remain fixed under modest updates, explicitly identifies white-box access requirements, and proposes an untested surrogate/prompt route to black-box use (F.2 and F.4). It also adds interpretations of sampling stability and comparative recovery, plus an extended discussion of ECO's detector vulnerabilities. The original text-only and small-model limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds Algorithm 1, fixed-selection and typical 1-3-layer guidance, OpenUnlearning framework/access information, and documentation for the new benchmark metrics. The abstract supplies an implementation URL where v1 only promised a future release. v2 nevertheless retains that future-release wording in Appendix D, so the PDFs establish added access information rather than verified repository availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds copyrighted news-content unlearning through MUSE News and fictitious-author entity unlearning through TOFU (Section 5.2). These introduce distinct data domains and forgetting requirements beyond v1's harmful-knowledge evaluations. WMDP, WikiText and MMLU coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The new benchmark comparisons evaluate GradAscent, GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO and IdkDPO, with membership differing between MUSE and TOFU, alongside Finetuned and Retain reference models (Tables 2-3). RMU also becomes an explicit recovery-attack comparator in Table 12. The original harmful-knowledge comparator sets remain unchanged; ECO is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include 10-epoch MUSE/TOFU evaluations, Llama-2-7b-hf and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, first-order optimization, ROUGE and FQ/MU metrics, and TOFU 1/5/10% forget splits. MI analysis varies sampling from 10% to 100%. The reported conflict-case forget/retain weights also change from 0.2/1.8 in v1 D.5 to 0.5/1.5 in v2 D.2.5; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices E.3-E.4 add comparative runtime/throughput analysis and sensitivity analysis of MI selection across sample proportions, including stable selection of layer 3. Appendix E.7 adds a direct RMU-versus-FALCON recovery analysis. Original component-ablation scores, logit-lens probing and QA/chat recovery tests are retained, with the ablation moved to Appendix E.5.

E5.justification: The TOFU evaluation introduces KS-test p-values as Forget Quality (Appendix D.3.1 and Table 3), adding a statistical comparison absent from v1. Existing MMLU uncertainty reporting is retained. Table 12 adds recovery values with undefined ± terms, without establishing additional runs or supplying seed counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: MUSE FALCON scores of 0.02/0.03/0.54, TOFU Forget05 FQ/MU of 0.92/0.59, efficiency and MI-sampling measurements, and comparative recovery scores (Tables 2-3, 7-9 and 12). These are newly reported evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1. Most original scores remain unchanged, but RMU's Mistral WMDP-Bio score changes from 31.1 in v1 Table 4 to 34.1 in v2 Table 5.

M1.justification: The MI-guided selection, SVD-derived principal offset vectors, contrastive forget loss, retention loss and gradient-projection procedure remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm 1 and the fixed-layer discussion expand documentation. Different optimizer configurations and numerical gradient weights are reported experimental settings.

P1.justification: The introduction, related-work discussion and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around harmful-knowledge unlearning, cross-domain generalization, efficiency and recovery; component ablations move into the appendix. New practical-implications and discussion sections substantially expand the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive resizing and placement changes for figures and tables. Figure 1 is revised and moved into the introduction. Six new tables present benchmark, efficiency, MI and recovery results, while existing displays are reformatted or relocated, including the ablation table.

R1.justification: Related work expands to NPO/SimNPO, representation noising, circuit breakers, additional logit-based approaches and contrastive unlearning, alongside TOFU, MUSE and OpenUnlearning. Section 2 and Appendix F.3 introduce a substantive positioning argument distinguishing ECO's filtering from parameter-level unlearning. These changes extend beyond bibliographic and citation-style updates.

T1.justification: Equations 1-16 retain the same substantive definitions and mathematical formulations, including MI selection, KDE, principal offset vectors, losses, gradient projection and entropy. No theorem, proof or substantive derivation is added. New pseudocode and conceptual explanations document the existing formulation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially reduces gaps in v1's support for generalizability and efficiency: MUSE and TOFU test distinct forgetting objectives, Appendices E.3-E.4 quantify computational costs and selection stability, and E.7 supplies a recovery comparator. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FALCON, with matching core methodology and original experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and additions.

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong multi-modal reasoning capabilities, enabling direct action generation from visual perception and language instructions in an end-to-end manner. However, their substantial computational cost poses a challenge for real-time robotic control, where rapid decision-making is essential. This paper introduces VLA-Cache, a training-free inference acceleration method that reduces computational overhead by adaptively caching and reusing static visual tokens across frames. Exploiting the temporal continuity in robotic manipulation, VLA-Cache identifies minimally changed tokens between adjacent frames and reuses their cached key-value representations, thereby circumventing redundant computations. Additionally, to maintain action precision, VLA-Cache selectively re-computes task-relevant tokens that are environmentally sensitive, ensuring the fidelity of critical visual information. To further optimize efficiency, we introduce a layer adaptive token reusing strategy that dynamically adjusts the reuse ratio based on attention concentration across decoder layers, prioritizing critical tokens for recomputation. Extensive experiments on two simulation platforms (LIBERO and SIMPLER) and a real-world robotic system demonstrate that VLA-Cache achieves up to 1.7x speedup in CUDA latency and a 15% increase in control frequency, with negligible loss on task success rate. The code and videos can be found at our project page: https://vla-cache.github.io.
arxiv_record.authors: Siyu Xu, Yunke Wang, Chenghao Xia, Dihao Zhu, Tao Huang, Chang Xu
arxiv_record.title: VLA-Cache: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Manipulation via Adaptive Token Caching
