C1.justification: The central claim remains training-free acceleration through adaptive temporal token reuse with little loss of task success. V2 adds an explicit abstract claim of a 15% control-frequency increase and emphasizes compatibility with optimized, high-frequency VLA architectures. These extend the claimed benefits without replacing the core contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive applicability qualifications: extensive motion reduces reuse, other decoder backbones remain untested, and standalone diffusion policies are outside the method's direct scope. It also interprets the object-mask comparison through contextual relevance and discusses robustness under camera motion. The main interpretations of the retained benchmarks remain stable.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page pointer for code and videos and clarifies real-world success criteria, randomization, fixed-horizon single-attempt evaluation, and absence of intervention. Most hardware, preprocessing, precision, sampling, and fine-tuning details already appear in v1 and are relocated or condensed.

E1.justification: LIBERO, both SIMPLER settings, and the four real-world tasks remain. V2 adds PickPot evaluations with moving background objects and people, plus fixed-camera and moving wrist-camera inputs through OpenVLA-OFT. These extend input conditions within the retained manipulation tasks.

E2.justification: FastV and SparseVLM remain the OpenVLA acceleration comparators. V2 adds unaccelerated OpenVLA-OFT comparisons, an object-mask relevance variant using Efficient Track Anything in Table 8, and an explicit OpenVLA baseline row in the component ablation. Newly cited ToMe, PuMer, and MADTP are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds policy control frequency as an evaluation metric across the principal comparisons and evaluates the action-chunking OpenVLA-OFT configuration. New controlled experiments vary background motion, relevance proxies, token budgets, and relevance thresholds. The original default thresholds, fine-tuning budget, and hardware remain; newly disclosed real-world trial procedures do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and token-budget ablations, v2 tests robustness to moving backgrounds, compares attention against object-mask relevance selection, and studies OpenVLA-OFT sensitivity to token budgets and relevance thresholds (Tables 7–10). These substantially expand evidence about robustness and the selection mechanism.

E5.justification: Appendix E.4 newly specifies 20 randomized trials for PickPot and PutSausage and 30 for PlaceCube and WipeTable, with success/failure counts. This discloses evaluation repetitions rather than establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals, seed-level variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Most original LIBERO and SIMPLER scores are retained. V2 adds control-frequency results and substantial OpenVLA-OFT, robustness, and sensitivity results; its Table 2 reports 96.8% versus 97.4% success and 65.10 versus 78.98 Hz for OpenVLA-OFT without versus with caching. Real-world WipeTable success changes from 73.0% to 73.3%, and the average from 84.5% to 84.6%. Component-ablation FLOP entries are omitted.

M1.justification: Both versions use patch similarity to select static tokens, attention to exclude task-relevant tokens, entropy-based layer adaptation, and selective KV-cache reuse. Splitting the algorithm and testing additional architectures do not establish a changed proposed procedure; the object-mask alternative is an ablation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, acceleration discussion, and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Preliminary material is incorporated into Methodology, implementation receives a separate section, the algorithm is split, and the appendices are reorganized into limitations, impact, complexity, inference, and experimental sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn, simulation and real-world task illustrations are merged, and the main visualization gains dynamic-background and wrist-camera panels. Tables gain frequency columns and model rows, new analysis tables appear, and retained appendix visualizations are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion and citations for ToMe, PuMer, MADTP, π0-FAST, HiRT, OpenVLA-OFT, Gemma2, and Efficient Track Anything, while dropping several preliminary-background references. It more explicitly positions caching as complementary to high-frequency architectures. The original distinction from pruning and retraining-based acceleration remains.

T1.justification: The entropy-based reuse definition, KV-update equations, FLOP savings model, and selection-overhead analysis are mathematically retained. V1's complexity appendix becomes Appendix C in v2. Renotation and condensation of repeated inference equations introduce no substantive assumptions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central practical-efficiency argument through control-frequency measurements, an already optimized OpenVLA-OFT baseline, and targeted robustness and relevance-selection tests. These address important gaps in v1's evidence, while clearer limitations and trial protocols improve interpretability. Local reporting errors temper the gain: Table 7 implies approximately 29% FLOP and 26% latency reductions, not the stated 42% and 35%; Table 11's pooled counts imply 81% and 84%, whereas its displayed percentages are task averages. These problems do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VLA-Cache research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds OpenVLA-OFT evaluations, control-frequency measurements, dynamic-background tests, and further ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original LIBERO and SIMPLER evaluations, token-selection and token-budget ablations, and Kinova Jaco2 experiments, including success rates and computational measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: In recent years, nonlinear dynamic system identification using artificial neural networks has garnered attention due to its broad potential applications across science and engineering. However, purely data-driven approaches often struggle with extrapolation and may yield physically implausible forecasts. Furthermore, the learned dynamics can exhibit instabilities, making it difficult to apply such models safely and robustly. This article introduces stable port-Hamiltonian neural networks, a machine learning architecture that incorporates physical biases of energy conservation and dissipation while ensuring global Lyapunov stability of the learned dynamics. Through illustrative and real-world examples, we demonstrate that these strong inductive biases facilitate robust learning of stable dynamics from sparse data, while avoiding instability and surpassing purely data-driven approaches in accuracy and physically meaningful generalization. Furthermore, the model's applicability and potential for data-driven surrogate modeling are showcased on multi-physics simulation data.
arxiv_record.authors: Fabian J. Roth, Dominik K. Klein, Maximilian Kannapinn, Jan Peters, Oliver Weeger
arxiv_record.title: Stable Port-Hamiltonian Neural Networks

C1.justification: The central claims about physically structured, globally stable learning from sparse data and surrogate modeling remain. v2's introduction and conclusion add the claim that providing the equilibrium as prior knowledge improves accuracy and reduces data requirements. Its novelty claim is also refined through more specific comparisons with existing stable models.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the equilibrium prior, explaining its advantage under scarce data and distinguishing bounded trajectories from convergence to the appropriate equilibrium. It adds a low-pass-filter explanation for noise robustness and discusses sNODE trajectory-training failures. It also clarifies that convexity is sufficient rather than necessary, discusses input warping, and reframes applicability around globally stable behavior within the region of interest.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a stated code/model-weight access link, Glorot initialization, hardware and operating-system details, computational timings, additional training-trajectory identifiers and explicit latent encoder/decoder formulas. These materially improve reproducibility documentation. Some detail is lost when matrix parameterization is condensed, including explicit output dimensions and the softplus/absolute-value rules for Cholesky diagonals.

E1.justification: All four application domains remain. v2 adds a food-processing scenario with Gaussian-corrupted input and temperature observations during training, followed by evaluation on clean data (Section 4.3, Table 1). Additional food-processing trajectories otherwise remain within the existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares sPHNN with NODE and PHNN, adding sPHNN-LM for tanks. v2 evaluates bounded PHNNs across the applications, adds Kolter–Manek sNODEs to the rigid-body comparison, and extends sPHNN-LM to the other applications. The bPHNN comparator is an OnsagerNet-inspired adaptation supporting time-dependent inputs, not an evaluation of unchanged OnsagerNet.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled food-processing experiments varying training-set size from one to fifteen trajectories, plus 5%, 15% and 25% Gaussian-noise conditions with evaluation on clean training and test data. These substantially expand the evaluation design. Existing training budgets, learning rates, network widths and core benchmark settings remain; v1 already specifies the fifteen-trajectory food test set despite its erroneous Figure 6 caption.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of data requirements and noise robustness, expands fixed-versus-learned equilibrium comparisons, and tests the weaker boundedness constraint through bPHNN. Existing augmented-dimension and tank extrapolation studies remain, with saturation moved to Appendix D. Conversely, the direct comparison between learned Hamiltonians and physical energy in v1 Figure 3 is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten rigid-body model instances and twenty instances per configuration for the other benchmarks, using boxplots and interquartile means/ranges to summarize variability. Added comparisons retain these practices. No increased repeat counts, seed specifications, confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive comparator, data-size, noise and timing results. For example, Table 1 reports sPHNN test RMSEs of 1.170, 2.595 and 3.177 at increasing noise levels, versus bPHNN's 1.572, 2.828 and 5.231. Section 4.1 newly reports an equilibrium-estimation distance of 0.010 for sPHNN-LM. The learned-Hamiltonian curves and energy-recovery finding from v1 Figure 3 are dropped.

M1.justification: The proposed sPHNN retains its normalized convex Hamiltonian, constrained matrices and derivative/trajectory fitting procedures. Learning the equilibrium location was already supported and tested in v1. The POD description in v2 expands the existing truncated-SVD procedure. bPHNN is introduced as a comparison model.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: port-Hamiltonian motivation and rigid-body equations move into the background, the random-model experiment becomes part of the architecture explanation, matrix descriptions are consolidated, and tank setup/saturation material moves to a new appendix. P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with substantial figure redesign. Architecture and random dynamics are combined; comparison plots are split into panels; food-processing plots are expanded; manufacturing figures gain heat-source and comparator displays. New noise/timing tables and a latent-model diagram appear. The manufacturing error plot and tank saturation plots are relocated and expanded.

R1.justification: v2 replaces v1's broad statement that the intersection of physical structure and stability is largely unexplored with substantive comparisons to latent linear port-Hamiltonian identification, OnsagerNet and projection-based stable learning. Discussions of Rettberg, Yu and Schlaginhaufen distinguish nonlinear global stability, time-dependent inputs and trajectory-training compatibility. This changes the research positioning beyond routine citation updates.

T1.justification: The central stability theorem and proof remain. Appendix A adds a Hessian condition to Lemma A.1 and an alternative coercivity argument; the main text removes v1's asserted finite-time zero-dissipation condition for nonconverging solutions. These are limited mathematical revisions. The new assertion that strict convexity requires an everywhere positive-definite Hessian is incorrect.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central contribution. v1's comparisons largely establish advantages over models without stability guarantees; v2 adds bounded and stable comparators and controlled studies separating equilibrium knowledge, data availability and noise robustness. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sPHNN research, with matching architecture, stability theorem and four application domains. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions to be distinguished from relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds baseline comparisons, training-data and noise studies, equilibrium-estimation results and computational timings.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training and prediction results for a spinning rigid body, cascaded tanks, thermal food processing and additive manufacturing, including extrapolation and augmented-state experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Leveraging attention sparsity to accelerate long-context large language models (LLMs) has been a hot research topic. However, current algorithms such as sparse attention or key-value (KV) cache compression tend to use a fixed budget, which presents a significant challenge during deployment because it fails to account for the dynamic nature of real-world scenarios, where the optimal balance between accuracy and efficiency can vary greatly. In this paper, we find that borrowing top-$p$ sampling (nucleus sampling) to sparse attention can surprisingly achieve adaptive budgeting. Based on this, we propose Twilight, a framework to bring adaptive sparsity to any existing sparse attention algorithm without sacrificing their accuracy. Empirical results show that Twilight can adaptively prune at most 98% of redundant tokens, leading to $15.4\times$ acceleration in self-attention operations and $3.9\times$ acceleration in end-to-end per token latency in long context LLM decoding.

metadata.abstract: Leveraging attention sparsity to accelerate long-context large language models (LLMs) has been of great importance recently. However, most existing sparse attention algorithms use a fixed budget of how many tokens to use in their computations. This simple static decision raises critical issues in real-world deployment because it fails to account for the dynamic nature of real-world scenarios, where the optimal balance between accuracy and efficiency can vary greatly.  In this paper, we reveal a key insight that leveraging the idea of top-$p$ sampling (a.k.a., nucleus sampling) in sparse attention could enable efficient and adaptive budget decisions. Based on this, we propose Twilight, a framework that enhances any existing sparse attention algorithm with adaptive budget decision capabilities without sacrificing accuracy.  Empirical results show that Twilight can adaptively prune up to 98% tokens with nearly no accuracy loss in both mid- and long-context scenarios, leading to a $1.4\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art sparse attention mechanisms.

E4.justification: v3 adds threshold-p sensitivity measurements (Figure 9), quantization-dependent SpGEMV latency (Figure 12), and padded versus head/group-variable-length attention comparisons (Figure 13). E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. Added averages and relative score changes remain point summaries rather than new uncertainty-reporting practices.

arxiv_record.abstract: While neural networks have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, accurately quantifying uncertainty in their predictions is essential to ensure their trustworthiness and enable widespread adoption in critical systems. Several Bayesian uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods exist that are either cheap or reliable, but not both. We propose a post-hoc, sampling-based UQ method for over-parameterized networks at the end of training. Our approach constructs efficient and meaningful deep ensembles by employing a (stochastic) gradient-descent sampling process on appropriately linearized networks. We demonstrate that our method effectively approximates the posterior of a Gaussian process using the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel. Through a series of numerical experiments, we show that our method not only outperforms competing approaches in computational efficiency-often reducing costs by multiple factors-but also maintains state-of-the-art performance across a variety of UQ metrics for both regression and classification tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: Joseph Wilson, Chris van der Heide, Liam Hodgkinson and Fred Roosta
arxiv_record.title: Uncertainty Quantification with the Empirical Neural Tangent Kernel

C1.justification: The abstract's principal NUQLS, GP-connection, and efficiency claims remain. v2 makes VMSP, already proposed in v1 Section 5.3, an explicit fourth introductory contribution. Remark 1.1 additionally argues that Bayesian methods should prioritize uncertainty estimation over predictive gains, refining the paper's stated contribution and focus.

C2.justification: New Appendix C substantially develops the distinction between epistemic uncertainty and prediction quality, including critiques of NLL, calibration, and OOD-detection metrics. Appendix H.1 interprets NUQLS and PNC as complementary across training/width regimes, and the conclusion adds dependence on adequate training and local linearization as a limitation. The cross-entropy theoretical caveat already existed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a separate NUQLS package link, pretrained ImageNet-weight provenance, implementation settings for convergence and coverage experiments, and detailed BDE, BatchEnsemble, SNGP, and SGLD configurations. Appendix E adds computational and memory guidance. Existing experimental-code access and much original implementation documentation are retained, while classification tuning guidance is shortened.

E1.justification: v2 adds SVHN classification with CIFAR-10 as OOD data, ImageNet classification with ImageNet-O evaluation, Gaussian synthetic regression for convergence testing, and sinusoidal regression for confidence-interval evaluation. The original UCI, toy-regression, and image-classification coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds PNC to confidence-interval comparisons and evaluates BatchEnsemble, SNGP, and SGLD in classification comparisons. BDE, already evaluated on toy regression in v1, is additionally compared on UCI datasets and FashionMNIST. These are actual comparator additions in Tables 3–4, 8, and 11 and Figure 6.

E3.justification: v2 introduces explicit NTK-variance convergence and confidence-interval coverage/width protocols. Existing settings also change: ResNet9/FashionMNIST NUQLS uses 2 instead of 5 epochs and gamma 0.1 instead of 0.6; ResNet20 uses 100 instead of 50 ensemble members. Table 7 adds a ResNet32 configuration. UCI runtime reporting now includes base-network training while separately retaining post-hoc costs. These are protocol and accounting changes, not same-setting performance comparisons.

E4.justification: New Section 4.1/Figure 2 tests convergence toward NTK-GP variance across training duration, ensemble size, and network configurations. Appendix H.1 compares confidence-interval behavior under extremely wide, partially trained versus finite-width, fully trained networks. Conversely, v1 Appendix C.2/Figure 3's classification sensitivity analysis over gamma, learning rate, and epochs is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 2 reports 95% sample confidence intervals over 10 random realizations, and Appendix I.5 specifies 100 or 50 repetitions for coverage experiments. Conversely, NUQLS's ResNet20 standard deviations disappear between v1 Table 5 and v2 Table 7. The established repeated-run reporting for UCI and LeNet experiments is retained.

E6.justification: v2 adds convergence curves, coverage/width results, BDE regression scores, and additional classification results. ResNet9/FashionMNIST incorrect/OOD VMSP medians change from 0.041/0.119 to 0.182/0.217 alongside changed training settings. ResNet20 NLL changes from 0.236±0.001 to 0.228 with a larger ensemble. Original UCI predictive metrics remain unchanged; larger reported runtimes reflect added base-training costs, such as Energy NUQLS changing from 0.151 seconds to 8.374 seconds total, retaining 0.151 in parentheses.

M1.justification: The core linearized sampler, training objective, Gaussian initialization, and eNUQLS extension are retained. For the new confidence-interval experiments, however, v2 Appendix I.5 adds a 1.5 multiplier to NUQLS variances alongside the existing gamma-tuning procedure, a limited adaptation of uncertainty postprocessing.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: main-text related work is consolidated into Appendix B, predictive classification evaluation moves to Appendix G, and experiments begin with convergence validation. The introduction is reframed around uncertainty evaluation, classification tuning discussion is shortened, and the appendices are reorganized into dedicated interpretation, cost, and experimental sections.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. v2 adds convergence Figure 2, four-panel Figure 6, confidence-interval and BDE tables, and expanded comparison/settings tables; removes v1's sensitivity Figure 3; and relocates predictive Table 2 to the appendix. Table 7 also introduces grouped model columns and colored rankings. Several original plots are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands positioning against PNC, SNGP, efficient ensemble methods, and Miani et al. (2024b)'s null-space posterior approach. Additional literature supports the new discussion of epistemic uncertainty and limitations of calibration metrics. BDE's positioning changes from largely explaining its exclusion to discussing broader direct comparisons.

T1.justification: The main assumptions, convergence theorem, GP derivation, and Appendix A proofs are substantively retained. New Appendix D presents an almost-sure noncollapse argument for parameter samples, while Appendix E derives approximate per-epoch computational costs and ensemble-memory scaling. These supplement rather than replace the central theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through direct NTK-convergence testing, broader comparator evaluations, and an explicit failure-regime study. Including base-network training costs makes the central efficiency comparison more complete, while expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. Removing the hyperparameter sensitivity study and ResNet20 error bars weakens some reporting, and ImageNet is compared only with a random baseline. Nevertheless, the gains in empirical support, applicability assessment, and cost transparency provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NUQLS research, with matching authors, core algorithm, theory, and retained experiments. The complete 24-page v1 and 39-page v2, including appendices and v2's checklist, provide readable material for a reliable comparison.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present a novel video generation framework that integrates 3-dimensional geometry and dynamic awareness. To achieve this, we augment 2D videos with 3D point trajectories and align them in pixel space. The resulting 3D-aware video dataset, PointVid, is then used to fine-tune a latent diffusion model, enabling it to track 2D objects with 3D Cartesian coordinates. Building on this, we regularize the shape and motion of objects in the video to eliminate undesired artifacts, e.g., non-physical deformation. Consequently, we enhance the quality of generated RGB videos and alleviate common issues like object morphing, which are prevalent in current video models due to a lack of shape awareness. With our 3D augmentation and regularization, our model is capable of handling contact-rich scenarios such as task-oriented videos, where 3D information is essential for perceiving shape and motion of interacting solids. Our method can be seamlessly integrated into existing video diffusion models to improve their visual plausibility.

arxiv_record.abstract: With the development of large language models (LLMs), efficient inference through Key-Value (KV) cache compression has attracted considerable attention, especially for long-context generation. To compress the KV cache, recent methods identify critical KV tokens through static modeling of attention scores. However, these methods often struggle to accurately determine critical tokens as they neglect the temporal patterns in attention scores, resulting in a noticeable degradation in LLM performance. To address this challenge, we propose AttentionPredictor, which is the first learning-based method to directly predict attention patterns for KV cache compression and critical token identification. Specifically, AttentionPredictor learns a lightweight, unified convolution model to dynamically capture spatiotemporal patterns and predict the next-token attention scores. An appealing feature of AttentionPredictor is that it accurately predicts the attention score and shares the unified prediction model, which consumes negligible memory, among all transformer layers. Moreover, we propose a cross-token critical cache prefetching framework that hides the token estimation time overhead to accelerate the decoding stage. By retaining most of the attention information, AttentionPredictor achieves 13$\times$ KV cache compression and 5.6$\times$ speedup in a cache offloading scenario with comparable LLM performance, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-arts. The code is available at https://github.com/MIRALab-USTC/LLM-AttentionPredictor.

arxiv_record.abstract:
High-quality supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data are crucial for eliciting strong capabilities from pretrained large language models (LLMs). Typically, instructions are paired with multiple responses sampled from other LLMs, which are often out of the distribution of the target model to be fine-tuned. This, at scale, can lead to diminishing returns and even hurt the models' performance and robustness. We propose **GRAPE**, a novel SFT framework that accounts for the unique characteristics of the target model. For each instruction, it gathers responses from various LLMs and selects the one with the highest probability measured by the target model, indicating that it aligns most closely with the target model's pretrained distribution; it then proceeds with standard SFT training.
  We first evaluate GRAPE with a controlled experiment, where we sample various solutions for each question in UltraInteract from multiple models and fine-tune commonly used LMs like LLaMA3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B on GRAPE-selected data. GRAPE significantly outperforms strong baselines, including distilling from the strongest model with an absolute gain of up to 13.8%, averaged across benchmarks, and training on 3x more data with a maximum performance improvement of 17.3%. GRAPE's strong performance generalizes to realistic settings. We experiment with the post-training data used for Tulu3 and Olmo-2. GRAPE outperforms strong baselines trained on 4.5 times more data by 6.1% and a state-of-the-art data selection approach by 3% on average performance. Remarkably, using 1/3 of the data and half the number of epochs, GRAPE enables LLaMA3.1-8B to surpass the performance of Tulu3-SFT by 3.5%.

arxiv_record.title: The Best Instruction-Tuning Data are Those That Fit

GRAPE's strong performance generalizes to realistic settings. We experiment with the post-training data used for Tulu3 and Olmo-2. GRAPE outperforms strong baselines trained on 4.5 times more data by 6.1% and a state-of-the-art data selection approach by 3% on average performance. metadata.abstract: High-quality supervised finetuning (SFT) data are essential for unlocking pretrained LLMs’ capabilities. Typically, instructions are paired with responses from various sources—by human annotators or other LMs—which are often out of the distribution of the target model to be finetuned. At scale, this mismatch can lead to diminishing returns and even hurt model performance and robustness. We hypothesize that SFT is most effective when the data is aligned with the model’s pretrained distribution, and propose **GRAPE**—a novel SFT framework that tailors supervision to the target model. For each instruction, it **g**athers **r**esponses from various sources and selects the one that **a**ligns most closely to the model’s **pre**trained distribution, as measured by the normalized probability. Standard SFT is then performed on these selected responses.  We first evaluate GRAPE in a controlled experiment, sampling multiple responses per question in the UltraInteract dataset from diverse models. We finetune using GRAPE-selected data on LMs from different families, including LLaMA-1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B. GRAPE significantly outperforms strong baselines—including distilling from the strongest model—with absolute gains up to **13.8%** averaged across benchmarks, and outperforms a 3× larger data baseline with improvements up to **17.3%**.  GRAPE's benefits generalize to off-the-shelf SFT data. When used to subsample from the post-training data of Tulu3 and Olmo-2, GRAPE surpasses strong baselines trained on 4.5× more data by **6.1%**, and outperforms state-of-the-art selection methods by **3.9%** on average. Notably, with only **1/3 the data** and **half the training epochs**, GRAPE enables LLaMA-1-8B to **exceed Tulu3-SFT performance by 3.5%**.  Our findings highlight that aligning supervision with the pretrained distribution provides a simple yet powerful strategy to improve both the **efficiency** and **effectiveness** of SFT.

C1.justification: The central claim remains that matching supervision to the target model's distribution improves SFT performance and efficiency over stronger-teacher responses, larger datasets and existing selection approaches. The headline gains in the abstracts are retained; the additional experiments support this existing claim.

C2.justification: v3 Section 7 explicitly qualifies GRAPE's applicability by candidate-pool quality and the base model's inherent capabilities. It also explains that response selection can complement instruction-level selection. These are useful qualifications beyond v1's existing warning about self-generation and reduced diversity.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the Question/Answer scoring template and length-normalized log probabilities in Section 3.2. Appendix C adds LESS and NV-Embed implementation details, and the checklist discloses greedy pass@1 evaluation. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained experiments; the GPU and batch-size disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendices B.3–B.4 add long-chain-of-thought training using an OpenR1-Math/LUFFY subset and OpenThoughts-114k. Evaluation expands to AIME24/25, AMC, Minerva, OlympiadBench, ARC-C, GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro. OpenHermes coverage is retained through relocation to Appendix B.2.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds evaluated LESS and Emb-NV baselines for all three target models. Appendix B.1/Table 7 adds response selection using Skywork-Reward-Llama3.1-8B-v0.2. LESS was discussed in v1's related-work appendix but was not an evaluated comparator there; the original comparison methods remain.

E3.justification: The original main experiments retain their reported one-epoch training and learning rate. Added experiments introduce Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B configurations, a second selection-and-training round, and a study sampling 1,000 Tulu instructions. The new LESS comparison specifies four warmup epochs on 5% of the data and 8192-dimensional gradient projection.

E4.justification: Figure 4 and Appendix H newly examine how response-source preferences differ across base models. Appendix G tests whether selection remains useful after initial fine-tuning, while Appendix B.4 tests extending likelihood-based supervision to token losses. The earlier single-generator, self-distillation, parameter-distance and UltraInteract subset analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests for its experimental results. v3's checklist invokes greedy pass@1 evaluation, but this adds no uncertainty estimates or statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: The original benchmark results are retained, but v3 adds substantial results for new comparators and experiments. Table 9 reports Qwen2.5-1.5B MATH accuracy of 0.396 with GRAPE versus 0.330 with highest-perplexity selection. Table 10 reports token-level GRAPE versus baseline scores of 60.20 versus 55.60 on MATH, but 3.23 versus 4.38 on AIME-25. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The main response-selection procedure is retained, but Appendix B.4 introduces a distinct training objective that weights token losses by token likelihood. Appendix G also adds iterative selection using the fine-tuned checkpoint before another training round. These extend the procedure beyond selecting responses followed by standard SFT.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites the abstract, experimental introductions, baseline descriptions and conclusion. P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column formatting with extensive figure and table repositioning. The original three figures are retained and rearranged; a response-selection heatmap is added. R1.justification: v3 adds references and discussion concerning SPIN, newer data-selection work by Dai and Ivison, NV-Embed, and long-chain-of-thought resources. T1.justification: The computational-cost definitions, assumptions and derivations in v1 Appendix E are retained in v3 Appendix F. No new theorem or proof is introduced. The standard perplexity formula added in Section 3.2 explains score computation without adding a theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument by supplementing v1's S2L and data/response controls with gradient-based, embedding-based and reward-based selection comparisons. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRAPE study. Their text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments on UltraInteract, Tulu–Olmo, OpenHermes and Magpie-Zoo, together with self-distillation and other analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point of a nonconvex function with a Lipschitz continuous Hessian is a central problem in optimization. Regularized Newton methods are a classical tool and have been studied extensively, yet they still face a trade-off between global and local convergence. Whether a parameter-free algorithm of this type can simultaneously achieve optimal global complexity and quadratic local convergence remains an open question. To bridge this long-standing gap, we propose a new class of regularizers constructed from the current and previous gradients, and leverage the conjugate gradient approach with a negative curvature monitor to solve the regularized Newton equation. The proposed algorithm is adaptive, requiring no prior knowledge of the Hessian Lipschitz constant, and achieves a global complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-3/2})$ in terms of the second-order oracle calls, and $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-7/4})$ for Hessian-vector products, respectively. When the iterates converge to a point where the Hessian is positive definite, the method exhibits quadratic local convergence. Preliminary numerical results, including training the physics-informed neural networks, illustrate the competitiveness of our algorithm.
arxiv_record.authors: Yuhao Zhou, Jintao Xu, Bingrui Li, Chenglong Bao, Chao Ding, Jun Zhu
arxiv_record.title: A Regularized Newton Method for Nonconvex Optimization with Global and Local Complexity Guarantees

Appendix A.2 newly identifies multiple CG iterations as a computational limitation and notes that nonsmooth activations such as ReLU may violate the Hessian assumption. The earlier CUTEst tradeoffs and failure-mode discussion remain.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds substantial implementation information: Python version, P100 GPUs, network architecture, double precision, tanh activation, Xavier initialization, sampling mesh, preconditioning and optimizer schedules. Appendix G adds the ARCqK implementation source. The checklist promises a code release, but the PDFs do not establish that release occurred.

E1.justification: v3 retains the 124 CUTEst problems and adds PINN training for convection, reaction and wave PDEs. This substantially extends evaluation from conventional optimization benchmarks to neural approximation of physical equations.

E2.justification: v3 adds adaptive cubic regularization method ARCqK to the CUTEst comparisons and NNCG with regularization coefficients 0.1 and 0.01 to the new PINN comparisons. CAT and AN2CER remain. Adam and L-BFGS serve as shared preliminary training stages.

E3.justification: The added PINN experiments introduce an 81,201-parameter network, 10,000 residual training points, a 101×257 evaluation mesh, Adam/L-BFGS warm starts and final-stage time budgets of 7.5, 2 and 18 hours. Training loss and test relative error are new evaluation metrics. The existing CUTEst tolerance, iteration limit and time limit remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The fallback, regularization-exponent and linesearch sweeps, together with the HIMMELBG and ROSENBR local-convergence cases, are retained from Appendix F as Appendix G. Their tested questions and reported outcomes remain unchanged; the added PINN material supplies optimizer comparisons rather than a new targeted ablation or robustness study.

E5.justification: v1 reports benchmark aggregates without repeated-seed uncertainty. v3 introduces eight random-seed runs per PINN experiment, mean and individual trajectories, and mean-plus-standard-deviation results in Table 7. Checklist item 7 identifies the uncertainty as standard deviation and explicitly describes CUTEst experiments as deterministic.

E6.justification: Existing CUTEst table entries are unchanged, while Tables 3–6 add ARCqK results, including 16.16 s shifted geometric mean runtime and 87.10% success. Tables 2 and 7 and Figures 3 and 7 add substantial PINN results. For example, Table 7 reports reaction mean training loss of 2.04×10^-9 for ARNCGg versus 5.20×10^-8 for NNCG0.01.

M1.justification: The central regularizers, fallback logic, capped CG and linesearch procedures remain unchanged; LipEstimation separates previously inline update rules. Appendix H.1 adds randomized Nyström preconditioning to CG for the PINN implementation, a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: The abstract and introductory framing are rewritten, Section 2.1 substantially expands the method's intuition, and Section 3 reorganizes the technical narrative. Related work and the summarized descent lemma move into appendices. These changes substantially restructure existing exposition beyond simply adding experiments.

P2.justification: v3 adds PINN Figures 3 and 7 and Tables 2 and 7, expands CUTEst displays with ARCqK, and revises the theoretical comparison table. Conference formatting substantially resizes and repositions displays, while algorithm formatting adds line numbers and a separate LipEstimation block.

R1.justification: The earlier related-work discussion is substantially expanded in Appendix A.1, distinguishing regularization, linesearch, adaptivity and proof techniques from Royer, He, Gratton and trust-region methods. v3 also adds positioning against adaptive cubic regularization and PINN optimization literature, including Dussault, Rathore and Nyström-preconditioning work.

Section 3 adds an argument about a theta-independent neighborhood with order-3/2 convergence and a K1+K2 bound on additional iterations before quadratic convergence. improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the practical evidence beyond v1's CUTEst evaluation through three PINN tasks, a specialist comparator, matched time budgets and eight-seed uncertainty reporting. The PINN evidence remains limited to three PDE settings, but the combined gains in empirical support and clarity are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARNCG research and contain readable text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Material can be reliably matched across the extensive reformatting and renumbering.

arxiv_record.abstract: Prompt tuning has emerged as a key technique for adapting large pre-trained Decision Transformers (DTs) in offline Reinforcement Learning (RL), particularly in multi-task and few-shot settings. The Prompting Decision Transformer (PDT) enables task generalization via trajectory prompts sampled uniformly from expert demonstrations -- without accounting for prompt informativeness. In this work, we propose a bandit-based prompt-tuning method that learns to construct optimal trajectory prompts from demonstration data at inference time. We devise a structured bandit architecture operating in the trajectory prompt space, achieving linear rather than combinatorial scaling with prompt size. Additionally, we show that the pre-trained PDT itself can serve as a powerful feature extractor for the bandit, enabling efficient reward modeling across various environments. We theoretically establish regret bounds and demonstrate empirically that our method consistently enhances performance across a wide range of tasks, high-dimensional environments, and out-of-distribution scenarios, outperforming existing baselines in prompt tuning.
arxiv_record.authors: Finn Rietz, Oleg Smirnov, Sara Karimi, Lele Cao
arxiv_record.title: Prompt Tuning Decision Transformers with Structured and Scalable Bandits

C1.justification: v3 adds theoretical regret guarantees as a headline contribution and makes structured linear scaling and compact PDT representations central to its claimed advantages over earlier prompt tuners. v1 primarily foregrounds empirical improvement of frozen PDTs and the custom environment, without a theoretical contribution. The core claim of adaptation without backbone weight updates remains.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes high variance from ignoring segment correlations. v3 instead develops a weak-interaction explanation based on independent prompt sampling during pretraining, supported by attention analyses, while acknowledging possible prompt overfitting. It also reframes encoded features primarily as an efficiency benefit rather than a prerequisite for strong returns and adds an explicit limitation concerning offline-RL extrapolation.

D1.justification: v3 adds optimizer names, approximate pretraining/adaptation times, hyperparameter-selection information, and MuJoCo implementation provenance. Its checklist describes a supplementary code archive with reproduction instructions, replacing v1's placeholder access statement; the archive itself is not available in the supplied PDFs. Shared hyperparameters are largely unchanged, and v1's explicit Half Cheetah held-out task IDs are no longer listed.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Sparse 2D Point and Half Cheetah tasks, v3 evaluates Ant directional locomotion and Meta-world Pick-place manipulation, including held-out tasks. Section 5.3 also introduces an evaluated synthetic vector-selection task with combinatorial choices and aggregate reward, substantially broadening task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: v3 evaluates ZORankSGD explicitly rather than only citing its source paper. Its Half Cheetah comparisons additionally include CQL oracle and hill-climbing results absent from the corresponding v1 tables. The synthetic experiment adds standard flat epsilon-greedy, UCB, and Thompson-sampling comparators. v1's Gaussian-perturbation baseline is retained under the hill-climbing name.

E3.justification: v3 adds 2,000-round synthetic size sweeps, controlled prompt permutations and attention masking, and runtime evaluations. MuJoCo aggregation is now described as covering all training tasks rather than v1's selected set, while retaining 250 rollouts and final-10 averaging. An extended ZORankSGD evaluation adds a larger budget, although Figure 6 inconsistently labels it as 1,500 episodes versus 1,250 rollouts in the caption.

E4.justification: New analyses test segment independence through permutations and attention interventions, scaling through synthetic problem-size sweeps, and feature-encoding efficiency through runtime comparisons. Extended-budget ZORankSGD curves are also added. The expert/novice mixture analysis is retained in Appendix D.2, whereas v1's Appendix C.3 diagnostic comparing offline loss with OOD online performance is removed.

E5.justification: The three-seed design and standard-deviation bands are retained. v3 explicitly identifies main-table entries as mean ± standard deviation and states the uncertainty convention globally in the checklist; v1 leaves its main-table ± notation undefined while defining standard deviation for appendix plots. This clarifies reporting without establishing additional runs or new significance tests.

E6.justification: Many shared 2D and in-distribution Half Cheetah entries remain unchanged, but Half Cheetah OOD results are replaced: for example, untuned PDT at J=1,H=5 is −36.83±2.58 in v1 Table 5 and −64.78±36.91 in v3 Table 2. These are revised reported outcomes, not established matched-setting gains. v3 adds extensive benchmark, comparator, regret, attention, and timing results, while removing the dedicated 2D OOD table and fine-tuning diagnostic.

M1.justification: v3 adds Thompson sampling as an evaluated exploration option alongside epsilon-greedy and UCB. The underlying procedure remains unchanged: independent reward models select prompt segments, receive rollout-return feedback, and optionally use frozen PDT features. Factorization and PDT-based feature extraction already appear in v1; Algorithms 1–3 are relocated to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, its abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, and the experimental narrative shifts from the custom 2D environment to MuJoCo benchmarks first. Algorithms and existing demonstration-quality discussion move to appendices, which are reorganized substantially; a conference checklist is also inserted.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Benchmark tables expand into multi-environment comparisons, and Figure 3 replaces the bandit's temporal sequence with a cross-method visualization paired with a results table. New regret plots, attention heatmaps, learning curves, and timing tables accompany extensive relocation and resizing of retained displays.

R1.justification: v3 substantially sharpens positioning against earlier PDT prompt tuners through claims about goal-conditioning expressiveness, causal consistency, and unstructured search scaling. It adds distinctions from MGPO, Meta-DT, and future-conditioned DT, while removing v1's discussion of LLM demonstration selection and ordering. This changes the novelty argument beyond merely expanding the bibliography.

T1.justification: v1 has no corresponding original regret theorem. v3 Section 4.3 adds a reward decomposition with bounded segment interactions, Theorem 4.1 bounding total regret by average slot regret plus 2Kε, and Corollary 4.2. improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation: Ant and pick-place evaluations and a dedicated ZORankSGD comparison address v1's narrow coverage and reliance on an approximate comparator. arxiv_record.abstract: The mean of a random variable can be understood as a linear functional on the space of probability distributions. Quantum computing is known to provide a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo methods for mean estimation. In this paper, we investigate whether a similar quadratic speedup is achievable for estimating non-linear functionals of probability distributions. We propose a quantum-inside-quantum Monte Carlo algorithm that achieves such a speedup for a broad class of non-linear estimation problems, including nested conditional expectations and stochastic optimization. Our algorithm improves upon the direct application of the quantum multilevel Monte Carlo algorithm introduced by An et al. (2021). The existing lower bound indicates that our algorithm is optimal up polylogarithmic factors. A key innovation of our approach is a new sequence of multilevel Monte Carlo approximations specifically designed for quantum computing, which is central to the algorithm's improved performance.

C1.justification: The central claim of near-optimal Õ(ε^-1) nested-expectation estimation and quadratic advantage over classical MLMC remains. The introduction changes its claim about directly applying QA-MLMC: v1 reports a partial speedup, whereas v2 reports no improvement over classical MLMC, strengthening the stated comparative advantage.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the mechanism explanation: the new hierarchy improves bias and variance exponents while retaining a similar cost exponent, rather than preserving statistical exponents and improving cost. V2 also explicitly identifies fault-tolerance requirements and current NISQ limitations, and clarifies that vector-valued applications require an extension.

D1.justification: V1 largely refers readers elsewhere for its computational access model. V2 Section 3 explains the requirement for sampling-procedure access and describes reversible circuit implementation using Toffoli/NOT gates and work registers. These are additional implementation disclosures, not evidence of a newly implemented or tested system.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or executes training or evaluation tasks. Conditional stochastic optimization already appears in v1; v2 develops a theoretical application rather than adding an evaluated domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the nested estimator of Rainforth et al., classical MLMC of Giles, and QA-MLMC of An et al. V2 Section 3.1 additionally analyzes directly nested quantum mean estimation as an alternative costing Õ(ε^-2). This is an analytical comparison, not an empirical baseline experiment.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an empirical evaluation protocol. Revised accuracy allocations, oracle assumptions, and success guarantees concern the algorithm and its mathematical analysis, not experimental settings.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, sensitivity experiments, robustness tests, error analyses, or instantiated case studies. The additional application bounds and lower-bound construction are theoretical analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repetitions, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's explicit median-trick proof and failure-probability corrections concern theoretical algorithm guarantees rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes An et al.'s analytical cost from Õ(ε^-1.5) to Õ(ε^-2), now matching classical MLMC rather than improving its exponent. The proposed method remains Õ(ε^-1). Section 4 adds parameter-dependent application costs and a finite-optimization bound; these are theoretical results, not measured performance gains.

M1.justification: The quantum-inside-quantum construction is retained. Algorithm 4 corrects the returned sum to include level zero, changes per-level accuracy from ε/(2L) to ε/(2L+2), and changes failure probability from 0.1^l to 0.1^(l+1). Section 4 also adds a finite-decision-set optimization procedure combining the estimator with quantum minimum finding.

P1.justification: V2 substantially condenses and rewrites the introduction, removes the standalone preliminary examples section while retaining overlapping applications, and standardizes quantum-accelerated terminology. It adds a proof agenda and reorganizes Appendix A into four named subsections. These changes substantially revise the narrative and organization beyond adding mathematical content.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively retypeset into a compact conference format with a redesigned title/author block and substantially different spacing and equation placement. Table 1 and Algorithm 1 become wrapped displays, and median amplification receives boxed instructions. The single comparison table is retained; neither version contains figures.

R1.justification: V2 adds literature supporting reversible computation, quantum minimum finding, the lower-bound reduction, and hardware limitations, and explicitly distinguishes its approach from classical many-body Quantum Monte Carlo. It also positions An et al.'s general QA-MLMC framework as worst-case optimal while retaining the principal nested-expectation literature.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 2.3 and Appendix C's COUNT–PARITY lower-bound construction, plus the median-trick proof in Appendix A.4. It changes the formal treatment from vector-valued to scalar inner functions, revises the main parameter dependence from S+KV to K√(SV), and corrects telescoping, variance, and cost calculations. The high-confidence theorem also replaces v1's corollary that still stated 80% success.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs important correctness defects in Algorithm 4 and Appendix A, including the missing level-zero contribution and inconsistent error/failure budgets, and corrects the central QA-MLMC comparison. The new lower-bound proof and clearer applicability conditions substantially strengthen the paper. A qualification remains necessary: v2 drops S ≥ 1 while Appendix A.3 simplifies its cost as though S were bounded away from zero. This limits the revised parameter guarantee but does not outweigh the substantial corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same nested-expectation algorithm despite retitling and substantial revision. The main text, equations, algorithms, table, and complete appendices—A–B in v1 and A–C in v2—support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 remains theoretical. Its additional lower bound and application analyses do not report executed experiments, simulation studies, or data analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports algorithms, complexity bounds, proofs, and illustrative applications. Table 1 contains theoretical costs; neither the main text nor the appendices report original empirical outcomes.

metadata.abstract: Modern foundation models are trained on diverse datasets to enhance generalization across tasks and domains. A central challenge in this process is determining how to effectively mix and sample data from multiple sources. This naturally leads to a multi-task learning (MTL) perspective. While prior work in MTL has emphasized mitigating gradient conflicts, we observe that large-scale pretraining scenarios—such as multilingual or multi-domain training—often exhibit little to no gradient conflict. Motivated by this observation, we propose $\textbf{PiKE}$ ($\textbf{P}$ositive gradient $\textbf{i}$nteraction-based $\textbf{K}$-task weights $\textbf{E}$stimator), an adaptive data mixing algorithm that dynamically adjusts sampling weights during training. PiKE exploits non-conflicting gradient interactions to minimize a near-tight upper bound on the average loss decrease at each step, while incurring negligible computational overhead. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees and  show that PiKE  outperforms static and non-adaptive mixing baselines. Furthermore, we extend PiKE to promote balanced learning across tasks. Extensive experiments on large-scale language model pretraining confirm that PiKE achieves faster convergence and improved downstream performance compared to existing approaches.

C1.justification: The core adaptive-mixing, convergence, fairness, and empirical-performance contributions remain. v2 adds explicit claims of a near-tight bound and near-optimal per-iteration decrease, and broadens the stated comparison beyond static and heuristic mixing. This refines and strengthens the contribution statement without changing the central research objective.

C2.justification: v2 explains that the variance term prevents excessive emphasis on noisy tasks and interprets the estimation ablation as supporting single-batch statistics. It expands the rationale for balanced task learning and suggests downstream-feedback integration. The existing data-abundance limitation and perplexity-versus-accuracy interpretation remain.

D1.justification: Table 7 revises hyperparameters and newly specifies an estimation batch size of 256. Appendix G.7 documents task-specific batch portions and averaging across sample subsets, while Table 8 supplies detailed runtime and overhead measurements. The underlying hardware, training infrastructure, tokenization, and general implementation disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same mC4 language coverage, including the six-language gradient study, the same six GLaM domains, and the same HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, CommonsenseQA, and PIQA tasks. Added shot settings and ablations reuse these datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates FAMO and ADO across multilingual and GLaM configurations in Tables 1–2 and 13–14; v1 only cites these methods. This substantially extends comparisons to scalable multitask optimization and adaptive mixing. Existing baselines, including the PCGrad/AdaTask comparison in Figure 7, remain.

E3.justification: Table 7 replaces the reported tuning grid: for example, zeta2 changes from {5, 10, 15} to values between 0.001 and 0.01 in specified parameter pairs. Tables 9–12 add complementary zero-/seven-shot evaluations and controlled variance-coefficient and estimation-budget sweeps. The small three-language model header changes from 300M to 270M. These reported changes do not establish reruns of retained results.

E4.justification: New Appendices G.6–G.7 test whether the variance term matters and whether averaging additional gradient-statistic estimates improves performance. Appendix G.4 adds training-overhead profiling. These substantially extend v1's analyses, while retaining its gradient-interaction, sampling-trajectory, and fairness investigations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Table 12's additional gradient-statistic estimates concern an algorithmic estimation budget, not replicated performance measurements or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original numerical benchmark rows are retained, but v2 adds extensive results for FAMO, ADO, Balanced-PiKE on GLaM, complementary shot settings, overhead, and ablations. For example, Table 2 adds 48.2% average accuracy for Balanced-PiKE with tau=5; Table 11 reports 47.0% with zeta2=0.005 versus 45.3% when the variance term is omitted.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same conceptual optimization, practical sampling update, and tilted-risk extension. Fair-PiKE becomes Balanced-PiKE, and removing the common exponential factor from its normalized weights is algebraically equivalent. Newly documented gradient-estimation details do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the former preliminaries/motivation sequence becomes three 'building blocks.' Gradient-study discussion moves into Appendix C, method and proof sections are reorganized, and Fair-PiKE is renamed Balanced-PiKE throughout. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 expands the main benchmark tables and the former appendix Tables 8–9, now Tables 13–14, and adds five tables for profiling, shot comparisons, and ablations. It introduces a boxed feature summary and colored equation annotations, and resizes or relocates retained figures, including a text-wrapped Figure 3.

R1.justification: v2 expands the existing scalability critique in Appendix B and explicitly positions its gradient observations as extending GradVaccine from multilingual BERT to larger autoregressive models. It adds references on fair resource allocation and metadata conditioning and removes the Gemma reference. The fundamental positioning around scalable optimization under low conflict remains.

T1.justification: v2 adds a tightness construction for the descent bound at zero conflict/alignment in Theorem H.4 and a static-uniform-SGD complexity comparison in Appendix H.3. It also revises stochastic conditioning and convergence reasoning and changes the main theorem's step-size and iteration expressions. These extend the formal content beyond v1's existing proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for PiKE's advantage and practicality: FAMO/ADO comparisons address missing adaptive competitors, component and estimation ablations test design choices, and measured 1.2–2.4% overhead substantiates the efficiency claim. These resolve important evidentiary gaps in v1. Formal analysis and implementation reporting also expand. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and Theorems 3.5 and H.5 disagree on the iteration bound, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial empirical improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PiKE research, with matching algorithms and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions to be distinguished from renaming and relocation.

arxiv_record.abstract: Scaling laws are typically fit using a family of models with a narrow range of frozen hyperparameter choices. In this work we study scaling laws using multiple architectural shapes and hyperparameter choices, highlighting their impact on resulting prescriptions. As a primary artifact of our research, we release the Gemstones: an open-source scaling law dataset, consisting of over 4000 checkpoints from transformers with up to 2 billion parameters and diverse architectural shapes; including ablations over learning rate and cooldown. Our checkpoints enable more complex studies of scaling, such as analyzing the relationship between width and depth. By examining our model suite, we find that the prescriptions of scaling laws can be highly sensitive to the experimental design process and the specific model checkpoints used during fitting.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds optimal architectural prescriptions and the efficiency of overtraining. v2 replaces these headline contributions with evidence that deeper models improve loss and benchmark performance per FLOP while wider models train faster under its parallelism setup. The abstract also drops the claim that Gemstones is the most comprehensive open-source scaling-law dataset.

C2.justification: v2 interprets cross-dataset rank stability as supporting alternative validation distributions, attributes benchmark-fit variability to architectural diversity, and links leave-one-out robustness to convex-hull fitting. It identifies poor accuracy extrapolation and develops the distinction between compute-efficient depth and time-efficient width. The existing limitation concerning parallelism-dependent timing results is retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies Dolma 1.7, documents task-loss construction and benchmark checkpoint selection, and explains recalibrating GPU-hour analyses using measured step times on other hardware. Most architecture, optimizer, initialization, and FLOP-counting details are retained. v1's promise of a later training-code release is dropped, without establishing an actual availability change.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained Dolma evaluation, v2 evaluates FineWeb, FineWeb-Edu, and DCLM-baseline. It also adds MMLU, WinoGrande, OpenBookQA, ARC-Easy/Challenge, CommonsenseQA, PIQA, SIQA, and HellaSwag evaluations. These substantially expand task and validation-distribution coverage.

E2.justification: Kaplan and Chinchilla remain the central scaling-law comparators. v2 drops the configuration-level comparisons against Gemma, Llama, and Qwen2 models accompanying v1's shape prescriptions in Figure 5 and Appendix D. Selected Qwen2.5 and Llama validation-loss references remain in the retained overtraining analysis.

E3.justification: v2 introduces benchmark evaluation at 10B-token intervals, length-normalized accuracy comparisons, held-out 2B-model extrapolation using a 1.8B cutoff, and validation-loss relative error measured over 250B–350B tokens. Leave-one-model-out fitting adds another evaluation design. The reported learning-rate validation budget also changes from 2B tokens to 1,000 steps totaling 4.2B tokens; this does not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of validation-distribution stability, larger-model extrapolation, and sensitivity to omitting individual model shapes (Section 4.3 and Appendices D–E). Conversely, v1's dedicated width/depth-law ablations, including alternative functional forms and relaxed integer constraints, disappear. Existing learning-rate, cooldown, and grid-size analyses are partly retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds minimum/maximum prescription ranges across leave-one-model-out refits in Figure 13 and error bars in benchmark Figures 8 and 15. The benchmark bars' construction is not explained. Neither version reports training-seed replication or confidence intervals, so additional repeated training runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: v2 adds benchmark scores, stable model rankings across validation corpora, and contrasting error-versus-accuracy extrapolation findings. Appendix D reports validation-loss relative errors of 0.68% when fitting all checkpoints and 0.63% when withholding the largest models; these use different fitting conditions. v1's detailed optimal-width/depth prescription results are removed, while its overspending and overtraining results remain.

M1.justification: v2 removes the explicit width/depth-aware loss models and exhaustive architecture-search procedure developed in v1 Section 4.1 and Appendix D. It adds loss-to-benchmark-error and task-loss-to-accuracy predictors in Section 4.3. The transformer architecture, learning-rate scaling rule, and convex-hull fitting procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution statements, related-work narrative, and experimental organization are substantially rewritten. Architecture and learning-rate explanations move into Appendix A, while overspending and overtraining move into Appendices H–I. The appendices are extensively reorganized around the revised narrative.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, adds numerical sensitivity tables and benchmark, extrapolation, and uncertainty displays, and removes the extensive shape-prescription figure series. Several existing figures are resized or relocated, including the retained overspending and overtraining plots.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around downstream scaling through Gadre and Bhagia, depth benefits and pruning through Gemma 2, Zuo, and Gromov, and newer depth-transfer work. It also positions Gemstones against a gap associated with Pile-trained model suites. Earlier literature is largely retained, sometimes relocated.

T1.justification: The mathematical modeling scope changes: v1's four-term width/depth/parameter/token loss definition and alternative three-term law are absent from v2, which instead defines exponential benchmark-error and sigmoidal accuracy mappings in Equations (2)–(3). Appendix B.1 restates previously used Chinchilla mathematics rather than supplying a new derivation. Neither version contains theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation: v1 lacked direct downstream evaluation and held-out extrapolation tests, whereas Section 4.3 and Appendices D–E test practical performance, distribution stability, extrapolation, and model-selection sensitivity. Reporting poor accuracy extrapolation also exposes an important boundary. Removing the width/depth-law specification makes the retained overtraining analysis less self-contained, and benchmark error bars remain unexplained, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger support for the paper's central empirical contributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Gemstones study and retain the same underlying model suite. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, supporting comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains original training and scaling results and adds downstream benchmarking, validation across text datasets, extrapolation tests, and leave-one-model-out analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) are a class of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that propagate information across the graph via local neighborhoods. The scheme gives rise to two key challenges: over-smoothing and over-squashing. While several Dropout-style algorithms, such as DropEdge and DropMessage, have successfully addressed over-smoothing, their impact on over-squashing remains largely unexplored. This represents a critical gap in the literature, as failure to mitigate over-squashing would make these methods unsuitable for long-range tasks -- the intended use case of deep MPNNs. In this work, we study the aforementioned algorithms, and closely related edge-dropping algorithms -- DropNode, DropAgg and DropGNN -- in the context of over-squashing. We present theoretical results showing that DropEdge-variants reduce sensitivity between distant nodes, limiting their suitability for long-range tasks. To address this, we introduce DropSens, a sensitivity-aware variant of DropEdge that explicitly controls the proportion of information lost due to edge-dropping, thereby increasing sensitivity to distant nodes despite dropping the same number of edges. Our experiments on long-range synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the predicted limitations of existing edge-dropping and feature-dropping methods. Moreover, DropSens consistently outperforms graph rewiring techniques designed to mitigate over-squashing, suggesting that simple, targeted modifications can substantially improve a model's ability to capture long-range interactions. Our conclusions highlight the need to re-evaluate and re-design existing methods for training deep GNNs, with a renewed focus on modelling long-range interactions.
arxiv_record.authors: Jasraj Singh, Keyue Jiang, Brooks Paige and Laura Toni
arxiv_record.title: Effects of Dropout on Performance in Long-range Graph Learning Tasks

C1.justification: v2 expands the central contribution from diagnosing edge-dropping failures to proposing a sensitivity-preserving remedy and claiming superiority over graph-rewiring methods. The abstract and introduction also foreground feature/message dropout and synthetic and graph-level tasks. These materially broaden the paper's claims beyond v1's diagnostic focus.

C2.justification: v2 introduces the interpretation that graph-level pooling may reduce over-squashing's impact, explicitly questions homophily as a task-range proxy, and discusses potentially loose sensitivity bounds. It adds architecture-specific limitations of DropSens supported by poor GIN results, while removing v1's GraphSAGE/ResGCN extrapolation. The local-overfitting explanation is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds hardware specifications, dataset splits, synthetic-data construction, readout details, learning-rate scheduling, DropSens parameter searches and a Python implementation. Table 9 records selected configurations. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's explicit failed-GAT-run exclusion thresholds are no longer documented.

E1.justification: v2 adds SyntheticZINC regression, PubMed and Actor node classification, and graph classification on Mutag, Proteins, Enzymes, Reddit-Binary, IMDb-Binary and Collab. Proteins appeared in v1 only in sensitivity simulations. The additional datasets surveyed in Appendix A.2 are not all experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: SkipNode, evaluated in v1 Table 2, disappears from v2's comparisons. v2 adds DropSens comparisons against fully adjacent layers, DIGL, SDRF, FoSR, GTR and undirected variants (Tables 2 and 8). Table 2 explicitly imports comparator scores from prior papers rather than reporting new baseline runs.

E3.justification: The primary evaluation shifts from correlations across dropping probabilities to comparisons of selected dropout configurations against NoDrop. Reported real-world training changes from learning rate 0.003 and weight decay 0.0005 to 0.001 and no weight decay. New protocols include 11-layer SyntheticZINC regression with MAE and a two-parameter DropSens search.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled information-mixing experiments, direct Monte Carlo influence comparisons in nonlinear GCNs, and an exact-versus-approximate DropSens probability analysis. Existing propagation-matrix analyses switch from Proteins to Cora. The underfitting investigation survives in Appendix F.3, but v1's ResGCN influence study and homophilic probability-sweep panels are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports five runs per configuration and probability–accuracy correlations. v2 reports 20 runs for configuration selection and 30 additional runs for final 50-sample comparisons, adding one-sided t-tests, normality checks, power calculations and Hedges' g. Appendix F also adds error bars, although their meaning is not specified in the captions.

E6.justification: v1's correlation table is replaced by accuracy differences, synthetic MAEs, effect sizes and rewiring-comparison results. For example, v2 Table 2 reports DropSens at 53.01% versus SDRF plus Undirected at 44.46% on Chameleon, but 22.38% versus SDRF at 28.42% on Actor. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: v1 analyzes existing dropping methods without proposing a replacement. v2 introduces DropSens: incoming-edge dropping probabilities depend on the receiving node's degree and a prescribed fraction of preserved expected message weight, with probability clipping and an approximate solution (Section 4; Appendix E.3).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Nonlinear theory and several experimental discussions move into reorganized appendices, while DropSens and the expanded evaluation become central sections. An appendix contents page and separate experimental-analysis sections considerably change navigation and narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Figure 1, adds synthetic-performance and DropSens plots, introduces several comparison and configuration tables, and replaces the correlation display with significance-colored accuracy tables. Probability-sweep figures are revised with error bars and fewer panels; the ResGCN figure disappears. The document also adopts a different title, heading and table layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial review of homophily bias in previous evaluations, including a dataset inventory and exceptions (Appendix A.2). New citations support expanded benchmarking, architectures, implementation and statistics. DropSens also changes the research positioning from critique of existing methods to an alternative compared with established rewiring techniques.

T1.justification: The central sensitivity lemmas, theorem, proofs and nonlinear extensions are retained, with substantial relocation. v2 adds the DropSens retained-information equation and its approximate solution, corrects the linear Monte Carlo propagation expression, and changes Appendix D.2's erroneous equality to an upper-bound inequality.

improvement.justification: v1 relies chiefly on homophily proxies and correlations across dropping probabilities. v2 substantially strengthens the central evidence through controlled SyntheticZINC mixing experiments, selected-configuration comparisons against NoDrop, statistical analysis and a documented constructive method. The gain is tempered by overstated DropSens superiority: Table 2 contains clear losses and Table 8 shows poor GIN performance, contradicting the abstract's consistency claim. Nevertheless, the stronger experimental design and reproducibility address important weaknesses of v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on random dropping and over-squashing, with matching core sensitivity results. All 24 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original sensitivity simulations, synthetic regression and real-world classification experiments, and evaluations of the newly proposed DropSens method.

before.justification: v1 reports original node-classification experiments, sensitivity simulations, and a ResGCN influence analysis in the main text and appendices.
