arxiv_record.abstract:
The canonical approach in generative modeling is to split model fitting into two blocks: define first how to sample noise (e.g. Gaussian) and choose next what to do with it (e.g. using a single map or flows). We explore in this work an alternative route that ties sampling and mapping. We find inspiration in moment measures, a result that states that for any measure $ho$, there exists a unique convex potential $u$ such that $ho=
abla u \sharp e^{-u}$. While this does seem to tie effectively sampling (from log-concave distribution $e^{-u}$) and action (pushing particles through $
abla u$), we observe on simple examples (e.g., Gaussians or 1D distributions) that this choice is ill-suited for practical tasks. We study an alternative factorization, where $ho$ is factorized as $
abla w^*\sharp e^{-w}$, where $w^*$ is the convex conjugate of a convex potential $w$. We call this approach conjugate moment measures, and show far more intuitive results on these examples. Because $
abla w^*$ is the Monge map between the log-concave distribution $e^{-w}$ and $ho$, we rely on optimal transport solvers to propose an algorithm to recover $w$ from samples of $ho$, and parameterize $w$ as an input-convex neural network. We also address the common sampling scenario in which the density of $ho$ is known only up to a normalizing constant, and propose an algorithm to learn $w$ in this setting.
arxiv_record.authors: Nina Vesseron, Louis B\'ethune, Marco Cuturi
arxiv_record.title: Sample and Map from a Single Convex Potential: Generation using Conjugate Moment Measures

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion expand the methodological contribution from learning a conjugate potential using samples to learning it using either samples or an unnormalized target density. The central factorization claim and claimed first ICNN generation of MNIST remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: The interpretation that conjugate Gibbs factors better match target distributions remains. v2 adds explanations of ELU/Hessian difficulties, the LMC efficiency–quality tradeoff, and why ordinary moment-potential regression is harder. It removes v1's concluding qualification that ICNN training difficulties currently hinder performance.

D1.justification: v2 adds code listings for the previously described 1D algorithms (Appendix B.3), explicit benchmark energy formulas, quadratic-input architecture details, and CMFMA hyperparameter tables, including Softplus with beta 10. It documents Cartoon preprocessing with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.2. Reported hardware changes from V100 or A100-40GB to V100-32GB.

E1.justification: The original Gaussian mixtures, five synthetic 2D distributions and MNIST remain. v2 adds the Cartoon dataset, three energy-defined 2D target distributions, learning with energy-function access, and reconstruction of half-masked MNIST and Cartoon images. These substantially extend the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Gaussian-to-data generative ICNN baselines for the retained 2D datasets and MNIST, as well as Cartoon (Figures 13, 5 and 15). Amos (2023) supplied a solver in v1 but was not evaluated there as this generative comparator. The original standard moment-measure comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 revise reported training budgets: 2D gradient steps increase from 700,000 to 1,000,000, MNIST steps decrease from 100,000 to 50,000, and generation-time LMC steps increase from 6,000 to 10,000. Diag-Checkerboard batches change from 4,096 to 1,024. v2 also introduces architecture-matched baseline comparisons, Sinkhorn evaluation with 2,048-sample batches, and half-image masking protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds brief qualitative sensitivity and failure analyses: reducing training LMC steps to 50 degrades performance, and ELU activations cause discontinuities in learned 1D CMFMA potentials, motivating Softplus. These are limited supplementary observations rather than a substantial ablation or robustness study.

E5.justification: v1 provides no seed-based variability assessment. v2 introduces evaluations across 100 random seeds and boxplots of Sinkhorn divergences for all five 2D datasets (Appendix D.1, Figure 13). This establishes a new variability-reporting practice. The seeds vary generated and reference samples; 100 independent training runs are not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds quantitative Sinkhorn comparisons, CMFMA energy-fitting and pushforward results, Cartoon generation, and MNIST/Cartoon reconstruction outcomes. Figure 13 shows broadly overlapping ICNN and CMFGen distributions with modest differences. The original 1D findings remain, including v1 Figure 5 as v2 Figure 8. Revised settings prevent interpreting refreshed generation examples as controlled before-and-after performance gains.

M1.justification: The original fixed-point learner is retained as CMFGen. v2 adds CMFMA, which learns from an unnormalized density through a Monge–Ampère regression objective involving the Hessian determinant (Section 4.3). It also replaces fixed LMC step sizes with a Hessian-adaptive rule and introduces learned-density optimization for inpainting.

P1.justification: Existing material is substantially reorganized: Background is condensed, the main proof sketch moves to Appendix A, the univariate transport recipe moves from experiments into methods, and the fixed-point method is named CMFGen. The methods and experimental narratives are rewritten, and the appendix is reorganized into separate theory, sample-based, energy-based, evaluation and implementation sections.

P2.justification: The 2D display changes from two rows with overlaid targets and potentials to three separate rows. MNIST receives a baseline-comparison panel, while Cartoon uses the earlier schematic format. New energy plots, Sinkhorn boxplots and reconstruction grids substantially expand the visual evidence. Hyperparameter tables separate shared solver settings and add CMFMA configurations; the original 1D convergence display is retained.

R1.justification: The main moment-measure and optimal-transport positioning remains. v2 adds Dalalyan (2016), Ramdas et al. (2017), Rezende and Mohamed (2015), and Royer et al. (2018), supporting sampling, evaluation, the normalizing-flow analogy and Cartoon data. It also explicitly positions its ordinary moment-measure solver as addressing a previously unavailable method.

T1.justification: v2 adds the Monge–Ampère density and energy characterizations in equations (8)–(9), providing the mathematical basis for energy-based learning, and an additional variational proof of Proposition 1. It corrects the 1D transport formula from B to its gradient and removes the earlier entropy–OT variational formulation. The central existence theorem and Schauder proof are retained; v1 Theorem 2 becomes Appendix A's Lemma 1.

improvement.justification: v1's practical generative claims relied mainly on qualitative demonstrations. v2 materially strengthens their assessment through architecture-matched ICNN comparisons and repeated sample-level quantitative evaluations (Appendix D.1), while adding a tested energy-based method and substantial reproducibility details. Image evaluation remains qualitative, the earlier general training caveat is removed, and Section 4.3 contains a log-determinant sign inconsistency with equation (9). These drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support, methodological utility and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same conjugate moment measure framework. All 16 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including proofs, experimental appendices, figures and tables, support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B–E report original sample-based and energy-based experiments, quantitative ICNN comparisons, Cartoon generation and image reconstruction.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original experiments on univariate Gaussian mixtures, five synthetic 2D distributions and MNIST generation.

arxiv_record.abstract: The growing use of generative models in daily life calls for efficient mechanisms to control their generation, to e.g., produce safe content or provide users with tools to explore style changes. Ideally, such mechanisms should require low volume of unpaired data (i.e., without explicit preference), and should be cheap, both at train and inference time, while preserving output quality. Recent research has shown that such mechanisms can be obtained by intervening exclusively on model activations, with the goal of correcting distributional differences between activations seen when using prompts from a source vs. a target set (e.g., toxic and non-toxic sentences). While cheap, these fast methods are inherently crude: their maps are tuned locally, not accounting for their impact on downstream layers, resulting in interventions that cause unintended shifts when used out-of-sample. We propose in this work linear end-to-end activation steering (LinEAS), an approach trained with a global loss that accounts simultaneously for all layer-wise distributional shifts. In addition to being more robust, the loss used to train LinEAS can be regularized with sparsifying norms, which can automatically carry out neuron selection. LinEAS only requires a handful of unpaired samples to be effective, and beats similar baselines on toxicity mitigation in language models, becoming competitive with oracle-dependent methods that have access to strong supervision. LinEAS is modality-agnostic and we empirically find that it outperforms existing activation steering methods at mitigating and including new concepts at the output of single-step text-to-image generation models.
arxiv_record.authors: Pau Rodriguez, Michal Klein, Eleonora Gualdoni, Valentino Maiorca, Arno Blaas, Luca Zappella, Marco Cuturi, Xavier Suau
arxiv_record.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss

C1.justification: The central contribution remains joint distributional learning of sparse affine interventions. V3 expands the headline image claim to concept mitigation and induction, narrows the advertised support reduction from 100–1000 times to 100 times, and deemphasizes compositionality as a headline contribution while retaining its results.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive qualifications about evaluating paired-data methods on unpaired toxicity data and applying interventions indiscriminately to all tokens. arxiv_record.abstract: Expensive communication cost is a common performance bottleneck in Federated Learning (FL), which makes it less appealing in real-world applications. Many communication-efficient FL methods focus on discarding a part of model updates mostly based on gradient magnitude. In this study, we find that recycling previous updates, rather than simply dropping them, more effectively reduces the communication cost while maintaining FL performance. We propose FedLUAR, a Layer-wise Update Aggregation with Recycling scheme for communication-efficient FL. We first define a useful metric that quantifies the extent to which the aggregated gradients influences the model parameter values in each layer. FedLUAR selects a few layers based on the metric and recycles their previous updates on the server side. Our extensive empirical study demonstrates that the update recycling scheme significantly reduces the communication cost while maintaining model accuracy. For example, our method achieves nearly the same AG News accuracy as FedAvg, while reducing the communication cost to just 17%.
arxiv_record.authors: Jisoo Kim, Sungmin Kang, Sunwoo Lee
arxiv_record.title: Layer-wise Update Aggregation with Recycling for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting have led to rapid improvements in efficient scene reconstruction from sparse views. However, most existing approaches construct Gaussian primitives directly aligned with the pixels in one or more of the input images. This leads to redundancies in the representation when input views overlap and constrains the position of the primitives to lie along the input rays without full flexibility in 3D space. Moreover, these pixel-aligned approaches do not naturally generalize to dynamic scenes, where effectively leveraging temporal information requires resolving both redundant and newly appearing content across frames. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel Fuse-and-Refine module that enhances existing feed-forward models by merging and refining the primitives in a canonical 3D space. At the core of our method is an efficient hybrid Splat-Voxel representation: from an initial set of pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives, we aggregate local features into a coarse-to-fine voxel hierarchy, and then use a sparse voxel transformer to process these voxel features and generate refined Gaussian primitives. By fusing and refining an arbitrary number of inputs into a consistent set of primitives, our representation effectively reduces redundancy and naturally adapts to temporal frames, enabling history-aware online reconstruction of dynamic scenes. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both static and streaming scene reconstructions while running at interactive rates (15 fps with 350ms delay) on a single H100 GPU.

C1.justification: V1 presents a history-aware streaming reconstruction framework as its primary contribution. V2 redefines the central contribution as a reusable Fuse-and-Refine module for existing feed-forward Gaussian models, emphasizing redundancy reduction and flexible primitive placement, with streaming as an application. Static-only training, interactive speed, and strong static/dynamic reconstruction claims are retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations concerning pixel-aligned redundancy, constrained primitive placement, and why learned refinement improves upon heuristic fusion. It interprets the new temporal controls and explicitly limits gains when initial primitives are poor or camera baselines are large. The conclusion replaces v1's emphasis on repeated per-frame reconstruction and high-resolution scalability with these input-quality limits and persistent dynamic-region warping artifacts.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page link, component runtime details, an A100 timing comparison, and concrete retraining details for the DepthSplat extension. Most architecture, optimizer, training-budget, voxel-grid, and tracking parameters were already supplied in v1's appendix. The PDFs alone do not establish whether the new project link provides downloadable code.

E1.justification: Both versions use RealEstate10K, DL3DV, Neural3DVideo, and LongVolumetricVideo for the same reconstruction tasks. V2 adds input-availability scenarios involving train/test camera-count mismatches: four-view training with two-, eight-, and sixteen-view inference, and two-view training with four-view inference. No new dataset or domain is introduced.

E2.justification: V2 adds TranSplat, HiSplat, OmniScene, and DepthSplat to the RealEstate10K comparison, plus Gaussian Graph Network and a retrained DepthSplat comparison in Tables 13–14. Table 5 adds GS-LRM with warping and with warping plus concatenation/dropout. The DL3DV 'Non-learning Fusion' baseline matches v1's 'Naive Baseline (Mean GS)' rather than introducing another comparator.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation designs for varying inference-view counts, joint versus staged training, and simple temporal-fusion controls. The DepthSplat experiment uses 128×192 images, 1,000 training scenes, ten test scenes, and two-view training/four-view testing. Joint DL3DV training uses the existing 200K total budget instead of the 100K-plus-100K staged schedule; the original benchmark protocols and metrics otherwise remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test camera-count robustness, whether warping or simple fusion suffices, joint versus staged training, component runtime costs, and portability to DepthSplat (Tables 3, 5, 6, 8, and 14). These substantially extend the original spatial and temporal component ablations. The earlier convergence plot is retained, not newly generated evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The retained training curves contain no uncertainty bands.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial numerical evidence for new comparators, view-count robustness, fusion controls, training schemes, and runtime. Its DL3DV headline PSNR changes from 30.34 to 30.61 through the newly reported joint-training variant; the original two-stage result remains in Table 8. The new DepthSplat comparison reports 16.57 versus 17.66 PSNR. Most retained streaming results are unchanged, but 3DGS's LongVolumetricVideo PSNR changes from 18.588 to 18.56.

M1.justification: V2 adds joint training from scratch as an alternative to staged training and integrates the refinement module with DepthSplat. The core voxel hierarchy, transformer, warping, and error-aware fusion remain unchanged. Explicitly concatenating Gaussian attributes in the fusion equation clarifies information already documented in v1 Appendix A.2.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around fusion and refinement. V2 introduces reconstruction preliminaries, separates the general module from its streaming application, moves detailed streaming mathematics into the appendix, and adds a societal-impact section.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from two-column to single-column formatting, adds a dedicated Fuse-and-Refine diagram and several experimental tables, and restructures existing tables. The original streaming overview, teaser, and close-ups move to the appendix; earlier qualitative grids and the convergence plot remain. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against learned Gaussian graph, voxel, and point-based methods, including Gaussian Graph Network, SCube, EvolSplat, and Splatformer. It also discusses point-voxel processing networks and heuristic Gaussian merging, while shortening earlier dynamic-scene and animation coverage. This changes the research context beyond citation updates.

T1.justification: The interpolation kernel, triangulation derivation, residual decoding, linear-blend skinning, losses, and flicker definition are retained, sometimes relocated. V2's standard 3DGS rendering preliminaries explain the existing component rather than changing its mathematics. No new theorem, proof, or substantive formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification for learned refinement. The new temporal-fusion controls, camera-count tests, Gaussian Graph Network comparison, and DepthSplat integration address v1's limited evidence about alternative fusion strategies and applicability beyond its original configuration. Runtime breakdowns and more specific failure conditions also make the claims easier to assess. arxiv_record.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) technologies, synthetic images have become increasingly prevalent in everyday life, posing new challenges for authenticity assessment and detection. Despite the effectiveness of existing methods in evaluating image authenticity and locating forgeries, these approaches often lack human interpretability and do not fully address the growing complexity of synthetic data. To tackle these challenges, we introduce FakeVLM, a specialized large multimodal model designed for both general synthetic image and DeepFake detection tasks. FakeVLM not only excels in distinguishing real from fake images but also provides clear, natural language explanations for image artifacts, enhancing interpretability. Additionally, we present FakeClue, a comprehensive dataset containing over 100,000 images across seven categories, annotated with fine-grained artifact clues in natural language. FakeVLM demonstrates performance comparable to expert models while eliminating the need for additional classifiers, making it a robust solution for synthetic data detection. Extensive evaluations across multiple datasets confirm the superiority of FakeVLM in both authenticity classification and artifact explanation tasks, setting a new benchmark for synthetic image detection. The code, model weights, and dataset can be found here: https://github.com/opendatalab/FakeVLM.

C2.justification: V2 introduces substantive limitations absent from v1: inherited annotation-model biases, missed fine-grained artifacts, and reduced sensitivity to high-fidelity synthetic images (Appendix F). It adds interpretations concerning alignment with human artifact perception and category-dependent performance, plus discussion of deployment errors and computational-access limitations in Appendix G.

D1.justification: Appendix H supplies seven real/fake prompt pairs and aggregation instructions previously unavailable in v1. V2 also explicitly identifies Qwen2-VL as aggregator, specifies the GPT-4o snapshot, and marks FakeClue-trained expert baselines. The abstract changes a promised code/data release to reported availability of code, model weights, and data; external availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The named benchmarks and detection/explanation tasks are retained. Appendix C adds testing on compressed, resized, noisy, and otherwise transformed FakeClue images, extending input conditions. Appendix D disaggregates existing LOKI coverage rather than establishing a newly added domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds CNNSpot, FreqNet, Fatformer, UnivFD, AIDE, and NPR to the FakeClue/LOKI comparison; CNNSpot and UnivFD previously appeared only in the DMimage comparison. New Table 8 substantially broadens LOKI comparators, including MiniCPM-V-2.6, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and Gemini-1.5-Pro.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 revises the stated learning rate from 2e-4 to 2e-5, retaining two epochs, eight A100 GPUs, and batch size 32 per GPU. Appendix C introduces specified distortion settings, including JPEG qualities, resizing scales, and Gaussian-noise variances. The learning-rate revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices C–D add systematic robustness testing across twelve perturbation conditions and category-level generalization analysis. Appendix B supplies benchmark-separated training-strategy results. The existing explanatory-text ablation is retained; the dedicated DD-VQA explanation examples in v1 Figure 6 are removed, while the real-image case figure gains another example.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for its experiments. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds expert-baseline, perturbation, and category results in Tables 2 and 7–8, including 89.5% FakeClue accuracy under Blur3 versus 98.6% on original images. arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advancements in LLM pretraining have featured ever-expanding context windows to process longer sequences. However, our pilot study reveals that models pretrained with shorter context windows consistently outperform their long-context counterparts under a fixed token budget. This finding motivates us to explore an optimal context window scheduling strategy to better balance long-context capability with pretraining efficiency. To this end, we propose SkyLadder, a simple yet effective approach that implements a short-to-long context window transition. SkyLadder preserves strong standard benchmark performance, while matching or exceeding baseline results on long context tasks. Through extensive experiments, we pre-train 1B-parameter models (up to 32K context) and 3B-parameter models (8K context) on 100B tokens, demonstrating that SkyLadder yields consistent gains of up to 3.7% on common benchmarks, while achieving up to 22% faster training speeds compared to baselines. The code is at https://github.com/sail-sg/SkyLadder.
arxiv_record.authors: Tongyao Zhu, Qian Liu, Haonan Wang, Shiqi Chen, Xiangming Gu, Tianyu Pang, Min-Yen Kan
arxiv_record.title: SkyLadder: Better and Faster Pretraining via Context Window Scheduling

The headline claims of gains up to 3.7% and training-time savings up to 22% remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds an optimization-stability explanation connecting shorter contexts to smaller attention logits, smoother losses, and more controlled gradients. It newly attributes RULER differences to synthetic-benchmark variability and discusses compatibility with alternative attention architectures. Appendix A.1 explicitly identifies computational scaling limits and the absence of theoretical analysis; Section 4.3 also narrows improvement over IntraDoc from all benchmarks to many.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial resource and data documentation: A.9 specifies A100/H100 hardware and training costs, including approximately 200 hours on eight A100s for a 1B, 8K-context run; A.10 supplies corpus and benchmark length statistics; A.11 supplies asset licenses. It also clarifies baseline use of Flash Attention 2. The code link, core configuration tables, and implementation pseudocode already existed in v1.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix A.7.3 substantially expands evaluation coverage with TOEFL and QuALITY reading comprehension, PopQA within retrieval-augmented QA, and many-shot classification on DBpedia, AGNews, Amazon, Yelp, and SST2. Existing training corpora and earlier evaluation tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Random, IntraDoc, BM25, Dataset Decomposition with one or eight cycles, continual pretraining, and alternative schedules. New architecture and task experiments compare Random with SkyLadder rather than introducing another competing algorithm. The expanded discussion of Li and Jin does not establish additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Gemma3-like 120M/360M and Qwen2.5-0.5B experimental configurations, stability measurements over the first 30K training steps, and FLOPs evaluation. Its new McNemar tests use full benchmark test sets, explicitly distinguished from OLMES's sampled evaluations. These are additions to the experimental design; the original training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's attention-sink and entropy analysis, v2 Section 4.6 investigates maximum attention logits, loss fluctuations, and gradient norms across context lengths. Appendix A.7.4 adds tests of applicability to hybrid attention and Qwen-style architectures, while A.10 analyzes corpus and benchmark length distributions. Existing scheduling ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates and a heuristic loss-difference threshold. v2 introduces paired McNemar significance tests for the main benchmark comparisons, with significance markers in Table 1 and procedures in A.7.3. Its checklist newly states that pretraining runs were not repeated because of cost; this is disclosure, not an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Most existing benchmark scores are retained, but Table 7 changes continual pretraining's long-context score from 2.7 to 10.0 under the same reported schedule. New results include Random versus SkyLadder RAG averages of 30.3 versus 35.5 and many-shot classification averages of 73.9 versus 76.5. v2 also adds architecture, stability, dataset-statistics, and FLOPs results, including reported compute reductions of 14.7% and 26.3%.

M1.justification: The blockwise causal mask, linear window-expansion rule, integration with intra-document masking, and Flash Attention pseudocode retain the same procedure. Hybrid-attention and Qwen-style models are additional experimental configurations; no new SkyLadder algorithmic component is specified.

P1.justification: The main five-section narrative remains recognizable. v2 tightens wording, moves coding experiments into the results subsection, and consolidates efficiency, attention analysis, and related-method comparison under Analysis and Discussion. It expands appendix organization and adds a conference checklist, but largely preserves the existing exposition rather than rewriting the paper wholesale.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training-stability plot and tables for stability, new tasks, architectures, and dataset statistics. It moves long-context columns from Table 1 into Table 2, adds significance markers and a FLOPs column, and revises captions. The NeurIPS formatting also substantially changes typography, equation placement, and figure/table positioning.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Gemma3, Kimi K2, and additional reading-comprehension benchmarks, and replaces the unrelated Zhang 2020 citation for SlimPajama with its actual dataset reference. Appendix A.8 expands comparisons with sequence-length warmup and GrowLength, while retaining the original positioning around simultaneous efficiency and performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 A.6 adds an explicit mathematical definition of per-token context size as the number of accessible, unmasked tokens and derives its uniform distribution under Random causal masking. v1 displayed this distribution without that formalization. The scheduling mathematics is unchanged, and neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs of effectiveness.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for preserving long-context capability: v1 relied mainly on MDQA/RULER, whereas v2 adds broader 3B reading-comprehension, retrieval-augmented QA, and many-shot evaluations. Architecture tests and stability diagnostics address generality and mechanism, while significance testing and resource disclosures improve assessability. These gains address important validation gaps rather than merely increasing reported performance. Statistical assurance remains incomplete because training runs are not repeated and the McNemar significance threshold is unspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SkyLadder and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched despite reorganization, renumbering, and additional material in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds long-context evaluations, architecture comparisons, training-stability measurements, and dataset analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Instruction tuning improves the ability of large language models (LLMs) to follow diverse human instructions, but achieving strong performance on specific target tasks remains challenging. A critical bottleneck is selecting the most relevant data to maximize task-specific performance. Existing data selection approaches include unstable influence-based methods and more stable distribution alignment methods, the latter of which critically rely on the underlying sample representation. In practice, most distribution alignment methods, from shallow features (e.g., BM25) to neural embeddings (e.g., BGE, LLM2Vec), may fail to capture how the model internally processes samples. To bridge this gap, we adopt a model-centric strategy in which each sample is represented by its neuronal activation pattern in the model, directly reflecting internal computation. However, directly using raw neuron activations leads to spurious similarity between unrelated samples due to neuron polysemanticity, where a single neuron may respond to multiple, unrelated concepts. To address this, we employ sparse autoencoders to disentangle polysemantic activations into sparse, monosemantic representations, and introduce a dedicated similarity metric for this space to better identify task-relevant data. Comprehensive experiments across multiple instruction datasets, models, tasks, and selection ratios show that our approach consistently outperforms existing data selection baselines in both stability and task-specific performance.

To address this, we employ sparse autoencoders to disentangle polysemantic activations into sparse, monosemantic representations, and introduce a dedicated similarity metric for this space to better identify task-relevant data. Comprehensive experiments across multiple instruction datasets, models, tasks, and selection ratios show that our approach consistently outperforms existing data selection baselines in both stability and task-specific performance.

arxiv_record.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful representation for real-time, high-performance rendering, enabling a wide range of applications. However, representing 3D scenes with numerous explicit Gaussian primitives imposes significant storage and memory overhead. Recent studies have shown that high-quality rendering can be achieved with a substantially reduced number of Gaussians when represented with high-precision attributes. Nevertheless, existing 3DGS compression methods still rely on a relatively large number of Gaussians, focusing primarily on attribute compression. This is because a smaller set of Gaussians becomes increasingly sensitive to lossy attribute compression, leading to severe quality degradation. Since the number of Gaussians is directly tied to computational costs, it is essential to reduce the number of Gaussians effectively rather than only optimizing storage. In this paper, we propose Optimized Minimal Gaussians representation (OMG), which significantly reduces storage while using a minimal number of primitives. First, we determine the distinct Gaussian from the near ones, minimizing redundancy without sacrificing quality. Second, we propose a compact and precise attribute representation that efficiently captures both continuity and irregularity among primitives. Additionally, we propose a sub-vector quantization technique for improved irregularity representation, maintaining fast training with a negligible codebook size. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OMG reduces storage requirements by nearly 50% compared to the previous state-of-the-art and enables 600+ FPS rendering while maintaining high rendering quality. Our source code is available at https://maincold2.github.io/omg/.
arxiv_record.authors: Joo Chan Lee, Jong Hwan Ko, Eunbyung Park

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: compact sparse-Gaussian representation, SVQ and local-distinctiveness pruning. The headline claims of approximately 49–50% storage reduction, approximately 4.1 MB on Mip-NeRF 360 and 600+ FPS are unchanged.

C2.justification: New Section 5 explicitly bounds OMG by its underlying densification method, explains failures on large Zip-NeRF scenes and discusses integration with MCMC. New appendix discussion interprets sparse-compressor failures, Morton-order scalability and deployment on weaker GPUs. These substantially expand applicability and mechanism discussion. However, Appendix B's claimed Morton speedup contradicts the timing assignments in Table 9.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies lambda=2 and documents the Zip-NeRF/MCMC training budget, densification interval, feature-introduction schedule and larger SVQ codebooks. Appendix A also explains how the sparse comparator combinations were trained. Most original implementation details and the project URL are retained; the checklist additionally states that supplementary code is provided.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on the larger, more complex scenes of the Zip-NeRF dataset (Table 7 and Section 5), extending coverage to a regime where the original baseline densification becomes inadequate. All three original datasets and their per-scene coverage are retained.

E2.justification: The comparison set expands substantially: Mini-Splatting joins Tables 1–3, LocoGS-L is added to the Tanks&Temples and Deep Blending comparison, and RVQ joins the quantization comparison. New experiments evaluate 3DGS-MCMC, Zip-NeRF and SMERF, plus Mini-Splatting combinations with Compact-3DGS and LocoGS. These are reported comparisons, not citation-only additions.

E3.justification: New protocols include MCMC evaluations at 500K/1M Gaussians, Zip-NeRF training with 3M Gaussians for 150K iterations, COLMAP-initialized LocoGS comparisons and GTX 1080 Ti timing. The VQ comparison changes appearance codebooks from 2^13 to 2^14 entries, expands to three OMG sizes and reports codebook-initialization time instead of total training time. The original OMG training schedule remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds LD scoring without attribute compression (Figure 5), removal of SVQ (Table 4), RVQ and expanded VQ comparisons (Table 5), and transfer to MCMC (Table 6). Appendices A–C additionally test competing compressors with sparse Gaussians, Morton-order approximation against KNN, and rendering on weaker hardware. These substantially extend the questions tested beyond v1's ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new checklist explicitly acknowledges the absence of error bars but introduces no statistical estimation or uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Original OMG benchmark and per-scene values are retained, but substantial new results are added. Examples include MCMC+OMG achieving 26.69 PSNR at 29.0 MB on Zip-NeRF and OMG-XS rendering at 106 FPS versus LocoGS's 73 FPS on GTX 1080 Ti. Table 5 replaces the VQ-XS result of 26.97 PSNR/3.99 MB with 27.06/4.21 under revised codebooks, not a same-setting gain. Figure 4 also uses different views and results.

M1.justification: The architecture, SVQ procedure and training objective remain intact. Equation (8) changes the stated local-distinctiveness score normalization from 1/K, the neighbor count, to 1/D, the feature dimension. This is a limited scoring-formula revision, without evidence of different pruning decisions. The generalized feature notation still uses D=3 in the documented original setup.

P1.justification: Most introductory, methodological and concluding prose is retained. Local wording is refined, the ablation discussion is reordered and rewritten in places, and a limitations section, acknowledgements and NeurIPS checklist are added. The appendix is reorganized into lettered sections; this is not a wholesale rewrite of the scientific narrative.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column NeurIPS format. Figure 4 replaces its views and OMG-M/stump panels with a LocoGS comparison and enlarged crops; Figure 5 is new. Tables gain comparisons, Table 5 is substantially restructured, and the retained post-processing table is transposed. Existing appendix results are relocated and reformatted rather than removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Zip-NeRF, SMERF and 3DGS-MCMC, connecting OMG to large-scene rendering and an alternative densification framework. The existing related-work taxonomy and positioning against Gaussian compression approaches remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (8) revises the mathematical definition of the LD score by replacing normalization by K with normalization by D. The remaining rendering and quantization equations are retained. Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs, and none are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central design choices through direct RVQ comparisons, uncompressed LD controls and sparse-compressor experiments. MCMC and Zip-NeRF evaluations, paired with explicit baseline-dependent limitations, address important gaps in v1's evidence about applicability. The new Morton/KNN timing table remains internally inconsistent: it assigns 4100 ms to OMG and 28 ms to KNN while the text claims Morton is 146 times faster. This weakens that specific conclusion, but the broader validation and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMG research, with matching architecture, core experiments and per-scene results. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison despite substantial formatting changes.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds quantization comparisons, MCMC integration, Zip-NeRF evaluation, sparse-baseline experiments, neighbor-search comparisons and lower-end GPU measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original OMG rendering, compression, timing and ablation results on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks&Temples and Deep Blending, including per-scene and compression analyses in the appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract: Model customization necessitates high-quality and diverse datasets, but acquiring such data remains time-consuming and labor-intensive. Despite the great potential of large language models (LLMs) for data synthesis, current approaches are constrained by limited seed data, model biases, and low-variation prompts, resulting in limited diversity and biased distributions with the increase of data scales. To tackle this challenge, we introduce TREESYNTH, a tree-guided subspace-based data synthesis approach inspired by decision trees. It constructs a spatial partitioning tree to recursively divide a task-specific full data space (i.e., root node) into numerous atomic subspaces (i.e., leaf nodes) with mutually exclusive and exhaustive attributes to ensure both distinctiveness and comprehensiveness before synthesizing samples within each atomic subspace. This globally dividing-and-synthesizing method finally collects subspace samples into a comprehensive dataset, effectively circumventing repetition and space collapse to ensure the diversity of large-scale data synthesis. Furthermore, the spatial partitioning tree enables sample allocation into atomic subspaces, allowing the rebalancing of existing datasets for more balanced and comprehensive distributions. Empirically, extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks consistently demonstrate the superior data diversity, model performance, and robust scalability of TREESYNTH compared to both human-crafted datasets and peer data synthesis methods, with an average performance gain reaching 10%. Besides, the consistent improvements of TREESYNTH-balanced datasets highlight its efficacious application to redistribute existing datasets for more comprehensive coverage and the induced performance enhancement. The code is available at https://github.com/cpa2001/TreeSynth.

arxiv_record.abstract: Offline multi-objective optimization aims to identify Pareto-optimal solutions given a dataset of designs and their objective values. In this work, we propose a preference-guided diffusion model that generates Pareto-optimal designs by leveraging a classifier-based guidance mechanism. Our guidance classifier is a preference model trained to predict the probability that one design dominates another, directing the diffusion model toward optimal regions of the design space. Crucially, this preference model generalizes beyond the training distribution, enabling the discovery of Pareto-optimal solutions outside the observed dataset. We introduce a novel diversity-aware preference guidance, augmenting Pareto dominance preference with diversity criteria. This ensures that generated solutions are optimal and well-distributed across the objective space, a capability absent in prior generative methods for offline multi-objective optimization. We evaluate our approach on various continuous offline multi-objective optimization tasks and find that it consistently outperforms other inverse/generative approaches while remaining competitive with forward/ surrogate-based optimization methods. Our results highlight the effectiveness of classifier-guided diffusion models in generating diverse and high-quality solutions that approximate the Pareto front well.
arxiv_record.authors: Yashas Annadani, Syrine Belakaria, Stefano Ermon, Stefan Bauer, Barbara E Engelhardt
arxiv_record.title: Preference-Guided Diffusion for Multi-Objective Offline Optimization

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent efforts in neural compression have focused on the rate-distortion-perception (RDP) tradeoff, where the perception constraint ensures the source and reconstruction distributions are close in terms of a statistical divergence. Theoretical work on RDP describes properties of RDP-optimal compressors without providing constructive and low complexity solutions. While classical rate distortion theory shows that optimal compressors should efficiently pack space, RDP theory additionally shows that infinite randomness shared between the encoder and decoder may be necessary for RDP optimality. In this paper, we propose neural compressors that are low complexity and benefit from high packing efficiency through lattice coding and shared randomness through shared dithering over the lattice cells. For two important settings, namely infinite shared and zero shared randomness, we analyze the RDP tradeoff achieved by our proposed neural compressors and show optimality in both cases. Experimentally, we investigate the roles that these two components of our design, lattice coding and randomness, play in the performance of neural compressors on synthetic and real-world data. We observe that performance improves with more shared randomness and better lattice packing.
arxiv_record.authors: Eric Lei, Hamed Hassani, Shirin Saeedi Bidokhti
arxiv_record.title: Optimal Neural Compressors for the Rate-Distortion-Perception Tradeoff

These changes extend beyond scientific additions and renumbering.

Appendix D introduces explicit flatness-factor conditions, achievable-region bounds in Lemma D.5, revised Wasserstein arguments, a polar-lattice construction, and an extension to perfect perception. Denser figures and the unspecified empirical choice of s remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in theoretical justification.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B and D report original Gaussian, Physics, and Speech experiments, ablations, and empirical sliced-Wasserstein estimates.

arxiv_record.abstract: Image geolocalization is a fundamental yet challenging task, aiming at inferring the geolocation on Earth where an image is taken. State-of-the-art methods employ either grid-based classification or gallery-based image-location retrieval, whose spatial generalizability significantly suffers if the spatial distribution of test images does not align with the choices of grids and galleries. Recently emerging generative approaches, while getting rid of grids and galleries, use raw geographical coordinates and suffer quality losses due to their lack of multi-scale information. To address these limitations, we propose a multi-scale latent diffusion model called LocDiff for image geolocalization. We also propose a novel SirenNet-based architecture (CS-UNet) to learn an image-based conditional backward process in the latent SHDD space by minimizing a latent KL-divergence loss. arxiv_record.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is now recognized as a key framework for communication-efficient collaborative learning. Most theoretical and empirical studies, however, rely on the assumption that clients have access to pre-collected data sets, with limited investigation into scenarios where clients continuously collect data. In many real-world applications, particularly when data is generated by physical or biological processes, client data streams are often modeled by non-stationary Markov processes. Unlike standard i.i.d. sampling, the performance of FL with Markovian data streams remains poorly understood due to the statistical dependencies between client samples over time. In this paper, we investigate whether FL can still support collaborative learning with Markovian data streams. Specifically, we analyze the performance of Minibatch SGD, Local SGD, and a variant of Local SGD with momentum. We answer affirmatively under standard assumptions and smooth non-convex client objectives: the sample complexity is proportional to the inverse of the number of clients with a communication complexity comparable to the i.i.d. scenario. However, the sample complexity for Markovian data streams remains higher than for i.i.d. sampling.
arxiv_record.authors: Tan-Khiem Huynh, Malcolm Egan, Giovanni Neglia, Jean-Marie Gorce
arxiv_record.title: Streaming Federated Learning with Markovian Data

arxiv_record.abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in various artificial intelligence problems. However, they fail to plan reliably, even when prompted with a detailed definition of the planning task. Attempts to improve their planning capabilities, such as chain-of-thought prompting, fine-tuning, and explicit "reasoning" still yield incorrect plans and usually fail to generalize to larger tasks. In this paper, we show how to use LLMs to generate correct plans, even for out-of-distribution tasks of increasing size. For a given planning domain, we ask an LLM to generate several domain-dependent heuristic functions in the form of Python code, evaluate them on a set of training tasks within a greedy best-first search, and choose the strongest one. The resulting LLM-generated heuristics solve many more unseen test tasks than state-of-the-art domain-independent heuristics for classical planning. They are even competitive with the strongest learning algorithm for domain-dependent planning. These findings are especially remarkable given that our proof-of-concept implementation is based on an unoptimized Python planner and the baselines all build upon highly optimized C++ code. In some domains, the LLM-generated heuristics expand fewer states than the baselines, revealing that they are not only efficiently computable, but sometimes even more informative than the state-of-the-art heuristics. Overall, our results show that sampling a set of planning heuristic function programs can significantly improve the planning capabilities of LLMs.
arxiv_record.authors: Augusto B. Corr\^ea and Andr\'e G. Pereira and Jendrik Seipp
arxiv_record.title: Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics: Challenging the State of the Art with Python Code

metadata.abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance in many problems. However, they fail to plan reliably. Specialized attempts to improve their planning capabilities still produce incorrect plans and fail to generalize to larger tasks. Furthermore, LLMs designed for explicit "reasoning" fail to compete with automated planners while increasing computational costs, which reduces one of the advantages of using LLMs. In this paper, we show how to use LLMs to always generate correct plans, even for out-of-distribution tasks of increasing size. For a given planning domain, we ask an LLM to generate several domain-dependent heuristic functions in the form of Python code, evaluate them on a set of training tasks with a greedy best-first search, and choose the best one. The resulting LLM-generated heuristic functions solve substantially more unseen out-of-distribution test tasks than end-to-end LLM planning, particularly for non-reasoning LLMs. Moreover, they also solve many more tasks than state-of-the-art domain-independent heuristics for classical planning, and are competitive with the strongest learning algorithm for domain-dependent planning. These results are impressive given that our implementation is based on a Python planner and the baselines all build upon highly optimized C++ code. In some domains, the LLM-generated heuristics expand fewer states than the baselines, showing that they are not only efficiently computable but also more informative than the state-of-the-art heuristics. Overall, our results show that sampling a set of planning heuristic functions can significantly improve the planning capabilities of LLMs.

native_events.abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance in many problems. However, they fail to plan reliably. Specialized attempts to improve their planning capabilities still produce incorrect plans and fail to generalize to larger tasks. Furthermore, LLMs designed for explicit "reasoning" fail to compete with automated planners while increasing computational costs, which reduces one of the advantages of using LLMs. In this paper, we show how to use LLMs to always generate correct plans, even for out-of-distribution tasks of increasing size. For a given planning domain, we ask an LLM to generate several domain-dependent heuristic functions in the form of Python code, evaluate them on a set of training tasks with a greedy best-first search, and choose the best one. The resulting LLM-generated heuristic functions solve substantially more unseen out-of-distribution test tasks than end-to-end LLM planning, particularly for non-reasoning LLMs. Moreover, they also solve many more tasks than state-of-the-art domain-independent heuristics for classical planning, and are competitive with the strongest learning algorithm for domain-dependent planning. These results are impressive given that our implementation is based on a Python planner and the baselines all build upon highly optimized C++ code. In some domains, the LLM-generated heuristics expand fewer states than the baselines, showing that they are not only efficiently computable but also more informative than the state-of-the-art heuristics. Overall, our results show that sampling a set of planning heuristic functions can significantly improve the planning capabilities of LLMs.

The central contribution of reusable domain-dependent heuristics outperforming traditional heuristics remains intact.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning reasoning versus memorization, useful candidate diversity, and imperfect heuristic selection. Section 6 explicitly discusses dependence on PDDL, uncertain generalization, prompt dependence, and implementation constraints. Appendix B additionally explains heuristic behavior and failure mechanisms across six previously undescribed domains.

D1.justification: Appendices A, C, and D add extensive generation, end-to-end, and ablation prompt listings, including example heuristic code and planner structures; embedded PDDL files are abridged. V2 also documents domain parameter ranges, identifies V3 version 0324, specifies training-run memory limits, and supplies a code-and-experiment-data archive reference. These disclosures do not by themselves establish changes to existing experiments.

E1.justification: V2 retains the eight IPC domains and adds reusable-spanner dynamics, Blocksworld with randomly renamed symbols, and the new Rod-Rings domain. These extend evaluation to changed action semantics, obfuscated inputs, and a distinct planning domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds direct end-to-end planning with Gemini Flash, Flash Thinking, DeepSeek V3, and R1 as evaluated comparators. Table 3 additionally includes V3-generated heuristics in the Fast Downward comparison. The existing classical and learned heuristic baselines remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include one LLM call per test task with VAL validation, ablations evaluating all 25 candidates under five-minute limits, and additional o3 configurations. Appendix E measures expansions per second on jointly solved tasks, excluding preprocessing. The main selected-heuristic evaluation retains its 30-minute/8-GiB limits.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's candidate-count analysis, v2 adds eight prompt-component ablations, tests probing memorization through modified, obfuscated, and novel domains, and a cross-planner throughput analysis. These examine prompt dependence, generalization mechanisms, selection quality, and implementation efficiency.

E5.justification: Table 4 newly reports standard deviations of candidate performance and specifies exclusion of failed heuristics from average coverage. V1 reports averages without comparable dispersion reporting. This characterizes candidate variability; it does not establish repeated full-pipeline experiments or uncertainty estimates for the headline comparisons.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces V3's total coverage of 283 with 343, changing its ranking; v2 specifies version 0324 while v1 leaves the version unspecified, so this is not an established same-configuration gain. R1's 373 and Pyperplan hFF's 243 remain unchanged. V2 adds direct-planning, ablation, robustness, o3, and throughput results, while removing the original per-model failure rates and detailed sampling curve.

M1.justification: Both versions generate candidate Python heuristics, evaluate them with GBFS, select by training coverage with an agile-score tie-breaker, and reuse the selected heuristic. The Blocksworld and Spanner code listings are unchanged. Expanded documentation and additional evaluated models do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The method exposition is substantially condensed, prompt and checklist material is reorganized into Appendix A, and existing heuristic explanations are consolidated in Appendix B. Experimental discussion is reordered, related work is tightened, and a dedicated limitations section and additional appendices substantially restructure the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 expands Tables 2 and 3, adds parameter-range, ablation, and throughput tables, and removes v1's cost/failure table and candidate-count figure. R1.justification: V2 adds discussion and citations for Tree of Thoughts, Algorithm of Thoughts/AoT+, planning formalization, and supporting theoretical background. improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's evidence with direct end-to-end baselines, component ablations, and altered/novel-domain tests. arxiv_record.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a critical component of large language model (LLM) post-training. However, on-policy algorithms used for post-training are not naturally robust to a diversified content of experience replay buffers, which asynchronous off-policy actors can efficiently populate in parallel to training. We propose efficiently learning on such off-policy data via Trajectory Balance with Asynchrony (TBA), an approach to asynchronous RL for LLMs that leverages the principled off-policy TB objective. On math, preference-tuning, and automated red-teaming tasks, we post-train models ranging from Pythia 410M to Qwen 2.5 7B, finding TBA offers speed and performance boosts over strong baselines like Online DPO and Dr. GRPO. Beyond TBA's performance benefits (high accuracy even as asynchrony grows) and speedups ($4\times$ or more), we show its reward- and recency-prioritizing sampling enable further gains as data generation is scaled. Our code is available at https://github.com/bbartoldson/TBA.

C1.justification: The central claim of faster asynchronous post-training with competitive or better performance remains. v2 narrows the abstract's categorical claim that on-policy algorithms are inherently incompatible with replay buffers to a lack of natural robustness to diversified replay data. It also foregrounds robustness as asynchrony increases and applicability through 7B models, without replacing the main contribution.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's exploration and replay-based explanations, v2 interprets the new ablations through KL regularization, reference resetting and task-dependent benefits of importance sampling. Appendix D discusses the stability/adherence tradeoff controlled by beta and reset frequency, explains differences from Kimi's reference policy, and identifies reward-hacking settings as an untested direction. These substantially expand the mechanism discussion and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a code-repository link, PRIME-RL implementation information, TBA′ hyperparameters in Table 4, and detailed GRPO reproduction settings in Appendix E.1, including TRL 0.17.0, DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 2 and 4×A100 80 GB hardware. The original TBA hyperparameter tables are largely retained and renumbered.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates GSM8K, TL;DR summarization and GPT-2/Llama red-teaming. v2 retains that coverage and adds MATH training with MATH-500 evaluation and generated Countdown problems for TBA′ (Section 6; Appendix C), substantially expanding reasoning-task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds an evaluated synchronous GRPO baseline on GSM8K, Dr. GRPO and IcePop comparisons on MATH/Countdown, and a Kimi-K2-style objective comparison on Countdown (Figures 1, 6, 10 and 11). These extend the actual comparator set beyond v1; CISPO's appearance in gradient comparisons alone is not counted as a separate evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: New TBA′ protocols use Qwen2.5-7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, 2- and 10-step staleness, 400/500 training steps, and a 9,000/1,000 Countdown training/test split (Section 6; Appendix C; Table 4). v2 also expands PFT comparisons to asynchronous settings and tests K=20 versus 40 completions at fixed batch size on GSM8K. Original TBA settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: The original GSM8K and TL;DR ablations remain as Figures 12 and 14. v2 adds tests of disabling importance sampling or reference resetting, replacing clipping with masking, and robustness to increased staleness (Figures 6–10). Table 5 and Appendix E.1 additionally examine completion-count effects, GRPO training dynamics and unsuccessful asynchronous GRPO configurations.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 newly specifies three runs per GPT-2 red-teaming configuration, where v1 only stated multiple runs. v2 also reports standard deviations for the completion-count ablation and displays separate Countdown replicates. Existing mean/standard-error reporting remains; the newly disclosed red-teaming count does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports GRPO's 49.05% GSM8K accuracy and the K=20/40 ablation accuracies of 54.61%/54.89%. Figures 6–11 add TBA′ results showing greater stability than Dr. GRPO/IcePop at 10-step staleness and similar Countdown performance to Kimi-K2-style training. Table 1 adds asynchronous baseline scores. The original 54.6% TBA headline result and relocated red-teaming table remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 retains buffer-based TBA and introduces TBA′ in PRIME-RL: fixed-staleness training without the original replay sampling, constant beta with periodic reference-policy resetting, and clipped importance sampling. Appendix D also evaluates an IcePop-masking variant. These additions change the update and data-use procedures, rather than merely documenting another implementation.

P1.justification: v2 revises the abstract and introduction, reorganizes the method overview around two implementations, combines metric/baseline paragraphs and subdivides the preliminaries. Appendix organization and discussion headings also change. Much of the retained experimental prose remains close to v1; the substantial scientific additions do not amount to a pervasive rewrite of existing text.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 6–11 and 13 and Tables 4–5, expands Table 1 into staleness blocks, and adds GRPO to Figure 1. The original red-teaming Table 2 moves to Appendix G as Table 6, while original ablation figures become Figures 12 and 14. NeurIPS formatting also changes typography, captions and page layout.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against recent asynchronous RL objectives and systems. Sections 2–3 and Appendix D distinguish near-on-policy approaches, connect GFlowNets with maximum-entropy RL/path consistency, and discuss ProRL-style resetting, Dr. GRPO, CISPO, IcePop and Kimi K1.5/K2. This adds substantive relationships and novelty qualifications beyond v1's related-work discussion.

T1.justification: v1 provides the TB/VarGrad objectives without the later gradient analysis. v2 adds Section 3.3, Appendix A's derivation, and Appendix D's formal gradient comparisons with Proximal RLOO, CISPO, Dr. GRPO and Kimi-K2-style objectives. It establishes the stated on-policy connection to mean-baseline REINFORCE with KL-regularized rewards and qualifies that connection off-policy.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrates useful speedups but provides limited objective-level analysis and component isolation. v2 substantially strengthens that foundation through gradient derivations, controlled resetting/importance-sampling ablations, modern baseline comparisons and larger-model experiments, supported by additional implementation details. The Kimi comparison also usefully qualifies the method's positioning. Larger-model evidence concerns the new TBA′ variant, and uncertainty reporting remains uneven, but the gains in explanatory support and empirical scrutiny are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TBA research, and their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation, including the original ablations and red-teaming table.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original MATH/Countdown evaluations, GRPO benchmarking and component ablations in Section 6 and Appendices C–E.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A–C report original TBA experiments on GSM8K, TL;DR summarization and automated red-teaming, including scaling and hyperparameter ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Video camouflaged object segmentation (VCOS), aiming at segmenting camouflaged objects that seamlessly blend into their environment, is a fundamental vision task with various real-world applications. With the release of SAM2, video segmentation has witnessed significant progress. However, SAM2's capability of segmenting camouflaged videos is suboptimal, especially when given simple prompts such as point and box. To address the problem, we propose Camouflaged SAM2 (CamSAM2), which enhances SAM2's ability to handle camouflaged scenes without modifying SAM2's parameters. Specifically, we introduce a decamouflaged token to provide the flexibility of feature adjustment for VCOS. To make full use of fine-grained and high-resolution features from the current frame and previous frames, we propose implicit object-aware fusion (IOF) and explicit object-aware fusion (EOF) modules, respectively. Object prototype generation (OPG) is introduced to abstract and memorize object prototypes with informative details using high-quality features from previous frames. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our approach. While CamSAM2 only adds negligible learnable parameters to SAM2, it substantially outperforms SAM2 on three VCOS datasets, especially achieving 12.2 mDice gains with click prompt on MoCA-Mask and 19.6 mDice gains with mask prompt on SUN-SEG-Hard, with Hiera-T as the backbone. The code is available at https://github.com/zhoustan/CamSAM2.
arxiv_record.authors: Yuli Zhou and Yawei Li and Yuqian Fu and Luca Benini and Ender Konukoglu and Guolei Sun
arxiv_record.title: CamSAM2: Segment Anything Accurately in Camouflaged Videos

E4.justification: The original component, distance-metric and prototype-count ablations remain. v3 adds tests of logit averaging, first-frame performance, token count, sampling/clustering choices and click sensitivity, plus efficiency profiling, prototype-similarity maps and further qualitative cases (A.3, A.5-A.8 and A.11-A.12). These substantially expand investigation of design choices and behavior.

E5.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies random seed 42 for sampling click prompts; v1 gives no seed. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3 explicitly acknowledges the absence of statistical significance reporting in its checklist.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for new comparisons, sensitivity tests, ablations and computational costs. Table 2 also revises existing Hiera-S entries: CamSAM2 box-prompt mDice/mIoU changes from 75.5/65.4 to 76.4/66.1. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting gains given the changed training-budget description. Original Hiera-T, CAD, SUN-SEG and Tables 5-7 values are retained.

M1.justification: The decamouflaged token, IOF, EOF, FPS plus one-iteration k-means in OPG, BCE/Dice objective and logit-averaging inference remain unchanged. Appendix explanations, including bypassing the added modules to recover SAM2, do not establish a revised VCOS algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative and much of the prose remain closely matched. v3 tightens explanatory and results paragraphs, moves training/inference from Section 3.6 into Section 4.1, updates author information and adds acknowledgments, appendix subsections and a checklist. P2.justification: v3 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column conference format, redraws Figure 1 and restructures Table 2 with backbones in adjacent columns. arxiv_record.abstract: This paper introduces Completion Pruning Policy Optimization (CPPO) to accelerate the training of reasoning models based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). GRPO, while effective, incurs high training costs due to the need to sample multiple completions for each question. Our experiment and theoretical analysis reveal that the number of completions impacts model accuracy yet increases training time multiplicatively, and not all completions contribute equally to policy training -- their contribution depends on their relative advantage. To address these issues, we propose CPPO, which prunes completions with low absolute advantages, significantly reducing the number needed for gradient calculation and updates. Additionally, we introduce a dynamic completion allocation strategy to maximize GPU utilization by incorporating additional questions, further enhancing training efficiency. Experiments show that CPPO achieves up to $7.98\times$ speedup on GSM8K and $3.48\times$ on Math while preserving or even enhancing the accuracy compared to the original GRPO. We release our code at \href{https://github.com/lzhxmu/CPPO}{https://github.com/lzhxmu/CPPO}.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhihang Lin, Mingbao Lin, Yuan Xie, Rongrong Ji
arxiv_record.title: CPPO: Accelerating the Training of Group Relative Policy Optimization-Based Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction revise headline speedups from 8.32×/3.51× to 7.98×/3.48× for GSM8K/MATH. The conclusion adds qualifications about a suitable pruning rate and sometimes preserving or improving accuracy. The central contributions remain completion pruning and dynamic allocation.

C2.justification: Section 5 newly explains that CPPO does not accelerate completion generation, limiting speedup when generation dominates, and identifies inference acceleration as complementary. It updates the model-scale limitation and future priorities. Appendix E also explains the smaller GSM8K accuracy improvement for the 7B model through its higher initial accuracy and limited remaining headroom.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds pseudocode specifying pruning-dependent batch and step counts and explains that implementation allocates questions before pruning to exploit parallel generation and prefix sharing. v2 also documents use of verl. These clarify reproducibility, while the principal hyperparameters, reward specifications, prompt templates and code-access link are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions train on GSM8K and MATH and evaluate on their test subsets plus AMC2023 and AIME2024. The added experiments vary models, frameworks and optimizers within this retained mathematical task coverage.

E2.justification: v1's principal comparison is against GRPO. v2 adds evaluated DAPO and DrGRPO comparisons, including their CPPO combinations, in Table 3, and REINFORCE++ and PPO without KL divergence in Table 11. This substantially broadens the competing optimization methods considered.

E3.justification: v2 adds experiments on verl, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on MATH, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on GSM8K, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on GSM8K. Table 11 also introduces a PPO comparison using group size 1 versus 16 for the other algorithms. These expand experimental configurations substantially; the existing decoding rules, metrics and principal hyperparameters remain.

E4.justification: The completion-count study, matched-question-batch comparison, pruning-metric ablation and component ablation retain their evidence. The reward curves and case studies are moved into Appendices H–J, with the same examples and findings. The added model and optimizer benchmark scores do not introduce a distinct diagnostic or stress test.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 newly specify three independent training runs and report means and standard deviations for GSM8K/MATH accuracy, training time and CPPO speedup. v1 provides point estimates without run-count or uncertainty reporting. This materially strengthens statistical reporting, although the OOD columns and added comparison tables remain point estimates; v1's actual run count is unspecified.

E6.justification: Main-table point estimates are replaced by three-run summaries: for example, GSM8K CPPO accuracy at 87.5% pruning changes from 80.41% to 80.01±0.38%, and speedup at 93.75% changes from 8.32 to 7.98±0.23. Tables 3 and 8–11 add substantial results, including DAPO+CPPO retaining 78.01% accuracy with 1.78× speedup. These additions use distinct configurations and do not establish gains over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 and Table 3 add DAPO+CPPO and DrGRPO+CPPO training variants, extending the pruning approach to other policy optimizers. The original CPPO objective, absolute-advantage selection, reward functions and allocation strategy remain. Appendix B principally clarifies implementation rather than establishing a changed original algorithm.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative and appendix organization are substantially reworked: stability discussion, case studies and completion examples move from the main text into Appendices H–J; algorithm documentation receives Appendix B; and references move before the appendices. Experimental subsections are reorganized and limitations rewritten, although much introductory and methodological prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds five experimental tables and an algorithm display, reformats Tables 1–2 for uncertainty reporting, and relocates several existing displays. v1's two-panel reward Figure 4 becomes enlarged separate Figures 5–6 in the appendix, while its completion examples and case tables are redistributed. These are substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for DAPO, DrGRPO, REINFORCE++, HybridFlow/verl, speculative sampling and EAGLE. These support targeted positioning of CPPO as compatible with other optimizers and complementary to inference acceleration. The existing related-work narrative is largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The explanation following Eq. (7) corrects the positive-advantage clipping condition from probability ratio < 1+epsilon to > 1+epsilon. This repairs a mathematical condition; the objectives, gradient derivation and reward definitions otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves variability in its central speed–accuracy comparisons unreported and evaluates a narrow optimizer/model selection. v2's three-run summaries in Tables 1–2 and broader comparisons in Tables 3 and 8–11 substantially improve the evidence for reliability and applicability. Appendix B clarifies implementation, and Section 5 identifies the generation-time bottleneck. Uncertainty reporting remains incomplete for supplementary comparisons, but the revision materially strengthens empirical support and qualification of the claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CPPO. All 16 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support matching content across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds three-run summaries, other RL algorithm comparisons, and evaluations with larger and different model backbones.

before.justification: v1 reports original CPPO-versus-GRPO accuracy and training-time measurements, pruning and component ablations, training curves and generated examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) focuses on the perceptual visual quality of images, playing a crucial role in downstream tasks such as image reconstruction, compression, and generation. The rapid advancement of multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) has significantly broadened the scope of IQA, moving toward comprehensive image quality understanding that incorporates content analysis, degradation perception, and comparison reasoning beyond mere numerical scoring. Previous MLLM-based methods typically either generate numerical scores lacking interpretability or heavily rely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using large-scale annotated datasets to provide descriptive assessments, limiting their flexibility and applicability. In this paper, we propose Q-Insight, a reinforcement learning-based model built upon group relative policy optimization (GRPO), which demonstrates strong visual reasoning capability for image quality understanding while requiring only a limited amount of rating scores and degradation labels. By jointly optimizing score regression and degradation perception tasks with carefully designed reward functions, our approach effectively exploits their mutual benefits for enhanced performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Q-Insight substantially outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both score regression and degradation perception tasks, while exhibiting impressive zero-shot generalization to comparison reasoning tasks. Code will be available at https://github.com/lwq20020127/Q-Insight.
arxiv_record.authors: Weiqi Li, Xuanyu Zhang, Shijie Zhao, Yabin Zhang, Junlin Li, Li Zhang, Jian Zhang
arxiv_record.title: Q-Insight: Understanding Image Quality via Visual Reinforcement Learning
