arxiv_record.abstract: Naive DDIM inversion process usually suffers from a trajectory deviation issue, i.e., the latent trajectory during reconstruction deviates from the one during inversion. To alleviate this issue, previous methods either learn to mitigate the deviation or design cumbersome compensation strategy to reduce the mismatch error, exhibiting substantial time and computation cost. In this work, we present a nearly free-lunch method (named FreeInv) to address the issue more effectively and efficiently. In FreeInv, we randomly transform the latent representation and keep the transformation the same between the corresponding inversion and reconstruction time-step. It is motivated from a statistical perspective that an ensemble of DDIM inversion processes for multiple trajectories yields a smaller trajectory mismatch error on expectation. Moreover, through theoretical analysis and empirical study, we show that FreeInv performs an efficient ensemble of multiple trajectories. FreeInv can be freely integrated into existing inversion-based image and video editing techniques. Especially for inverting video sequences, it brings more significant fidelity and efficiency improvements. Comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluation on PIE benchmark and DAVIS dataset shows that FreeInv remarkably outperforms conventional DDIM inversion, and is competitive among previous state-of-the-art inversion methods, with superior computation efficiency.
arxiv_record.authors: Yuxiang Bao, Huijie Liu, Xun Gao, Huan Fu, Guoliang Kang
arxiv_record.title: FreeInv: Free Lunch for Improving DDIM Inversion

C1.justification: The introduction's contribution summary and conclusion shift toward explicit comparable-or-better image/video reconstruction claims across U-Net and DiT architectures, whereas v1 emphasizes competitive image editing and superior video editing. The abstract, ensemble motivation and central efficiency claim remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix F newly acknowledges that FreeInv can preserve source content too strongly and restrict editability, and that editing quality depends on the selected editing framework. Section 3.3 also adds a rationale for using transformed branches without spatial or semantic correspondence. These are substantive qualifications of otherwise retained interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a direct code-access statement, specifies 25-step FLUX and 12-step VI schedules, and documents the retained survey's 15 images, 165 votes, instructions and interface. Conversely, it removes v1's V100-32GB/A100-80GB hardware specifications and explicit statement that rotation is the default comparison transformation. These are documentation changes, not evidence of reruns.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate image reconstruction/editing on PIE and video reconstruction/editing using DAVIS and Internet videos. Additional qualitative examples and human comparisons remain within this coverage. SDXL adds a model configuration, not a new dataset or task.

E2.justification: ReNoise joins the P2P editing comparison. More substantially, v2 Table 1 introduces direct U-Net reconstruction comparisons against NTI, EDICT, DI, VI, ReNoise, BELM and PI, beyond v1's editing comparisons. Appendix D also adds human preferences across alternative inversion methods; v1 only reports preferences with versus without FreeInv.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce an SDXL configuration, inverse-transformation and NTI-combination controls, and a multi-method preference study reporting 130 votes. Existing PIE coverage, image resolution, 120-frame video preparation and evaluation metrics remain unchanged. Newly disclosed details of retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained sampling-count, branch-construction and transformation ablations, v2 adds color jitter and tests three substantive questions: whether inverse noise transformation affects reconstruction versus editing, whether FreeInv complements NTI, and whether its benefits transfer to SDXL (Appendices A–C, Tables 7–9). The earlier FLUX analysis is retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. Newly disclosed survey vote counts describe sample sizes rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive reconstruction comparisons, ReNoise editing scores, FLUX resource costs and appendix results, including NTI+FreeInv PSNR 28.15 and FreeInv preference of 30.0% in Table 10. Patch-shuffle PSNR changes from 27.45 to 27.61, with LPIPS and MSE also revised (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 6). Matched existing editing, FLUX reconstruction, video and original preference results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The ensemble formulation, one-sample-per-step approximation and matched latent transformations remain unchanged. The inverse transformation of predicted noise moves from v1 Section 3.3 to v2 Appendix A. The additional transformation and integration experiments do not introduce a newly specified inversion algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 polishes language and front matter, rewrites the contribution summary, conclusion and portions of Section 4 around reconstruction, and moves editing integration into Appendix A. FLUX discussion moves into the main reconstruction comparison. The principal section sequence and most methodological and related-work prose are retained.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column layout. Reconstruction and efficiency comparisons are consolidated, editing-table cost columns move into the reconstruction table, and existing qualitative panels are rearranged. Appendix Tables 7–10 and Figures 8–13 add substantial displays; some examples repeat earlier figures rather than provide new evidence.

R1.justification: New citations include ReNoise, SDXL, DiT and rectified-flow architectures, ensemble learning, CLIP, LatentWarp and WAVE. The related-work narrative and positioning against optimization-based and error-compensation inversion methods remain largely intact.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 explicitly specifies independently sampled initial images from the natural-image distribution and writes the mismatch-error expectation over that distribution. This refines the premises of the unbiasedness argument. The triangle inequality and subsequent Monte Carlo derivation otherwise remain mathematically unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 fills an important evidential gap by directly benchmarking reconstruction against competing U-Net inversion methods. Appendices A–C test the editing adaptation, compatibility with NTI and transfer to SDXL; comparative human evaluation and explicit limitations further strengthen and qualify the conclusions. These gains substantially improve support for the paper's central claims, outweighing the loss of hardware documentation while preserving the established editing and video results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FreeInv work, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes Appendices A–F. No reading gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 retains original empirical results, while Appendices A–D report additional inverse-transformation, NTI-combination, SDXL and human-preference experiments.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original image and video reconstruction/editing experiments, ablations and human preferences, including Tables 1–6 and Figure 5.

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce IntrinsiX, a novel method that generates high-quality intrinsic images from text description. In contrast to existing text-to-image models whose outputs contain baked-in scene lighting, our approach predicts physically-based rendering (PBR) maps. This enables the generated outputs to be used for content creation scenarios in core graphics applications that facilitate re-lighting, editing, and texture generation tasks. In order to train our generator, we exploit strong image priors, and pre-train separate models for each PBR material component (albedo, roughness, metallic, normals). We then align these models with a new cross-intrinsic attention formulation that concatenates key and value features in a consistent fashion. This allows us to exchange information between each output modality and to obtain semantically coherent PBR predictions. To ground each intrinsic component, we propose a rendering loss which provides image-space signals to constrain the model, thus facilitating sharp details also in the output BRDF properties. Our results demonstrate detailed intrinsic generation with strong generalization capabilities that outperforms existing intrinsic image decomposition methods used with generated images by a significant margin. Finally, we show a series of applications, including re-lighting, editing, and text-conditioned room-scale PBR texture generation.
arxiv_record.authors: Peter Kocsis (1), Lukas H\"ollein (1), Matthias Nie{\ss}ner (1) ((1) Technical University of Munich)
arxiv_record.title: IntrinsiX: High-Quality PBR Generation using Image Priors

C1.justification: The central claims about direct text-to-PBR generation, generalization, and the two-stage method remain. v2 newly claims first-time room-scale PBR texturing in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The introduction drops v1's assertion that direct generation eliminates decomposition ambiguity, replacing it with a claim about self-contained generation and generalization.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops the generalization explanation: matching an input image may distract decomposition models from learning the PBR distribution, while a pretrained PBR prior can benefit even image-conditioned decomposition. New limitations acknowledge reduced compositional diversity, lost detail, and incorrect intrinsic predictions relative to FLUX. Rank sensitivity and alternative lighting sampling also receive new interpretations and qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 specifies LoRA projection targets and documents CFG=10, flow normalization, and inverse-observation weighting for the existing scene-texturing application. It adds GPU memory, A6000 inference hardware, approximately 12-second sampling time, resource licenses, and user-study anonymity information. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings. Code and weights are newly promised for release, rather than demonstrated to be available.

E1.justification: The quantitative out-of-distribution evaluation changes from Hypersim indoor scenes and BlenderKit outdoor scenes to GObjaverse Daily-Used objects. This replaces the represented evaluation domain, rather than merely enlarging the same dataset. InteriorVerse training and the existing scene-texturing demonstrations remain.

E2.justification: IID, RGBX, and ColorfulShading remain. Table 1 and v2 Figure 15 add IID w/ FLUX-LoRA, trained with the same architecture and small dataset as the proposed method. Figure 15 also adds the image-conditioned IntrinsiX variant. ColorfulShading's additional mention in Section 5.1 does not establish new participation in Figure 6.

E3.justification: Section 5 expands the main InteriorVerse FID evaluation from 100 to all 2,595 test images and replaces the 40-image OOD evaluation with 1,000 GObjaverse samples. The new IID comparison controls backbone and training data. Reported user-study totals also change from 37 participants and 2,336 responses to 36 and 2,274, without explaining the revision. Appendix Table 2 retains its 100-image evaluation.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether pretrained PBR priors benefit image decomposition, compare LoRA ranks from 16 through 256, and investigate Disney BRDF lighting sampling. Appendix C adds an illustrated failure case concerning lost detail and incorrect normals. The previous dataset-size, diversity, stage-alignment, dropout, and rendering-loss analyses remain after matching their relocated figures.

E5.justification: Table 1 adds standard deviations to rendering-quality, specularity, and prompt-coherence ratings that previously had means only; the checklist identifies these as standard deviations. It also explicitly mentions different seeds for the retained diversity examples. Neither addition establishes more repeated training runs, and no confidence intervals or formal significance tests are supplied.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the main FID results under changed evaluation conditions: IntrinsiX's ID/OOD values change from 186.60/220.12 to 72.09/71.39, not a same-setting improvement. New results include IID w/ FLUX-LoRA at 103.36/79.29, image-conditioned OOD FID of 70.51, BRDF-sampled results of 75.26/68.87, and the rank sweep. The w/o CIA-Dropout specularity and prompt-coherence means change from 2.82/4.48 to 3.21/4.52. Dataset-size Table 2 is unchanged.

M1.justification: The core two-stage LoRA training, cross-intrinsic attention, and rendering-loss procedure remain. Section 5.2 adds an image-conditioned variant by introducing RGB as another modality and applying conditioning dropout. Appendix B also introduces a BRDF-sampled training variant. These extend the method without replacing its main architecture.

P1.justification: The main narrative and most original prose remain. v2 makes localized introductory and application rewrites, improves several cross-references, reorders ablation discussion, and incorporates Individual PBR Priors into Appendix A. New appendix sections and a conference checklist extend the structure without a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds rank-sensitivity Figure 9, limitations Figure 17, and license Table 3. Table 1 gains a comparator row and uncertainty displays, while the supplementary albedo comparison gains two rows. Figure 5 is redesigned to show the input mesh and combined roughness/metallic panels. The existing dataset-size grid is transposed and relocated; most other imagery is retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through material reconstruction and generation, including rendering-aware SVBRDF estimation, Material Palette, MaterialPicker, and concurrent diffusion-based G-buffer generation. It distinguishes independent priors and a fixed renderer from shared-ControlNet and diffusion-renderer approaches. Separately, the VFDS citation changes from the text-to-3D FlowDreamer work to a different robot-manipulation FlowDreamer paper, making that attribution questionable.

T1.justification: The probability definitions, flow-matching objective, attention formulation, and combined loss remain substantively unchanged. Equation (3) makes the incident-light argument explicit and expresses the cosine factor as a normal-light dot product, clarifying the existing rendering model. Neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The matched FLUX-LoRA baseline and image-conditioned experiment address an important weakness in v1: differences in backbone and training data complicated its explanation of superiority over decomposition methods. Larger held-out evaluations, additional design tests, rating dispersions, and illustrated failures substantially strengthen the evidence and qualify the generalization claims. There are tradeoffs: the earlier scene-based OOD evaluation is replaced, the user-study count revision is unexplained, and the VFDS attribution becomes questionable. These issues limit the gains but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IntrinsiX by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports revised evaluations, an additional baseline, image-conditioned generation, rank sensitivity, and alternative lighting-sampling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original FID evaluations, a participant study, component and dataset-size ablations, and generated image and scene-texturing results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion Models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in handling inverse problems, offering high-quality posterior-sampling-based solutions. Despite significant advances, a fundamental trade-off persists regarding the way the conditioned synthesis is employed: Zero-shot approaches can accommodate any linear degradation but rely on approximations that reduce accuracy. In contrast, training-based methods model the posterior correctly, but cannot adapt to the degradation at test-time. Here we introduce InvFusion, the first training-based degradation-aware posterior sampler. InvFusion combines the best of both worlds -- the strong performance of supervised approaches and the flexibility of zero-shot methods. This is achieved through a novel architectural design that seamlessly integrates the degradation operator directly into the diffusion denoiser. We compare InvFusion against existing general-purpose posterior samplers, both degradation-aware zero-shot techniques and blind training-based methods. Experiments on the FFHQ and ImageNet datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. Beyond posterior sampling, we further demonstrate the applicability of our architecture, operating as a general Minimum Mean Square Error predictor, and as a Neural Posterior Principal Component estimator.
arxiv_record.authors: Noam Elata, Hyungjin Chung, Jong Chul Ye, Tomer Michaeli, Michael Elad
arxiv_record.title: InvFusion: Bridging Supervised and Zero-shot Diffusion for Inverse Problems

C1.justification: v2 explicitly claims the first training-based degradation-aware posterior sampler in its abstract and introduction. It also replaces adaptation to 'virtually any degradation' with a 'wide range' and emphasizes comparisons among models handling multiple tasks. The central architectural, sampling, MMSE and NPPC contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the broad noise-generalization expectation with observed failure under high Poisson noise and explains limitations of comparing DIP methods with posterior samplers. It also discusses unseen matrix operators as generalization evidence and connects a prospective nonlinear extension to latent diffusion. Existing training-coverage, linearity and computational limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.2 supplies pseudocode for feature degradation and joint attention, including key construction. Appendix A.1 adds hardware, approximate training times, licenses and per-experiment precision information. Its planned code/checkpoint-release statement becomes a statement of code availability; v1 already contained a repository link, so the link itself is not a new resource disclosure.

E1.justification: The datasets, resolutions and principal tasks remain unchanged. v2 Table 12 adds a high-Poisson-noise scenario for FFHQ64 motion blur and in-painting, extending the existing noiseless and Gaussian-noise coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MGPS and InDI to the FFHQ64, ImageNet64 and FFHQ256 comparisons; MGPS is spelled MPGS in Table 13. Tables 14–15 additionally compare against end-to-end unrolled DDRM and ASeq-DIP. This substantially broadens the evaluated comparator families. InDI was previously cited but not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 adds LPIPS and measurement-space MSE evaluations, controlled block-resolution configurations, ten-step DDRM unrolling trained with MSE, and a 1,024-image PSNR/KID/LPIPS comparison with ASeq-DIP. Table 6 also reports bf16 for FFHQ256, whereas v1 Appendix A.1 specified fp16 generally. These are new evaluation designs and a reported setting revision, without establishing which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained out-of-distribution, Gaussian-noise and MMSE-training analyses, v2 adds progressive block-placement ablations (Table 8), direct measurement-consistency diagnostics (Table 10), and a high-Poisson-noise failure test (Table 12). These examine architectural contribution and robustness limits not directly tested in v1. The dedicated MMSE-versus-Palette visual comparison in v1 Figure 4 is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions describe deterministic sampling with matched seeds for qualitative comparisons. Neither introduces repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The existing NPPC uncertainty-estimation application is retained.

E6.justification: Changes exceed rounding: FFHQ64 motion-blur CFID changes from 4.69 to 4.2 (Table 1), and FFHQ unconditional FID changes from 6.27 to 6.36 (Table 4). ImageNet in-painting CFID changes from 6.44 to 5.9, reversing the comparison with Palette's 6.20/6.2. Numerous new analysis and comparator results, plus FFHQ256 MMSE rows, substantially expand the findings. Updated FFHQ256 scores accompany a revised reported precision setting.

M1.justification: The feature-degradation layer, joint-attention conditioning, diffusion and MMSE objectives, and NPPC procedure are retained. The new pseudocode documents implementation details without establishing an algorithm revision. Applying blocks selectively was already described in v1 Appendix A.1.

P1.justification: InvFussion is renamed InvFusion, the abstract is substantially rewritten, and introduction and explanatory passages receive localized revisions. The main section sequence remains intact. The appendix gains pseudocode and ablation sections, while Additional Results moves from Appendix C to D; most existing exposition is retained.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column NeurIPS format, with extensive relocation and resizing of displays. Six new tables and code listings are added, and existing comparison tables expand. v1 Figure 4 is removed; the NPPC figure is redrawn with explicit model-flow annotations, while the unconditional sample grids are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for ASeq-DIP, MGPS, an algorithm-unrolling review, KID and LPIPS. It more explicitly distinguishes posterior sampling from distortion-oriented unrolling and DIP objectives, and strengthens its novelty positioning. Most of the existing related-work discussion and cited literature remain.

T1.justification: The diffusion formulation, posterior-mixture reasoning, feature-degradation equation, training objectives and high-noise MMSE argument are retained. Some definitions move inline and equations are renumbered, but no substantive mathematical definition, proof or derivation is added or revised.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central architecture through previously missing block-placement controls and direct consistency measurements, while the Poisson experiment establishes a concrete failure boundary. Broader comparators and implementation pseudocode improve credibility and reproducibility. New reporting problems include incorrect LPIPS highlighting in Table 9 and unexplained MMSE differences between Tables 1 and 7, but these limited issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InvFussion/InvFusion research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable matching despite renaming and reformatting.

after.justification: The original empirical evaluations remain, supplemented by architectural ablations, consistency measurements, Poisson-noise experiments and additional method comparisons.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendices B–C report original FFHQ and ImageNet restoration, generation, MMSE and neural posterior principal-component results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Although significant progress has been made in audio-driven talking head generation, text-driven methods remain underexplored. In this work, we present OmniTalker, a unified framework that jointly generates synchronized talking audio-video content from input text while emulating the speaking and facial movement styles of the target identity, including speech characteristics, head motion, and facial dynamics. Our framework adopts a dual-branch diffusion transformer (DiT) architecture, with one branch dedicated to audio generation and the other to video synthesis. At the shallow layers, cross-modal fusion modules are introduced to integrate information between the two modalities. In deeper layers, each modality is processed independently, with the generated audio decoded by a vocoder and the video rendered using a GAN-based high-quality visual renderer. Leveraging the in-context learning capability of DiT through a masked-infilling strategy, our model can simultaneously capture both audio and visual styles without requiring explicit style extraction modules. Thanks to the efficiency of the DiT backbone and the optimized visual renderer, OmniTalker achieves real-time inference at 25 FPS. To the best of our knowledge, OmniTalker is the first one-shot framework capable of jointly modeling speech and facial styles in real time. Extensive experiments demonstrate its superiority over existing methods in terms of generation quality, particularly in preserving style consistency and ensuring precise audio-video synchronization, all while maintaining efficient inference.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhongjian Wang, Peng Zhang, Jinwei Qi, Guangyuan Wang, Chaonan Ji, Sheng Xu, Bang Zhang, Liefeng Bo

C1.justification: Joint generation, multimodal style replication and 25-FPS inference remain the central claims. v2 additionally foregrounds novelty as the first unified one-shot text-to-audio-video framework and no longer lists the data pipeline and multistage training as a separate principal contribution. The zero-shot/one-shot terminology change does not establish a different reference-conditioning task.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific limitations concerning head-only generation and GAN artifacts under large motion, explanations of gaze–head coordination and text-conditioning design, and clarification that baseline FPS excludes preceding TTS. Existing multitask-learning and frontal-view metric-bias interpretations remain. These additions qualify and explain the retained conclusions rather than replacing them.

D1.justification: v2 supplies extensive previously absent implementation information: training on eight A100s for 750,000 iterations, batch size and learning rate, feature extraction and temporal alignment, masking/dropout rates, CFG settings, sampling steps, renderer losses, preprocessing thresholds and model configurations. These disclosures substantially improve reproducibility, although prose specifying 512-dimensional audio/visual embeddings conflicts with Table 5's 1024-dimensional entries.

E1.justification: Reported evaluation coverage changes from v1's pooled VFHQ, MEAD and real-world collection to separate SEED speech, VoxCeleb2 video and Chinese Custom evaluations. Appendix B.3 adds RAVDESS emotional-reference examples. Several SEED speech columns reproduce earlier scores, so their new dataset label alone should not be mistaken for new experimental coverage.

E2.justification: The external TTS and talking-head baseline sets remain unchanged. However, v2 Table 4 adds Cross-Attention alongside Add and Linear as an evaluated comparator in the fusion experiment corresponding to v1 Table 3.

E3.justification: v1 describes 1,000 pooled test samples; v2 specifies 500 VoxCeleb2 clips and 100 Custom clips. AniTalker's reported evaluation resolution changes from 256×256 to 512×512 with super-resolution. PSNR, SSIM and image FID are dropped. A new user-study protocol uses 50 references, 50 participants and six dimensions rated from 1 to 5. These are reported protocol changes, not proof that all retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond extending the fusion ablation with Cross-Attention, v2 adds substantial qualitative investigation of gaze dynamics, coordination with head motion and reference-eye-style inheritance in Figures 7–9, plus emotional-reference transfer in Figure 10. The earlier yaw trajectories and motion heatmaps are retained rather than newly added analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bars for the experimental results. The new user study reports mean ratings without uncertainty estimates; participant counts are evaluation-design information.

E6.justification: v2 adds VoxCeleb2, Custom-speech, MOS and Cross-Attention results, while removing PSNR/SSIM/FID entries and the earlier fully conditioned ZH/EN speech scores. In the largely retained video-results block, Sync-C changes from 0.597 to 4.17 for StyleTalk, 6.548 to 5.52 for Hallo, and 5.354 to 5.48 for OmniTalker. Changed test-set descriptions prevent treating these as established same-setting gains. Reported renderer speed changes from 30 to 50 FPS, while overall generation remains 25 FPS.

M1.justification: The dual-branch DiT, joint attention, reference conditioning and decoders remain. Localized procedural revisions include stated L1 rather than squared-error training, logit-normal rather than uniform timestep sampling, and condition-specific guidance replacing generic scalar CFG. v2 also describes multiple masked segments instead of v1's reference/target pair. Newly documented renderer details alone do not establish a new renderer.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much related-work prose are rewritten. Method subsections are reorganized around alignment, fusion, generation and decoding; experimental setup is consolidated and qualitative evaluation separated. Flow-matching background moves into an appendix, alongside newly organized technical, experimental, limitations and impact sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. The introductory pipeline illustration disappears, and the architecture diagram is redrawn to show four fusion variants. Benchmark tables gain dataset groupings, while MOS and configuration tables and several appendix figures are added. The original yaw plot and qualitative heatmap comparison are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: The main research positioning and closest competing approaches remain. v2 adds an explicit distinction from MMAudio's separate text branch and references such as StyleTalk++, MimicTalk and LivePortrait, alongside dataset and preprocessing sources. The earlier NeRF/Gaussian-splatting discussion and ChatAnyone citation are removed. This updates supporting context without fundamentally changing the research position.

T1.justification: v2 adds explicit landmark-fitting and renderer-loss formulations and revises the mathematical formulation of CFG to use condition-specific weights. Appendix A.1 expands the conditional-flow derivation with marginalization identities, while retaining its underlying OT objective. No new theorem or proved guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's sparse reproducibility documentation through Appendices A–B and adds human evaluation and gaze/emotion analyses directly relevant to its central style-replication claim. Specific failure conditions also improve assessability. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including ambiguous provenance of reused scores, inconsistent embedding dimensions, overbroad metric-superiority wording and absent uncertainty estimates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniTalker, with matching architecture, baselines and substantial shared results. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, fusion ablations, a 50-participant user study and additional gaze and emotional-generation examples, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original speech and video generation experiments, fusion ablations and qualitative motion analyses in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–4.

arxiv_record.abstract: The increasing number of satellites and orbital debris has made space congestion a critical issue, threatening satellite safety and sustainability. Challenges such as collision avoidance, station-keeping, and orbital maneuvering require advanced techniques to handle dynamic uncertainties and multi-agent interactions. Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise in this domain, enabling adaptive, autonomous policies for space operations; however, many existing RL frameworks rely on custom-built environments developed from scratch, which often use simplified models and require significant time to implement and validate the orbital dynamics, limiting their ability to fully capture real-world complexities. To address this, we introduce OrbitZoo, a versatile multi-agent RL environment built on a high-fidelity industry standard library, that enables realistic data generation, supports scenarios like collision avoidance and cooperative maneuvers, and ensures robust and accurate orbital dynamics. The environment is validated against a real satellite constellation, Starlink, achieving a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 0.16% compared to real-world data. This validation ensures reliability for generating high-fidelity simulations and enabling autonomous and independent satellite operations.
arxiv_record.authors: Alexandre Oliveira and Katarina Dyreby and Francisco Caldas and Cl\'audia Soares
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted at the 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
arxiv_record.title: OrbitZoo: Real Orbital Systems Challenges for Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a customizable, high-fidelity orbital RL environment, and the abstract's 0.16% MAPE claim is unchanged. v2 adds prominent claims about fast parallel scaling, concludes that continuous action spaces generally improve performance under realistic dynamics, and extends the platform's stated relevance to broader autonomy research.

C2.justification: v2 makes parallelization benefits conditional on force complexity and adds substantive mission-specific limitations: stochastic precision problems in Hohmann transfers, inclination-related chase failures, collision-policy generalization difficulties, and slow or unstable GEO coordination. It also attributes advantages to continuous control and federated knowledge sharing. These extend the scientific interpretation beyond relocating v1's existing caveats.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an explicit experiment-code repository link, DDPG/DDQN architectures and replay settings, a discrete collision-action table, and previously unspecified numerical reward weights across missions. It also documents the propagation-mode configuration. These materially expand reproducibility information; newly disclosed reward coefficients do not themselves establish changed objectives.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix E.2 adds a Kolosa-inspired low-thrust transfer requiring simultaneous changes to several orbital elements, extending the existing Hohmann and moving-target transfer coverage. The collision-avoidance, GEO coordination, and Starlink validation domains remain; no new real satellite dataset is reported.

E2.justification: The PPO-only mission evaluations expand to DDQN versus PPO for collision avoidance and independent versus FedAvg-based PPO for GEO coordination (v2 Appendices E.5–E.6). Appendix E.2 also introduces a Kolosa-inspired reproduction and qualitative comparison with the published implementation, explicitly acknowledging implementation differences.

E3.justification: Reported chase-target steps change from 70 to 500 seconds. GEO episodes change from 2000 to 500 steps, with revised learning rates, epochs, clipping, and update budgets; the new comparison uses matched initial constellations. Hohmann initial action standard deviation changes from 0.4 to 0.5. These are reported protocol changes, without establishing that every retained plot was regenerated.

E4.justification: v2 adds learning-speed and fuel analyses to the existing Hohmann reward-shaping comparison, examines DDQN robustness to realistic perturbations, and tests knowledge sharing in GEO coordination. Parallelization analysis now compares computation modes across force configurations. Conversely, v1's four-day collision-avoidance stress test and associated failure evidence are removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figures 10–11 add ±1 standard-deviation bands to timing measurements, retaining the stated 100 propagation steps. GEO evaluation still reports thirty Monte Carlo simulations, but v2 Figure 29 shows averages without the individual trial traces displayed in v1 Figure 21. arxiv_record.abstract: Creativity in AI imagery remains a fundamental challenge, requiring not only the generation of visually compelling content but also the capacity to add novel, expressive, and artistically rich transformations to images. Unlike conventional editing tasks that rely on direct prompt-based modifications, creative image editing requires an autonomous, iterative approach that balances originality, coherence, and artistic intent. To address this, we introduce CREA, a novel multi-agent collaborative framework that mimics the human creative process. Our framework leverages a team of specialized AI agents who dynamically collaborate to conceptualize, generate, critique, and enhance images. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that CREA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in diversity, semantic alignment, and creative transformation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to introduce the task of creative editing.

arxiv_record.abstract: Existing methods to enhance the reasoning capability of large language models predominantly rely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) on reasoning-specific data. These approaches critically depend on external supervisions--such as labeled reasoning traces, verified golden answers, or pre-trained reward models. In this work, we propose Entropy Minimized Policy Optimization (\ours), which makes an early attempt at fully unsupervised LLM reasoning incentivization. By continuously minimizing the predictive entropy of LLMs on unlabeled questions in a latent semantic space, \ours achieves competitive performance compared to supervised counterparts on both mathematical and free-form natural reasoning tasks. Specifically, without any supervised signals, \ours boosts the accuracy of Qwen2.5-Math-7B Base from 30.7\% to 48.1\% on mathematical benchmarks and improves the accuracy of Qwen2.5-7B Base from 32.1\% to 50.1\% on MMLU-Pro. Primary experiments and analysis are also provided to interpret the effectiveness of \ours. Code is available at https://github.com/QingyangZhang/EMPO.
arxiv_record.authors: Qingyang Zhang, Haitao Wu, Changqing Zhang, Peilin Zhao, Yatao Bian
arxiv_record.comments: Ongoing work. First released on April 8, 2025

arxiv_record.abstract: Existing methods for solving Riemannian bilevel optimization (RBO) problems require prior knowledge of the problem's first- and second-order information and curvature parameter of the Riemannian manifold to determine step sizes, which poses practical limitations when these parameters are unknown or computationally infeasible to obtain. In this paper, we introduce the Adaptive Riemannian Hypergradient Descent (AdaRHD) algorithm for solving RBO problems. To our knowledge, AdaRHD is the first method to incorporate a fully adaptive step size strategy that eliminates the need for problem-specific parameters in RBO. We prove that AdaRHD achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon)$ iteration complexity for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point, thus matching the complexity of existing non-adaptive methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that substituting exponential mappings with retraction mappings maintains the same complexity bound. Experiments demonstrate that AdaRHD achieves comparable performance to existing non-adaptive approaches while exhibiting greater robustness.
arxiv_record.authors: Xu Shi, Rufeng Xiao, Rujun Jiang
arxiv_record.title: An Adaptive Algorithm for Bilevel Optimization on Riemannian Manifolds

native_events.abstract: Existing methods for solving Riemannian bilevel optimization (RBO) problems require prior knowledge of the problem's first- and second-order information and curvature parameter of the Riemannian manifold to determine step sizes, which poses practical limitations when these parameters are unknown or computationally infeasible to obtain. In this paper, we introduce the Adaptive Riemannian Hypergradient Descent (AdaRHD) algorithm for solving RBO problems. To our knowledge, AdaRHD is the first method to incorporate a fully adaptive step size strategy that eliminates the need for problem-specific parameters in RBO. We prove that AdaRHD achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon)$ iteration complexity for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point, thus matching the complexity of existing non-adaptive methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that substituting exponential mappings with retraction mappings maintains the same complexity bound. Experiments demonstrate that AdaRHD achieves comparable performance to existing non-adaptive approaches while exhibiting greater robustness.

arxiv_record.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained large language models (LLMs) presents a dual challenge of balancing parameter efficiency and model capacity. Existing methods like low-rank adaptations (LoRA) are efficient but lack flexibility, while Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enhance model capacity at the cost of more & under-utilized parameters. To address these limitations, we propose Structural Mixture of Residual Experts (S'MoRE), a novel framework that seamlessly integrates the efficiency of LoRA with the flexibility of MoE. Conceptually, S'MoRE employs hierarchical low-rank decomposition of expert weights, yielding residuals of varying orders interconnected in a multi-layer structure. By routing input tokens through sub-trees of residuals, S'MoRE emulates the capacity of numerous experts by instantiating and assembling just a few low-rank matrices. We craft the inter-layer propagation of S'MoRE's residuals as a special type of Graph Neural Network (GNN), and prove that under similar parameter budget, S'MoRE improves structural flexibility of traditional MoE (or Mixture-of-LoRA) by exponential order. Comprehensive theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that S'MoRE achieves superior fine-tuning performance, offering a transformative approach for efficient LLM adaptation. Our implementation is available at: https://github.com/ZimpleX/SMoRE-LLM.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances in inference-time compute have significantly improved performance on complex tasks by generating long chains of thought (CoTs) using Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). However, this improved accuracy comes at the cost of high inference latency due to the length of generated reasoning sequences and the autoregressive nature of decoding. Our key insight in tackling these overheads is that LRM inference, and the reasoning that it embeds, is highly tolerant of approximations: complex tasks are typically broken down into simpler steps, each of which brings utility based on the semantic insight it provides for downstream steps rather than the exact tokens it generates. Accordingly, we introduce SpecReason, a system that automatically accelerates LRM inference by using a lightweight model to (speculatively) carry out simpler intermediate reasoning steps and reserving the costly base model only to assess (and potentially correct) the speculated outputs. Importantly, SpecReason's focus on exploiting the semantic flexibility of thinking tokens in preserving final-answer accuracy is complementary to prior speculation techniques, most notably speculative decoding, which demands token-level equivalence at each step. Across a variety of reasoning benchmarks, SpecReason achieves $1.4-3.0\times$ speedup over vanilla LRM inference while improving accuracy by $0.4-9.0\%$. Compared to speculative decoding without SpecReason, their combination yields an additional $8.8-58.0\%$ latency reduction. We open-source SpecReason at https://github.com/ruipeterpan/specreason.
arxiv_record.authors: Rui Pan, Yinwei Dai, Zhihao Zhang, Gabriele Oliaro, Zhihao Jia, Ravi Netravali

C2.justification: V1 attributes accuracy gains primarily to explicit scoring augmenting self-reflection. V2 makes reduced token consumption under a fixed budget the primary explanation, while retaining scoring as another contributor. Figure 4b shows the reported AIME advantage shrinking from 16.2% at 4096 tokens to 4.7% at 8192. V2 also discusses Skywork's weaker instruction following and consequent need for stricter acceptance thresholds.

D1.justification: V2 documents the added model identities and configuration values for new experiments, including the initial-step sweep n=0,10,20,30,40. Existing vLLM 0.8.2, GPU and tensor-parallel settings, cache handling, sequential execution, and repository access information remain unchanged. The added details do not establish a change to the underlying inference engine.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate AIME 2024, MATH500, and GPQA Diamond. The added model pairings, token budgets, and control experiments remain within these mathematical and scientific reasoning tasks. Adding GPQA to the threshold analysis does not introduce a previously unevaluated task.

E2.justification: Matched main comparisons retain vanilla base-model inference, vanilla small-model inference, SpecDecode, and SpecReason+Decode. E5.justification: Both versions calculate accuracy from 16 responses per query at temperature 0.6. Neither reports seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results continue the existing practice of reporting point estimates and averages.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for three main model pairings and the new supplementary analyses. M1.justification: V2 Section 4.1 introduces an optional control that forces the base model to generate the first n reasoning steps before speculation. The core proposal, utility scoring, threshold acceptance, fallback regeneration, and hierarchical speculative decoding procedures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references and discussion covering SuffixDecoding, token recycling, Lookahead, and additional reasoning models. arxiv_record.abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) pretraining is more scalable than dense Transformer pretraining, because MoEs learn to route inputs to a sparse set of their feedforward parameters. However, this means that MoEs only receive a sparse backward update, leading to training instability and suboptimal performance. We present a lightweight approximation method that gives the MoE router a dense gradient update while continuing to sparsely activate its parameters. Our method, which we refer to as Default MoE, substitutes missing expert activations with default outputs consisting of an exponential moving average of expert outputs previously seen over the course of training. This allows the router to receive signals from every expert for each token, leading to significant improvements in training performance. Our Default MoE outperforms standard TopK routing in a variety of settings without requiring significant computational overhead. Code: https://github.com/vatsal0/default-moe.

C2.justification: v3 Sections 4.4–5 develop explanations connecting router entropy, default-vector similarity, gradient approximation, and training stability, and attribute competing methods' weaker results to globally reduced auxiliary loss. New Appendix A.1 qualifies industrial applicability of dropless MoEs and identifies untested reasoning, specialized coding/math, and finetuning settings. v1 lacks this substantive mechanism and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: Most architecture, optimizer, batch-size, and auxiliary-loss details are relocated to Appendix A.2. v3 adds explicit active-parameter counts, identifies Liger as the Triton-kernel source, discloses 64-GPU AWS execution, and replaces the GitHub pointer with anonymous code and configuration links. The previously printed minimum learning rate is omitted. These are limited documentation and access-information changes.

E1.justification: FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu were already used in v1. v3 adds BoolQ, PubMedQA, and SciQ to benchmark evaluation, and Appendix B.1 adds routing-specialization evaluations across ArXiv, GitHub, Pile-CC, PubMed Central, and StackExchange domains. These additions substantially broaden the evaluated data and task coverage.

E2.justification: TopK and SparseMixer comparisons are retained. v3 Section 4.4 additionally evaluates ReMoE, reporting failure to recover from training divergence, and Loss-Free Balancing with a tuned bias-update coefficient. Both were only discussed or cited in v1, so the evaluated routing alternatives expand substantially.

E3.justification: The main benchmark comparison changes from 320B-token 8c1 models to 160B-token 8c1 and 32c4 models. New protocols include a 1/64-sparsity configuration and varying K from 1 to 7 against a fully activated gradient reference. Benchmark random-reference values and improvement-over-random normalization also change. Global auxiliary-loss reduction was already documented in v1.

E4.justification: v3 adds scored-versus-unscored EMA sensitivity tests, a more extreme sparsity ablation, and extensive analyses of router entropy, dense-gradient similarity, default-vector similarity, domain specialization, load balance, and expert coactivation. These test mechanisms and potential side effects beyond v1's architecture and EMA ablations, many of which remain in the appendix.

E5.justification: v1's benchmark table lacks uncertainty estimates. v3 Table 2 adds standard errors throughout the benchmark comparisons; the checklist attributes them to lm-eval-harness and states that pretraining is typically conducted once per configuration. Section 4.6 also adds throughput variability estimates. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting without establishing additional training runs.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports a 2.8% average benchmark advantage; v3 Table 2 reports 2.1% for 8c1 and 0.3% for 32c4, with some task-level losses. These are different-budget, different-coverage comparisons, not same-setting performance changes. New findings include Loss-Free Balancing perplexity of 24.22 versus Default MoE's 23.48, ReMoE nonconvergence, and gradient-similarity results. The throughput table's numerical results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core sparse computation and EMA-based dense-router-gradient approximation remain. v3 Sections 4.3 and A.4 introduce router-score-weighted accumulation into the default-vector update and explicitly describe it as the final method. This refines v1's unweighted averaging to reduce sensitivity to the EMA decay parameter.

P1.justification: v3 condenses the introduction, moves implementation details into the appendix, separates routing comparisons and empirical analysis into dedicated subsections, and rewrites the discussion around a mechanistic explanation. The appendices are reorganized around limitations, experimental details, ablations, and detailed analyses, followed by a checklist. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: The opening benchmark bar chart is removed, the benchmark table is transposed and expanded, and an active-parameter table is added. Separate ablation plots are consolidated into Figure 2, while several retained curves move to the appendix. New heatmaps, domain-routing charts, and polar gradient-similarity plots substantially change the visual presentation.

(2024) for Liger kernels, while removing several background references, including Dai et al. (2024) and Kaplan et al. (2020). The comparison framing changes, but the core positioning as a lightweight improvement to sparse MoE routing remains.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central mechanism: Section 4.5 and Appendix B directly test dense-gradient approximation and examine routing behavior, which v1 did not. arxiv_record.abstract: We study whether and how the choice of optimization algorithm can impact group fairness in deep neural networks. Through stochastic differential equation analysis of optimization dynamics in an analytically tractable setup, we demonstrate that the choice of optimization algorithm indeed influences fairness outcomes, particularly under severe imbalance. Furthermore, we show that when comparing two categories of optimizers, adaptive methods and stochastic methods, RMSProp (from the adaptive category) has a higher likelihood of converging to fairer minima than SGD (from the stochastic category). Building on this insight, we derive two new theoretical guarantees showing that, under appropriate conditions, RMSProp exhibits fairer parameter updates and improved fairness in a single optimization step compared to SGD. We then validate these findings through extensive experiments on three publicly available datasets, namely CelebA, FairFace, and MS-COCO, across different tasks as facial expression recognition, gender classification, and multi-label classification, using various backbones. Considering multiple fairness definitions including equalized odds, equal opportunity, and demographic parity, adaptive optimizers like RMSProp and Adam consistently outperform SGD in terms of group fairness, while maintaining comparable predictive accuracy. Our results highlight the role of adaptive updates as a crucial yet overlooked mechanism for promoting fair outcomes. We release the source code at: https://github.com/Mkolahdoozi/Some-Optimizers-Are-More-Equal.
arxiv_record.authors: Mojtaba Kolahdouzi, Hatice Gunes, Ali Etemad
arxiv_record.title: Some Optimizers are More Equal: Understanding the Role of Optimizers in Group Fairness

E4.justification: v2 adds checks of whether fairness advantages survive joint hyperparameter tuning, whether optimizer variants support the second-moment-normalization explanation, and whether benefits complement FairBatch. E5.justification: v2 specifies ten-run averages for the added tabular experiment. E6.justification: Tables 1, 4 and 6 add substantial result sets while previously reported results remain unchanged. arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) demonstrate that sophisticated behaviors such as multi-step reasoning and self-reflection can emerge via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards~(\textit{RLVR}). However, existing \textit{RLVR} approaches are inherently ``on-policy'', limiting learning to a model's own outputs and failing to acquire reasoning abilities beyond its initial capabilities. To address this issue, we introduce \textbf{LUFFY} (\textbf{L}earning to reason \textbf{U}nder o\textbf{FF}-polic\textbf{Y} guidance), a framework that augments \textit{RLVR} with off-policy reasoning traces. LUFFY dynamically balances imitation and exploration by combining off-policy demonstrations with on-policy rollouts during training. Specifically, LUFFY combines the Mixed-Policy GRPO framework, which has a theoretically guaranteed convergence rate, alongside policy shaping via regularized importance sampling to avoid superficial and rigid imitation during mixed-policy training. Compared with previous RLVR methods, LUFFY achieves an over \textbf{+6.4} average gain across six math benchmarks and an advantage of over \textbf{+6.2} points in out-of-distribution tasks. Most significantly, we show that LUFFY successfully trains weak models in scenarios where on-policy RLVR completely fails. These results provide compelling evidence that LUFFY transcends the fundamental limitations of on-policy RLVR and demonstrates the great potential of utilizing off-policy guidance in RLVR.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes improved benchmark performance, generalization and selective imitation. v4 makes successful training of weak models where on-policy RL fails a central abstract claim and explicit contribution. It also expands headline superiority claims to alternative off-policy training methods and highlights computational efficiency.

C2.justification: v4 adds explicit limitations concerning verifiable-reward tasks, model scale and using one off-policy trajectory per question. New interpretations explain Llama training failure through missing positive rewards and attribute SFT-based alternatives' computational overhead to excessively long imitated reasoning. The earlier selective-imitation and exploration interpretations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds the verl/vLLM implementation stack, detailed SFT hyperparameters, baseline construction, difficulty-selection thresholds, subset sizes and Llama prompting. Table 2 newly reports GPU hours and on/off-policy data usage. Several existing disclosures, including hardware and the Qwen system prompt, are relocated rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: Training remains based on OpenR1-Math-220k, and evaluation retains the same six mathematical and three out-of-distribution benchmarks. The new Easy/Hard selections and held-out SFT+RL portion change sampling within the existing source and task coverage; additional backbones change model configurations.

E2.justification: v4 Table 1 adds RL w/ SFT Loss and SFT+RL as evaluated comparators for both mathematical and out-of-distribution performance, substantially extending v1's comparison with plain SFT and on-policy methods. The new Llama experiment also includes its corresponding instruction-tuned model.

E3.justification: New protocols include 860-step LUFFY† training to match SFT+RL GPU hours, Llama-specific prompting, 7.3k/25.4k difficulty-filtered training subsets, and an approximately 49k-prompt held-out RL stage for SFT+RL. v4 separately specifies an SFT learning rate of 5e-5, whereas v1 gives an unqualified 1e-6 training rate. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds the Llama Easy/Hard training-failure analysis, a five-value shaping-parameter sensitivity study, and generation-length dynamics comparing RL w/ SFT Loss with LUFFY. Existing component ablations, BLEU analysis, temperature study and case study remain, often relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: v4 introduces paired-bootstrap significance testing with 1,000 resamples in Appendix C.3 and p < 0.05 markers for the headline comparisons in Table 1. v1 reports point estimates without this statistical testing. Bootstrap resampling does not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: Reported math scores change throughout: for example, 7B LUFFY's average changes from 49.6 to 50.1 and SFT's from 47.6 to 44.1, while shared OOD scores remain unchanged. New results cover additional baselines, Llama, sensitivity tests and the longer-budget LUFFY† run, reporting 50.4 math and 61.8 OOD averages. v4 also corrects v1's trained-1.5B averages, which omitted AIME 2025.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains mixed-policy advantage estimation, importance weighting with practical πφ = 1, shaping with f(x) = x/(x + γ), and removal of clipping. On-policy clipping removal moves from v1 Section 2.4 to v4 Appendix E.1. The added experiments do not introduce a new LUFFY component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, with RLVR replacing much zero-RL terminology and an explicit contribution list added. GRPO and reward background become a separate section. Training details, clipping discussion, ablations and reasoning analyses are reorganized into expanded appendices with a contents list.

P2.justification: v4 merges the separate math and OOD tables into a grouped, shaded Table 1 and adds a resource table and several new plots. The opening performance bar chart is removed, the method diagram is relocated, and Figure 6 is redrawn with an entropy axis and fewer displayed variants. Existing analysis figures and tables are extensively relocated.

R1.justification: v4 updates citations with additional work on RL capability limits, TTRL, Absolute Zero, NFT, reward gaming and statistical testing, while removing some classical RL references. It makes the claim of being first to incorporate off-policy guidance into RLVR explicit. These changes refine the existing positioning between on-policy RL and imitation.

T1.justification: The existing convergence theorem and proof move from Appendix A to B.1. New Appendix B.2 adds a first-order Taylor variance analysis and a derivation for exponentially distributed importance weights, providing conditional mathematical support for shaping. The mixed-advantage numerator is also corrected from τi in v1 Equation 2 to R(τi) in v4 Equation 4.

improvement.justification: v4 resolves important empirical gaps in v1 through stronger SFT+RL and joint-loss comparisons, matched GPU budgets, and a direct demonstration of on-policy failure on difficult Llama training data. Added significance testing, sensitivity analysis and implementation details substantially improve assessability. Reporting problems remain: Section 5.1 claims a 16.1-point OOD advantage over SFT+RL, although Table 1 supports 13.0 points. This limited error does not outweigh the stronger support for the central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LUFFY research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds alternative training baselines, Llama experiments, a compute-matched comparison and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, training dynamics, component ablations, model extensions and reasoning analyses in Sections 4–5 and Appendix B.

arxiv_record.abstract: Event cameras offer a promising avenue for multi-view stereo depth estimation and Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) due to their ability to detect blur-free 3D edges at high-speed and over broad illumination conditions. However, traditional deep learning frameworks designed for conventional cameras struggle with the asynchronous, stream-like nature of event data, as their architectures are optimized for discrete, image-like inputs. We propose a scalable, flexible and adaptable framework for pixel-wise depth estimation with event cameras in both monocular and stereo setups. The 3D scene structure is encoded into disparity space images (DSIs), representing spatial densities of rays obtained by back-projecting events into space via known camera poses. Our neural network processes local subregions of the DSIs combining 3D convolutions and a recurrent structure to recognize valuable patterns for depth prediction. Local processing enables fast inference with full parallelization and ensures constant ultra-low model complexity and memory costs, regardless of camera resolution. Experiments on standard benchmarks (MVSEC and DSEC datasets) demonstrate unprecedented effectiveness: (i) using purely monocular data, our method achieves comparable results to existing stereo methods; (ii) when applied to stereo data, it strongly outperforms all state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches, reducing the mean absolute error by at least 42%; (iii) our method also allows for increases in depth completeness by more than 3-fold while still yielding a reduction in median absolute error of at least 30%. Given its remarkable performance and effective processing of event-data, our framework holds strong potential to become a standard approach for using deep learning for event-based depth estimation and SLAM. Project page: https://github.com/tub-rip/DERD-Net

C1.justification: The abstract's central method, accuracy, completeness and efficiency claims are unchanged. The introduction and conclusion add explicit claims of robustness to imperfect camera poses and demonstrated downstream applicability, extending the earlier general claim of suitability for SLAM.

C2.justification: V2 adds an accuracy-versus-computation rationale for the chosen patch size, explains excluded MVSEC sequences, and interprets pose-noise results with attention to changing point coverage. Appendix A.4 explicitly limits tracking results to offline maps built using ground-truth poses, without accumulated drift or direct comparability to online SLAM. These substantive qualifications were absent from v1.

D1.justification: V2 clarifies moving-camera ray casting, output-depth rescaling and layer resizing in the existing patch-size experiment. Section 4.7 documents preprocessing workload, CPU hardware and approximately 45/26/0.2 ms for DSI creation, fusion and pixel selection. V2 also explicitly states that code, trained models and videos are provided, while retaining the existing project link and training hyperparameters.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates depth estimation on MVSEC indoor_flying 1–3 and DSEC Zurich_City_04_a. V2 adds offline camera tracking across Zurich_City_04_a–f, including five previously unused sequences, and depth-estimation scenarios with noisy poses from odometry systems.

E2.justification: SGM and GTS are added to the DSEC comparison in v2 Tables 3 and 15; v1 Tables 4 and 12 omit them, although both already participate in MVSEC comparisons. The existing deep-stereo comparator set is retained. ESVO2 supplies poses for robustness experiments rather than a separately scored competing depth method.

E3.justification: V2 introduces protocols using ES-PTAM/ESVO2 poses, offline depth-to-tracking-to-DSI reprojection, and camera tracking against maps constructed using ground-truth poses. Tracking adds ATE and ARE RMSE evaluation. The original benchmark splits, training epochs, filters and depth metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.6 and Appendix A.3 add substantial tests of sensitivity to estimated poses and feedback from DERD-Net's own depth errors. Appendix A.1 adds computational-cost analysis to the patch-size study. The reflection, patch-size and per-sequence no-ensemble analyses already existed in v1 and are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, seed values, confidence intervals or significance tests. Both describe the same two independently initialized ensemble models and cross-validation arrangements. V2's percentage changes and tracking RMSE values are performance summaries, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: New Tables 5 and 8–10 report pose-noise, reprojection and tracking outcomes, including 17.07 cm tracking ATE RMSE on zc04a. Existing DERD-Net benchmark scores remain unchanged. DSEC ESVO changes from 3.88 m MAE and 3.40 million points to 3.93 m and 9.40 million points; the PDFs do not explain this replacement. DSEC SGM/GTS scores and an averaged no-ensemble row are also added.

M1.justification: The Sub-DSI processing, 3D convolution, GRU, dense outputs, MAE loss and two-model ensemble remain unchanged. V2 clarifies ray origins and normalized-depth rescaling. The reprojection loop is introduced as an evaluation protocol rather than a revision to the proposed depth estimator.

P1.justification: Most core prose and the top-level narrative are retained, with selective explanatory rewrites. The deep-stereo comparison moves from Section 4.8 to 4.5; detailed patch-size and reflection discussions move into Appendix A.1–A.2; detailed benchmark tables form Appendix B.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column format to a single-column NeurIPS layout. V1 Tables 3–4 merge into v2 Table 3, existing sensitivity displays are consolidated and relocated, and new pose/tracking Tables 5 and 8–10 are introduced. The three figures retain their substantive content but are resized and relabeled.

R1.justification: V2 adds references concerning event-based SLAM, ESVO2, deep visual odometry and simulation-to-real transfer, and strengthens discussion of practical pose sources. Its central positioning as learning depth from geometrically constructed DSIs remains unchanged. Publication updates and duplicate-reference cleanup do not represent new research positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–3 for Sub-DSI normalization, convolution outputs and GRU representations are retained. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs. The added depth-rescaling explanation is an implementation clarification.

improvement.justification: V1's SLAM-suitability claim lacked estimated-pose and tracking tests. V2 substantially strengthens practical validation through estimated-pose experiments on both benchmarks, reprojection testing and offline tracking on six DSEC sequences. It also discloses preprocessing costs and the offline-map limitation. Changing point coverage limits direct robustness comparisons, and Tables 8–9 apparently mislabel centimetre-scale errors as metres, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DERD-Net and contain readable methods, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched reliably despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains the original experiments and adds depth estimation using estimated camera poses, a reprojection experiment and downstream camera-tracking results in Section 4.6 and Appendix A.

before.justification: Sections 4 and Appendix A report original DERD-Net experiments on MVSEC and DSEC, including depth-estimation results, reflection tests, patch-size sensitivity and runtime measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) offers a flexible and general approach to performing Bayesian inference: In SBI, a neural network is trained on synthetic data simulated from a model and used to rapidly infer posterior distributions for observed data. A key goal for SBI is to achieve accurate inference with as few simulations as possible, especially for expensive simulators. In this work, we address this challenge by repurposing recent probabilistic foundation models for tabular data: We show how tabular foundation models -- specifically TabPFN -- can be used as pre-trained autoregressive conditional density estimators for SBI. We propose Neural Posterior Estimation with Prior-data Fitted Networks (NPE-PFN) and show that it is competitive with current SBI approaches in terms of accuracy for both benchmark tasks and two complex scientific inverse problems. Crucially, it often substantially outperforms them in terms of simulation efficiency, sometimes requiring orders of magnitude fewer simulations. NPE-PFN eliminates the need for inference network selection, training, and hyperparameter tuning. We also show that it exhibits superior robustness to model misspecification and can be scaled to simulation budgets that exceed the context size limit of TabPFN. NPE-PFN provides a new direction for SBI, where training-free, general-purpose inference models offer efficient, easy-to-use, and flexible solutions for a wide range of stochastic inverse problems.
arxiv_record.authors: Julius Vetter, Manuel Gloeckler, Daniel Gedon, Jakob H. Macke
arxiv_record.title: Effortless, Simulation-Efficient Bayesian Inference using Tabular Foundation Models

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) offers a flexible and general approach to performing Bayesian inference: In SBI, a neural network is trained on synthetic data simulated from a model and used to rapidly infer posterior distributions for observed data. A key goal for SBI is to achieve accurate inference with as few simulations as possible, especially for expensive simulators. In this work, we address this challenge by repurposing recent probabilistic foundation models for tabular data: We show how tabular foundation models -- specifically TabPFN -- can be used as pre-trained autoregressive conditional density estimators for SBI. We propose Neural Posterior Estimation with Prior-data Fitted Networks (NPE-PFN) and show that it is competitive with current SBI approaches in terms of accuracy for both benchmark tasks and two complex scientific inverse problems. Crucially, it often substantially outperforms them in terms of simulation efficiency, sometimes requiring orders of magnitude fewer simulations. NPE-PFN eliminates the need for inference network selection, training, and hyperparameter tuning. We also show that it exhibits superior robustness to model misspecification and can be scaled to simulation budgets that exceed the context size limit of TabPFN. NPE-PFN provides a new direction for SBI, where training-free, general-purpose inference models offer efficient, easy-to-use, and flexible solutions for a wide range of stochastic inverse problems.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims of training-free TabPFN-based inference, strong simulation efficiency, robustness to misspecification and scalability through filtering. The additional experiments strengthen support without materially redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 expands the existing causal-structure explanation into a hypothesis about exploiting sparse conditional dependencies. It adds interpretations of tuning and filter-size trade-offs, makes runtime limitations more explicit, and replaces the spatial/continuous-parameter caveat with a limitation concerning parameter spaces beyond 500 dimensions.

D1.justification: v2 adds operational pseudocode, a benchmark-dimensionality overview in Table C-1, and hardware, search-budget and configuration details for the added studies. The existing libraries, hardware disclosures and training defaults are largely retained. D.6 inconsistently mentions a 100,000-point context despite specifying a 10,000-point default elsewhere, so this does not reliably establish a changed default.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix D.1 adds Weinberg, Stellar Streams, M/G/1 queue, Tree and HMM experiments, substantially extending coverage to further physics, queuing and structured inference problems. The original SBI benchmarks, neuroscience applications, embedding tasks and UCI datasets remain; the UCI experiments move from D.1 to D.9.

E2.justification: v2 adds the hyperparameter-optimized NPE (Sweep) comparator in Appendix D.2 and Fig. D-4. The default NPE and other existing comparators remain. NRE and NPE ensembles were already evaluated in v1, so they are not new baselines.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include ten-hour random searches for each of seven tasks and four budgets, runtime measurements across parameter dimensions, observation dimensions and context sizes, and filter-size sweeps at a fixed 100,000-simulation budget. v2 also tests a 50-dimensional HMM configuration and pyloric parameter-order permutations. The original benchmark budgets and training defaults are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands the diagnostic evidence with baseline-tuning analysis, systematic inference-speed analysis, filter-size sensitivity and a 50-permutation pyloric ordering study (D.2, D.3, D.6 and C.4). These supplement the existing misspecification, embedding, density-evaluation, noise-distribution and benchmark-ordering analyses.

E5.justification: The new pyloric ordering study reports fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles across 50 random permutations, adding a statistical summary of ordering sensitivity. Existing reporting practices, including five-run confidence intervals in Fig. 2 and three-seed benchmark-ordering experiments, remain unchanged; no increase in their run counts is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds task-performance, calibration, optimized-baseline, filtering and runtime results while retaining the original principal results. For example, Table D-2 reports 516 seconds for 10,000 posterior samples with 32 parameter dimensions, 32 observation dimensions and 10,000 context simulations. New C.4 results report pyloric ordering quantile ranges of 0.081–0.094 for energy score and 96–98% for validity.

M1.justification: The autoregressive TabPFN estimator, simulation filtering, ratio-based density evaluation, sequential inference, embedding approach and unconditional mixture construction are retained. Renaming NPE-PF to NPE-PFN and adding Algorithms 1–2 document the existing procedure rather than establish a new method.

P1.justification: The method is renamed throughout, explanations of TabPFN and sequential inference are refined, and the appendix gains subsections while moving UCI density estimation to its end. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain recognizable. The preprint header is replaced by NeurIPS 2025 identification.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with three new experimental figures (D-1, D-4 and D-7), benchmark and runtime tables, and two algorithm boxes. Existing figures are relabeled and rearranged; notably, the original UCI Fig. D-1 becomes Fig. D-10, and calibration plots share a page with the new tuning comparison.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to quantile-regression SBI, Groschner et al.'s neuroscience application and graphically structured diffusion models. It also makes the relationship to existing nearest-neighbor filtering more explicit. The broader positioning within SBI, in-context learning and tabular foundation models remains.

T1.justification: The autoregressive factorization, posterior-invariance argument for filtering, embedding loss, mixture decomposition and existing synthetic-task equations are retained. There is no new theorem, proof or substantive derivation; the added pseudocode documents computations already described in v1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by testing whether the advantage survives baseline optimization and extends to additional domains, including expensive stellar-stream simulations. Runtime scaling and filter-size analyses also give practical substance to previously less-tested usability claims. These gains, together with clearer procedural documentation, outweigh the localized context-size inconsistency in D.6.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the method rename and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments on further inference tasks, optimized baselines, runtime scaling and sensitivity to filtering and parameter ordering.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation-based inference experiments, Hodgkin–Huxley and pyloric-network results, and appendix experiments on density estimation, calibration and robustness.
