C1.justification: V1 primarily guarantees detection and leaves recovery conjectural. V2's introductory Theorem 1.9 guarantees both strong detection and weak recovery for the compressed estimator when beta exceeds 0.76. The abstract and main theorem also qualify the earlier general claim of a unique signal-strength threshold.

C2.justification: V2 explains that general signed signal distributions may permit repeated appearance and disappearance of outliers. It qualifies BP/AMP efficiency and initialization comparisons and discusses applicability beyond the assumed random-matrix models in Appendix B. Existing dense-signal and compression limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A changes the code-access pointer from an anonymous repository to the named NonlinearLaplacian GitHub repository. Appendix B documents graph preprocessing and vertex selection. Existing architecture, training hyperparameters, hardware and runtime disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds dense-subgraph search on the 297-vertex C. elegans network, a limited extension to real graph data. Planted-clique numerical experiments were already mentioned in v1 Section 4.2; displaying them in v2 does not establish newly introduced coverage.

E2.justification: Direct spectral estimation remains the evaluated comparator, including in the added graph results. The compared nonlinearity families are retained. Correcting the discussion of cited AMP methods to BP does not introduce a newly evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix B introduces a protocol that makes the network binary and symmetric, selects 15 vertices using leading eigenvector coordinates, and measures the fraction of possible edges present. Existing synthetic-data and MLP settings are retained; Figure 5 uses the Figure 2 setup.

E4.justification: V2 adds a real-network applicability case study and compares the new theoretical eigenvector predictions with simulations in Figure 2. Figure 5 explicitly illustrates the planted-clique correspondence. The parameter-sensitivity and cross-distribution transferability analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 2 still reports averages over 500 inputs with plus/minus one standard deviation, and MLP optimization still uses 10 random initializations. Figure 5 adopts the existing uncertainty-reporting practice; no new statistical estimation or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Appendix B newly reports 65% versus 73% edge density for 15-vertex subgraphs found by naive spectral and nonlinear-Laplacian methods. Figure 2 adds theoretical overlap predictions, and Figure 5 displays results identified as planted-clique validation, although one caption sentence inconsistently names the Gaussian model. Existing tuning thresholds and transferability values are retained.

M1.justification: Definition 1.5 extends the explicitly defined compressed algorithm from detection to recovery using Vv1(tilde L). Appendix B adds extraction of vertex subsets from the eigenvector's largest coordinates. The nonlinear-Laplacian construction and three approaches to tuning sigma remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 expands introductory motivation and related-work explanations, streamlines proof exposition, changes the eigenvector-analysis subsection from challenges to a proof, and adds Appendix B. The main section organization and most method and experimental prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 adds theoretical eigenvector markers and adjusts its vertical-axis presentation. A new Figure 5 displays the planted-clique comparison; the original transferability figure becomes Figure 6 without substantive display changes. Overall formatting is retained, although the new Figure 5 caption contains inconsistent model identification.

R1.justification: Section 1.7 adds connections to combined linear/spectral estimators, optimized phase-retrieval methods, robust AMP and large-scale eigenvector computation. It corrects the characterization of HWX17 and DM15 as dense BP rather than AMP. References supporting the new proof and network example are added, while some references tied to replaced arguments are removed.

T1.justification: Theorem 1.8 gains an explicit eigenvector-overlap limit, proved through eigenvalue differentiation and convexity in Section 3.5. Definition 1.1 relaxes subgaussianity to a finite third absolute moment and the sparsity lower bound from omega((log n)^c/n), c>6, to omega(log n/n). Sections 2.2 and 3.1–3.2 replace concentration and complex-analysis arguments with simpler convergence arguments. The unique-threshold guarantee is restricted to nonnegative signals.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important theoretical gap: recovery was conjectural in v1, whereas Theorem 1.8 and Section 3.5 provide an explicit overlap formula and proof for the compressed estimator. Weaker assumptions and a corrected threshold scope further strengthen the central contribution. These gains outweigh limited reporting weaknesses in the added empirical material, particularly Figure 5's inconsistent caption and the sparsely specified real-network example.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same nonlinear-Laplacian research. Their main text, equations, figures, references and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v2's new Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds an explicit planted-clique comparison figure and a C. elegans network experiment in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original Gaussian planted-submatrix simulations, numerical optimization of nonlinearities, sensitivity analysis and transferability results in Figures 1–5.

arxiv_record.abstract: 3D visual illusion is a perceptual phenomenon where a two-dimensional plane is manipulated to simulate three-dimensional spatial relationships, making a flat artwork or object look three-dimensional in the human visual system. In this paper, we reveal that the machine visual system is also seriously fooled by 3D visual illusions, including monocular and binocular depth estimation. In order to explore and analyze the impact of 3D visual illusion on depth estimation, we collect a large dataset containing almost 3k scenes and 200k images to train and evaluate SOTA monocular and binocular depth estimation methods. We also propose a 3D visual illusion depth estimation framework that uses common sense from the vision language model to adaptively fuse depth from binocular disparity and monocular depth. Experiments show that SOTA monocular, binocular, and multi-view depth estimation approaches are all fooled by various 3D visual illusions, while our method achieves SOTA performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Chengtang Yao, Zhidan Liu, Jiaxi Zeng, Lidong Yu, Yuwei Wu, Yunde Jia
arxiv_record.title: 3D Visual Illusion Depth Estimation

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations involving conflicting monocular priors and planar-label bias, acknowledges the ablation's EPE tradeoff, and introduces computational-cost and composite/novel-illusion limitations. The LoRA-potential caveat disappears. Booster interpretation changes from 'ours best' to favoring monocular methods, especially DepthPro, although unchanged Table 2 supports only region- and metric-specific advantages.

D1.justification: The appended material supplies loss definitions, data-processing pseudocode and thresholds, filtering/video-generation prompts, calibration details, LoRA targets, and training resources: four H100 GPUs, batch size six per GPU and approximately 20 days. Tables 1–2 explicitly identify fine-tuning status. v4 also adds direct dataset and model access links alongside the existing code link. E1.justification: v4 extends evaluation beyond illusion-depth benchmarks to ordinary-scene generalization on Middlebury (Table 5) and qualitative 3D object detection using YOLO3D on real illusion images (Appendix C.5, Figure 15). E2.justification: The quantitative comparator sets in Tables 1–2 are unchanged; DA V2 abbreviates DepthAnything V2. E3.justification: v4 adds fine-tuning versus no-fine-tuning controls, Sparse/Dense augmentation comparisons, half-resolution whole-image Middlebury evaluation without a maximum-disparity restriction, and an H100 resource benchmark at 1920×1080. Section 3 also replaces 178,912 training frames with 'over 200,000', although Appendix C.2 still lists components totaling 178,912; actual dataset expansion is unresolved.

E4.justification: The original module ablation is retained as Table 6. New analyses test whether fine-tuning monocular and stereo baselines resolves illusions, evaluate confidence-map errors under zero-shot transfer, and illustrate VLM recognition and downstream detection failures. These substantially expand the investigation of adaptation, reliability and failure modes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v4's approximately 20% confidence-map error evaluates a model output; it is not uncertainty reporting across experimental runs.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in the original Tables 1–2 and module ablation are unchanged. v4 adds substantial results: its Marigold fine-tuning comparison reports illusion-region EPE changing from 21.16 to 13.67 while bad2 worsens from 65.67 to 74.82; Middlebury EPE is 1.50 for the proposed method. Confidence error, additional stereo fine-tuning results, and 53,959 MB/4.77 s per iteration resource measurements are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The dual-branch prediction, flow-matching confidence and affine-alignment fusion remain. However, v4's introduction and Figure 4 depict RGB-only input to the VLM, replacing v1's RGB plus monocular and binocular maps, while v4 Section 4.2 still specifies all three inputs. This inconsistency prevents establishing whether the actual input procedure changed. Newly documented losses alone do not establish a method revision.

P1.justification: The introduction, dataset explanation, experimental narrative and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Separate dataset-result subsections are consolidated into 'Influence of 3D Visual Illusions', ablations are reorganized, and a dedicated discussion places expanded limitations before the conclusion. Appendices organize the additional technical material; author and publication information also change.

P2.justification: v4 redraws Figure 4, adds fine-tuning columns to Tables 1–2, introduces new experimental tables and appendix algorithm displays, and places the original Figures 5–6 side by side at reduced size. Appendix figures add pipeline, calibration, VLM and detection displays and extend qualitative comparisons, while reusing some original examples. The original ablation table is relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for Black Forest Labs' FLUX, Flask and Mousavian et al.'s 3D bounding-box estimation work. The stereo, monocular-depth and VLM related-work organization and most research positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: The main geometric reasoning and Equations 1–10 are retained. Appendix A.2 explicitly formulates normalized constrained plane fitting, while Appendix B.1 defines weighted disparity losses and focal confidence supervision, including its binary target (Equations 11–14). These add mathematical specification, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's missing reproducibility documentation through included losses, processing algorithms, prompts and implementation details. New fine-tuning controls test whether ordinary adaptation suffices, while Middlebury and resource measurements clarify generalization and practical cost. These gains outweigh the remaining weaknesses, including inconsistent VLM-input descriptions and training-frame counts, and an overgeneralized Booster interpretation. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset and VLM-driven depth-fusion work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds fine-tuning comparisons, Middlebury evaluation, confidence-map analysis, computational measurements and qualitative appendix studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on 3D-Visual-Illusion and Booster in Tables 1–2 and a Booster module ablation in Table 3.

arxiv_record.abstract: Designing neural networks within a Hamiltonian framework offers a principled way to ensure that conservation laws are respected in physical systems. While promising, these capabilities have been largely limited to discrete, analytically solvable systems. In contrast, many physical phenomena are governed by PDEs, which govern infinite-dimensional fields through Hamiltonian functionals and their functional derivatives. Building on prior work, we represent the Hamiltonian functional as a kernel integral parameterized by a neural field, enabling learnable function-to-scalar mappings and the use of automatic differentiation to calculate functional derivatives. This allows for an extension of Hamiltonian mechanics to neural PDE solvers by predicting a functional and learning in the gradient domain. We show that the resulting Hamiltonian Neural Solver (HNS) can be an effective surrogate model through improved stability and conserving energy-like quantities across 1D and 2D PDEs. This ability to respect conservation laws also allows HNS models to better generalize to longer time horizons or unseen initial conditions.

arxiv_record.comments: Published at NeurIPS 2025. Code and datasets are at http://github.com/anthonyzhou-1/hamiltonian_pdes/tree/main

arxiv_record.abstract: Learning the underlying dynamics of single cells from snapshot data has gained increasing attention in scientific and machine learning research. The destructive measurement technique and cell proliferation/death result in unpaired and unbalanced data between snapshots, making the learning of the underlying dynamics challenging. In this paper, we propose joint Velocity-Growth Flow Matching (VGFM), a novel paradigm that jointly learns state transition and mass growth of single-cell populations via flow matching. VGFM builds an ideal single-cell dynamics containing velocity of state and growth of mass, driven by a presented two-period dynamic understanding of the static semi-relaxed optimal transport, a mathematical tool that seeks the coupling between unpaired and unbalanced data. To enable practical usage, we approximate the ideal dynamics using neural networks, forming our joint velocity and growth matching framework. A distribution fitting loss is also employed in VGFM to further improve the fitting performance for snapshot data. Extensive experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that VGFM can capture the underlying biological dynamics accounting for mass and state variations over time, outperforming existing approaches for single-cell dynamics modeling.
arxiv_record.authors: Dongyi Wang, Yuanwei Jiang, Zhenyi Zhang, Xiang Gu, Peijie Zhou, Jian Sun

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: joint velocity–growth modeling derived from semi-relaxed optimal transport, accurate state/mass reconstruction, and improved scalability and training efficiency. The added experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds a Malthusian-growth rationale for time-independent growth, an accumulated-error explanation for distribution fitting, and spatial/temporal interpretations of predictive uncertainty. Appendix B.8 links learned growth and gene-gradient rankings to Acinar/Ductal proliferation, adding substantive biological interpretation. The existing limitations concerning simulation dependence and potentially misleading observed cell counts remain.

D1.justification: v2 changes the code-release promise into a stated release with a concrete repository link in the abstract and checklist. Appendix B.6 newly identifies POT/emd and GeomLoss and explains gradient handling; new analyses document dropout, resampling and gene-selection details. Most architecture, batching and preprocessing information was already present in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds developing mouse Pancreas data at days 14.5 and 15.5, evaluated using 2,000 highly variable genes, extending real biological coverage beyond the retained embeddings. It also introduces a biased-observation scenario by perturbing simulated branch proportions. Simulation Gene, Dyngen, Gaussian, EB, CITE and mouse hematopoiesis coverage remains.

E2.justification: Table 2 removes WLF-UOT from the EB/CITE hold-out comparison while retaining the other named comparators. Tables 3 and A-10 introduce comparisons with Sinkhorn-loss variants. The mouse hematopoiesis comparator set is unchanged, matching v1 Table A-6 to v2 Table A-9.

E3.justification: Section 4 revises the warm-up learning rate from 10^-4 to 10^-3 and the general warm-up schedule from 200–800 iterations to 500 for synthetic and 5,000 for real datasets. Appendices change Simulation Gene epsilon from 0.001 to 0.003, EB/CITE tau from 30 to 5, Dyngen batch size from 32 to 60, and hematopoiesis fitting epochs from 50 to 100. New analyses introduce additional evaluation protocols. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices B.2, B.6 and B.8 add intermediate-time growth-rate validation, branch/time uncertainty analysis, sampling-bias robustness, Sinkhorn regularization sensitivity, and Pancreas mean–variance and gene-attribution analyses. The Pancreas experiment also tests the distribution-fitting loss. v1's CITE training/hold-out loss curves in Figure A-14 are replaced by a with/without-loss trajectory comparison; the EB convergence analysis remains.

E5.justification: v1 lacks predictive uncertainty estimation or explicit repeated-seed reporting. v2 introduces variance estimation using dropout at rate 0.1 with five stochastic forward passes and reports sampling-bias results averaged over three random seeds (Tables A-7–A-8). This substantially adds statistical estimation, although main benchmark tables still lack error bars or significance tests. It does not establish increased run counts for retained benchmarks.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises VGFM's CITE W1 values from 0.650/34.182 to 0.745/37.386 and DeepRUOT's from 0.648/35.539 to 0.845/38.681; OT-MFM now leads both CITE columns. These accompany changed training settings and are not controlled across-version performance differences. Table 1 replaces UDSB's Gaussian W1/RME of 25.304/0.965 with nonconvergence. Substantial additions include Pancreas W1/RME of 24.416/0.017, growth correlations of 0.980–0.996, uncertainty and bias results, and Sinkhorn-variant scores and timing.

M1.justification: v2 adds VGFM(*), which replaces the original Wasserstein distribution-fitting loss with Sinkhorn divergence (Table 3; Appendix B.6). Appendix B.2 also introduces dropout-based uncertainty inference. These are limited adaptations; the original semi-relaxed transport construction, joint matching formulation and training algorithm remain.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. v2 expands explanations in Sections 3.4 and A.4, adds focused experimental subsections and Appendix B.8, and includes acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist. These are localized narrative and structural extensions rather than a broad rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with five new experimental tables and Pancreas Figures A-15–A-18. Figure 2 is redrawn and relabeled, several trajectory plots are revised, Table 3 gains a variant row, and Figure A-14 replaces CITE loss curves with trajectory comparisons. The existing hematopoiesis table is merely renumbered from A-6 to A-9.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds optimal-transport application context, and references expand to recent unbalanced-dynamics work, Malthusian growth, Sinkhorn divergences and the Pancreas dataset. The Deep Momentum Multi-Marginal Schrödinger Bridge citation is removed. The central positioning against velocity-only flow matching and existing unbalanced dynamics models remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 corrects Equation A-15 by restoring the density factor p_t(x) inside the Benamou–Brenier kinetic-energy integral. The central proposition, endpoint-equivalence theorem, their proofs and the growth-energy minimization argument remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for biological applicability and reliability: it adds real 2,000-gene evaluation and interpretation, directly quantifies growth accuracy at unseen times, and tests sensitivity to biased observations. arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, equivariant neural networks for policy learning have shown promising improvements in sample efficiency and generalization, however, their wide adoption faces substantial barriers due to implementation complexity. Equivariant architectures typically require specialized mathematical formulations and custom network design, posing significant challenges when integrating with modern policy frameworks like diffusion-based models. In this paper, we explore a number of straightforward and practical approaches to incorporate symmetry benefits into diffusion policies without the overhead of full equivariant designs. Specifically, we investigate (i) invariant representations via relative trajectory actions and eye-in-hand perception, (ii) integrating equivariant vision encoders, and (iii) symmetric feature extraction with pretrained encoders using Frame Averaging. We first prove that combining eye-in-hand perception with relative or delta action parameterization yields inherent SE(3)-invariance, thus improving policy generalization. We then perform a systematic experimental study on those design choices for integrating symmetry in diffusion policies, and conclude that an invariant representation with equivariant feature extraction significantly improves the policy performance. Our method achieves performance on par with or exceeding fully equivariant architectures while greatly simplifying implementation.
arxiv_record.authors: Dian Wang, Boce Hu, Shuran Song, Robin Walters, Robert Platt
arxiv_record.title: A Practical Guide for Incorporating Symmetry in Diffusion Policy

E1.justification: Both versions use the same MimicGen tasks, Robomimic demonstration populations, and ImageNet-1k pretraining source. The new experiments reuse existing tasks and camera configurations; they expand model comparisons and controls rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The existing Diffusion Policy and image/voxel EquiDiff comparisons remain. Table 5 adds an encoder-augmented EquiDiff variant alongside ordinary EquiDiff and Diffusion Policy variants; the other added comparisons predominantly reuse existing method families.

E3.justification: Appendices E–H substantially expand the controlled evaluation design across encoder, camera, and action configurations, including proprioception removal, C2/C4/C8 groups, and EquiDiff with only an in-hand camera. The principal demonstration budgets and evaluation schedule remain unchanged. Appendix C also qualifies v1's general two-observation-step setting: pretrained variants use one visual step and two proprioceptive steps, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's action-representation and encoder comparisons, v3 adds targeted component ablations, proprioception removal, symmetry-group sensitivity, and EquiDiff camera controls in Tables 6–9. Appendices E–F additionally test whether encoder benefits transfer across observation/action configurations and policy architectures.

E5.justification: Existing three-seed means and standard errors are retained, and the checklist repeats this practice. However, new Tables 7–8 report only point estimates, making uncertainty reporting uneven despite the checklist's claim that all experiments include standard errors. No increased run count or new significance procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 are unchanged, but Tables 4–9 add substantial results. arxiv_record.abstract: We study Transformers through the perspective of optimal control theory, using tools from continuous-time formulations to derive actionable insights into training and architecture design. This framework improves the performance of existing Transformer models while providing desirable theoretical guarantees, including generalization and robustness. Our framework is designed to be plug-and-play, enabling seamless integration with established Transformer models and requiring only slight changes to the implementation. We conduct seven extensive experiments on tasks motivated by text generation, sentiment analysis, image classification, and point cloud classification. Experimental results show that the framework improves the test performance of the baselines, while being more parameter-efficient. On character-level text generation with nanoGPT, our framework achieves a 46% reduction in final test loss while using 42% fewer parameters. On GPT-2, our framework achieves a 9.3% reduction in final test loss, demonstrating scalability to larger models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that applies optimal control theory to both the training and architecture of Transformers. It offers a new foundation for systematic, theory-driven improvements and moves beyond costly trial-and-error approaches.

arxiv_record.abstract: As AI systems become more capable, deceptive behaviors can undermine evaluation and mislead users at deployment. Recent work has shown that lie detectors can accurately classify deceptive behavior, but they are not typically used in the training pipeline due to concerns around contamination and objective hacking. We examine these concerns by incorporating a lie detector into the labelling step of LLM post-training and evaluating whether the learned policy is genuinely more honest, or instead learns to fool the lie detector while remaining deceptive. Using DolusChat, a novel 65k-example dataset with paired truthful/deceptive responses, we identify three key factors that determine the honesty of learned policies: amount of exploration during preference learning, lie detector accuracy, and KL regularization strength. We find that preference learning with lie detectors and GRPO can lead to policies which evade lie detectors, with deception rates of over 85\%. However, if the lie detector true positive rate (TPR) or KL regularization is sufficiently high, GRPO learns honest policies. In contrast, off-policy algorithms (DPO) consistently lead to deception rates under 25\% for realistic TPRs. Our results illustrate a more complex picture than previously assumed: depending on the context, lie-detector-enhanced training can be a powerful tool for scalable oversight, or a counterproductive method encouraging undetectable misalignment.
arxiv_record.authors: Chris Cundy, Adam Gleave
arxiv_record.title: Preference Learning with Lie Detectors can Induce Honesty or Evasion

arxiv_record.abstract: World models predict state transitions in response to actions and are increasingly developed across diverse modalities. However, standard training objectives such as maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) often misalign with task-specific goals of world models, i.e., transition prediction metrics like accuracy or perceptual quality. In this paper, we present RLVR-World, a unified framework that leverages reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) to directly optimize world models for such metrics. Despite formulating world modeling as autoregressive prediction of tokenized sequences, RLVR-World evaluates metrics of decoded predictions as verifiable rewards. We demonstrate substantial performance gains on both language- and video-based world models across domains, including text games, web navigation, and robot manipulation. Our work indicates that, beyond recent advances in reasoning language models, RLVR offers a promising post-training paradigm for enhancing the utility of generative models more broadly. Code, datasets, models, and video samples are available at the project website: https://thuml.github.io/RLVR-World.

arxiv_record.comments: NeurIPS 2025. Code is available at project website: https://thuml.github.io/RLVR-World/

However, standard training objectives such as maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) often misalign with task-specific goals of world models, i.e., transition prediction metrics like accuracy or perceptual quality. In this paper, we present RLVR-World, a unified framework that leverages reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) to directly optimize world models for such metrics. Despite formulating world modeling as autoregressive prediction of tokenized sequences, RLVR-World evaluates metrics of decoded predictions as verifiable rewards. We demonstrate substantial performance gains on both language- and video-based world models across domains, including text games, web navigation, and robot manipulation. Our work indicates that, beyond recent advances in reasoning language models, RLVR offers a promising post-training paradigm for enhancing the utility of generative models more broadly. Code, datasets, models, and video samples are available at the project website: https://thuml.github.io/RLVR-World.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs), such as OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1, have significantly enhanced their reasoning capabilities by generating longer chains of thought, demonstrating outstanding performance across a variety of tasks. However, this performance gain comes at the cost of a substantial increase in redundant reasoning during the generation process, leading to high computational overhead and exacerbating the issue of overthinking. Although numerous existing approaches aim to address the problem of overthinking, they often rely on external interventions. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Self-Braking Tuning (SBT), which tackles overthinking from the perspective of allowing the model to regulate its own reasoning process, thus eliminating the reliance on external control mechanisms. We construct a set of overthinking identification metrics based on standard answers and design a systematic method to detect redundant reasoning. This method accurately identifies unnecessary steps within the reasoning trajectory and generates training signals for learning self-regulation behaviors. Building on this foundation, we develop a complete strategy for constructing data with adaptive reasoning lengths and introduce an innovative braking prompt mechanism that enables the model to naturally learn when to terminate reasoning at an appropriate point. Experiments across mathematical benchmarks (AIME, AMC, MATH500, GSM8K) demonstrate that our method reduces token consumption by up to 60% while maintaining comparable accuracy to unconstrained models.

E3.justification: Added analyses introduce component-removal controls, beta values 0.05–0.2, additional thresholds 0.05, 0.1 and 0.5, and early-exit stratification and average-step measurements. These extend the experimental settings; the retained experiments preserve their model sizes, training budget, temperature 0.7 and eight samples per question.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct masking and no-guidance ablations, beta sensitivity, broader threshold robustness tests, and analyses of spontaneous stopping and reasoning depth. Appendix C also tests transfer from mathematical training to other domains. These substantially expand the investigation beyond v1's retained threshold, masking-length, granularity and guidance comparisons.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging accuracy over eight samples per question. v3 introduces no new seed information, repeated-training-run reporting, confidence intervals, error bars or significance-testing procedures.

For example, v3 Table 4 reports 57.83% accuracy and 1,673 tokens with MRT versus 58.02% and 2,306 without it. New Table 10 reports GPQA-Diamond accuracy of 24.24% for Llama-3.2-1B SBT-E versus its 17.99% baseline; this is a newly reported comparison, not a performance increase over v1.

arxiv_record.abstract: Protein fitness optimization involves finding a protein sequence that maximizes desired quantitative properties in a combinatorially large design space of possible sequences. Recent advances in steering protein generative models (e.g., diffusion models and language models) with labeled data offer a promising approach. However, most previous studies have optimized surrogate rewards and/or utilized large amounts of labeled data for steering, making it unclear how well existing methods perform and compare to each other in real-world optimization campaigns where fitness is measured through low-throughput wet-lab assays. In this study, we explore fitness optimization using small amounts (hundreds) of labeled sequence-fitness pairs and comprehensively evaluate strategies such as classifier guidance and posterior sampling for guiding generation from different discrete diffusion models of protein sequences. We also demonstrate how guidance can be integrated into adaptive sequence selection akin to Thompson sampling in Bayesian optimization, showing that plug-and-play guidance strategies offer advantages over alternatives such as reinforcement learning with protein language models. Overall, we provide practical insights into how to effectively steer modern generative models for next-generation protein fitness optimization.
arxiv_record.authors: Jason Yang, Wenda Chu, Daniel Khalil, Raul Astudillo, Bruce J. Wittmann, Frances H. Arnold, Yisong Yue

arxiv_record.abstract: Many natural systems, including neural circuits involved in decision making, are modeled as high-dimensional dynamical systems with multiple stable states. While existing analytical tools primarily describe behavior near stable equilibria, characterizing separatrices--the manifolds that delineate boundaries between different basins of attraction--remains challenging, particularly in high-dimensional settings. Here, we introduce a numerical framework leveraging Koopman Theory combined with Deep Neural Networks to effectively characterize separatrices. Specifically, we approximate Koopman Eigenfunctions (KEFs) associated with real positive eigenvalues, which vanish precisely at the separatrices. Utilizing these scalar KEFs, optimization methods efficiently locate separatrices even in complex systems. We demonstrate our approach on synthetic benchmarks, ecological network models, and high-dimensional recurrent neural networks trained on either neuroscience-inspired tasks or fit to real neural data. Moreover, we illustrate the practical utility of our method by designing optimal perturbations that can shift systems across separatrices, enabling predictions relevant to optogenetic stimulation experiments in neuroscience.
arxiv_record.authors: Kabir V. Dabholkar, Omri Barak
arxiv_record.title: Finding separatrices of dynamical flows with Deep Koopman Eigenfunctions

arxiv_record.abstract: Policy exploration is critical in reinforcement learning (RL), where existing approaches include greedy, Gaussian process, etc. However, these approaches utilize preset stochastic processes and are indiscriminately applied in all kinds of RL tasks without considering task-specific features that influence policy exploration. Moreover, during RL training, the evolution of such stochastic processes is rigid, which typically only incorporates a decay in the variance, failing to adjust flexibly according to the agent's real-time learning status. Inspired by the analyzing and reasoning capability of large language models (LLMs), we design LLM-Explorer to adaptively generate task-specific exploration strategies with LLMs, enhancing the policy exploration in RL. In our design, we sample the learning trajectory of the agent during the RL training in a given task and prompt the LLM to analyze the agent's current policy learning status and then generate a probability distribution for future policy exploration. Updating the probability distribution periodically, we derive a stochastic process specialized for the particular task and dynamically adjusted to adapt to the learning process. Our design is a plug-in module compatible with various widely applied RL algorithms, including the DQN series, DDPG, TD3, and any possible variants developed based on them. Through extensive experiments on the Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, we demonstrate LLM-Explorer's capability to enhance RL policy exploration, achieving an average performance improvement up to 37.27%. Our code is open-source at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/LLM-Explorer for reproducibility.
arxiv_record.authors: Qianyue Hao, Yiwen Song, Qingmin Liao, Jian Yuan, Yong Li
arxiv_record.title: LLM-Explorer: A Plug-in Reinforcement Learning Policy Exploration Enhancement Driven by Large Language Models

arxiv_record.abstract: Algorithmic fairness has emerged as a central issue in ML, and it has become standard practice to adjust ML algorithms so that they will satisfy fairness requirements such as Equal Opportunity. In this paper we consider the effects of adopting such fair classifiers on the overall level of ecosystem fairness. Specifically, we introduce the study of fairness with competing firms, and demonstrate the failure of fair classifiers in yielding fair ecosystems. Our results quantify the loss of fairness in systems, under a variety of conditions, based on classifiers' correlation and the level of their data overlap. We show that even if competing classifiers are individually fair, the ecosystem's outcome may be unfair; and that adjusting biased algorithms to improve their individual fairness may lead to an overall decline in ecosystem fairness. In addition to these theoretical results, we also provide supporting experimental evidence. Together, our model and results provide a novel and essential call for action.
arxiv_record.authors: Ronen Gradwohl and Eilam Shapira and Moshe Tennenholtz
arxiv_record.title: Fairness under Competition

Specifically, we introduce the study of fairness with competing firms, and demonstrate the failure of fair classifiers in yielding fair ecosystems. Our results quantify the loss of fairness in systems, under a variety of conditions, based on classifiers' correlation and the level of their data overlap. We show that even if competing classifiers are individually fair, the ecosystem's outcome may be unfair; and that adjusting biased algorithms to improve their individual fairness may lead to an overall decline in ecosystem fairness. In addition to these theoretical results, we also provide supporting experimental evidence. Together, our model and results provide a novel and essential call for action.

arxiv_record.abstract:
The attention mechanism is a core primitive in modern large language models (LLMs) and AI more broadly. Since attention by itself is permutation-invariant, position encoding is essential for modeling structured domains such as language. Rotary position encoding (RoPE) has emerged as the de facto standard approach for position encoding and is part of many modern LLMs. However, in RoPE the key/query transformation between two elements in a sequence is only a function of their relative position and otherwise independent of the actual input. This limits the expressivity of RoPE-based transformers.
  This paper describes PaTH, a flexible data-dependent position encoding scheme based on accumulated products of Householder(like) transformations, where each transformation is data-dependent, i.e., a function of the input. We derive an efficient parallel algorithm for training through exploiting a compact representation of products of Householder matrices, and implement a FlashAttention-style blockwise algorithm. Across both targeted synthetic benchmarks and moderate-scale real-world language modeling experiments, we find that PaTH improves upon RoPE and other recent baselines. Finally, we show that we can convert pretrained RoPE transformers into PaTH with continued pretraining.
arxiv_record.authors: Songlin Yang, Yikang Shen, Kaiyue Wen, Shawn Tan, Mayank Mishra, Liliang Ren, Rameswar Panda, Yoon Kim

The preprint footer becomes a NeurIPS 2025 conference footer. These edits do not amount to extensive rewriting or reorganization.

R1.justification: v2 adds RADLADS as the conversion precedent, references for new data and models, and connections to ENTP and Causal Attention with Lookahead Keys. It shortens the positional-encoding survey and removes several references, including Cable, ModuleFormer, and the automata-cascade citations. The central positioning relative to RoPE, algebraic positional encodings, and linear RNNs remains.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical applicability by demonstrating conversion of existing 1.7B and 7B models, addressing a question left open by v1's 760M training-from-scratch experiments. arxiv_record.abstract: Building generative models for relational databases (RDBs) is important for many applications, such as privacy-preserving data release and augmenting real datasets. However, most prior works either focus on single-table generation or adapt single-table models to the multi-table setting by relying on autoregressive factorizations and sequential generation. These approaches limit parallelism, restrict flexibility in downstream applications, and compound errors due to commonly made conditional independence assumptions. In this paper, we propose a fundamentally different approach: jointly modeling all tables in an RDB without imposing any table order. By using a natural graph representation of RDBs, we propose the Graph-Conditional Relational Diffusion Model (GRDM), which leverages a graph neural network to jointly denoise row attributes and capture complex inter-table dependencies. Extensive experiments on six real-world RDBs demonstrate that our approach substantially outperforms autoregressive baselines in modeling multi-hop inter-table correlations and achieves state-of-the-art performance on single-table fidelity metrics. Our code is available at https://github.com/ketatam/rdb-diffusion.

arxiv_record.comments: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)

The additional experiments support practical applications without redefining these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of dimension tables as fixed metadata, graph-generator adequacy and its limits on more strongly correlated structures, DCR evidence concerning memorization, and size invariance from local GNN processing. These extend interpretation and applicability boundaries beyond v1's receptive-field discussion and general future-work paragraph.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code repository link and states that reproduction instructions are available there. It documents dimension-table selection and counts, revised model and training configurations, and a hardware change from RTX 2080 Ti to A100-PCIE-40GB. Appendix E adds experimental procedures and reports generation within two hours for the scaling experiments.

E1.justification: The six synthesis databases remain unchanged, but Appendix E.2 extends evaluated task coverage to conditional missing-value imputation on California. It tests missing parent or child tables and missing rows or cells; v1 mentioned imputation only as a potential application.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains SDV, SingleTable, Denorm, and ClavaDDPM with unchanged participation. Within Table 2, a real-graph comparison variant replaces the separate neighborhood-size comparison, while Sequential remains. The comparator change is therefore confined to internal variants; new privacy and structural comparisons reuse ClavaDDPM.

E3.justification: v2 uses K = 1 throughout instead of K = 2 on three databases, increases GNN width from 128 to 256, reduces MLP depth for small tables, and changes GRDM's batch size from 1024 to 4096. New protocols introduce holdout-based imputation with masking, DCR and structural metrics, and 0.5x–10x size experiments using smaller MLPs.

E4.justification: The K = 1 versus K = 2 sensitivity study is removed. v2 adds real-versus-generated graph ablations across all six databases, a memorization/privacy sanity check, higher-order structural analysis, masking experiments, and size-extrapolation tests. These substantially broaden the questions examined beyond the retained joint-versus-sequential ablation.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains standard deviations over three seeds. v2's checklist newly specifies that Table 2 also reports averages and standard deviations across three seeds; v1 displayed its uncertainty without explicitly specifying the ablation run count. E6.justification: Table 1 changes 24 of 28 GRDM mean/standard-deviation entries while retaining every baseline value. For example, Berka 3-hop fidelity changes from 93.13 ± 0.47 to 92.43 ± 0.69 under revised settings, so this is not a controlled performance decline. Neighborhood-size results disappear, while Tables 4–9 add privacy, imputation, graph, and scaling outcomes.

M1.justification: Section 3.5 adds dimension-table conditioning: whereas v1 describes noising and generating all rows, v2 keeps detected dimension tables fixed at t = 0 during training and sampling. P1.justification: The abstract and introductory prose are polished, method explanations are clarified, and cross-references are updated. A dimension-table subsection, related-work and experiment appendices, broader-impact text, and a checklist are inserted. The existing scientific narrative and most methodological prose remain intact rather than undergoing extensive rewriting.

arxiv_record.abstract: While recent diffusion-based generative image codecs have shown impressive performance, their iterative sampling process introduces unpleasing latency. In this work, we revisit the design of a diffusion-based codec and argue that multi-step sampling is not necessary for generative compression. Based on this insight, we propose OneDC, a One-step Diffusion-based generative image Codec -- that integrates a latent compression module with a one-step diffusion generator. Recognizing the critical role of semantic guidance in one-step diffusion, we propose using the hyperprior as a semantic signal, overcoming the limitations of text prompts in representing complex visual content. To further enhance the semantic capability of the hyperprior, we introduce a semantic distillation mechanism that transfers knowledge from a pretrained generative tokenizer to the hyperprior codec. Additionally, we adopt a hybrid pixel- and latent-domain optimization to jointly enhance both reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneDC achieves SOTA perceptual quality even with one-step generation, offering over 39% bitrate reduction and 20x faster decoding compared to prior multi-step diffusion-based codecs. Project: https://onedc-codec.github.io/

arxiv_record.abstract: One persistent challenge in LLM research is the development of attention mechanisms that are able to generalise from training on shorter contexts to inference on longer contexts. We propose two conditions that we expect all effective long context attention mechanisms to have: scale-invariant total attention, and scale-invariant attention sparsity. Under a Gaussian assumption, we show that a simple position-dependent transformation of the attention logits is sufficient for these conditions to hold. Experimentally we find that the resulting scale-invariant attention scheme gives considerable benefits in terms of validation loss when zero-shot generalising from training on short contexts to validation on longer contexts, and is effective at long-context retrieval.
arxiv_record.authors: Ben Anson and Xi Wang and Laurence Aitchison
arxiv_record.title: Scale-invariant Attention

arxiv_record.abstract: With the growing demand for deploying large language models (LLMs) across diverse applications, improving their inference efficiency is crucial for sustainable and democratized access. However, retraining LLMs to meet new user-specific requirements is prohibitively expensive and environmentally unsustainable. In this work, we propose a practical and scalable alternative: composing efficient hybrid language models from existing pre-trained models. Our approach, Zebra-Llama, introduces a family of 1B, 3B, and 8B hybrid models by combining State Space Models (SSMs) and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) layers, using a refined initialization and post-training pipeline to efficiently transfer knowledge from pre-trained Transformers. Zebra-Llama achieves Transformer-level accuracy with near-SSM efficiency using only 7-11B training tokens (compared to trillions of tokens required for pre-training) and an 8B teacher. Moreover, Zebra-Llama dramatically reduces KV cache size -down to 3.9%, 2%, and 2.73% of the original for the 1B, 3B, and 8B variants, respectively-while preserving 100%, 100%, and >97% of average zero-shot performance on LM Harness tasks. Compared to models like MambaInLLaMA, X-EcoMLA, Minitron, and Llamba, Zebra-Llama consistently delivers competitive or superior accuracy while using significantly fewer tokens, smaller teachers, and vastly reduced KV cache memory. Notably, Zebra-Llama-8B surpasses Minitron-8B in few-shot accuracy by 7% while using 8x fewer training tokens, over 12x smaller KV cache, and a smaller teacher (8B vs. 15B). It also achieves 2.6x-3.8x higher throughput (tokens/s) than MambaInLlama up to a 32k context length. We will release code and model checkpoints upon acceptance.
arxiv_record.authors: Mingyu Yang, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Guihong Li, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
arxiv_record.title: Zebra-Llama: Towards Extremely Efficient Hybrid Models

arxiv_record.abstract: Token embeddings play a crucial role in language modeling but, despite this practical relevance, their theoretical understanding remains limited. Our paper addresses the gap by characterizing the structure of embeddings obtained via gradient descent. Specifically, we consider a one-layer softmax attention model with a linear head for binary classification, i.e., $\texttt{Softmax}( p^\top E_X^\top ) E_X v = \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^T \exp(p^\top E_{x_i}) E_{x_i}^\top v}{\sum_{j=1}^T \exp(p^\top E_{x_{j}}) }$, where $E_X = [ E_{x_1} , \dots, E_{x_T} ]^\top$ contains the embeddings of the input sequence, $p$ is the embedding of the $\mathrm{\langle cls \rangle}$ token and $v$ the output vector. First, we show that, already after a single step of gradient training with the logistic loss, the embeddings $E_X$ capture the importance of tokens in the dataset by aligning with the output vector $v$ proportionally to the frequency with which the corresponding tokens appear in the dataset. Then, after training $p$ via gradient flow until convergence, the softmax selects the important tokens in the sentence (i.e., those that are predictive of the label), and the resulting $\mathrm{\langle cls \rangle}$ embedding maximizes the margin for such a selection. Experiments on real-world datasets (IMDB, Yelp) exhibit a phenomenology close to that unveiled by our theory.

arxiv_record.abstract: Restoring images degraded by adverse weather remains a significant challenge due to the highly non-uniform and spatially heterogeneous nature of weather-induced artifacts, e.g., fine-grained rain streaks versus widespread haze. Accurately estimating the underlying degradation can intuitively provide restoration models with more targeted and effective guidance, enabling adaptive processing strategies. To this end, we propose a Morton-Order Degradation Estimation Mechanism (MODEM) for adverse weather image restoration. Central to MODEM is the Morton-Order 2D-Selective-Scan Module (MOS2D), which integrates Morton-coded spatial ordering with selective state-space models to capture long-range dependencies while preserving local structural coherence. Complementing MOS2D, we introduce a Dual Degradation Estimation Module (DDEM) that disentangles and estimates both global and local degradation priors. These priors dynamically condition the MOS2D modules, facilitating adaptive and context-aware restoration. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that MODEM achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks and weather types, highlighting its effectiveness in modeling complex degradation dynamics. Our code will be released at https://github.com/hainuo-wang/MODEM.git.
arxiv_record.authors: Hainuo Wang, Qiming Hu, Xiaojie Guo
arxiv_record.title: MODEM: A Morton-Order Degradation Estimation Mechanism for Adverse Weather Image Recovery

arxiv_record.abstract: Scaling deep reinforcement learning in pixel-based environments presents a significant challenge, often resulting in diminished performance. While recent works have proposed algorithmic and architectural approaches to address this, the underlying cause of the performance drop remains unclear. In this paper, we identify the connection between the output of the encoder (a stack of convolutional layers) and the ensuing dense layers as the main underlying factor limiting scaling capabilities; we denote this connection as the bottleneck, and we demonstrate that previous approaches implicitly target this bottleneck. As a result of our analyses, we present global average pooling as a simple yet effective way of targeting the bottleneck, thereby avoiding the complexity of earlier approaches.

arxiv_record.abstract: The quality of foundation models depends heavily on their training data. Consequently, great efforts have been put into dataset curation. Yet most approaches rely on manual tuning of coarse-grained mixtures of large buckets of data, or filtering by hand-crafted heuristics. An approach that is ultimately more scalable (let alone more satisfying) is to \emph{learn} which data is actually valuable for training. This type of meta-learning could allow more sophisticated, fine-grained, and effective curation. Our proposed \emph{DataRater} is an instance of this idea. It estimates the value of training on any particular data point. This is done by meta-learning using `meta-gradients', with the objective of improving training efficiency on held out data. In extensive experiments across a range of model scales and datasets, we find that using our DataRater to filter data is highly effective, resulting in significantly improved compute efficiency.

arxiv_record.abstract: Tabular data have been playing a vital role in diverse real-world fields, including healthcare, finance, etc. With the recent success of Large Language Models (LLMs), early explorations of extending LLMs to the domain of tabular data have been developed. Most of these LLM-based methods typically first serialize tabular data into natural language descriptions, and then tune LLMs or directly infer on these serialized data. However, these methods suffer from two key inherent issues: (i) data perspective: existing data serialization methods lack universal applicability for structured tabular data, and may pose privacy risks through direct textual exposure, and (ii) model perspective: LLM fine-tuning methods struggle with tabular data, and in-context learning scalability is bottle-necked by input length constraints (suitable for few-shot learning). This work explores a novel direction of integrating LLMs into tabular data throughough logical decision tree rules as intermediaries, proposes a decision tree enhancer with LLM-derived rule for tabular prediction, DeLTa. The proposed DeLTa avoids tabular data serialization, and can be applied to full data learning setting without LLM fine-tuning. Specifically, we leverage the reasoning ability of LLMs to redesign an improved rule given a set of decision tree rules. Furthermore, we provide a calibration method for original decision trees via new generated rule by LLM, which approximates the error correction vector to steer the original decision tree predictions in the direction of ``errors'' reducing. Finally, extensive experiments on diverse tabular benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Hangting Ye, Jinmeng Li, He Zhao, Dandan Guo, Yi Chang
arxiv_record.title: LLM Meeting Decision Trees on Tabular Data

Furthermore, we provide a calibration method for original decision trees via new generated rule by LLM, which approximates the error correction vector to steer the original decision tree predictions in the direction of ``errors'' reducing. Finally, extensive experiments on diverse tabular benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

arxiv_record.abstract: Given a large pool of unlabelled data and a smaller amount of labels, prediction-powered inference (PPI) leverages machine learning predictions to increase the statistical efficiency of confidence interval procedures based solely on labelled data, while preserving fixed-time validity. In this paper, we extend the PPI framework to the sequential setting, where labelled and unlabelled datasets grow over time. Exploiting Ville's inequality and the method of mixtures, we propose prediction-powered confidence sequence procedures that are asymptotically valid uniformly over time and naturally accommodate prior knowledge on the quality of the predictions to further boost efficiency. We carefully illustrate the design choices behind our method and demonstrate its effectiveness in real and synthetic examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: While deep learning has achieved remarkable success across many domains, it has historically underperformed on tabular learning tasks, which remain dominated by gradient boosting decision trees. However, recent advancements are paving the way for Tabular Foundation Models, which can leverage real-world knowledge and generalize across diverse datasets, particularly when the data contains free-text. Although incorporating language model capabilities into tabular tasks has been explored, most existing methods utilize static, target-agnostic textual representations, limiting their effectiveness. We introduce TabSTAR: a Tabular Foundation Model with Semantically Target-Aware Representations. TabSTAR is designed to enable transfer learning on tabular data with textual features, with an architecture free of dataset-specific parameters. It unfreezes a pretrained text encoder and takes as input target tokens, which provide the model with the context needed to learn task-specific embeddings. TabSTAR achieves state-of-the-art performance for both medium- and large-sized datasets across known benchmarks of classification tasks with text features, and its pretraining phase exhibits scaling laws in the number of datasets, offering a pathway for further performance improvements.
arxiv_record.authors: Alan Arazi, Eilam Shapira, Roi Reichart
arxiv_record.title: TabSTAR: A Tabular Foundation Model for Tabular Data with Text Fields

arxiv_record.abstract: Many real-world problems require reasoning across multiple scales, demanding models which operate not on single data points, but on entire distributions. We introduce generative distribution embeddings (GDE), a framework that lifts autoencoders to the space of distributions. In GDEs, an encoder acts on sets of samples, and the decoder is replaced by a generator which aims to match the input distribution. This framework enables learning representations of distributions by coupling conditional generative models with encoder networks which satisfy a criterion we call distributional invariance. We show that GDEs learn predictive sufficient statistics embedded in the Wasserstein space, such that latent GDE distances approximately recover the $W_2$ distance, and latent interpolation approximately recovers optimal transport trajectories for Gaussian and Gaussian mixture distributions. We systematically benchmark GDEs against existing approaches on synthetic datasets, demonstrating consistently stronger performance. arxiv_record.abstract: Generating realistic brain connectivity matrices is key to analyzing population heterogeneity in brain organization, understanding disease, and augmenting data in challenging classification problems. Functional connectivity matrices lie in constrained spaces, such as the set of symmetric positive definite or correlation matrices, that can be modeled as Riemannian manifolds. However, using Riemannian tools typically requires redefining core operations (geodesics, norms, integration), making generative modeling computationally inefficient. In this work, we propose DiffeoCFM, an approach that enables conditional flow matching (CFM) on matrix manifolds by exploiting pullback metrics induced by global diffeomorphisms on Euclidean spaces. We show that Riemannian CFM with such metrics is equivalent to applying standard CFM after data transformation. This equivalence allows efficient vector field learning, and fast sampling with standard ODE solvers. We instantiate DiffeoCFM with two different settings: the matrix logarithm for covariance matrices and the normalized Cholesky decomposition for correlation matrices. We evaluate DiffeoCFM on three large-scale fMRI datasets with more than 4600 scans from 2800 subjects (ADNI, ABIDE, OASIS-3) and two EEG motor imagery datasets with over 30000 trials from 26 subjects (BNCI2014-002 and BNCI2015-001). It enables fast training and achieves state-of-the-art performance, all while preserving manifold constraints. Code: https://github.com/antoinecollas/DiffeoCFM
arxiv_record.authors: Antoine Collas, Ce Ju, Nicolas Salvy, Bertrand Thirion
arxiv_record.title: Riemannian Flow Matching for Brain Connectivity Matrices via Pullback Geometry

Added evidence supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds uncertainty about alternative connectivity estimators, including partial correlations and graphical-Lasso precision, and strengthens the dimensionality limitation to exponential sample-complexity growth. Section 3.2 also explains the embeddings' selection for simplicity and identifies alternatives. These refine applicability and interpretation without changing the central conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 adds project-code and implementation links, RIEMCFM configuration details, and the One-Class SVM explanation for the already-used EvaGeM evaluator. Most existing training and hardware details move into Section 4.3. Conversely, v1's explicit affine-invariant tangent-space preprocessing description for CAS is omitted; this does not establish that the preprocessing itself changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ABIDE, ADNI, OASIS-3, BNCI2014-002, and BNCI2015-001, retaining the same disease-classification and motor-imagery tasks and simulated-SPD scalability study. The new architecture experiments use the existing ABIDE coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds affine-invariant RIEMCFM to both EEG comparisons in Table 1, providing an important direct manifold-based comparator. v1 discussed Riemannian CFM but excluded it as inapplicable. Existing comparators, including the separate SPD-DDPM timing comparison, are retained.

E3.justification: The reported integration setting changes from fixed-step midpoint to dopri5. Added experiments specify RIEMCFM's six-layer network and learning rate, and ABIDE sweeps over widths 8–1024 and one to four hidden layers. Figure 3 additionally summarizes performance through an average of quality F1 and CAS F1. These are bounded extensions within the retained evaluation framework.

E4.justification: New Appendix K systematically tests sensitivity to network width and depth, reporting quality and computational costs in Tables 3–4. This adds substantive evidence for the chosen shallow, 512-unit architecture that v1 lacked. Existing projection, constraint-satisfaction, and neurophysiological analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: v2 increases the reported fMRI repetitions from five to ten subject-grouped splits and newly explains EEG standard deviations as computed over five inner splits and averaged over sessions. Table 1 adds one-sided paired Wilcoxon tests at alpha = 0.05, replacing bolding of numerical winners with significance-aware comparisons. Mean and standard-deviation reporting already existed in v1.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds RIEMCFM outcomes and training/sampling times, while Tables 3–4 add architecture-sensitivity results. Existing scores also change: DIFFEOCFM's ADNI CAS F1 is 0.35 ± 0.09 in v1 and 0.47 ± 0.10 in v2. These are revised results under changed reported settings, not an established same-setting gain. The OASIS-3 connectome panel is also replaced.

M1.justification: The pullback-CFM formulation, embeddings, objectives, and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. However, the reported numerical sampling procedure changes from midpoint integration with step size 10^-3 in v1 Appendix J to dopri5 in v2 Section 4.3, constituting a limited inference-procedure revision.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained. Changes include localized explanatory additions, moving implementation details into the main text, reorganizing appendices, revising the conclusion heading, and appending a NeurIPS checklist. These do not amount to a broad scientific rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially redesigned with runtime columns, RIEMCFM rows, highlighted DIFFEOCFM rows, and revised bolding. v2 adds the performance-versus-cost Figure 3 and two ablation tables, and adopts NeurIPS formatting throughout. Figure 9b replaces v1 Figure 8b's duplicated ABIDE imagery with a distinct OASIS-3 panel; most other figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: Related work adds connections to Lie-group reparameterization, manifold diffusion processes, and metric flow matching, including acknowledgment of an earlier precursor. The baseline discussion corrects v1's characterization of Riemannian CFM as inapplicable, recognizing its usable but costlier SPD implementation. The overall novelty positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Propositions 1–3 and their proofs remain substantively identical, as do the pullback identities, affine-invariant quotient geometry, and projection derivation. Discussion of alternative embeddings and dimensionality limitations does not introduce a new formal result.

improvement.justification: The direct RIEMCFM comparison resolves an important baseline gap in v1 and substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency claim at similar EEG generation quality. arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a dominant AI paradigm due to their exceptional text understanding and generation capabilities. However, their tendency to generate inconsistent or erroneous outputs challenges their reliability, especially in high-stakes domains requiring accuracy and trustworthiness. Existing research primarily focuses on detecting and mitigating model misbehavior in general-purpose scenarios, often overlooking the potential of integrating domain-specific knowledge. In this work, we advance misbehavior detection by incorporating domain knowledge. The core idea is to design a general specification language that enables domain experts to customize domain-specific predicates in a lightweight and intuitive manner, supporting later runtime verification of LLM outputs. To achieve this, we design a novel specification language, ESL, and introduce a runtime verification framework, RvLLM, to validate LLM output against domain-specific constraints defined in ESL. We evaluate RvLLM on three representative tasks: violation detection against Singapore Rapid Transit Systems Act, numerical comparison, and inequality solving. Experimental results demonstrate that RvLLM effectively detects erroneous outputs across various LLMs in a lightweight and flexible manner. The results reveal that despite their impressive capabilities, LLMs remain prone to low-level errors due to limited interpretability and a lack of formal guarantees during inference, and our framework offers a potential long-term solution by leveraging expert domain knowledge to rigorously and efficiently verify LLM outputs.
arxiv_record.authors: Yedi Zhang, Sun Yi Emma, Annabelle Lee Jia En, Jin Song Dong
arxiv_record.title: RvLLM: LLM Runtime Verification with Domain Knowledge

native_events.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a dominant AI paradigm due to their exceptional text understanding and generation capabilities. However, their tendency to generate inconsistent or erroneous outputs challenges their reliability, especially in high-stakes domains requiring accuracy and trustworthiness. Existing research primarily focuses on detecting and mitigating model misbehavior in general-purpose scenarios, often overlooking the potential of integrating domain-specific knowledge. In this work, we advance misbehavior detection by incorporating domain knowledge. The core idea is to design a general specification language that enables domain experts to customize domain-specific constraints in a lightweight and intuitive manner, supporting later runtime monitoring of LLM outputs. To achieve this, we design a novel specification language ESL, and introduce a runtime verification framework RvLLM to validate LLM output against domain-specific constraints defined in ESL. RvLLM operates in two main stages: interpretation and reasoning. During interpretation, it derives interpretations of the specification based on the context, which then guide the reasoning process to identify inconsistencies. When new knowledge is derived, RvLLM issues a follow-up query to the LLM to further verify the consistency. We evaluate RvLLM on three representative tasks: violation detection against Singapore Rapid Transit Systems Act, numerical comparison, and inequality solving. Experimental results show that RvLLM effectively detects erroneous outputs across various LLMs in a lightweight and flexible manner. The results reveal that despite their impressive capabilities, LLMs remain prone to low-level errors due to a lack of formal guarantees during inference, and our framework offers a potential long-term solution by leveraging expert domain knowledge to rigorously and efficiently verify LLM outputs.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated SelfCheckGPT and domain-constraint prompt augmentation, termed LLM-as-a-judge, across all three tasks (Figure 3 and Tables 3, 9–11). v1 discusses SelfCheckGPT in related work but provides no corresponding experimental comparison. arxiv_record.abstract: The go-to strategy to apply deep networks in settings where uncertainty informs decisions--ensembling multiple training runs with random initializations--is ill-suited for the extremely large-scale models and practical fine-tuning workflows of today. We introduce a new cost-effective strategy for improving the uncertainty quantification and downstream decisions of a large model (e.g. a fine-tuned ViT-B): coupling it with a less accurate but much smaller "sidekick" (e.g. a fine-tuned ResNet-34) with a fraction of the computational cost. We propose aggregating the predictions of this Asymmetric Duo by simple learned weighted averaging. Surprisingly, despite their inherent asymmetry, the sidekick model almost never harms the performance of the larger model. In fact, across five image classification benchmarks and a variety of model architectures and training schemes (including soups), Asymmetric Duos significantly improve accuracy, uncertainty quantification, and selective classification metrics with only ${\sim}10-20\%$ more computation.
arxiv_record.authors: Tim G. Zhou, Evan Shelhamer, Geoff Pleiss
arxiv_record.title: Asymmetric Duos: Sidekicks Improve Uncertainty

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the central claim that a small, appropriately weighted sidekick improves prediction and uncertainty with fractional additional computation. The new comparisons support this existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: v2 attributes advantages over deep ensembles to architectural diversity and temperature aggregation, recommends choosing the strongest affordable base model, and discusses IVON compatibility and Laplace hardware constraints. Some new interpretations overreach: the claimed IVON advantage across all metrics contradicts Table 3, and Table 4 shows lower Laplace AUROC despite the prose claiming improvement.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability statement and repository link, specifies NVIDIA L40S training hardware, documents ensemble checkpoint sources and construction, and describes the last-layer Kronecker-factored Laplace implementation. These extend the existing reproducibility documentation; repository contents were not inspected.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate ImageNet, ImageNet V2, Caltech 256, and in-distribution and out-of-distribution iWildCam classification. New comparisons use these existing datasets. Adding ConvNeXt results on iWildCam expands model configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated pool-then-calibrate ResNet-50 deep ensembles with 2, 5, and 8 members, IVON with deterministic and sampled inference, and last-layer Laplace approximation (Tables 1–4). These substantive comparator families were not evaluated against Duos in v1.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 changes iWildCam linear probing from 5 to 8 epochs, fine-tuning from 10 to 12 epochs, and Caltech fine-tuning from 20 to 16 epochs. Adaptive batch sizing becomes fixed sizes of 128 and 16. Soup construction changes from 32 candidates with 5 selected to 16 candidates with 3 selected. v2 also introduces base-model-controlled and FLOPs-controlled comparisons. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish their execution history.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of ensemble-size and computational-budget scaling, including allocating compute to stronger Duo base models, and examines IVON inference with 2–32 samples. The original unweighted and UQ-only ablations, entropy comparison, and temperature-weight analysis remain.

E5.justification: v2 adds tabular ± summaries and specifies 32 sampled ensemble subsets drawn from 10 independently trained ResNet-50 checkpoints (Appendix A.5). This does not mean 32 independent training runs. The new ± quantities are not explicitly defined; Figure 1's standard deviation across model choices already appeared in v1.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 add substantial comparative results. For example, Table 1 reports accuracy of 81.87±0.19 for ResNet-50 plus EfficientNet-B2 versus 81.97±0.13 for five ResNet-50 ensemble members, at 27% versus 400% additional FLOPs. Numerous existing plots change, and Figure 14 gains ConvNeXt iWildCam results. Revised fine-tuning settings prevent treating affected scores as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains independently trained large and small models combined through two logit weights optimized for validation negative log likelihood. Revised training budgets and additional comparator implementations do not change the Duo algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 adds Section 5.6, Appendix A.5, comparison Appendices E–F, and a NeurIPS checklist, moving full results to Appendix G. Local wording, spelling, affiliation, and publication-header edits accompany these additions; the existing narrative is largely retained.

P2.justification: v2 introduces four multi-metric comparison tables and expands the ConvNeXt result grids from three to five dataset columns. Several plots have revised axes and legends. Figure 8 changes its plotted base-model label and correlation value while retaining an inconsistent caption and discussion.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Laplace Redux and IVON references and positions Duos against these scalable Bayesian approaches. It also clarifies the distinction from Gontijo-Lopes et al. through fine-tuning paired models on the same data. Existing related-work coverage is retained.

T1.justification: The prediction, uncertainty, weighted-logit, and FLOPs-balance definitions remain substantively unchanged. A corrected closing parenthesis is typographical; neither version introduces theoretical results or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 presents Duos as a cheaper alternative to deep ensembles without directly benchmarking that alternative. v2 substantially closes this central evidential gap through calibrated comparisons controlling the base model and inference FLOPs (Tables 1–2), supplemented by Bayesian baselines and additional reproducibility information. Unsupported interpretations of Tables 3–4, undefined ± summaries, and stale Figure 8 text weaken reporting reliability, but do not outweigh the stronger evidence for the paper's central efficiency argument.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Asymmetric Duos research, with readable text, equations, figures, and complete appendices. v1's full-results Appendix E is retained as Appendix G in v2.

arxiv_record.abstract: Flow-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art sample quality, but require the expensive solution of a differential equation at inference time. Flow map models, commonly known as consistency models, encompass many recent efforts to improve inference-time efficiency by learning the solution operator of this differential equation. Yet despite their promise, these models lack a unified description that clearly explains how to learn them efficiently in practice. Here, building on the methodology proposed in Boffi et. al. (2024), we present a systematic algorithmic framework for directly learning the flow map associated with a flow or diffusion model. By exploiting a relationship between the velocity field underlying a continuous-time flow and the instantaneous rate of change of the flow map, we show how to convert any distillation scheme into a direct training algorithm via self-distillation, eliminating the need for pre-trained teachers. We introduce three algorithmic families based on different mathematical characterizations of the flow map: Eulerian, Lagrangian, and Progressive methods, which we show encompass and extend all known distillation and direct training schemes for consistency models. We find that the novel class of Lagrangian methods, which avoid both spatial derivatives and bootstrapping from small steps by design, achieve significantly more stable training and higher performance than more standard Eulerian and Progressive schemes. Our methodology unifies existing training schemes under a single common framework and reveals new design principles for accelerated generative modeling. Associated code is available at https://github.com/nmboffi/flow-maps.
arxiv_record.authors: Nicholas M. Boffi, Michael S. Albergo, and Eric Vanden-Eijnden
arxiv_record.title: How to build a consistency model: Learning flow maps via self-distillation
