C1.justification: The general self-distillation contribution remains, but the headline empirical claim changes. v1 emphasizes avoiding temporal and spatial derivatives for image synthesis, favoring PSD. v2 instead presents Lagrangian methods as more stable and better performing than Eulerian and Progressive methods, and explicitly claims that the framework encompasses all known consistency-model distillation and direct-training schemes.

C2.justification: v2 shifts the explanation toward spatial Jacobians, stopgradient placement, and LSD's avoidance of bootstrapping. It newly attributes PSD's theoretical difficulty to compounding errors and distribution shift (Section 2.3), discusses uncertain convergence of stopgradient updates, and expands limitations concerning untested parameterizations, stabilization choices, hybrid objectives, and guidance. These materially revise the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code link, method-specific pseudocode, a configuration table, explicit histogram-based KL computation, FID checkpoint-selection procedures, EMA values, clipping, and embedding details. arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating scientific hypothesis generation, yet existing approaches primarily yield coarse-grained hypotheses lacking critical methodological and experimental details. We introduce and formally define the new task of fine-grained scientific hypothesis discovery, which entails generating detailed, experimentally actionable hypotheses from coarse initial research directions. We frame this as a combinatorial optimization problem and investigate the upper limits of LLMs' capacity to solve it when maximally leveraged. Specifically, we explore four foundational questions: (1) how to best harness an LLM's internal heuristics to formulate the fine-grained hypothesis it itself would judge as the most promising among all the possible hypotheses it might generate, based on its own internal scoring-thus defining a latent reward landscape over the hypothesis space; (2) whether such LLM-judged better hypotheses exhibit stronger alignment with ground-truth hypotheses; (3) whether shaping the reward landscape using an ensemble of diverse LLMs of similar capacity yields better outcomes than defining it with repeated instances of the strongest LLM among them; and (4) whether an ensemble of identical LLMs provides a more reliable reward landscape than a single LLM. To address these questions, we propose a hierarchical search method that incrementally proposes and integrates details into the hypothesis, progressing from general concepts to specific experimental configurations. We show that this hierarchical process smooths the reward landscape and enables more effective optimization. Empirical evaluations on a new benchmark of expert-annotated fine-grained hypotheses from recent literature show that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines.

arxiv_record.abstract: Securing personal identity against deepfake attacks is increasingly critical in the digital age, especially for celebrities and political figures whose faces are easily accessible and frequently targeted. Most existing deepfake detection methods focus on general-purpose scenarios and often ignore the valuable prior knowledge of known facial identities, e.g., "VIP individuals" whose authentic facial data are already available. In this paper, we propose \textbf{VIPGuard}, a unified multimodal framework designed to capture fine-grained and comprehensive facial representations of a given identity, compare them against potentially fake or similar-looking faces, and reason over these comparisons to make accurate and explainable predictions. Specifically, our framework consists of three main stages. First, fine-tune a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to learn detailed and structural facial attributes. Second, we perform identity-level discriminative learning to enable the model to distinguish subtle differences between highly similar faces, including real and fake variations. Finally, we introduce user-specific customization, where we model the unique characteristics of the target face identity and perform semantic reasoning via MLLM to enable personalized and explainable deepfake detection. Our framework shows clear advantages over previous detection works, where traditional detectors mainly rely on low-level visual cues and provide no human-understandable explanations, while other MLLM-based models often lack a detailed understanding of specific face identities. To facilitate the evaluation of our method, we built a comprehensive identity-aware benchmark called \textbf{VIPBench} for personalized deepfake detection, involving the latest 7 face-swapping and 7 entire face synthesis techniques for generation. The code is available at https://github.com/KQL11/VIPGuard .

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: personalized detection as fine-grained identity recognition, the three-stage multimodal VIPGuard framework, VIPBench, and superior detection and explainability. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability boundaries: sensitivity to head rotations exceeding roughly 50 degrees, age differences, and limited use of audio or temporal information. It also adds interpretations concerning stage synergy, possible token overfitting, transfer enabling annotation-free customization, and semantic cues explaining corruption robustness. These qualifications and mechanisms were not developed in the supplied v1.

D1.justification: Appendices D.1 and E supply previously unavailable optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size, epoch, resizing and prediction-scoring details, plus face filtering, sampling ratios and annotation prompts. TransFace is identified as the default similarity model. The release-on-acceptance promise is supplemented by a code URL and noncommercial, reviewed-request dataset access terms; external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: The underlying training sources, 22-identity VIPEval benchmark, forgery generators, CelebDF and DF40 coverage remain unchanged. v2 adds evaluation under Gaussian noise, blur and JPEG compression, plus automatic identity/token selection when multiple VIPs are protected. These extend input and deployment scenarios within the existing task.

E2.justification: Tables 1–4 retain the same conventional detectors, identity-aware methods and MLLM competitors. The added backbone, face-recognition component and training-stage comparisons vary VIPGuard itself rather than add competing detectors to those benchmark comparisons.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce substantial controlled variation: textual supervision in Stage 3, training-stage combinations, available authentic-image counts, token lengths from 8 to 128, and 3B/7B/11B backbones. Appendix D.4 specifies three intensities for each corruption. These are additional experimental protocols; newly disclosed settings for the retained experiments are reproducibility information rather than evidence of rerunning them.

E4.justification: v1 mentions supplementary ablations but supplies none. v2 provides stage-removal, reference-image-count, token-size, backbone and face-recognition-component analyses, along with annotation-free and adaptive-selection comparisons and corruption robustness tests. Figures 8–11 also add genuine-pair and forgery explanation cases beyond the retained Figure 5 examples.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, detector-training seed studies, confidence intervals, significance tests or error bars. The added results remain point estimates. Varying generation seeds to create synthetic images was already described in v1 and is not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–4 are unchanged. v2 adds extensive results in Tables 5–10 and Figures 6–11, including adaptive selection averaging 98.01% AUC versus 98.23% with supplied tokens, and strongest-noise performance of 94.12%. Table 5 reports image-only customization at 95.86%, but its annotated InSwap value of 99.43% conflicts with 96.40% in Table 1, limiting interpretation of that comparison.

M1.justification: The three-stage VIPGuard architecture remains intact. Appendix D.3 adds Adaptive VIPGuard, which uses face recognition to select the appropriate VIP token automatically. Section 5.1 also introduces a Stage 3 variant without textual annotations. These are limited procedural extensions; expanded attention formulas and implementation disclosures do not establish a redesigned core method.

P1.justification: Most original main-text prose, contribution bullets and the conclusion are retained. Changes include localized copyediting, separating problem formulation from method overview, revising reference/query terminology, adding an annotation-free subsection and appendix roadmap, and updating publication and funding text. The supplementary expansion primarily adds content rather than extensively rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with ablation curves, robustness and variant tables, full explanation conversations, facial-attribute examples, annotation prompts and dataset-construction diagrams. Tables 1–4 are relocated or reformatted while retaining their results; existing diagrams and captions receive smaller revisions. The new displays make previously unavailable analyses and procedures inspectable.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable results across diverse downstream tasks, but their monolithic nature restricts scalability and efficiency in complex problem-solving. While recent research explores multi-agent collaboration among LLMs, most approaches rely on static organizational structures that struggle to adapt as task complexity and agent numbers grow, resulting in coordination overhead and inefficiencies. To this end, we propose a puppeteer-style paradigm for LLM-based multi-agent collaboration, where a centralized orchestrator ("puppeteer") dynamically directs agents ("puppets") in response to evolving task states. This orchestrator is trained via reinforcement learning to adaptively sequence and prioritize agents, enabling flexible and evolvable collective reasoning. Experiments on closed- and open-domain scenarios show that this method achieves superior performance with reduced computational costs. Analyses further reveal that the key improvements consistently stem from the emergence of more compact, cyclic reasoning structures under the orchestrator's evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev/tree/puppeteer.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: dynamic centralized orchestration, reinforcement-driven adaptation, improved quality and efficiency, and emergent compact cyclic structures. The abstract's added code link does not alter these scientific claims.

C2.justification: Appendices A and C add explanations for uneven efficiency gains, possible limitations from optimization budget and hyperparameters, and difficulties comparing training costs across methods. Appendix D newly identifies coarse terminal rewards, a fixed agent/tool pool, miscoordination, and deceptive agreement as limitations. These substantially expand the qualifications surrounding the retained claims.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-repository link, agent/action inventories, and role and action prompt templates in Appendix B. It explicitly documents the 200-sample optimization limit and reports eight A800 GPUs, 28.8–78.4 GB peak memory per GPU, and 2–6 hours of training in Table 3. These substantially improve implementation and resource disclosure.

E1.justification: The four quantitative benchmarks are retained. Appendix A.4 adds ALFWorld embodied interaction, illustrated through one THOR task involving a remote control and floor lamp. This extends coverage to an interactive scenario, but no aggregate ALFWorld evaluation is reported.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same foundation-model comparators, Self-Refine, AFlow, MacNet, and EvoAgent in both model subspaces. The added embodied case study introduces no evaluated comparator; the new related-work citations are not additional baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 adds evaluation using performance divided by token cost. The new ALFWorld case uses a maximum chain length of 50, one exploration trajectory, and GPT-4o-mini for all agents. Existing benchmark settings are unchanged; the explicit 200-sample optimization limit is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: Appendix A substantially expands analysis of efficiency and collaboration: cost dynamics across the remaining model configurations, performance-per-token trajectories, concrete agent-interaction motifs, and an embodied execution case study. The original reward-weight and depth/width sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are supplied. LOWESS smoothing is retained for the additional curves; the computational-resource ranges are not reported as uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 is numerically unchanged, including the evolved Titan Puppeteer average of 0.7731. However, Figures 8–9 add extensive cost, agent-count, and performance/cost trajectories, including settings without consistent improvement. Figures 10–11 add qualitative interaction and embodied-execution evidence, substantially expanding the reported results.

M1.justification: The centralized agent-selection procedure, REINFORCE optimization, aggregation, and quality–cost reward remain unchanged. Appendix B documents agent prompts; Appendix A.4 applies the framework to another environment without introducing a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The main section order and nearly all existing prose are retained. v2 clarifies the explanation accompanying Equation (6), updates contact and conference information, adds an acknowledgement, and organizes new material into appendices. arxiv_record.abstract: Long-context supervised fine-tuning (Long-SFT) plays a vital role in enhancing the performance of large language models (LLMs) on long-context tasks. To smoothly adapt LLMs to long-context scenarios, this process typically entails training on mixed datasets containing both long and short sequences. However, this heterogeneous sequence length distribution poses significant challenges for existing training systems, as they fail to simultaneously achieve high training efficiency for both long and short sequences, resulting in sub-optimal end-to-end system performance in Long-SFT. In this paper, we present a novel perspective on data scheduling to address the challenges posed by the heterogeneous data distributions in Long-SFT. We propose Skrull, a dynamic data scheduler specifically designed for efficient long-SFT. Through dynamic data scheduling, Skrull balances the computation requirements of long and short sequences, improving overall training efficiency. Furthermore, we formulate the scheduling process as a joint optimization problem and thoroughly analyze the trade-offs involved. Based on those analysis, Skrull employs a lightweight scheduling algorithm to achieve near-zero cost online scheduling in Long-SFT. Finally, we implement Skrull upon DeepSpeed, a state-of-the-art distributed training system for LLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that Skrull outperforms DeepSpeed by 3.76x on average (up to 7.54x) in real-world long-SFT scenarios.
arxiv_record.authors: Hongtao Xu, Wenting Shen, Yuanxin Wei, Ang Wang, Guo Runfan, Tianxing Wang, Yong Li, Mingzhen Li, Weile Jia

E3.justification: V2 introduces 14B/32B LoRA configurations, a bucket-size sweep, rollback controls and per-iteration memory measurements. E6.justification: Original Figure 3 values remain, while v2 adds sorted-batching scores, 1.40x versus 1.17x Skrull/RR speedups, rollback-related OOMs, bucket-size results, LoRA speedups of 2.37x/2.54x and similar training-loss curves. Its prose inconsistently attributes 3.76x to both DeepSpeed and sorted batching before separately reporting 3.45x against sorted batching; these should not be treated as equivalent comparisons.

M1.justification: The proposed DACP/GDS scheduling rules, objectives and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. Algorithm 3 makes state arguments explicit and permits an absent load array, without establishing changed behavior for Skrull's normal scheduling path. The added round-robin algorithm is a comparator.

P1.justification: Most introductory, methodological and concluding prose is retained. Changes include localized evaluation and related-work revisions, author affiliations, acknowledgments, small wording corrections and appendix reorganization into precision validation, scheduling algorithms and performance modeling.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 2, adds a comparator series to Figure 3, and replaces the small batch-size plot with a two-panel Figure 4 covering sensitivity and LoRA. It adds two case-study tables and a loss figure. The original FLOPs figure and communication table are retained and relocated. New Table 4's latency caption conflicts with its memory interpretation in the text.

R1.justification: V2 removes the assertion that LongAlign's sorted batching breaks training equivalence and drops the separate ChatQA 2 paper reference while retaining its dataset citation. Several other references receive publication metadata updates, without representing newly cited research.

T1.justification: The scheduling formulations and performance-modeling equations 1–16 are unchanged. V1's performance-modeling Appendix A becomes Appendix C in v2. The new loss comparison supplies empirical validation, not a new mathematical derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked an evaluated competing scheduling strategy, direct rollback validation and a convergence check. V2 addresses these important gaps through sorted-batching comparisons, controlled OOM/memory analyses and training-loss validation, substantially strengthening support for the scheduler's benefits and behavior in the tested settings. Sparse LoRA settings and numerical/caption inconsistencies limit reproducibility and clarity, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Skrull and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be matched reliably across the appendix reorganization and expanded evaluation.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by sorted-batching comparisons, bucket-size and rollback studies, larger-model LoRA results and training-loss validation.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original training-speed measurements on three datasets, DACP/GDS component ablations and batch-size sensitivity experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable success in understanding complex real-world scenarios and supporting data-driven decision-making processes. However, VLMs exhibit significant vulnerability against adversarial examples, either text or image, which can lead to various adversarial outcomes, e.g., jailbreaking, hijacking, and hallucination, etc. In this work, we empirically and theoretically demonstrate that VLMs are particularly susceptible to image-based adversarial examples, where imperceptible perturbations can precisely manipulate each output token. To this end, we propose a novel attack called Vision-language model Manipulation Attack (VMA), which integrates first-order and second-order momentum optimization techniques with a differentiable transformation mechanism to effectively optimize the adversarial perturbation. Notably, VMA can be a double-edged sword: it can be leveraged to implement various attacks, such as jailbreaking, hijacking, privacy breaches, Denial-of-Service, and the generation of sponge examples, etc, while simultaneously enabling the injection of watermarks for copyright protection. Extensive empirical evaluations substantiate the efficacy and generalizability of VMA across diverse scenarios and datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-AI-Group/VMA.
arxiv_record.authors: Xiaosen Wang and Shaokang Wang and Zhijin Ge and Yuyang Luo and Shudong Zhang
arxiv_record.title: Attention! Your Vision Language Model Could Be Maliciously Manipulated

Notably, VMA can be a double-edged sword: it can be leveraged to implement various attacks, such as jailbreaking, hijacking, privacy breaches, Denial-of-Service, and the generation of sponge examples, etc, while simultaneously enabling the injection of watermarks for copyright protection. Extensive empirical evaluations substantiate the efficacy and generalizability of VMA across diverse scenarios and datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-AI-Group/VMA.

arxiv_record.abstract: Dependency parsing is the task of inferring natural language structure, often approached by modeling word interactions via attention through biaffine scoring. This mechanism works like self-attention in Transformers, where scores are calculated for every pair of words in a sentence. However, unlike Transformer attention, biaffine scoring does not use normalization prior to taking the softmax of the scores. In this paper, we provide theoretical evidence and empirical results revealing that a lack of normalization necessarily results in overparameterized parser models, where the extra parameters compensate for the sharp softmax outputs produced by high variance inputs to the biaffine scoring function. We argue that biaffine scoring can be made substantially more efficient by performing score normalization. We conduct experiments on semantic and syntactic dependency parsing in multiple languages, along with latent graph inference on non-linguistic data, using various settings of a $k$-hop parser. We train $N$-layer stacked BiLSTMs and evaluate the parser's performance with and without normalizing biaffine scores. Normalizing allows us to achieve state-of-the-art performance with fewer samples and trainable parameters. Code: https://github.com/paolo-gajo/EfficientSDP

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. V2 makes localized language edits, standardizes BiLSTM-depth notation to N, adds acknowledgements, and reorganizes the appendices: the original full-results discussion moves from Appendix A to E, following the new studies and retained ablations.

P2.justification: V2 adds four tables and a GAT architecture diagram, and replaces the four-panel depth plot with a six-panel plot. Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn, Table 1 is reformatted, and retained figures and tables are relocated, including the full-results table moving from Table 4 to Table 13. These substantially expand and revise the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 retains the original 44 references and adds ten covering latent graph inference, GATs, graph benchmarks, multilingual Universal Dependencies, and ACE corpora. Section 2 adds a brief broader graph-inference framing, while the principal positioning relative to biaffine dependency parsers remains.

T1.justification: Section 3 replaces Claim 1's Frobenius-norm covariance inequality with monotonicity of total variance measured by covariance trace. V2 explicitly defines nested truncated-SVD approximations and supplies a new trace/Loewner-order proof, avoiding v1's unjustified assertion that increasing rank adds a positive-semidefinite covariance increment.

improvement.justification: V2 replaces an unsupported step in the central mathematical argument with a valid trace/SVD proof and substantially strengthens applicability testing through multilingual, GAT, and non-linguistic experiments. arxiv_record.abstract: While large reasoning models demonstrate strong performance on complex tasks, they lack the ability to adjust reasoning token usage based on task difficulty. This often leads to the "overthinking" problem -- excessive and unnecessary reasoning -- which, although potentially mitigated by human intervention to control the token budget, still fundamentally contradicts the goal of achieving fully autonomous AI. In this work, we propose Adaptive Reasoning Model (ARM), a reasoning model capable of adaptively selecting appropriate reasoning formats based on the task at hand. These formats include three efficient ones -- Direct Answer, Short CoT, and Code -- as well as a more elaborate format, Long CoT. To train ARM, we introduce Ada-GRPO, an adaptation of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), which addresses the format collapse issue in traditional GRPO. Ada-GRPO enables ARM to achieve high token efficiency, reducing tokens by an average of 30%, and up to 70%, while maintaining performance comparable to the model that relies solely on Long CoT. Furthermore, not only does it improve inference efficiency through reduced token generation, but it also brings a 2x speedup in training. In addition to the default Adaptive Mode, ARM supports two additional reasoning modes: 1) Instruction-Guided Mode, which allows users to explicitly specify the reasoning format via special tokens -- ideal when the appropriate format is known for a batch of tasks. 2) Consensus-Guided Mode, which aggregates the outputs of the three efficient formats and resorts to Long CoT in case of disagreement, prioritizing performance with higher token usage.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances have demonstrated the effectiveness of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in improving the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing works inevitably rely on high-quality instructions and verifiable rewards for effective training, both of which are often difficult to obtain in specialized domains. In this paper, we propose Self-play Reinforcement Learning (SeRL) to bootstrap LLM training with limited initial data. Specifically, SeRL comprises two complementary modules: self-instruction and self-rewarding. The former module generates additional instructions based on the available data at each training step, employing robust online filtering strategies to ensure instruction quality, diversity, and difficulty. The latter module introduces a simple yet effective majority-voting mechanism to estimate response rewards for additional instructions, eliminating the need for external annotations. Finally, SeRL performs conventional RL based on the generated data, facilitating iterative self-play learning. Extensive experiments on various reasoning benchmarks and across different LLM backbones demonstrate that the proposed SeRL yields results superior to its counterparts and achieves performance on par with those obtained by high-quality data with verifiable rewards. Our code is available at https://github.com/wantbook-book/SeRL.

arxiv_record.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a popular method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of generative models, valued for its simplicity and effectiveness. Despite recent enhancements, LoRA still suffers from a fundamental limitation: overfitting when the bottleneck is widened. It performs best at ranks 32-64, yet its accuracy stagnates or declines at higher ranks, still falling short of full fine-tuning (FFT) performance. We identify the root cause as LoRA's structural bottleneck, which introduces gradient entanglement to the unrelated input channels and distorts gradient propagation. To address this, we introduce a novel structure, Granular Low-Rank Adaptation (GraLoRA) that partitions weight matrices into sub-blocks, each with its own low-rank adapter. With negligible computational or storage cost, GraLoRA overcomes LoRA's limitations, effectively increases the representational capacity, and more closely approximates FFT behavior. Experiments on code generation and commonsense reasoning benchmarks show that GraLoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and other baselines, achieving up to +8.5% absolute gain in Pass@1 on HumanEval+. These improvements hold across model sizes and rank settings, making GraLoRA a scalable and robust solution for PEFT. Code, data, and scripts are available at https://github.com/SqueezeBits/GraLoRA.git

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances in computational pathology have led to the emergence of numerous foundation models. These models typically rely on general-purpose encoders with multi-instance learning for whole slide image (WSI) classification or apply multimodal approaches to generate reports directly from images. However, these models cannot emulate the diagnostic approach of pathologists, who systematically examine slides at low magnification to obtain an overview before progressively zooming in on suspicious regions to formulate comprehensive diagnoses. Instead, existing models directly output final diagnoses without revealing the underlying reasoning process. To address this gap, we introduce CPathAgent, an innovative agent-based approach that mimics pathologists' diagnostic workflow by autonomously navigating across WSI based on observed visual features, thereby generating substantially more transparent and interpretable diagnostic summaries. To achieve this, we develop a multi-stage training strategy that unifies patch-level, region-level, and WSI-level capabilities within a single model, which is essential for replicating how pathologists understand and reason across diverse image scales. Additionally, we construct PathMMU-HR2, the first expert-validated benchmark for large region analysis. This represents a critical intermediate scale between patches and whole slides, reflecting a key clinical reality where pathologists typically examine several key large regions rather than entire slides at once. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CPathAgent consistently outperforms existing approaches across benchmarks at three different image scales, validating the effectiveness of our agent-based diagnostic approach and highlighting a promising direction for computational pathology.

Rewriting and additional supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the above-expert PathMMU results through discussion of textual shortcuts and the expert lead on PathMMU-Pro. It adds interpretations of component contributions and OOD performance. Appendix D introduces substantive limitations concerning synthetic rather than observed clinical trajectories, restricted task scope, and training-data scale.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents patient-level splitting, clarifies that the complete cropped-view sequence enters reasoning together, and describes matched-split CPath-Omni retraining. Appendix C.2 adds benchmark construction details. Hardware, stage runtimes, optimization hyperparameters, and detailed prompts remain unchanged, with no new code or data access instructions.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained PathMMU and TCGA evaluations, v2 adds CPTAC-Lung WSI classification and BRACS benign/atypical/malignant region classification, extending evaluation to external cohorts. PathMMU-Pro adds questions designed to require visual discrimination while reducing textual shortcuts (Section 4.4 and Appendix B.3).

E2.justification: v2 adds CPath-Omni to the PathMMU-HR² comparison and a retrained CPath-Omni* to TCGA WSI classification. PRISM and TITAN become evaluated comparators in Figure 4. Quilt-LLaVA and PathGen-LLaVA WSI comparisons already existed in v1's Table 4 and are relocated into Table 3.

E3.justification: New controls replace learned screening with random selection of 70% of regions and replace navigation/reasoning with single-view descriptions. The added CPath-Omni* comparison uses matched-split retraining. PathMMU-HR²'s reported total changes from 1,688 to 1,668, matching the unchanged tissue counts; this supports a reporting correction, not an inference that the benchmark was resampled.

E4.justification: v2 adds component ablations, external-distribution testing, and a shortcut-focused PathMMU-Pro analysis, addressing component contributions, generalization, and benchmark bias. The 40-region pathologist study and Gemini agent failure analysis are retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report MIL results averaged over five random seeds and pass@k from eight generations across 40 regions. Relocating and explaining the pathologist study adds no new repetition or uncertainty-reporting practice. No confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: New results include 88.1% CPTAC-Lung and 64.3% BRACS balanced accuracy, 65.3% PathMMU-Pro full-set accuracy, and 80.3%/75.0% WSI balanced accuracy for the two component ablations. New comparisons place TITAN ahead on CPTAC-Lung and experts ahead on PathMMU-Pro Tiny. Existing CPathAgent headline scores in Tables 1–3 are retained; these additions do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The Qwen3-14B/CPath-CLIP architecture, three-stage training, and screening–navigation–reasoning pipeline are retained. The pathologist evaluation moves into Appendix B.2, WSI comparisons are consolidated, and the appendices are reorganized around a new limitations section.

P2.justification: v1's architecture/training Figure 4 is removed, a new OOD Figure 4 is added, and the pass@k plot moves and is redrawn as Figure A9. arxiv_record.abstract: The integration of image and event streams offers a promising approach for achieving robust visual object tracking in complex environments. However, current fusion methods achieve high performance at the cost of significant computational overhead and struggle to efficiently extract the sparse, asynchronous information from event streams, failing to leverage the energy-efficient advantages of event-driven spiking paradigms. To address this challenge, we propose the first fully Spiking Frame-Event Tracking framework called SpikeFET. This network achieves synergistic integration of convolutional local feature extraction and Transformer-based global modeling within the spiking paradigm, effectively fusing frame and event data. To overcome the degradation of translation invariance caused by convolutional padding, we introduce a Random Patchwork Module (RPM) that eliminates positional bias through randomized spatial reorganization and learnable type encoding while preserving residual structures. Furthermore, we propose a Spatial-Temporal Regularization (STR) strategy that overcomes similarity metric degradation from asymmetric features by enforcing spatio-temporal consistency among temporal template features in latent space. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior tracking accuracy over existing methods while significantly reducing power consumption, attaining an optimal balance between performance and efficiency.
arxiv_record.authors: Jingjun Yang, Liangwei Fan, Jinpu Zhang, Xiangkai Lian, Hui Shen, Dewen Hu
arxiv_record.title: Fully Spiking Neural Networks for Unified Frame-Event Object Tracking

arxiv_record.abstract: Stylizing 3D scenes instantly while maintaining multi-view consistency and faithfully resembling a style image remains a significant challenge. Current state-of-the-art 3D stylization methods typically involve computationally intensive test-time optimization to transfer artistic features into a pretrained 3D representation, often requiring dense posed input images. In contrast, leveraging recent advances in feed-forward reconstruction models, we demonstrate a novel approach to achieve direct 3D stylization in less than a second using unposed sparse-view scene images and an arbitrary style image. To address the inherent decoupling between reconstruction and stylization, we introduce a branched architecture that separates structure modeling and appearance shading, effectively preventing stylistic transfer from distorting the underlying 3D scene structure. Furthermore, we adapt an identity loss to facilitate pre-training our stylization model through the novel view synthesis task. This strategy also allows our model to retain its original reconstruction capabilities while being fine-tuned for stylization. Comprehensive evaluations, using both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, demonstrate that our approach produces high-quality stylized 3D content that achieve a superior blend of style and scene appearance, while also outperforming existing methods in terms of multi-view consistency and efficiency.
arxiv_record.authors: Peng Wang, Xiang Liu, Peidong Liu
arxiv_record.title: Styl3R: Instant 3D Stylized Reconstruction for Arbitrary Scenes and Styles

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent studies show that the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) can be improved by applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to question-answering (QA) tasks in areas such as math and coding. With a long context length, LLMs may learn to perform search, as indicated by the self-correction behavior observed in DeepSeek R1. However, this search behavior is often imprecise and lacks confidence, resulting in long, redundant responses and highlighting deficiencies in intuition and verification. Inspired by the Dual Process Theory in psychology, we introduce a simple modification to the QA task that includes four stages: Fast Thinking, where the LLM must answer within a strict token budget; Verification, where the model evaluates its initial response; Slow Thinking, where it refines the initial response with more deliberation; and Summarization, where it distills the refinement from the previous stage into precise steps. Our proposed task improves average accuracy from 25.6% to 27.3% for Qwen2.5-1.5B, and from 45.9% to 51.0% for DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-1.5B. Notably, for Qwen2.5-1.5B, the Fast Thinking mode alone achieves 25.2% accuracy using fewer than 1000 tokens, demonstrating substantial inference efficiency gains. These findings suggest that intuition and deliberative reasoning are distinct, complementary systems benefiting from targeted training. Additionally, we have open-sourced both the trained models and the source code.
arxiv_record.authors: Stephen Chung, Wenyu Du, Jie Fu
arxiv_record.title: Thinker: Learning to Think Fast and Slow

arxiv_record.abstract: Agent-Based Models (ABMs) are powerful tools for studying emergent properties in complex systems. In ABMs, agent behaviors are governed by local interactions and stochastic rules. However, these rules are, in general, non-differentiable, limiting the use of gradient-based methods for optimization, and thus integration with real-world data. We propose a novel framework to learn a differentiable surrogate of any ABM by observing its generated data. Our method combines diffusion models to capture behavioral stochasticity and graph neural networks to model agent interactions. Distinct from prior surrogate approaches, our method introduces a fundamental shift: rather than approximating system-level outputs, it models individual agent behavior directly, preserving the decentralized, bottom-up dynamics that define ABMs. We validate our approach on two ABMs (Schelling's segregation model and a Predator-Prey ecosystem) showing that it replicates individual-level patterns and accurately forecasts emergent dynamics beyond training. Our results demonstrate the potential of combining diffusion models and graph learning for data-driven ABM simulation.
arxiv_record.authors: Francesco Cozzi, Marco Pangallo, Alan Perotti, Andr\'e Panisson, Corrado Monti
arxiv_record.title: Learning Individual Behavior in Agent-Based Models with Graph Diffusion Networks

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve impressive reasoning capabilities at the cost of substantial inference overhead, posing substantial deployment challenges. Although distilled Small Language Models (SLMs) significantly enhance efficiency, their performance suffers as they fail to follow LLMs' reasoning paths. Luckily, we reveal that only a small fraction of tokens genuinely diverge reasoning paths between LLMs and SLMs. Most generated tokens are either identical or exhibit neutral differences, such as minor variations in abbreviations or expressions. Leveraging this insight, we introduce **Roads to Rome (R2R)**, a neural token routing method that selectively utilizes LLMs only for these critical, path-divergent tokens, while leaving the majority of token generation to the SLM. We also develop an automatic data generation pipeline that identifies divergent tokens and generates token-level routing labels to train the lightweight router. We apply R2R to combine R1-1.5B and R1-32B models from the DeepSeek family, and evaluate on challenging math, coding, and QA benchmarks. With an average activated parameter size of 5.6B, R2R surpasses the average accuracy of R1-7B by 1.6x, outperforming even the R1-14B model. arxiv_record.abstract: Few-shot segmentation aims to segment unseen object categories from just a handful of annotated examples. This requires mechanisms that can both identify semantically related objects across images and accurately produce segmentation masks. We note that Segment Anything 2 (SAM2), with its prompt-and-propagate mechanism, offers both strong segmentation capabilities and a built-in feature matching process. However, we show that its representations are entangled with task-specific cues optimized for object tracking, which impairs its use for tasks requiring higher level semantic understanding. Our key insight is that, despite its class-agnostic pretraining, SAM2 already encodes rich semantic structure in its features. We propose SANSA (Semantically AligNed Segment Anything 2), a framework that makes this latent structure explicit, and repurposes SAM2 for few-shot segmentation through minimal task-specific modifications. SANSA achieves state-of-the-art performance on few-shot segmentation benchmarks specifically designed to assess generalization, outperforms generalist methods in the popular in-context setting, supports various prompts flexible interaction via points, boxes, or scribbles, and remains significantly faster and more compact than prior approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/ClaudiaCuttano/SANSA.
arxiv_record.authors: Claudia Cuttano, Gabriele Trivigno, Giuseppe Averta, Carlo Masone
arxiv_record.title: SANSA: Unleashing the Hidden Semantics in SAM2 for Few-Shot Segmentation

arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, test-time adaptation has attracted wide interest in the context of vision-language models for image classification. However, to the best of our knowledge, the problem is completely overlooked in dense prediction tasks such as Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation (OVSS). In response, we propose a novel TTA method tailored to adapting VLMs for segmentation during test time. Unlike TTA methods for image classification, our Multi-Level and Multi-Prompt (MLMP) entropy minimization integrates features from intermediate vision-encoder layers and is performed with different text-prompt templates at both the global CLS token and local pixel-wise levels. Our approach could be used as plug-and-play for any segmentation network, does not require additional training data or labels, and remains effective even with a single test sample. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive OVSS TTA benchmark suite, which integrates a rigorous evaluation protocol, nine segmentation datasets, 15 common synthetic corruptions, and additional real and rendered domain shifts, \textbf{with a total of 87 distinct test scenarios}, establishing a standardized and comprehensive testbed for future TTA research in open-vocabulary segmentation. Our experiments on this suite demonstrate that our segmentation-tailored method consistently delivers significant gains over direct adoption of TTA classification baselines. Code and data are available at https://github.com/dosowiechi/MLMP.

Unlike TTA methods for image classification, our Multi-Level and Multi-Prompt (MLMP) entropy minimization integrates features from intermediate vision-encoder layers and is performed with different text-prompt templates at both the global CLS token and local pixel-wise levels.  Our approach could be used as plug-and-play for any segmentation network, does not require additional training data or labels, and remains effective even with a single test sample. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive OVSS TTA benchmark suite, which integrates a rigorous evaluation protocol, nine segmentation datasets, 15 common synthetic corruptions, and additional real and rendered domain shifts, with a total of 87 distinct test scenarios, establishing a standardized and comprehensive testbed for future TTA research in open-vocabulary segmentation. Our experiments on this suite demonstrate that our segmentation-tailored method consistently delivers significant gains over direct adoption of TTA classification baselines. Code and data are available at https://github.com/dosowiechi/MLMP.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive applications such as virtual and augmented reality, where a first-person (egocentric) view captured by head-mounted cameras serves as key input. While this view offers fine-grained cues about user attention and hand-object interactions, its narrow field of view and lack of global context often lead to failures on spatially or contextually demanding queries. To address this, we introduce a framework that augments egocentric inputs with third-person (exocentric) views, providing complementary information such as global scene layout and object visibility to LVLMs. We present E3VQA, the first benchmark for multi-view question answering with 4K high-quality question-answer pairs grounded in synchronized ego-exo image pairs. Additionally, we propose M3CoT, a training-free prompting technique that constructs a unified scene representation by integrating scene graphs from three complementary perspectives. M3CoT enables LVLMs to reason more effectively across views, yielding consistent performance gains (4.84% for GPT-4o and 5.94% for Gemini 2.0 Flash) over a recent CoT baseline. Our extensive evaluation reveals key strengths and limitations of LVLMs in multi-view reasoning and highlights the value of leveraging both egocentric and exocentric inputs. The dataset and source code are available at https://github.com/Leeinsu1/Towards-Comprehensive-Scene-Understanding.

arxiv_record.abstract: Designing protein sequences of both high fitness and novelty is a challenging task in data-efficient protein engineering. Exploration beyond wild-type neighborhoods often leads to biologically implausible sequences or relies on surrogate models that lose fidelity in novel regions. Here, we propose ProSpero, an active learning framework in which a frozen pre-trained generative model is guided by a surrogate updated from oracle feedback. By integrating fitness-relevant residue selection with biologically-constrained Sequential Monte Carlo sampling, our approach enables exploration beyond wild-type neighborhoods while preserving biological plausibility. We show that our framework remains effective even when the surrogate is misspecified. ProSpero consistently outperforms or matches existing methods across diverse protein engineering tasks, retrieving sequences of both high fitness and novelty.
arxiv_record.authors: Michal Kmicikiewicz, Vincent Fortuin, Ewa Szczurek
arxiv_record.title: ProSpero: Active Learning for Robust Protein Design Beyond Wild-Type Neighborhoods

arxiv_record.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) is an established approach for performing Bayesian inference on scientific simulators. SBI so far works best on low-dimensional parametric models. However, it is difficult to infer function-valued parameters, which frequently occur in disciplines that model spatiotemporal processes such as the climate and earth sciences. Here, we introduce an approach for efficient posterior estimation, using a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architecture with a flow matching objective. We show that our approach, FNOPE, can perform inference of function-valued parameters at a fraction of the simulation budget of state of the art methods. In addition, FNOPE supports posterior evaluation at arbitrary discretizations of the domain, as well as simultaneous estimation of vector-valued parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark tasks and a challenging spatial inference task from glaciology. FNOPE extends the applicability of SBI methods to new scientific domains by enabling the inference of function-valued parameters.

arxiv_record.abstract: Machine unlearning algorithms aim to remove the influence of specific training samples, ideally recovering the model that would have resulted from training on the remaining data alone. We study unlearning in the overparameterized setting, where many models interpolate the data, and defining the solution as any loss minimizer over the retained set$\unicode{x2013}$as in prior work in the underparameterized setting$\unicode{x2013}$is inadequate, since the original model may already interpolate the retained data and satisfy this condition. In this regime, loss gradients vanish, rendering prior methods based on gradient perturbations ineffective, motivating both new unlearning definitions and algorithms. For this setting, we define the unlearning solution as the minimum-complexity interpolator over the retained data and propose a new algorithmic framework that only requires access to model gradients on the retained set at the original solution. We minimize a regularized objective over perturbations constrained to be orthogonal to these model gradients, a first-order relaxation of the interpolation condition. For different model classes, we provide exact and approximate unlearning guarantees and demonstrate that an implementation of our framework outperforms existing baselines across various unlearning experiments.
arxiv_record.authors: Jacob L. Block, Aryan Mokhtari, Sanjay Shakkottai
arxiv_record.title: Machine Unlearning under Overparameterization

arxiv_record.abstract: Chain-of-Thought reasoning has emerged as a powerful approach for solving complex mathematical and logical problems. However, it can often veer off track through incorrect or unsubstantiated inferences. Formal mathematical reasoning, which can be checked with a formal verifier, is one approach to addressing this issue. However, currently LLMs are simply not good enough to solve complex problems in a formal way, and even just formalizing an informal problem statement can be challenging. Motivated by this fact, in this work we consider the problem of learning reliable verifiers for natural language Chain-of-Thought reasoning. That is, given a problem statement and step-by-step solution in natural language, the aim of the verifier is to output [Yes] if the reasoning steps in the solution are all valid, and [No] otherwise. In this work we give a formal PAC-learning framework for studying this problem. We propose and analyze several natural verification goals, at different levels of strength, in this framework. We provide sample complexity upper-bounds for learning verifiers satisfying these goals, as well as lower-bound and impossibility results for learning other natural verification objectives without additional assumptions.
arxiv_record.authors: Maria-Florina Balcan, Avrim Blum, Zhiyuan Li, Dravyansh Sharma
arxiv_record.title: On Learning Verifiers and Implications to Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

C1.justification: The four principal contributions and sample-complexity conclusions remain. v2 explicitly adds a computational-separation claim in Section 1.2 and frames the abstract around sequential reasoning including CoT, modestly extending the stated contribution framing.

C2.justification: v1 presents trustable verification as guiding generation; v2 restricts this interpretation to stepwise soundness and small alphabets, explaining why it fails for overall soundness or large alphabets. New Remarks 2.1 and 4.2 clarify that acceptance need not establish proof completion and distinguish the guarantees from formal-logical soundness and completeness. These qualifications materially change the interpretation of central guarantees.

D1.justification: Both versions document abstract mathematical procedures. v2 adds no implementation package, hyperparameter or hardware specification, training-time measurement, data-processing recipe, or code/data-access information.

E1.justification: Neither version trains or evaluates on datasets or empirical tasks. The added planning and puzzle illustrations and USAT construction are conceptual or theoretical examples, not additional evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods against the proposed learners. Additional citations to verification and generation methods in v2 do not constitute evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, metrics, budgets, model configurations, or testing procedures. Changes to mathematical learning guarantees are theoretical changes rather than evaluation-protocol revisions.

E4.justification: No experimental ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness evaluations, or error analyses are added or removed. Appendix B retains its mathematical examples; the added puzzle illustration is explanatory and the USAT separation is theoretical.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Confidence parameters and probability bounds occur within theoretical proofs, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Neither version contains experimental scores or qualitative evaluation outcomes. New Table 1 summarizes existing theoretical sample-complexity rates; the new separation argument and revised proofs are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Prefix-by-prefix verification, ERM-based learning, gold-trace negative-example construction, Algorithm 1, and the online learners in Example B.5 are retained. The revised soundness definitions and proofs do not introduce a different learning or inference procedure.

P1.justification: v2 revises the title, polishes language, adds explanatory remarks and acknowledgments, and introduces the existing SVPAC loss before Definition 3.1 instead of first inside a proof. The main section sequence and Appendix A–C organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 comparing training data, algorithms, and theoretical sample complexities across verification goals. This consolidates material already present in v1. The single-column layout and Algorithm 1 display remain, with local pagination and spacing changes.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 substantially expands positioning through new discussions of interactive provers and exact learning, plus connections to planning, imitation learning, selective classification, robustly reliable learning, and strategic improvements. These additions explain relationships to several research directions beyond those covered in v1.

T1.justification: v2 Definition 4.1 explicitly defines acceptance through all prefixes and separates stepwise from overall soundness, with corresponding revisions to TVPAC definitions and guarantees. The proof of v1 Theorem 4.7, now Theorem 4.9, replaces an unjustified independence step with a union bound over verifier subsets. Remark 4.6 restricts generation–verification equivalence to small alphabets, and new Remark 4.7 establishes a USAT-based computational separation assuming RP differs from NP.

improvement.justification: Replacing the unjustified independence-based argument in v1 Theorem 4.7 with the subset union bound in v2 Theorem 4.9 repairs support for a central sample-complexity guarantee. The soundness distinctions and restricted generation–verification equivalence also reduce substantive ambiguity and overstatement. Together these changes substantially strengthen the mathematical reliability and precision of this theoretical paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same verifier-learning research. All 22 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including Appendices A–C, are readable and support comparison despite the revised title and renumbered results.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical. Its new summary table and computational-separation example report mathematical results, while empirical findings mentioned in related work are attributed to other papers.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical bounds, proofs, and illustrative mathematical constructions, including in its appendices. It contains no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

arxiv_record.abstract: Gaussian Splatting (GS) has recently emerged as an efficient representation for rendering 3D scenes from 2D images and has been extended to images, videos, and dynamic 4D content. However, applying style transfer to GS-based representations, especially beyond simple color changes, remains challenging. In this work, we introduce CLIPGaussian, the first unified style transfer framework that supports text- and image-guided stylization across multiple modalities: 2D images, videos, 3D objects, and 4D scenes. Our method operates directly on Gaussian primitives and integrates into existing GS pipelines as a plug-in module, without requiring large generative models or retraining from scratch. The CLIPGaussian approach enables joint optimization of color and geometry in 3D and 4D settings, and achieves temporal coherence in videos, while preserving the model size. We demonstrate superior style fidelity and consistency across all tasks, validating CLIPGaussian as a universal and efficient solution for multimodal style transfer.

arxiv_record.title: CLIPGaussian: Universal and Multimodal Style Transfer Based on Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the claims of universal text/image-guided Gaussian stylization, joint appearance and geometry optimization, preserved model size, and strong quality and consistency. The additional experiments and Light configuration do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: B.3.3 substantially expands the failure discussion beyond v1's reconstruction dependence and 2D quality limitations. It relates prompt generality, specificity, and length to CLIP representation problems, unwanted semantic features, and background artifacts, explicitly explaining how higher CLIP scores can accompany worse perceived quality. Section 4 also adds a patch-size explanation for repeated structures in 2D outputs.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies Light settings: learning rate 0.002 and patch-loss weights 35 for 3D and 45 for video. v2 also specifies video resolutions and UVG downsampling, revises the reported 4D-scene hardware from RTX 4090 to DGX A100, and states that code is available rather than forthcoming after review. Most implementation documentation is retained.

E1.justification: Appendix B.5 adds four UVG sequences to the previously DAVIS-only video evaluation, extending coverage to longer videos under image and text conditioning. The four-modality task scope and other datasets, including the existing PanopticSports experiments, are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds SGSST and ABC-GS to the 3D image-conditioned comparison (Table 1), and ViSt3D, AdaAttN, and ReReVST to the DAVIS image-conditioned video comparison (Table 18). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator sets. The user study retains its original methods.

E3.justification: v2 introduces flow-warped LPIPS/RMSE evaluation at frame offsets 1 and 7, and Farneback flow comparisons at offsets 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 (B.1.2). New protocols include Light configurations and 4D evaluation using 200 rendered views at 11 time points and 21 time points per test camera (B.3.4). The existing batch-size figure also relabels 3 as 4, without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: The existing hyperparameter analyses are retained, while B.3.3 adds prompt-specificity and prompt-length experiments crossed with background-loss settings, examining semantic and background artifacts. v2 also adds standard-versus-Light comparisons and camera/time consistency analyses across batch sizes (B.3.4, Tables 16-17 and Figure 33).

E5.justification: The Friedman and Conover-Friedman tests, their p-value tables, and survey participant counts are retained. The added experiments do not introduce repeated-run or seed information, error bars, confidence intervals, or additional significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline and Light results, UVG scores, non-CLIP consistency measurements, and prompt/time findings. In the corresponding DAVIS image-conditioned comparison, CCPL's CLIP-S changes from 18.89 to 68.89 and UniST's from 15.93 to 65.93, while CLIPGaussian remains at 74.31 (v1 Table 14; v2 Table 18). These are revised reported values, without a documented explanation for the increases.

M1.justification: The Gaussian representations, four-term loss, patch augmentation, and modality-specific optimization procedures remain unchanged. CLIPGaussian-Light adjusts existing learning rates and patch-loss weights; it introduces no new architecture, loss component, or algorithmic step.

P1.justification: Localized editing streamlines the introduction and expands selected explanations. v2 adds appendix subsections, a social-impact paragraph, acknowledgments, and a NeurIPS checklist, and updates affiliations and conference information. The main section order and most retained prose remain stable.

P2.justification: The two original 3D comparison tables are merged and expanded into v2 Table 1; the DAVIS tables are similarly combined into Table 18. Numerous new analysis and consistency tables and Figures 19 and 31-33 substantially extend the displays. Existing figures are relocated, the survey screenshot is enlarged, and Figure 7 gains resolution; retained qualitative galleries largely preserve their content.

R1.justification: Related work adds discussion of StyleDyRF, AdaAttN, ReReVST, ViSt3D, and StyleMaster, and elaborates the distinction from Instruct-GS2GS. Additional comparison and metric references include SGSST, ABC-GS, and StyleRF. This broadens the context while retaining the central novelty positioning; publication updates and consolidated duplicate references are bibliographic edits.

T1.justification: The representation and loss equations and existing CLIP metric definitions are unchanged. v2's added optical-flow formula documents an adopted evaluation metric; it introduces no new theoretical assumption, proof, derivation, or formal result.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative consistency evaluation relied on CLIP-derived measures. v2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of this central claim through non-CLIP consistency metrics, broader comparators, longer-video testing, and concrete prompt-failure analyses. These additions expose meaningful tradeoffs and applicability limits. The unchanged superiority wording remains overbroad: v2 Table 20 favors Rerender over standard CLIPGaussian on DAVIS LPIPS/RMSE. Despite that unresolved overstatement, the broader validation and explicit failure evidence provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLIPGaussian framework and provide readable methods, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-B. Retained material can be matched despite additions, renumbering, and layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds baseline comparisons, UVG experiments, consistency measurements, and failure-case analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original stylization experiments across four modalities, quantitative comparisons, a 3D user study, and hyperparameter analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on knowledge-intensive tasks. However, varying response quality across LLMs under RAG necessitates intelligent routing mechanisms, which select the most suitable model for each query from multiple retrieval-augmented LLMs via a dedicated router model. We observe that external documents dynamically affect LLMs' ability to answer queries, while existing routing methods, which rely on static parametric knowledge representations, exhibit suboptimal performance in RAG scenarios. To address this, we formally define the new retrieval-augmented LLM routing problem, incorporating the influence of retrieved documents into the routing framework. We propose RAGRouter, a RAG-aware routing design, which leverages document embeddings and RAG capability embeddings with contrastive learning to capture knowledge representation shifts and enable informed routing decisions. Extensive experiments on diverse knowledge-intensive tasks and retrieval settings, covering open and closed-source LLMs, show that RAGRouter outperforms the best individual LLM and existing routing methods. With an extended score-threshold-based mechanism, it also achieves strong performance-efficiency trade-offs under low-latency constraints. The code and data are available at https://github.com/OwwO99/RAGRouter.
arxiv_record.authors: Jiarui Zhang, Xiangyu Liu, Yong Hu, Chaoyue Niu, Fan Wu, Guihai Chen
arxiv_record.title: RAGRouter: Learning to Route Queries to Multiple Retrieval-Augmented Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the effectiveness claim to open- and closed-source candidate models. The abstract drops v1's specific improvement figures, while the introduction reports a broader 1.67%–9.33% improvement range. The central novelty, knowledge-shift modeling, and latency-trade-off claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting transfer performance to learned relative RAG capabilities and residual failures to retrieval-induced degradation, task difficulty, and model-selection overconfidence. It interprets the new embedding ablation as supporting separate capability modeling. v1's discussion of future applications beyond RAG is removed, while the central knowledge-shift explanation is retained.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code/data repository link, extends API-access disclosure to the added models, and explains the single-embedding ablation configuration and probabilistic supervision. Existing implementation settings remain unchanged. Inference-cost measurements move from v1 Appendix G to v2 Section 5.2; they are not newly reported.

E1.justification: v2 retains the five original QA datasets and adds HotpotQA multi-hop QA and WikiASP aspect-based summarization. Appendix F also introduces medical-to-Wikipedia QA and search-QA-to-medical transfer scenarios, substantially extending task requirements and domain-shift coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-Max, and DeepSeek-R1 as individually evaluated model comparators. GPT-4o previously served inside the Prompt LLM routing baseline rather than as a candidate answerer. The routing comparators in the retained experiments are unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a six-model candidate pool for the NQ/WebQ comparison, two cross-domain training/testing protocols, and ROUGE-L evaluation for summarization. Its failure analysis excludes cases where all candidate LLMs fail and categorizes the remaining failures. Original QA sample counts, metrics, and training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ablation of the RAG Capability Embedding Layer, quantitative failure categories and analysis of cases where baselines succeed but RAGRouter fails, and cross-domain generalization tests. The original retrieval-noise analysis, sensitivity sweeps, and two successful routing examples remain; moving their displays does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. Added results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice; probabilistic training-label sampling is not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained results are unchanged, including Table 2's 64.46% average accuracy. New results include 59.38% versus GPT-4o's 57.71% in Table 3, 63.70% without RAG capability embeddings, a 12.95% failure rate in Table 12, cross-domain accuracies of 21.20% and 68.89%, and WikiASP ROUGE-L of 0.1981 versus KNN Router's 0.1881. These are additional results under distinct settings, not improvements over corresponding v1 scores.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix H introduces score-based probabilistic label sampling for WikiASP: a normalized continuous score s produces a positive training label with probability s and a negative label with probability 1-s. This extends v1's binary-correctness supervision. The original architecture, contrastive objectives, and routing procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, edits selected abstract, contribution, and architecture passages, and reorganizes experimental and appendix subsections. It adds appendix contents and funding acknowledgments and moves inference-cost discussion into the main text. Most original prose and the main narrative sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation expands with tables for stronger-model comparisons, failure categories, cross-domain transfer, and summarization. v1's combined ablation table becomes separate architecture and contrastive-learning tables. Existing sensitivity heatmaps move into the main text, and appendix figures and case tables are regrouped; these retained figures are not new analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds the WikiASP and HotpotQA references and removes citations concerning distillation, parameter-efficient transfer learning, LoRA, and chain-of-thought prompting alongside the deleted future-work discussion. Related-work positioning against non-RAG-aware routers remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds a limited mathematical extension to training-label construction: continuous scores define positive and negative label probabilities s and 1-s. The original routing formulation, loss equations, and response-reversal definitions in Equations 1–11 remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by directly testing the distinctive RAG capability embedding, quantifying routing failures, and examining transfer beyond the original QA settings through stronger candidate models, cross-domain tests, and summarization. These additions address important gaps in mechanism attribution and applicability while preserving the original evidence. HotpotQA/WikiASP setup details remain incomplete and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, limiting the strength of the expanded generalization claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAGRouter work despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds stronger-model comparisons, failure analysis, cross-domain evaluations, and summarization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original routing-accuracy and latency experiments, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and retrieval-noise evaluations.

arxiv_record.abstract: In strategic classification, the standard supervised learning setting is extended to support the notion of strategic user behavior in the form of costly feature manipulations made in response to a classifier. While standard learning supports a broad range of model classes, the study of strategic classification has, so far, been dedicated mostly to linear classifiers. This work aims to expand the horizon by exploring how strategic behavior manifests under non-linear classifiers and what this implies for learning. We take a bottom-up approach showing how non-linearity affects decision boundary points, classifier expressivity, and model class complexity. Our results show how, unlike the linear case, strategic behavior may either increase or decrease effective class complexity, and that the complexity decrease may be arbitrarily large. Another key finding is that universal approximators (e.g., neural nets) are no longer universal once the environment is strategic. We demonstrate empirically how this can create performance gaps even on an unrestricted model class.
arxiv_record.authors: Benyamin Trachtenberg, Nir Rosenfeld
arxiv_record.title: Strategic Classification with Non-Linear Classifiers

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: In strategic classification, the standard supervised learning setting is extended to support the notion of strategic user behavior in the form of costly feature manipulations made in response to a classifier. While standard learning supports a broad range of model classes, the study of strategic classification has, so far, been dedicated mostly to linear classifiers. This work aims to expand the horizon by exploring how strategic behavior manifests under non-linear classifiers and what this implies for learning. We take a bottom-up approach showing how non-linearity affects decision boundary points, classifier expressivity, and model class complexity. Our results show how, unlike the linear case, strategic behavior may either increase or decrease effective class complexity, and that the complexity decrease may be arbitrarily large. Another key finding is that universal approximators (e.g., neural nets) are no longer universal once the environment is strategic. We demonstrate empirically how this can create performance gaps even on an unrestricted model class.

C1.justification: The introduction adds a central contribution establishing an upper bound on strategic complexity for bounded piecewise-linear classes, including fixed-size ReLU networks. This substantially extends v1's polytope-specific upper-bound claim, while retaining the claims about complexity collapse, non-universality, and approximation gaps.

C2.justification: New Appendices A.2-A.3, C.1, and C.10 substantially expand applicability and interpretation: bounded input domains, obstacles to a general VC bound, extensions beyond Euclidean costs, and limitations under instance-dependent costs. They also develop implications for inversion, curvature regularization, interpolation thresholds, and model selection.

D1.justification: v2 Section 6 adds a code-repository link for both experiments. Appendix D.1 further clarifies the existing grid approximation; the disclosed CPU allocation, sample counts, fitting procedure, and tolerance remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same bounded two-dimensional polynomial classifiers and synthetic class-conditional Gaussian classification problems. The additional discussion of other cost functions introduces no evaluated datasets or scenarios.

E2.justification: The approximation experiment retains the same comparators: unrestricted non-strategic classification and optimal linear classification, whose strategic and non-strategic classes coincide. No evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Appendix D retains the polynomial-degree and strategic-reach ranges, bounded input domain, 0.9 fitting tolerance, Gaussian-separation range, and 25 samples per class. The grid-based calculations and optimal-linear-classifier search are also unchanged.

E4.justification: The same experiments examine expressivity across polynomial degree and strategic reach, and accuracy across class separation and strategic reach. No empirical ablation, robustness test, or supplementary case study is added; the new appendix analyses concern theory and its implications.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 instances for expressivity and 20 for approximation, with means and standard-error confidence intervals. No repeated-run, seed, or uncertainty-reporting procedure changes.

E6.justification: The experimental plots in v1 Figure 6 and v2 Figure 5 are identical, and their reported trends and comparator relationships are retained. The revised mathematical examples preserve their intended findings and are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The underlying strategic-response model and experimental procedures are retained. Appendix C.10 discusses prospective inversion and curvature-regularization approaches without introducing an instantiated learning algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 combines 'Points' and 'Classifiers' under 'Underlying Mechanisms,' renames 'Model classes' to 'Class-level analysis,' and adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments. Copyediting and notation cleanup are widespread, but the original bottom-up sequence and most existing exposition remain.

P2.justification: Both versions retain eleven figures and no tables. v2 revises point-mapping arrows and explanatory captions, moves the curvature illustration from the main text to Appendix B.3, and relocates the unchanged experimental figure nearer the experiment descriptions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Huang (2020) and Petersen and Voigtlaender (2018) to connect piecewise-linear analysis with ReLU approximation. It also clarifies the borrowing from offset-curve theory and discusses restrictions of earlier optimization approaches, while retaining the existing related-work framework.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 3 and Appendix B.10, bounding strategic VC dimension for piecewise-linear classes by O(dm log m + nu_p k log k); the original polytope bound remains as Theorem 4. It also revises the classifier construction in Appendix B.8 and replaces the flawed strategic-accuracy example in v1 C.8 with a corrected construction in v2 C.9. Equation (1) corrects the response objective from h(x) to h(x').

improvement.justification: The new piecewise-linear VC bound and accompanying proof substantially broaden the central learnability analysis beyond v1's polytope result to classes relevant to ReLU networks. Corrected mathematical constructions, explicit applicability boundaries, and code-access information further improve reliability and usefulness. The fully general learnability question remains open, and the empirical evidence is unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, and Appendices A-D are readable and support reliable matching across the restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments in Sections 6.1-6.2, Figure 5, and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 Sections 7.1-7.2, Figure 6, and Appendix D report original experiments on polynomial expressivity and attainable classification accuracy using synthetic data.
