arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently refuse to respond to pseudo-malicious instructions: semantically harmless input queries triggering unnecessary LLM refusals due to conservative safety alignment, significantly impairing user experience. Collecting such instructions is crucial for evaluating and mitigating over-refusals, but existing instruction curation methods, like manual creation or instruction rewriting, either lack scalability or fail to produce sufficiently diverse and effective refusal-inducing prompts. To address these limitations, we introduce EVOREFUSE, a prompt optimization approach that generates diverse pseudo-malicious instructions consistently eliciting confident refusals across LLMs. EVOREFUSE employs an evolutionary algorithm exploring the instruction space in more diverse directions than existing methods via mutation strategies and recombination, and iteratively evolves seed instructions to maximize evidence lower bound on LLM refusal probability. Using EVOREFUSE, we create two novel datasets: EVOREFUSE-TEST, a benchmark of 582 pseudo-malicious instructions that outperforms the next-best benchmark with 85.34% higher average refusal triggering rate across 9 LLMs without a safety-prior system prompt, 34.86% greater lexical diversity, and 40.03% improved LLM response confidence scores; and EVOREFUSE-ALIGN, which provides 3,000 pseudo-malicious instructions with responses for supervised and preference-based alignment training. With supervised fine-tuning on EVOREFUSE-ALIGN, LLAMA3.1-8B-INSTRUCT achieves up to 29.85% fewer over-refusals than models trained on the second-best alignment dataset, without compromising safety. Our analysis with EVOREFUSE-TEST reveals models trigger over-refusals by overly focusing on sensitive keywords while ignoring broader context. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/FishT0ucher/EVOREFUSE.

C1.justification: The main claims now explicitly cover operation both with and without safety-prior prompting. The abstract highlights an 85.34% benchmark margin and 29.85% SFT mitigation improvement under the new setting, while the introduction retains the earlier prompted claims. The central contributions—evolutionary optimization, two datasets, and shortcut-learning insights—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies fitness improvement as heuristic evidence for increasing true refusal likelihood, explains system-prompt effects through refusal bias, and interprets DarkIdol's results as reducing dependence on GPT-4o for generation. The shortcut-learning and early-layer interpretations, and Appendix C's white-box, computational-cost, and annotation-subjectivity limitations, remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code/data repository link and release statements, the GPT refusal-judging prompt in Appendix A.7, a DarkIdol checkpoint reference, explicit decoding settings, and the annotator count. The original safety-prior prompt moves to B.5. Core implementation templates and EVOREFUSE hyperparameters in A.3–A.6 are retained.

E1.justification: The datasets, domains, and underlying tasks remain unchanged, including the 582-example EVOREFUSE-TEST and 3,000-example EVOREFUSE-ALIGN. v3 adds evaluation without the safety-prior system prompt, extending coverage to an additional input-conditioning scenario.

E2.justification: The eight benchmark comparators, alignment baselines using OR-BENCH/PHTEST/PromptAgent, Few-Shot and DRO defenses, and Figure 2 comparison methods are retained. Table 10 varies EVOREFUSE's mutator model within the same pipeline.

E3.justification: v3 introduces an unprompted evaluation protocol with temperature 0.01 and GPT-based CRR judging; the prompted appendix uses temperature 1.0 and the original binary classifier. Section 4 changes the stated fine-tuning budget from three to five epochs. New experiments also introduce single-round mutation testing and a DarkIdol configuration. These are substantial protocol changes, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 expands robustness analysis across prompted and unprompted evaluations, compares nine mutation strategies individually in Appendix B.4, and tests dependence on GPT-4o using DarkIdol in B.6. Table 10 reports five-iteration refusal rates of 0.46 for DarkIdol and 0.72 for GPT-4o. Existing component ablations remain, and Table 6 adds one attribution example.

E5.justification: Table 2 newly reports ranges across annotators, and Section 4 identifies three NLP practitioners. This adds uncertainty reporting for safety judgments. Figure 2 already contained standard-error shading in v1; v3 does not establish additional repeated model runs or newly specified random seeds.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial benchmark and mitigation results under the new settings in Tables 1 and 3; v1's corresponding tables remain numerically unchanged as Tables 8 and 9. In the new benchmark setting, PH-GEN exceeds EVOREFUSE-TEST on DeepSeek-V3, with PRR 0.45 versus 0.38. Table 2 changes EVOREFUSE-TEST's reported unsafe fraction from 0.00 to 0.02 ± 0.02. Tables 7 and 10 add strategy and mutator findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the fitness function in Equation 5, mutation/recombination templates, safety filtering, and simulated annealing remain unchanged. The GPT-based CRR judge changes evaluation, not fitness computation. The DarkIdol experiment tests a different backend within the existing procedure.

P1.justification: v3 makes targeted rewrites to the results summary, experimental settings, and theoretical explanation, and adds appendix subsections B.4–B.6. It also updates author/affiliation information and adds author contributions, acknowledgments, and a NeurIPS checklist. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The new main Table 1 uses a PRR-only layout; earlier Tables 1 and 3 move to appendix Tables 8 and 9. v3 adds compact Tables 7 and 10, annotator ranges in Table 2, and a row in Table 6. Table captions move above their displays. Figures 1–3 retain identical graphical content, with resizing and page reflow.

R1.justification: Reference 39, cited for TRIDENT-CORE, changes from Ji et al.'s PKU-SafeRLHF paper to Wu et al.'s TRIDENT paper. This changes the attributed source work. The related-work discussion and broader novelty positioning otherwise remain unchanged; other citation-number changes reflect reordering.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2 replace the earlier elitist ELBO/true-likelihood convergence argument and global-optimality discussion with convergence of record-best practical fitness only. Equation 6 restores the entropy term, refusal becomes response-dependent and stochastic, and assumptions are rewritten. v3 explicitly withdraws guarantees of monotonic improvement or convergence along the accepted-seed trajectory and of increasing true refusal likelihood.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is correcting an important mathematical overclaim: Appendix A.2 now limits convergence to record-best fitness and acknowledges that true refusal likelihood need not improve. Evaluations without forced safety-prior prompting and additional component tests substantially strengthen empirical support, while annotator ranges improve transparency. The prompt-effect interpretation remains confounded by different temperatures and CRR judges, but this does not outweigh the gains in validity and evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EVOREFUSE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison. The earlier main experimental tables can be matched exactly to tables retained in the later appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations without the safety-prior prompt, mutation-strategy comparisons, and an alternative-mutator experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, alignment experiments, attribution analyses, and optimization ablations in Tables 1–4, Figures 1–3, and the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Autonomous agentic AI systems powered by vision-language models (VLMs) are rapidly advancing toward real-world deployment, yet their cross-modal reasoning capabilities introduce new attack surfaces for adversarial manipulation that exploit semantic reasoning across modalities. Existing adversarial attacks typically rely on visible pixel perturbations or require privileged model or environment access, making them impractical for stealthy, real-world exploitation. We introduce TRAP, a novel generative adversarial framework that manipulates the agent's decision-making using diffusion-based semantic injections into the vision-language embedding space. Our method combines negative prompt-based degradation with positive semantic optimization, guided by a Siamese semantic network and layout-aware spatial masking. Without requiring access to model internals, TRAP produces visually natural images yet induces consistent selection biases in agentic AI systems. We evaluate TRAP on the Microsoft Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset, building multi-candidate decision scenarios. Across these scenarios, TRAP consistently induces decision-level preference redirection on leading models, including LLaVA-34B, Gemma3, GPT-4o, and Mistral-3.2, significantly outperforming existing baselines such as SPSA, Bandit, and standard diffusion approaches. These findings expose a critical, generalized vulnerability: autonomous agents can be consistently misled through visually subtle, semantically-guided cross-modal manipulations. Overall, our results show the need for defense strategies beyond pixel-level robustness to address semantic vulnerabilities in cross-modal decision-making. The code for TRAP is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/TRAP.
arxiv_record.authors: Hangoo Kang, Jehyeok Yeon, Gagandeep Singh
arxiv_record.title: TRAP: Targeted Redirecting of Agentic Preferences

These findings expose a critical, generalized vulnerability: autonomous agents can be consistently misled through visually subtle, semantically-guided cross-modal manipulations. Overall, our results show the need for defense strategies beyond pixel-level robustness to address semantic vulnerabilities in cross-modal decision-making. arxiv_record.abstract: Handwritten Mathematical Expression Recognition (HMER) remains a persistent challenge in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) due to the inherent freedom of symbol layouts and variability in handwriting styles. Prior methods have faced performance bottlenecks by proposing isolated architectural modifications, making them difficult to integrate coherently into a unified framework. Meanwhile, recent advances in pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong cross-task generalization, offering a promising foundation for developing unified solutions. In this paper, we introduce Uni-MuMER, which fully fine-tunes a VLM for the HMER task without modifying its architecture, effectively injecting domain-specific knowledge into a generalist framework. Our method integrates three data-driven tasks: Tree-Aware Chain-of-Thought (Tree-CoT) for structured spatial reasoning, Error-Driven Learning (EDL) for reducing confusion among visually similar characters, and Symbol Counting (SC) for improving recognition consistency in long expressions. Experiments on the CROHME and HME100K datasets show that Uni-MuMER achieves super state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the best lightweight specialized model SSAN by 16.31\% and the top-performing VLM Gemini2.5-flash by 24.42\% under zero-shot setting. Our datasets, models, and code are open-sourced at: {https://github.com/BFlameSwift/Uni-MuMER

arxiv_record.abstract: Multi-task model merging aims to consolidate knowledge from multiple fine-tuned task-specific experts into a unified model while minimizing performance degradation. Existing methods primarily approach this by minimizing differences between task-specific experts and the unified model, either from a parameter-level or a task-loss perspective. However, parameter-level methods exhibit a significant performance gap compared to the upper bound, while task-loss approaches entail costly secondary training procedures. In contrast, we observe that performance degradation closely correlates with feature drift, i.e., differences in feature representations of the same sample caused by model merging. Motivated by this observation, we propose Layer-wise Optimal Task Vector Merging (LOT Merging), a technique that explicitly minimizes feature drift between task-specific experts and the unified model in a layer-by-layer manner. LOT Merging can be formulated as a convex quadratic optimization problem, enabling us to analytically derive closed-form solutions for the parameters of linear and normalization layers. Consequently, LOT Merging achieves efficient model consolidation through basic matrix operations. Extensive experiments across vision and vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that LOT Merging significantly outperforms baseline methods, achieving improvements of up to 4.4% (ViT-B/32) over state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is available at https://github.com/SunWenJu123/model-merging.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: training-free feature-drift minimization, closed-form layer-wise merging, task-dependency analysis, and the reported 4.4-percentage-point ViT-B/32 advantage. The new appendix evidence does not redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: D.8 adds qualifications about narrower advantages on unseen tasks and task-dependent benefits from surrogate exemplars. D.11 interprets differing multimodal correlations through reasoning demands and modality interactions. The original limitations concerning strictly data-free use and more complex operations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit source-code link and clarifies that exemplars are randomly drawn from training data and kept separate from evaluation data. It also identifies the Qwen checkpoints used in the new experiments. The split statement is newly disclosed information, not evidence of a changed split; existing hardware and implementation disclosures remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds eight GLUE language tasks and MTEB retrieval and clustering tasks, extending evaluation beyond vision and vision-language. It also adds unseen-task and corrupted-input scenarios and uses AOKVQA and IconQA as auxiliary exemplar sources alongside existing datasets.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds the Individual fine-tuned BLIP models as a reference comparator, absent from that comparison in v1. Comparator membership in the retained vision experiments is unchanged; the new appendix evaluations primarily reuse existing comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include merging six experts and evaluating two held-out tasks, Gaussian-blurred or surrogate exemplars, seven corruptions applied to exemplars and test data, and restricted exemplar-class coverage. Language evaluations introduce RoBERTa and Qwen3-0.6B settings with classification, correlation, retrieval and clustering metrics. These are added designs, not demonstrated changes to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices D.8, D.9, D.11 and D.12 add substantial analyses of unseen-task transfer, calibration-data mismatch, corruption robustness, multimodal feature-drift correlations, and incomplete exemplar-class coverage. v1's existing parameter ablations, exemplar sensitivity, runtime and consistency analyses are retained.

E5.justification: D.11 and Table 17 add explicit Pearson correlation estimates between feature drift and loss changes across six BLIP tasks, extending the earlier visual association analysis. Three-random-exemplar averaging and the runs in Table 8 remain unchanged; no new confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Existing LOT results, including 82.7% for ViT-B/32 and 90.5% for ViT-L/14, are retained. v2 adds Individual BLIP scores and Tables 11–18, including a GLUE average of 63.13 and Qwen ArguAna performance of 47.36 versus Task Arithmetic's 30.86. These are additional results under new settings, not improvements over v1 under matched conditions.

M1.justification: The layer-wise objective, closed-form merging rules for linear weights, scaling factors and biases, and final lambda-weighted integration remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 corrects a comment without changing its operations; the additional backbones use the existing method.

P1.justification: The core exposition and section order are largely retained. Changes include updated author and affiliation text, expanded acknowledgments, corrected equation references and an algorithm comment, a NeurIPS checklist, and additional appendix subsections rather than extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: Tables 11–18 substantially expand the displayed evidence with generalization, corruption, language-model, correlation and exemplar-coverage results. Table 3 gains a reference row, and the NeurIPS format reflows existing material and resizes Figure 2. Figures 1–3 retain their underlying analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for RoBERTa, GLUE, MTEB and Qwen3 to support the language experiments. The related-work discussion and positioning against RegMean, Surgery and CAT Merging remain substantively unchanged; conversion to numbered citations is stylistic.

T1.justification: Appendix B corrects expert-side activations from f_k^(-1)(W_k) to f_k^(l-1)(W_k) in Equations 22–23 and subsequent steps, repairing the recursive proof's layer indexing. The feature-drift bound, assumptions, and closed-form derivations are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by testing language models and directly examining calibration representativeness, unseen-task transfer and corruption sensitivity, which v1 left untested. The Individual BLIP reference and clearer exemplar provenance also improve assessability. Localized reporting errors temper this gain: Table 11 reports 51.1 for an unseen-task average whose entries average 48.6, and D.8 claims surrogate-exemplar superiority despite OKVQA scoring 40.15 versus Task Arithmetic's 40.37. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LOT Merging. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and can be matched reliably despite formatting changes and additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original language-model evaluations, generalization tests, corruption studies, and feature-drift analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: We propose a method for discovering and visualizing the differences between two learned representations, enabling more direct and interpretable model comparisons. We validate our method, which we call Representational Differences Explanations (RDX), by using it to compare models with known conceptual differences and demonstrate that it recovers meaningful distinctions where existing explainable AI (XAI) techniques fail. Applied to state-of-the-art models on challenging subsets of the ImageNet and iNaturalist datasets, RDX reveals both insightful representational differences and subtle patterns in the data. Although comparison is a cornerstone of scientific analysis, current tools in machine learning, namely post hoc XAI methods, struggle to support model comparison effectively. Our work addresses this gap by introducing an effective and explainable tool for contrasting model representations.

These are substantial added evaluation protocols; the original training, dataset splits, and alignment settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 and Figure A11 add a systematic robustness experiment testing whether extracted concepts remain consistent when images are uniformly added or removed. It covers four retained ImageNet subsets and seven methods. Earlier distance-function, sampling, and alignment analyses remain present.

E5.justification: Tables A3–A6 add numerical mean ± summaries beyond v1's boxplots and point-valued tables. However, v2 does not clearly identify the statistic following ± or document additional repeated runs. The previously disclosed global seed remains unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds detailed BSR and SemanticLens results in Tables A3–A6 and consistency findings in Figure A11, where SAE is most consistent and RDX has relatively low disagreement. M1.justification: The RDX pipeline retains ranked Euclidean distances, the locally biased difference function, spectral clustering, KNA sampling, and optional CKA alignment. The stated rank range changes from 0–n to 1–n, but this wording correction does not establish a different ranking procedure. The new metrics concern evaluation.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose and caption revisions, clarifies visual concepts, separates the monosemanticity discussion, and moves limitations and societal impact from Appendix A into the main discussion. Appendix material is reorganized, but the central narrative and method exposition remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The quantitative presentation expands substantially through four detailed comparison tables and a new consistency plot. R1.justification: v2 adds eight references, including SemanticLens, NLMCD, k-sparse autoencoders, OpenCLIP, Hungarian matching, and Isomap. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RDX research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

arxiv_record.abstract: We develop practical and theoretically grounded membership inference attacks (MIAs) against both independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data and graph-structured data. Building on the Bayesian decision-theoretic framework of Sablayrolles et al., we derive the Bayes-optimal membership inference rule for node-level MIAs against graph neural networks, addressing key open questions about optimal query strategies in the graph setting. We introduce BASE and G-BASE, tractable approximations of the Bayes-optimal membership inference. G-BASE achieves superior performance compared to previously proposed classifier-based node-level MIA attacks. BASE, which is also applicable to non-graph data, matches or exceeds the performance of prior state-of-the-art MIAs, such as LiRA and RMIA, at a significantly lower computational cost. Finally, we show that BASE and RMIA are equivalent under a specific hyperparameter setting, providing a principled, Bayes-optimal justification for the RMIA attack.
arxiv_record.authors: Marcus Lassila, Johan \"Ostman, Khac-Hoang Ngo, Alexandre Graell i Amat
arxiv_record.comments: In NeurIPS 2025, 10 pages plus 15 pages of appendices

arxiv_record.abstract: Data attribution methods, which quantify the influence of individual training data points on a machine learning model, have gained increasing popularity in data-centric applications in modern AI. Despite a recent surge of new methods developed in this space, the impact of hyperparameter tuning in these methods remains under-explored. In this work, we present the first large-scale empirical study to understand the hyperparameter sensitivity of common data attribution methods. Our results show that most methods are indeed sensitive to certain key hyperparameters. However, unlike typical machine learning algorithms -- whose hyperparameters can be tuned using computationally-cheap validation metrics -- evaluating data attribution performance often requires retraining models on subsets of training data, making such metrics prohibitively costly for hyperparameter tuning. This poses a critical open challenge for the practical application of data attribution methods. To address this challenge, we advocate for better theoretical understandings of hyperparameter behavior to inform efficient tuning strategies. As a case study, we provide a theoretical analysis of the regularization term that is critical in many variants of influence function methods. Building on this analysis, we propose a lightweight procedure for selecting the regularization value without model retraining, and validate its effectiveness across a range of standard data attribution benchmarks. Overall, our study identifies a fundamental yet overlooked challenge in the practical application of data attribution, and highlights the importance of careful discussion on hyperparameter selection in future method development.
arxiv_record.authors: Weiyi Wang, Junwei Deng, Yuzheng Hu, Shiyuan Zhang, Xirui Jiang, Runting Zhang, Han Zhao, Jiaqi W. Ma
arxiv_record.title: Taming Hyperparameter Sensitivity in Data Attribution: Practical Selection Without Costly Retraining

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Data attribution methods, which quantify the influence of individual training data points on a machine learning model, have gained increasing popularity in data-centric applications in modern AI. Despite a recent surge of new methods developed in this space, the impact of hyperparameter tuning in these methods remains under-explored. In this work, we present the first large-scale empirical study to understand the hyperparameter sensitivity of common data attribution methods. Our results show that most methods are indeed sensitive to certain key hyperparameters. However, unlike typical machine learning algorithms -- whose hyperparameters can be tuned using computationally-cheap validation metrics -- evaluating data attribution performance often requires retraining models on subsets of training data, making such metrics prohibitively costly for hyperparameter tuning. This poses a critical open challenge for the practical application of data attribution methods. To address this challenge, we advocate for better theoretical understandings of hyperparameter behavior to inform efficient tuning strategies. As a case study, we provide a theoretical analysis of the regularization term that is critical in many variants of influence function methods. Building on this analysis, we propose a lightweight procedure for selecting the regularization value without model retraining, and validate its effectiveness across a range of standard data attribution benchmarks. Overall, our study identifies a fundamental yet overlooked challenge in the practical application of data attribution, and highlights the importance of careful discussion on hyperparameter selection in future method development.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: identifying costly hyperparameter tuning, characterizing sensitivity, and proposing theoretically motivated selection without retraining. The added conclusion sentence about checkpoint sensitivity restates a finding already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds a geometric explanation involving gradient directions, interprets the new constant estimates as support for assumptions in nonconvex settings, and suggests dataset redundancy explains limited effects from 10% removal. The original limitations concerning regularization-specific theory and reliance on LDS remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 documents projected-FIM diagonalization and gradient-based estimation for the new assumption checks. Appendix D changes the listed repository location from the data-attribution-hp organization to TRAIS-Lab. Existing hardware, timing, and default-hyperparameter disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix C.5 adds an actual downstream data-selection/removal task on MNIST, CIFAR-2, and MAESTRO, extending evaluation beyond LDS. No new dataset is introduced: WikiText2/GPT2, including its language-modeling setting, already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: The new downstream comparisons include random removal and explicit default-regularization IFFIM/TRAK comparisons against their selected-regularization variants, alongside a full-data reference. The original sensitivity-study methods and spectral-quantile selection baselines are retained.

E3.justification: The downstream evaluation introduces removal rates of 10%, 30%, and 50%, using test accuracy for MNIST/CIFAR-2 and test loss for MAESTRO. New assumption checks use projection dimension 4096 and epsilon_g = 0.5. These are added protocols; the original LDS evaluation using 50 independently retrained models remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix B.4 adds empirical checks of Assumptions B.7 and B.9 on CIFAR-2 and MAESTRO, estimating their constants relative to the smallest eigenvalue. Figure 7 also extends regularization-sensitivity diagnostics to IFFIM and LoGra on WikiText2/GPT2. The existing subset-fraction robustness analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.5 and Tables 2–4 introduce ten-seed experiments reported as means and standard errors. v1's LDS retrainings did not provide this uncertainty-reporting practice. This does not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments, and no formal significance test is specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds assumption-check measurements, Figure 7's LDS curves, and downstream results in Tables 2–4. For example, at 30% MNIST removal, TRAK Selected yields 83.84% accuracy versus 87.92% for TRAK Default; lower accuracy indicates stronger attribution. CIFAR-2 IFFIM Selected and Default have identical reported results. Original Figures 1–6 retain their results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 still selects the candidate regularization value whose average surrogate indicator is closest to 0.5. The attribution procedures and projection formulations are retained; expanded notation and explanations do not change the algorithm.

P1.justification: Section 4 separates problem formulation from analysis, introduces notation before the theorem, and adds intuition and a proof sketch. Appendix subsections are expanded and renumbered, with local wording and conference-footer updates. Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the two-panel Figure 7 and three downstream-result tables. Existing Figures 1–6 retain their displays, with local relocation, including placing Figures 2 and 3 together. Table 1's caption moves above the table.

R1.justification: v2 adds Deng et al.'s 2025 data-attribution survey as reference 9 and cites it in the introduction. The remaining references largely match after renumbering, and the main novelty positioning is unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds an assumption and derivation connecting the alpha weights to leave-one-out effects. Proposition B.8 restores a missing factor of n, propagated into the constants and inequalities in Lemma B.15's proof. The main sufficient-condition theorem and qualitative monotonicity result remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical validation beyond v1's LDS-only evaluation through ten-seed downstream experiments across three settings. It also repairs a proof-bound error and adds empirical scrutiny of theoretical assumptions. These address important evidential and mathematical weaknesses. The gains remain qualified: CIFAR-2 shows no IFFIM improvement, and the significance claims lack a specified formal test.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds empirical assumption checks, WikiText2/GPT2 surrogate evaluations, and downstream data-removal results.

before.justification: v1 reports original hyperparameter-sensitivity experiments, surrogate-selection evaluations, and subset-fraction analyses in Sections 3–4 and Appendices A and C.

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision-language models like CLIP have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot capabilities in classification and retrieval. However, these models often struggle with compositional reasoning - the ability to understand the relationships between concepts. A recent benchmark, SugarCrepe++, reveals that previous works on improving compositionality have mainly improved lexical sensitivity but neglected semantic understanding. In addition, downstream retrieval performance often deteriorates, although one would expect that improving compositionality should enhance retrieval. In this work, we introduce CLIC (Compositionally-aware Learning in CLIP), a fine-tuning method based on a novel training technique combining multiple images and their associated captions. CLIC improves compositionality across architectures as well as differently pre-trained CLIP models, both in terms of lexical and semantic understanding, and achieves consistent gains in retrieval performance. This even applies to the recent CLIPS, which achieves SOTA retrieval performance. Nevertheless, the short fine-tuning with CLIC leads to an improvement in retrieval and to the best compositional CLIP model on SugarCrepe++. All our models and code are available at https://clic-compositional-clip.github.io
arxiv_record.authors: Amit Peleg, Naman Deep Singh, Matthias Hein
arxiv_record.title: Advancing Compositional Awareness in CLIP with Efficient Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The original CLIP compositionality, retrieval and efficiency claims remain. v2 adds a third introductory contribution and a conclusion claim that CLIC vision features improve LLaVA compositional reasoning while preserving general VLM capabilities. This materially expands the claimed contribution beyond dual-encoder CLIP models.

C2.justification: v2 hypothesizes that reduced negative diversity explains the LLM-swapping variant's mixed results and interprets long-caption retrieval as evidence against concatenation shortcuts. Appendix A replaces v1's inability to test LLaVA with a limitation to the tested LLaVA setting. Figure 6 explicitly acknowledges persistent hallucinations in both LLaVA variants.

D1.justification: Section D.5 supplies model, dataset, resolution, batch size, training stages, baseline controls and codebase information for the new LLaVA pipeline. Appendix B.4 documents fine-grained POS processing, Gemini 2.5-Flash replacement candidates and preprocessing costs. Section D.1 also revises ambiguous GPU-hour wording to training durations on four A100 GPUs.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation beyond the retained CLIP benchmarks to GQA, TextVQA, ScienceQA-Images and MME perception through LLaVA. It also adds qualitative open-ended captioning and a long-caption retrieval scenario using multiple sentences describing one scene. These substantially broaden task and input-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: The original CLIP comparator sets are retained. New comparisons introduce an authors-trained standard LLaVA-1.5-7b control against its CLIC-equipped counterpart (Table 6), and an LLM SWAPS condition (Table 8). The earlier Non-random condition is retained as SAME NOUN, rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: The new LLaVA experiment introduces 336×336 CLIP fine-tuning, an effective batch size of 40×8, staged projector/language-model training, matched baseline training and VQAScore evaluation. Long-caption retrieval introduces punctuation-based truncation within CLIP's 77-token context. These are added protocols; the original CLIP experiments retain their previously documented settings.

E4.justification: Appendix B.4 adds an LLM-swapping ablation and a manual quality audit of 75 negatives from each generation approach. Appendix E adds a long-caption test of concatenation shortcuts, success/failure cases across four SugarCrepe++ categories, and LLaVA captioning examples. The original component ablation is retained, moving from v1 Table 10 to v2 Table 4.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v2 Tables 10–11 introduce means and standard deviations over three independent runs for CLIC-LAION and CLIC-RedCaps across compositionality and downstream benchmarks. This establishes a substantial new reporting practice, although v1's unspecified run counts prevent claiming a particular increase in runs.

E6.justification: Matched original table values are unchanged, but substantial new results appear. v2 Table 6 reports WinoGround text scores of 36.7 versus 43.5 for CLIP-based versus CLIC-based LLaVA, while SQA-I scores are 69.2 versus 68.2. Additional results cover long-caption retrieval, repeated-run summaries, failure cases and negative quality: the manual audit reports 69% meaningful, grammatical negatives for LLM SWAPS versus 28% for standard CLIC.

M1.justification: v2 adds a LLaVA adaptation pipeline that fine-tunes both CLIP encoders, transfers the vision encoder, and trains the projector and language model (Sections 4.5 and D.5). Appendix B.4 adds an LLM-guided negative-generation variant. Equation (5) also changes the stated loss aggregation. The original concatenation and alternating-update scheme remains; implementation changes for retained experiments are not established.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose revisions, expands explanatory examples in Appendix D.4, consolidates the former SOTA subsection into Section 4.4 and introduces dedicated LLaVA sections. Repetitive appendix ablation discussion is shortened, and front matter is updated. Most existing narrative and the appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds uncertainty tables, LLaVA and long-caption comparison tables, four illustrated success/failure tables with cosine scores, and a caption-response comparison figure. These substantially expand the visual evidence. The component ablation moves into the main text, while the original figures are retained and existing tables are redistributed.

R1.justification: Eight targeted references are added, including Gemini 2.5, VQAScore, Long-CLIP and works supporting the new VQA evaluations. The established positioning against NegCLIP, DAC, SVLC and TripletCLIP remains substantially unchanged; the additions mainly contextualize the new experiments.

T1.justification: Equation (5) moves the sum over four positive captions outside the logarithm: v1 takes the logarithm of summed positive-versus-negative probabilities, whereas v2 sums their logarithms. These expressions are not equivalent; v2 aligns with the stated per-positive penalty. This is a localized mathematical correction, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence by adding repeated-run uncertainty, direct tests of negative quality and concatenation shortcuts, and explicit failure examples. Its matched LLaVA experiment addresses v1's stated transfer limitation, while Equation (5) corrects an important specification error. These resolve meaningful reliability, applicability and documentation gaps. The gains remain qualified: LLaVA results lack repeated-run uncertainty, SQA-I decreases from 69.2 to 68.2, and captioning hallucinations persist.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLIC study by the same authors. The complete main texts and appendices A–E, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds authors-trained LLaVA comparisons, repeated-run measurements, long-caption retrieval and a manually assessed negative-generation experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original CLIC fine-tuning experiments, compositionality and downstream evaluations, and component, training-duration and encoder-freezing ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Developing high-performing, yet interpretable models remains a critical challenge in modern AI. Concept-based models (CBMs) attempt to address this by extracting human-understandable concepts from a global encoding (e.g., image encoding) and then applying a linear classifier on the resulting concept activations, enabling transparent decision-making. However, their reliance on holistic image encodings limits their expressiveness in object-centric real-world settings and thus hinders their ability to solve complex vision tasks beyond single-label classification. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Object-Centric Concept Bottlenecks (OCB), a framework that combines the strengths of CBMs and pre-trained object-centric foundation models, boosting performance and interpretability. We evaluate OCB on complex image datasets and conduct a comprehensive ablation study to analyze key components of the framework, such as strategies for aggregating object-concept encodings. The results show that OCB outperforms traditional CBMs and allows one to make interpretable decisions for complex visual tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: David Steinmann, Wolfgang Stammer, Antonia W\"ust, Kristian Kersting
arxiv_record.title: Object Centric Concept Bottlenecks

E2.justification: v3 adds CLIP+MLP across all five benchmark settings in Table 1 and Coarse-to-Fine CBM (C2F-CBM) on SUN397 and COCOLogic in Table 2. These substantially broaden v1's comparisons with standard and equal-capacity SpLiCE-based CBMs.

E3.justification: Section 5 revises the stated COCOLogic metric from accuracy to balanced accuracy; retained numerical scores do not establish recomputation. Added protocols use a common LAION-based vocabulary and nonsparse OCB for the C2F-CBM comparison, and vary feature inputs, sparsity and minimum proposal size from 0.005 to 0.05.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained proposal-model, aggregation and object-count analyses, v3 adds image-only versus object-only controls (Table 4), capacity sweeps (Figure 8), minimum-size sensitivity (Table 10), and duplicate/irrelevant detection examples (Figure 9). These test additional explanations for gains and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and standard deviations over five seeds. The new tables continue this practice, and the added checklist reiterates it. No increased run count, new uncertainty estimator or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 rows and v1 Tables 3–7, retained as v3 Tables 5–9, keep their numerical values. Substantial new results include C2F-CBM versus nonsparse OCB on SUN397 at 70.12 versus 89.60, object-only VOC performance of 77.48, CLIP+MLP scores, and capacity/size sweeps. M1.justification: The proposal filtering, image/object concept extraction, five aggregation options and linear predictor remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. The shared-vocabulary and sparsity discussion clarifies the existing framework; nonsparse and object-only evaluations vary its configuration without introducing a new proposed component.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose are retained. v3 locally rewrites the introduction, evaluation discussion and conclusion, renames Section 5.4, subdivides Appendix E, and appends a NeurIPS checklist. This is limited restructuring rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 expands Table 1, adds comparison/ablation Tables 2, 4 and 10, and introduces the capacity plot and failure illustrations in Figures 8 and 9. It also revises Figures 4–5 captions and rearranges existing figures and appendix tables, substantially expanding the visual presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds Prasse et al. (2025), DCBM, and distinguishes its image-level activation vector from OCB's combined image/object activations. The broader related-work coverage remains stable. Panousis et al.'s C2F-CBM was already cited in v1; its actual evaluation is new.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, filtering equations, aggregation formulas and COCOLogic rules are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs. improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited comparator breadth and incomplete attribution of performance gains. arxiv_record.abstract: Recent neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) methods have shown promising problem-solving ability without requiring domain-specific expertise. Most existing NCO methods use training and testing data with a fixed constraint value and lack research on the effect of constraint tightness on the performance of NCO methods. This paper takes the capacity-constrained vehicle routing problem (CVRP) as an example to empirically analyze the NCO performance under different tightness degrees of the capacity constraint. Our analysis reveals that existing NCO methods overfit the capacity constraint, and they can only perform satisfactorily on a small range of the constraint values but poorly on other values. To tackle this drawback of existing NCO methods, we develop an efficient training scheme that explicitly considers varying degrees of constraint tightness and proposes a multi-expert module to learn a generally adaptable solving strategy. Experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively overcome the overfitting issue, demonstrating superior performances on the CVRP and CVRP with time windows (CVRPTW) with various constraint tightness degrees.
arxiv_record.authors: Fu Luo, Yaoxin Wu, Zhi Zheng, Zhenkun Wang
arxiv_record.title: Rethinking Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Vehicle Routing Problems with Different Constraint Tightness Degrees

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: existing NCO models overfit particular constraint tightnesses, and varying-tightness training plus expert specialization mitigates this on CVRP and CVRPTW. The expanded appendix evidence does not materially redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly qualifies the module as switching between specialists rather than learning one continuously adaptable policy. New discussions interpret vehicle overuse, justify practical capacity-range selection, assess solution-quality/runtime tradeoffs, and discuss applicability to complex routing problems and sensitivity to demand distributions. The original uniform-sampling limitation and future-work paragraph remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v3 reports released code and supplies a repository link. v3 also documents Top-K settings, auxiliary-loss weight 0.01, long-tailed demand generation, heuristic procedures, and runtime measurement conditions, including the CPU/GPU distinction. Conversely, the explicit POMO decoder-expert equations are removed and replaced by a less detailed encoder-placement description.

E1.justification: v3 adds VRPBTW100 and VRPBLTW100, KP200 evaluations, and CVRP tests with long-tailed customer demands. Appendix L also analyzes 192 CVRPLIB instances descriptively. These extend task requirements, domains, and input distributions beyond v1's CVRP/CVRPTW evaluations and retained TSP/OVRP similarity analyses.

E2.justification: The original nine NCO comparators and HGS remain in the corresponding CVRP comparisons. v3 adds a learnable Top-K MoE comparator against discrete switching in Table 10 and introduces OR-Tools as the reference in the complex-routing and knapsack comparisons in Tables 11 and 17.

E3.justification: The original training budgets and greedy-inference settings are retained, but v3 adds substantial evaluation protocols: a MEM-only control, matched-settings Top-K gating evaluation, runtime measurements for 10,000-instance datasets, vehicle-count metrics, and heuristic-based tightness measurements. Appendix O additionally evaluates fixed-capacity KP200 checkpoints across five capacities. The newly stated equal training-data budget clarifies existing settings rather than establishing a budget change.

E4.justification: v3 adds the missing MEM-only ablation in Table 4, tests discrete versus learned gating in Table 10, analyzes vehicle overuse in Table 13, measures MEM's computational tradeoff in Table 14, and tests demand-distribution robustness in Table 16. It also adds capacity-range justification and a knapsack case study. The earlier problem-similarity and batch-versus-instance training analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. Both answer 'No' to checklist item 7 with the same justification about deterministic inference and reporting mean objectives or gaps. The added results retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original primary scores are retained, including Table 3's 1.86% average gap and Table 5's CVRPTW results. v3 adds substantial results: MEM alone averages 8.95% in Table 4; Top-K gating averages 2.17% versus switching's 1.86% in Table 10; augmented POMO averages 10.03% versus 20.91% on VRPBTW100 in Table 11. Runtime, vehicle-count, demand-shift, tightness, and knapsack outcomes are also new.

M1.justification: The varying-tightness training scheme and LEHD multi-expert architecture remain unchanged. However, v1 Appendix F replaces POMO's decoder with lightweight experts containing an added feed-forward layer; v3 Appendix G instead places the multi-expert module in POMO's encoder. This is an explicit architecture revision localized to the POMO adaptation.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized language corrections, a new introductory definition subsection, revised ablation and POMO descriptions, updated affiliations and funding text, and moving the checklist before the appendices. The standalone broader-impacts appendix is removed, with its general assessment retained in the checklist; the extensive new scientific content does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the tabular presentation with runtime comparisons, gating results, multiple task panels, tightness calculations, vehicle counts, and demand-distribution tables. Table 4 gains a MEM-only row. Existing appendix tables are relocated and renumbered, while the three original figures are retained with sizing and layout adjustments.

R1.justification: The introduction updates its cited literature, adding works including CaDA, URS, ARS, and Rethinking Light Decoder-Based Solvers, while removing citations to the dual-aspect transformer, flexible neural k-opt, and DPN papers. Section 7's substantive positioning against fixed-tightness and varying-capacity training remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix J introduces a general mathematical definition of tightness using normalized logarithmic changes in a reference heuristic's objective value between relaxed and extreme constraints. It specifies assumptions and instantiates the definition for CVRP, CVRPTW, and knapsack. This is distinct from v1's retained problem-similarity formula and time-window parameterization. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps in v1 through the MEM-only control, an alternative-gating comparison, broader task and distribution tests, and explicit computational-cost measurements. These strengthen both the overfitting diagnosis and the justification for the proposed design. The reported code release also improves reproducibility access. Statistical uncertainty remains absent, and the revised POMO implementation is less fully specified, but the additional controls and evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work on constraint-tightness overfitting and varying-tightness training with a multi-expert module. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable. Retained material can be matched across appendix renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds original gating comparisons, runtime measurements, complex-routing experiments, demand-distribution tests, and knapsack analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original CVRP and CVRPTW experiments, component ablations, and appendix analyses of problem similarity and training strategies.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have recently shown great promise in advancing robotics by combining embodied reasoning with robot control. A common approach involves training on embodied reasoning tasks related to robot control using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). However, SFT datasets are often heuristically constructed and not explicitly optimized for improving robot control. Furthermore, SFT often leads to issues such as catastrophic forgetting and reduced generalization performance. To address these limitations, we introduce Robot-R1, a novel framework that leverages reinforcement learning to enhance embodied reasoning specifically for robot control. Robot-R1 learns to predict the next keypoint state required for task completion, conditioned on the current scene image and environment metadata derived from expert demonstrations. Inspired by the DeepSeek-R1 learning approach, Robot-R1 samples reasoning-based responses and reinforces those that lead to more accurate predictions. To rigorously evaluate Robot-R1, we also introduce a new benchmark that demands the diverse embodied reasoning capabilities for the task. Our experiments show that models trained with Robot-R1 outperform SFT methods on embodied reasoning tasks. Despite having only 7B parameters, Robot-R1 even surpasses GPT-4o on reasoning tasks related to low-level action control, such as spatial and movement reasoning.
arxiv_record.authors: Dongyoung Kim, Sumin Park, Huiwon Jang, Jinwoo Shin, Jaehyung Kim, Younggyo Seo
arxiv_record.title: Robot-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Enhanced Embodied Reasoning in Robotics

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the claims of RL-enhanced embodied reasoning, the Robot-R1 benchmark, advantages over SFT and strong low-level reasoning relative to commercial models. The added evaluations supply evidence for these claims without materially redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for weak planning-judge agreement, optimizer differences, limited low-level transfer to Bridge images, VLABench failures and the LIBERO object-category decline. These materially expand applicability boundaries and mechanism hypotheses. It also introduces strong seed-robustness interpretations, although Table 8 does not show improvement for every task and seed. The original xyz-only limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents the high-quality SFT data-generation procedure and adds the GR00T-N1.5 implementation reference, diffusion-head training budgets, batch size, robot platform, demonstration counts and rollout counts. Appendix B.1 changes the stated 12-hour training account from one to five epochs while retaining the same hardware. These substantially expand implementation information without establishing a new code release.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained benchmarks, v2 evaluates real demonstration images from BridgeV2, VLABench reasoning categories, LIBERO manipulation tasks and four physical pick-and-place tasks using a Franka Research 3 arm. These substantially extend the represented environments and task requirements, including actual physical execution.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated RLOO and REINFORCE++ alternatives to GRPO in Table 7 and a high-quality CoT-SFT comparator in Table 13. The latter uses GPT-4.1-mini-generated reasoning rather than the original scripted supervision. These extend comparison to alternative RL optimizers and a different supervised-training regime; the original comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 revises the reported training budget from one to five epochs; the training-curve caption changes Open-End/MCQA budgets from two/one to ten/five epochs. This establishes changed reporting, not that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include blind scoring of 80 responses by eight experts, one-epoch Appendix C experiments, 50 rollouts per LIBERO task and 24 trials per physical task. Appendix C's one-epoch statement conflicts with Figure 11's blanket five-epoch description.

E4.justification: v2 adds studies of automatic-judge agreement with experts, dependence on the RL optimizer, sensitivity to sampling seeds, and RL following high-quality SFT initialization. These address evaluation validity and training robustness beyond v1's retained auxiliary-task and question-format ablations. The original qualitative examples are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports two additional sampling-seed runs and presents individual results, means and standard deviations across three seeds in Table 8. Table 6 also introduces Pearson correlations against median ratings from eight experts. v1 contains neither practice; v2 does not provide confidence intervals or a formal significance test supporting its significance language.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and QA-ablation values remain unchanged, while Tables 6–8 and 11–15 add substantial results. These include planning judge correlation of 0.3315 versus approximately 0.89 for other categories, mixed VLABench transfer, and new baseline-versus-Robot-R1 control averages of 69.0% versus 71.8% on LIBERO and 16.67% versus 23.96% on the physical robot. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The core MCQA construction, auxiliary tasks, rewards and GRPO procedure remain unchanged. v2 adds limited adaptations: supervised initialization before Robot-R1 in Appendix C and a diffusion-policy head attached to the LVLM for downstream control in Appendix F. Renaming primitive movement and subtask reasoning does not change their underlying procedures.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes terminology, corrects some wording and updates affiliations, the conference header and acknowledgements. P2.justification: v2 substantially expands quantitative presentation with tables for judge agreement, optimizers, seeds, transfer, cold start and VLA control. arxiv_record.abstract: Predicting accurate future trajectories of pedestrians is essential for autonomous systems but remains a challenging task due to the need for adaptability in different environments and domains. A common approach involves collecting scenario-specific data and performing fine-tuning via backpropagation. However, the need to fine-tune for each new scenario is often impractical for deployment on edge devices. To address this challenge, we introduce TrajICL, an In-Context Learning (ICL) framework for pedestrian trajectory prediction that enables adaptation without fine-tuning on the scenario-specific data at inference time without requiring weight updates. We propose a spatio-temporal similarity-based example selection (STES) method that selects relevant examples from previously observed trajectories within the same scene by identifying similar motion patterns at corresponding locations. To further refine this selection, we introduce prediction-guided example selection (PG-ES), which selects examples based on both the past trajectory and the predicted future trajectory, rather than relying solely on the past trajectory. This approach allows the model to account for long-term dynamics when selecting examples. Finally, instead of relying on small real-world datasets with limited scenario diversity, we train our model on a large-scale synthetic dataset to enhance its prediction ability by leveraging in-context examples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TrajICL achieves remarkable adaptation across both in-domain and cross-domain scenarios, outperforming even fine-tuned approaches across multiple public benchmarks. Project Page: https://fujiry0.github.io/TrajICL-project-page/.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion-based generative models are emerging as powerful tools for long-horizon planning in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly with offline datasets. However, their performance is fundamentally limited by the quality and diversity of training data. This often restricts their generalization to tasks outside their training distribution or longer planning horizons. To overcome this challenge, we propose State-Covering Trajectory Stitching (SCoTS), a novel reward-free trajectory augmentation method that incrementally stitches together short trajectory segments, systematically generating diverse and extended trajectories. SCoTS first learns a temporal distance-preserving latent representation that captures the underlying temporal structure of the environment, then iteratively stitches trajectory segments guided by directional exploration and novelty to effectively cover and expand this latent space. We demonstrate that SCoTS significantly improves the performance and generalization capabilities of diffusion planners on offline goal-conditioned benchmarks requiring stitching and long-horizon reasoning. Furthermore, augmented trajectories generated by SCoTS significantly improve the performance of widely used offline goal-conditioned RL algorithms across diverse environments.
arxiv_record.authors: Kyowoon Lee and Jaesik Choi
arxiv_record.title: State-Covering Trajectory Stitching for Diffusion Planners

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: reward-free trajectory augmentation using temporal embeddings, exploratory stitching and diffusion refinement to improve diffusion planning and offline GCRL. The added experiments broaden supporting evidence without changing these core claims.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 newly argues that local retrieval does not require globally accurate temporal distances. Appendix C explains novelty-driven detours around embedding distortions, interprets parameter sensitivities, and clarifies that reward-free describes stitching rather than downstream reward use. The existing computational-cost and asymmetric-MDP limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New experiment details specify reward-model training on original offline data and navigation preprocessing from 512-ray LiDAR to 64×64 occupancy grids and eight-dimensional beta-VAE representations, with trajectories collected over 5m ranges. Existing architecture specifications, hyperparameter table, hardware, runtimes and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: v3 retains the eight OGBench settings and adds Hopper and Walker2d medium/medium-replay datasets for dense-reward offline RL. It also evaluates noisy, partially observable LiDAR navigation in building and corridor environments, substantially extending task and input coverage.

E2.justification: Diffuser, previously discussed as prior work, becomes an evaluated comparator against Diffuser trained with SCoTS augmentation in Table 11. Comparator membership in the retained main experiments is unchanged; the navigation experiment reuses HIQL.

E3.justification: The original OGBench settings and Table 5 are unchanged. New protocols include component-removal controls and beta, segment-length and retrieval-count sweeps; D4RL normalized-return evaluation with horizon 32, segment length 4 and 2M samples; and navigation evaluation over 100 episodes using short-range collected trajectories and processed LiDAR observations.

E4.justification: v1 includes controller-horizon and replanning ablations, qualitative novelty comparisons and refinement Dynamic MSE analysis. v3 retains these and adds direct temporal-embedding ablation, downstream HD/HIQL refinement ablations, and quantitative sensitivity analyses for novelty weight, segment length and retrieved-candidate count (Tables 6–10).

E5.justification: Existing OGBench reporting remains five seeds, 50 episodes per task and standard deviations. The new D4RL results explicitly average over 50 planning seeds, adding a distinct seed-reporting protocol. Navigation results specify 100 episodes but do not clearly define their run count or reported uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their scores, while Tables 6–12 add substantial results. New comparisons include AntMaze-Giant-Stitch success of 7±2 without temporal embeddings versus 87±2 with them, D4RL average returns of 79.5 for Diffuser versus 87.2 with SCoTS, and building-navigation success of 27±7 for HIQL versus 53±4 with augmentation. These are newly reported comparisons, not revisions of earlier scores.

M1.justification: The core stitching algorithm, objectives and refinement procedure remain unchanged. Appendix C adds limited task-specific adaptations: a learned reward predictor labels augmented dense-reward trajectories, and a pretrained beta-VAE encodes LiDAR occupancy images for navigation.

P1.justification: Most prose and section organization are retained. v3 adds a methodological remark, notation clarification, Appendix C subsections, an impact statement and acknowledgements, alongside small language corrections and conference metadata. The code link moves to the abstract.

P2.justification: Appendix C gains a substantial suite of seven tables presenting component controls, parameter sweeps and additional benchmarks. Existing figures are retained; the novelty and long-horizon illustrations exchange order, Table 5 moves to a standalone page, and surrounding layouts reflow.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting the new experiments and planning context, including beta-VAE, HRL navigation and Fast Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion. The central positioning against reward-guided augmentation and test-time trajectory composition is unchanged. Publication updates to existing references do not introduce different works.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, temporal-distance formulation, expectile objective and stitching scores remain unchanged. No theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is added; the new embedding discussion provides qualitative reasoning.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the method's design and applicability. Tables 6–10 supply direct component and sensitivity tests where v1 relied partly on qualitative illustrations or indirect Dynamic MSE evidence. Dense-reward and LiDAR-navigation experiments test previously unexamined settings. These additions materially improve empirical support, although implementation and uncertainty reporting for the new navigation experiment remain limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCoTS research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite relocated material and added experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds component ablations, sensitivity analyses, D4RL locomotion results and mobile robot navigation results in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original SCoTS planning and data-augmentation experiments, including OGBench results and controller, refinement and replanning analyses. Appendix D separately identifies externally sourced baseline scores.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper studies reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for aligning large language models with human preferences. While RLHF has demonstrated promising results, many algorithms are highly sensitive to misspecifications in the underlying preference model (e.g., the Bradley-Terry model), the reference policy, or the reward function, resulting in undesirable fine-tuning. To address model misspecification, we propose a doubly robust preference optimization algorithm that remains consistent when either the preference model or the reference policy is correctly specified (without requiring both). Our proposal demonstrates superior and more robust performance than state-of-the-art algorithms, both in theory and in practice. The code is available at https://github.com/DRPO4LLM/DRPO4LLM
arxiv_record.authors: Erhan Xu, Kai Ye, Hongyi Zhou, Luhan Zhu, Francesco Quinzan, Chengchun Shi

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims of double robustness, semiparametric efficiency and favorable optimization-gap bounds. The additional experiments support the existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets HH results through pairwise preference noise and discusses DRPO's performance relative to noise-aware DPO variants, including a conjectured benefit from adopting a noise-aware preference model. It also adds discussion of bound tightness. The original importance-sampling variance and model-scale limitations are relocated to Appendix E.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds the 7B model's training information, TRL/BF16 defaults for DPO variants, the custom Dr. DPO loss adaptation and the AlpacaEval reference-response setup. Existing hardware disclosures, DRPO hyperparameters and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds general-purpose instructions from AlpacaEval 2.0 as an explicit out-of-distribution evaluation for HH-trained models, substantially extending evaluation beyond the original training domains. IMDb, TL;DR and HH remain; the added 7B IMDb experiment changes model configuration rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: Empirical comparisons expand beyond PPO and DPO to Dr. DPO, rDPO, cDPO, CPO, ORPO, IPO and RSO in v2 Tables 2–3. IPO and RSO were previously discussed but not evaluated as comparators. The new out-of-distribution comparison also uses SFT-generated responses as its reference.

E3.justification: The added AlpacaEval protocol uses a GPT-4-Turbo-based judge, ordinary and length-controlled win rates, and SFT responses instead of the benchmark's default GPT-4-Turbo references. Appendix C.1 adds Qwen2.5-7B preference evaluation at sample sizes 500–3000. These are additional settings; Appendix C.2 retains GPT-4o-mini for the original PPO/DPO comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit distribution-shift test from HH training to general-purpose instructions and extends the controlled four-way preference/reference-model misspecification analysis to a 7B model. This broadens robustness validation beyond the original settings. The temperature studies and eight qualitative examples are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report 500 simulations and 95% confidence bands for the original IMDb experiment. The added tables introduce no stated new seed or repeated-run protocol, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical evidence. Table 2 reports DRPO-BT win rates of 57.5% against ORPO and 98.5% against IPO. Table 3 reports length-controlled win rates against SFT of 86.38% for DRPO-GPM and 92.16% for Dr. DPO. Table 4 adds 7B MSEs, including 0.000390 with both models correct at 3000 samples. Existing Figures 3–6 and qualitative results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The DR estimator, optimization objective and practical procedure remain unchanged, including importance-ratio clipping, Monte Carlo sampling, stop-gradient construction and KL regularization in Appendix B and Algorithm 1. Testing a larger model does not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: Section 6 is reorganized and partly rewritten, the discussion is shortened, and limitations and broader impacts move to Appendix E. v2 also changes regret terminology to performance gap, corrects reversed DM/IS labels, and updates citation and author formatting. Most methodological and theoretical prose retains its original structure.

P2.justification: The document is extensively retypeset in NeurIPS format, changing typography, page geometry, author layout and float placement. Two main-text comparison tables and a 7B MSE table are added. Existing diagrams and plots are reused, while appendix tables are reflowed and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on noisy-preference optimization, multiple reference models, DR/OPE and the new evaluation benchmark. Section 5 explicitly positions its DPO analysis against bounds requiring linearity assumptions, while Appendix A.7 replaces an unresolved citation with rank-correlation references. The existing RLHF/DR positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an explicit derivation of the reference-policy tangent space. Appendix A.5 inserts a missing coverage factor in an intermediate empirical-process bound. The principal assumptions, theorem statements and convergence rates otherwise remain unchanged apart from equivalent notation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical comparison against PPO and DPO by adding relevant robust alternatives, explicit out-of-distribution testing and larger-model estimator validation. Table 3 also exposes limits to DRPO's comparative advantage, making the evidence more informative. The added win-rate tables lack uncertainty estimates and the main theory is largely unchanged, but the stronger comparative assessment constitutes a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DRPO research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds DPO-variant comparisons, out-of-distribution evaluation and 7B preference-estimation results in Tables 2–4.

before.justification: v1 reports original IMDb preference-estimation simulations and TL;DR/HH fine-tuning results, with temperature checks and qualitative examples in Appendix D.

arxiv_record.abstract: Graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for analyzing graph-structured data, achieving remarkable success across diverse applications. However, the theoretical understanding of the stability of these models, i.e., their sensitivity to small changes in the graph structure, remains in rather limited settings, hampering the development and deployment of robust and trustworthy models in practice. To fill this gap, we study how perturbations in the graph topology affect GCNN outputs and propose a novel formulation for analyzing model stability. Unlike prior studies that focus only on worst-case perturbations, our distribution-aware formulation characterizes output perturbations across a broad range of input data. This way, our framework enables, for the first time, a probabilistic perspective on the interplay between the statistical properties of the node data and perturbations in the graph topology. We conduct extensive experiments to validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate their benefits over existing baselines, in terms of both representation stability and adversarial attacks on downstream tasks. Our results demonstrate the practical significance of the proposed formulation and highlight the importance of incorporating data distribution into stability analysis.
arxiv_record.authors: Ning Zhang, Henry Kenlay, Li Zhang, Mihai Cucuringu, Xiaowen Dong
arxiv_record.title: On the Stability of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks: A Probabilistic Perspective
