C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: distribution-aware embedding stability, an exact graph-filter characterization, a multilayer bound, structural interpretation, and task-agnostic attacks. The additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly explains that maximizing embedding disruption need not maximize misclassification, using Squirrel as evidence. It also cautiously suggests extending the analysis to MPNNs and discusses the efficiency-versus-optimality tradeoff of restricted greedy search. Earlier structural and depth-related interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 newly specifies losses, Adam optimization, weight decay, training epochs, the 250-iteration PGD limit, and approximately ten-minute Cora attack times. v4 also clarifies the simplified GIN implementation and supplies technical details for the added experiments. The code URL and stated V100 hardware were already present in v1.

E1.justification: v4 retains the earlier datasets and adds Chameleon and Squirrel for heterophilic node classification, plus ogbn-arxiv, ogbn-mag, ogbn-products, and pokec for large-graph embedding attacks. This extends coverage to new graph populations, heterogeneous structure, and million-node environments.

E2.justification: Random and Wst-PGD remain the comparators in the existing experiments. Figure 5 adds a majority-class classifier reference, while Appendix C.8 evaluates a stochastic greedy version of the worst-case attack, Wst, alongside the new Prob approximation.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2 changes the reported node-classification learning rate from 0.001 to 0.01 and graph-classification hidden dimensions from 64 to {32,64}. Added experiments introduce deeper GIN configurations, H2GCN with specified heterophilic-data splits, and a 200-edge deletion protocol for large graphs. These are substantive reported setting changes and new evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix C.6 adds experiments varying the internal MLP depth of GIN to test applicability beyond the simplified convolutional architecture. Appendix C.8 adds computational scalability analysis with runtime and peak memory measurements. The earlier structural case study and five-layer depth/activation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports downstream averages over five attack repetitions without dispersion in Table 1. v4 reports averages over ten pretrained models with plus-minus values and explicitly reports means and standard deviations for the H2GCN experiments. The existing 200 random-weight trials remain; this is not simply a five-to-ten increase in the same repetition count.

E6.justification: Table 1 is extensively revised: for example, MUTAG GCN accuracy after Prob-PGD changes from 0.29 to 42.89 ± 4.86%. Revised settings and aggregation prevent treating this as a same-setting performance improvement. Figures 2 and 5 also change, and Tables 5-7 add substantial results, including Squirrel's larger embedding disruption without the greatest accuracy degradation.

M1.justification: The original Prob-PGD objective and Algorithm 1 remain, but Appendix C.8 introduces a distinct scalable approximation, Prob. It samples candidate existing edges and greedily deletes the objective-maximizing edge at each iteration, substantially changing the search procedure and restricting attacks to deletions.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section structure remain largely intact. v4 locally rewrites experimental descriptions, expands implementation explanations, moves second-moment estimation from Appendix C.5 to C.3, and adds acknowledgments and revised author information. The new scientific sections do not constitute a wholesale language rewrite.

P2.justification: v4 adds the filter-reference Table 3 and experimental Tables 5-7; the earlier architecture table is retained as Table 4. Table 1 is redesigned for percentages and uncertainty, Figure 2 corrects the adjacency/Laplacian axis labels, and Figure 5 is redrawn with a majority-class reference. Existing appendix plots are consolidated and relocated.

R1.justification: v4 adds two Parada-Mayorga stability papers to related work and references supporting OGB datasets, H2GCN, and standard graph filters. The central positioning against worst-case stability analysis remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Remark 2 changes the permutation-alignment criterion from the unscripted spectral norm to the Frobenius norm. The principal stability theorems, assumptions, structural proposition, and proof arguments remain substantively unchanged; added standard filter and architecture formulas mainly expand exposition.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens empirical assessment and reproducibility: central downstream results gain model-level variability reporting, training details become more explicit, and new experiments examine deeper architectures, heterophily, and computational feasibility beyond small graphs. The Squirrel discussion also qualifies the connection between embedding disruption and classification failure. These address important reporting and validation gaps in v1. The scalability evidence concerns the greedy approximation, however, and does not establish scalability of the original full PGD procedure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across section moves and renumbering.

after.justification: Original empirical results remain and are updated, with additional experiments on deeper GINs, heterophilic datasets, and large graphs in Appendices C.6-C.8.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original simulations and adversarial-attack experiments, including embedding perturbations and downstream classification results.

arxiv_record.abstract: As large language models increasingly gain popularity in real-world applications, processing extremely long contexts, often exceeding the model's pre-trained context limits, has emerged as a critical challenge. While existing approaches to efficient long-context processing show promise, recurrent compression-based methods struggle with information preservation, whereas random access approaches require substantial memory resources. We introduce REFORM, a novel inference framework that efficiently handles long contexts through a two-phase approach. First, it incrementally processes input chunks while maintaining a compressed KV cache, constructs cross-layer context embeddings, and utilizes early exit strategy for improved efficiency. Second, it identifies and gathers essential tokens via similarity matching and selectively recomputes the KV cache. Compared to baselines, REFORM achieves over 52% and 34% performance gains on RULER and BABILong respectively at 1M context length. It also outperforms baselines on Infinite-Bench, RepoEval, and MM-NIAH, demonstrating flexibility across diverse tasks and domains. Additionally, REFORM reduces inference time by 30% and peak memory usage by 5%, achieving both efficiency and superior performance.

C1.justification: The main framework, efficiency, and modality-generality claims remain. V2 adds an explicit superiority claim for repository-level code completion and revises the headline RULER/BABILong gains from over 50%/27% to over 52%/34%. The underlying RULER/BABILong tables are unchanged, so these numerical revisions do not demonstrate improved method performance.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations linking pooling to contextual preservation, faster decoding to the smaller recomputed cache, and complementary heads to structural versus semantic retrieval. Section 5 newly discusses gathering reliability and redundant attention-score computation with Flash Attention. Appendices D.2 and E expand the interpretation of efficiency and head specialization beyond v1's narrower discussion.

D1.justification: V2 lists exact head/layer choices for both Qwen2.5-Coder models, discloses redundant attention-score matrix multiplication, estimates offline head-selection cost, and adds dataset/model license information. The previously specified Mistral, Qwen-7B, and Pixtral head choices and cache budgets remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 expands ∞-Bench from four English text tasks to ten, adding passkey, number and key-value retrieval, Chinese QA, code debugging, and mathematical finding. RepoEval adds repository-level API and line completion. These substantially broaden language, domain, and task coverage beyond the retained benchmarks.

E2.justification: V1 Figure 3 compares REFORM with H2O, InfiniPot, and InfLLM on NIAH; v2 retains only REFORM's heatmap and removes those comparisons. The principal benchmark and RAG comparator sets otherwise remain unchanged, and the added experiments use existing comparator methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include RepoEval with Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/7B, repository context excluding the target file, and edit-similarity scoring; Qwen2.5-32B evaluation; and separate prefill/decoding measurements on H200 with 200 generated tokens at 256k, 512k, and 1M contexts. The original H100, 10-token efficiency experiment remains, so these are additional settings rather than replacements.

E4.justification: V2 Table 6a adds sensitivity tests reducing the default 129-token pooling window to 5 and 17 tokens, testing the importance of preserving neighboring context. Appendix D.2 adds prefill/decoding and compress-plus-gather/recomputation latency breakdowns across context lengths. These materially extend the existing component and efficiency analyses; the original compression and head-selection ablations are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Table 8 specifies averaging over 20 runs for the new H200 latency measurements. The retained H100 experiment still reports averaging over 10 samples; this does not establish an increase in runs for that experiment. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, dispersion estimates, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial benchmark, pooling, latency, and 32B-model results. For example, RepoEval 1.5B API completion scores 65.3 for REFORM versus 61.8 for InfLLM. The Mistral ∞-Bench average changes from 31.2 to 50.2 because coverage expands from four to ten tasks; all four shared task columns are unchanged. Matched RULER, BABILong, MM-NIAH, RAG, and H100 efficiency scores remain unchanged. NIAH baseline heatmaps and BABILong across-length averages are removed.

M1.justification: The compression, early exit, normalized head-embedding combination, similarity search, pooling, gathering, and KV recomputation procedure remains unchanged. The expanded head-selection explanation documents the existing procedure, and the code-model experiments apply it without introducing a new component.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A, appendix ablations move into Section 4.5, and realistic-text, code, and multimodal evaluations are consolidated in Section 4.3. Introduction and method explanations are revised, and the supplementary material gains separate discussion, impacts, and licensing sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column presentation. RULER and BABILong tables are merged, RepoEval is combined with MM-NIAH, and ablation/efficiency tables become paired panels. Figure 3 shrinks from four comparator heatmaps to one, while new latency and larger-model tables extend the appendix displays.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in sensitive domains, where their ability to infer personal data from seemingly benign text introduces emerging privacy risks. While recent LLM-based anonymization methods help mitigate such risks, they often rely on proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4), raising concerns about cost and the potential exposure of sensitive data to untrusted external systems. To address this, we introduce SElf-refining Anonymization with Language model (SEAL), a novel distillation framework for training small language models (SLMs) to perform effective anonymization without relying on external models at inference time. SEAL leverages adversarial interactions between an LLM anonymizer and an inference model to collect trajectories of anonymized texts and inferred attributes, which are then used to distill anonymization and critique capabilities into SLMs through supervised fine-tuning and preference learning. The resulting models learn both to anonymize text and to evaluate their outputs, enabling iterative improvement of anonymization quality via self-refinement. Experiments on SynthPAI, a dataset of synthetic personal profiles and text comments, demonstrate that SLMs trained with SEAL achieve substantial improvements in anonymization capabilities. Notably, 8B models attain a privacy-utility trade-off comparable to that of the GPT-4 anonymizer and, with self-refinement, even surpass it in terms of privacy protection. These results highlight the effectiveness of our adversarial distillation framework for training SLMs as efficient anonymizers.

arxiv_record.abstract: Neural models learn representations of high-dimensional data on low-dimensional manifolds. Multiple factors, including stochasticities in the training process, model architectures, and additional inductive biases, may induce different representations, even when learning the same task on the same data. However, it has recently been shown that when a latent structure is shared between distinct latent spaces, relative distances between representations can be preserved, up to distortions. Building on this idea, we demonstrate that exploiting the differential-geometric structure of latent spaces of neural models, it is possible to capture precisely the transformations between representational spaces trained on similar data distributions. Specifically, we assume that distinct neural models parametrize approximately the same underlying manifold, and introduce a representation based on the pullback metric that captures the intrinsic structure of the latent space, while scaling efficiently to large models. We validate experimentally our method on model stitching and retrieval tasks, covering autoencoders and vision foundation discriminative models, across diverse architectures, datasets, and pretraining schemes.
arxiv_record.authors: Hanlin Yu, Berfin Inal, Georgios Arvanitidis, Soren Hauberg, Francesco Locatello, Marco Fumero
arxiv_record.title: Connecting Neural Models Latent Geometries with Relative Geodesic Representations

arxiv_record.abstract: Correlated equilibria -- and their generalization $\Phi$-equilibria -- are a fundamental object of study in game theory, offering a more tractable alternative to Nash equilibria in multi-player settings. While computational aspects of equilibrium computation are well-understood in some settings, fundamental questions are still open in generalized games, that is, games in which the set of strategies allowed to each player depends on the other players' strategies. These classes of games model fundamental settings in economics and have been a cornerstone of economics research since the seminal paper of Arrow and Debreu [1954]. Recently, there has been growing interest, both in economics and in computer science, in studying correlated equilibria in generalized games. It is known that finding a social welfare maximizing correlated equilibrium in generalized games is NP-hard. However, the existence of efficient algorithms to find any equilibrium remains an important open question. In this paper, we answer this question negatively, showing that this problem is PPAD-complete.
arxiv_record.authors: Martino Bernasconi, Matteo Castiglioni, Andrea Celli, Gabriele Farina
arxiv_record.title: The Complexity of Correlated Equilibria in Generalized Games

C1.justification: The PPAD-completeness headline is retained, but the computational problem referenced by the main contribution now requires stability only against exactly safe deviations, rather than all ν-safe deviations. This substantively redefines the central guarantee. Section 1.1 also adds an explicit impossibility claim for general efficient no-regret convergence and its application to black-box autobidding.

C2.justification: The added discussion in Section 1.1 explains why equilibrium convergence matters for advertising platforms and argues that convergence guarantees must exploit application-specific structure. The existing interpretation of correlation versus coupled constraints and the open question about constant approximations remain.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies software implementation settings, hardware information, experimental processing instructions, or code/data access information. The added construction and normalization details concern mathematical proofs.

E1.justification: Neither version evaluates datasets or experimental tasks. The expanded discussion of Internet advertising introduces application context, not an evaluated domain.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. References to equilibrium algorithms and additional cited work are theoretical context, not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version contains an experimental evaluation protocol. Changes to approximation parameters concern mathematical reductions, not evaluation settings.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity experiments, or empirical case studies. Figure 1 and Appendix A retain their illustrative theoretical examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: There are no empirical result entries, performance rankings, or measured numerical outcomes in either version. Revised theoretical guarantees and bounds are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The reduction strategies remain the same, but the membership construction changes: Section 4 removes the identity blocks and corresponding zero entries from A and b, and Claim 4.5 revises the internal approximation parameters. These are localized changes to the computational reduction.

P1.justification: v2 adds a focused introductory discussion, reorganizes Claim 4.5's proof into three named steps, adds a normalization footnote and acknowledgment, and makes small wording and cross-reference edits. The overall section and appendix organization is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 and its caption are unchanged, but its placement relative to the surrounding argument shifts. The Appendix C.1 matrix display becomes shorter after block removal, and the expanded proof changes equation placement and page layout. There are no new figures or tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hart and Mas-Colell (2000), Agarwal et al. (2014), Balseiro et al. (2021), and Paes Leme et al. (2024) to support the learning and autobidding discussion. It also adds Ni et al. (2025) to the discussion of equilibrium existence without strict feasibility. The central positioning against earlier complexity results remains.

T1.justification: Sections 2.2–3 change admissible deviations from cost at most ν to cost at most zero, while allowing the equilibrium distribution itself cost at most ν. Lemma 3.3 and Equation (2) consequently require deviating marginals to match exactly. Section 4 and Appendix C revise the constraint correspondence, and Claim 4.5 receives new tolerance choices and a substantially rewritten proof of safety, deviation simulation, and equilibrium conditions. These changes alter the formal problem and its membership argument.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central membership argument. It removes v1's identity-block constraints, which imposed nonpositive coordinates alongside a unit-sum requirement, and replaces the unsupported deviation-simulation step with an explicit derivation and revised error bounds in Appendix C.2. The material tradeoff is that this argument establishes the revised, weaker incentive condition against exactly safe deviations, rather than v1's claimed guarantee against all ν-safe deviations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, The Complexity of Correlated Equilibria in Generalized Games. All pages, including Appendices A–C, are readable; the equations and illustrative figure support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical, including its appendices. The added autobidding discussion reports no original empirical results.

before.justification: v1 presents complexity reductions, mathematical proofs, and illustrative constructions, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis results.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Eliciting reliable human feedback is essential for many machine learning tasks, such as learning from noisy labels and aligning AI systems with human preferences. Peer prediction mechanisms incentivize truthful reporting without ground truth verification by scoring agents based on correlations with peers. Traditional mechanisms, which ensure that truth-telling maximizes the expected scores in equilibrium, can elicit honest information while assuming agents' utilities are linear functions of their scores. However, in practice, non-linear payment rules are usually preferred, or agents' utilities are inherently non-linear.
  We propose stochastically dominant truthfulness (SD-truthfulness) as a stronger guarantee: the score distribution of truth-telling stochastically dominates all other strategies, incentivizing truthful reporting for a wide range of monotone utility functions. Our first observation is that no existing peer prediction mechanism naturally satisfies this criterion without strong assumptions. A simple solution -- rounding scores into binary lotteries -- can enforce SD-truthfulness, but often degrades sensitivity, a key property related to fairness and statistical efficiency. We demonstrate how a more careful application of rounding can better preserve sensitivity. Furthermore, we introduce a new enforced agreement (EA) mechanism that is theoretically guaranteed to be SD-truthful in binary-signal settings under mild assumptions, and empirically achieves the highest sensitivity among all known SD-truthful mechanisms.
arxiv_record.authors: Yichi Zhang, Shengwei Xu, David Pennock, Grant Schoenebeck
arxiv_record.title: Stochastically Dominant Peer Prediction

Practical applicability is narrowed: tournaments used as a motivating application in v1 are replaced by threshold rewards, and v2's conclusion explicitly leaves tournament incentive guarantees unresolved.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly explains that correlated scores can let a dominated reporting strategy improve tournament rank, correcting v1's interpretation that SD-truthfulness supports tournament payments. It also adds a variance-control explanation for EA. Conversely, it removes v1's warning that optimal enforcement may overfit the simplified effort model.

D1.justification: V2 adds an experimental-code repository link, specifies the sensitivity simulation count, and documents threshold calibration and evaluation. However, v1 Appendix C.1's prior-sweep joint-distribution matrix and 0.01 step size disappear. The dataset information-structure parameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use binary compound-synthesis judgments and four-class tweet sentiment, with the same crowdsourcing-derived information structures. Prior sweeps, task-count sweeps, and multi-agent effort elicitation remain; reward functions and target effort values change within this coverage.

E2.justification: OA, PTS, CA, MA, and their existing partitioned or rounded variants remain in the comparisons. Original implementations move into Appendix E.2. The budgetary-efficiency plots retain the same six mechanism variants and optimal-linear-payment reference.

E3.justification: Section 7.3 replaces winner-take-all and Borda-count tournaments with fixed-threshold bonuses. Target efforts change from 0.7 and 0.9 to 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, and 0.9. V2 splits 10,000 simulations equally between estimating a 75th-percentile threshold and evaluating payments, substantially revising the payment-evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: The practical robustness check linking sensitivity to budgetary efficiency is substantially revised: tournament-based validation is replaced by threshold-payment validation across four effort levels. Enforcement-choice, prior-sensitivity, and task-count analyses remain. Appendix E.2 reorganizes the existing original-versus-rounded comparison rather than introducing a new ablation.

E5.justification: Section 7.1 newly specifies 20,000 independent Monte Carlo score samples, where v1 specified only T repetitions. This discloses a count without establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based variability.

E6.justification: V1 Figure 3's tournament-payment outcomes are replaced by v2 Figure 2's threshold-payment outcomes at four effort levels. EA-prior remains the lowest-payment mechanism among those plotted. These are substantially replaced results under different reward conditions, not evidence of a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Direct rounding, partition rounding, and EA's enforced distributions, report flipping, and agreement scoring are retained. The general-signal integer-programming enforcement and optimal-enforcement rule move to Appendix C. Changed payment schemes concern the effort-elicitation evaluation.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, model exposition, and mechanism discussion are rewritten and condensed. Sensitivity derivations, non-binary EA, optimal enforcement, and proofs are reorganized into Appendices A–F. Broader Impact and Acknowledgment sections are added.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a conference template with substantially different typography and title layout. Sensitivity plots are merged into a three-panel main figure and separated into four appendix panels; tournament plots are replaced by threshold-payment panels. Table 1 and plot legends are reformatted.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds focused comparisons with mutual-information mechanisms that v1 placed beyond detailed discussion. The Lu et al. (2024) citation is removed. The main research positioning and attribution of binary rounding to Miller et al. (2005) remain.

T1.justification: New Appendix A supplies explicit failure arguments for f-mutual-information, determinant-mutual-information, and pairing mechanisms, extending v1's largely intuitive discussion. The central rounding, binary and three-signal EA, optimal-enforcement, and MA results and proofs are retained after relocation.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important validity problem in v1's practical argument: SD-truthfulness was treated as sufficient for tournament incentives. Section 8 explains the correlated-score limitation, and Section 7.3 replaces tournaments with fixed-threshold rewards calibrated and evaluated on separate samples. This substantially improves alignment between the theoretical guarantee and experimental application, outweighing the loss of prior-sweep documentation and the optimal-enforcement caveat.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SD-truthfulness, rounding, and enforced-agreement study. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching extensively relocated material.

after.justification: Section 7 and Appendix E retain original sensitivity evaluations and report budgetary-efficiency simulations with threshold payments.

before.justification: Section 7 reports original sensitivity and budgetary-efficiency simulations using information structures estimated from crowdsourcing datasets.

arxiv_record.abstract: Perceiving the shape and material of an object from a single image is inherently ambiguous, especially when lighting is unknown and unconstrained. Despite this, humans can often disentangle shape and material, and when they are uncertain, they often move their head slightly or rotate the object to help resolve the ambiguities. Inspired by this behavior, we introduce a novel conditional denoising-diffusion model that generates samples of shape-and-material maps from a short video of an object undergoing differential motions. Our parameter-efficient architecture allows training directly in pixel-space, and it generates many disentangled attributes of an object simultaneously. Trained on a modest number of synthetic object-motion videos with supervision on shape and material, the model exhibits compelling emergent behavior: For static observations, it produces diverse, multimodal predictions of plausible shape-and-material maps that capture the inherent ambiguities; and when objects move, the distributions converge to more accurate explanations. The model also produces high-quality shape-and-material estimates for less ambiguous, real-world objects. By moving beyond single-view to continuous motion observations, and by using generative perception to capture visual ambiguities, our work suggests ways to improve visual reasoning in physically-embodied systems.
arxiv_record.authors: Xinran Nicole Han, Ko Nishino, Todd Zickler
arxiv_record.title: Generative Perception of Shape and Material from Differential Motion

arxiv_record.abstract: Flow-based latent generative models such as Stable Diffusion 3 are able to generate images with remarkable quality, even enabling photorealistic text-to-image generation. Their impressive performance suggests that these models should also constitute powerful priors for inverse imaging problems, but that approach has not yet led to comparable fidelity. There are several key obstacles: (i) the data likelihood term is usually intractable; (ii) learned generative models cannot be directly conditioned on the distorted observations, leading to conflicting objectives between data likelihood and prior; and (iii) the reconstructions can deviate from the observed data. We present FLAIR, a novel, training-free variational framework that leverages flow-based generative models as prior for inverse problems. To that end, we introduce a variational objective for flow matching that is agnostic to the type of degradation, and combine it with deterministic trajectory adjustments to guide the prior towards regions which are more likely under the posterior. To enforce exact consistency with the observed data, we decouple the optimization of the data fidelity and regularization terms. D1.justification: V2 adds a stated source-code access link in the abstract, tuned likelihood weights and a regularizer scale for pixel-space experiments, runtime/memory measurements, and explicit pFID patch counts. The existing detailed SD3 implementation, hardware, preprocessing, and default optimization disclosures are largely retained. The linked resource itself was not inspected.

E1.justification: V2 adds CelebA-HQ through a pretrained pixel-space flow model and evaluation on 1,000 images for inpainting and ×8 super-resolution (Section 5.2, Appendix A.9). E4.justification: New Appendix A.10 tests the speed, memory, and reconstruction-quality effects of a tiny VAE and at most five data-term steps. E5.justification: V1 already reports sample-wise standard deviations and 32-sample posterior variability. FLAIR's main Table 1 values and original component-ablation values remain unchanged. The new experiments have separate settings and do not establish improvements over v1's FLAIR scores.

P1.justification: V2 locally rewrites the abstract and contribution statements, clarifies initialization and terminology, corrects some notation and language, adds acknowledgments, and inserts new appendix subsections. arxiv_record.abstract: Unsigned distance fields (UDFs) are widely used in 3D deep learning due to their ability to represent shapes with arbitrary topology. While prior work has largely focused on learning UDFs from point clouds or multi-view images, extracting meshes from UDFs remains challenging, as the learned fields rarely attain exact zero distances. A common workaround is to reconstruct signed distance fields (SDFs) locally from UDFs to enable surface extraction via Marching Cubes. However, this often introduces topological artifacts such as holes or spurious components. Moreover, local SDFs are inherently incapable of representing non-manifold geometry, leading to complete failure in such cases. To address this gap, we propose MIND (Material Interface from Non-manifold Distance fields), a novel algorithm for generating material interfaces directly from UDFs, enabling non-manifold mesh extraction from a global perspective. The core of our method lies in deriving a meaningful spatial partitioning from the UDF, where the target surface emerges as the interface between distinct regions. We begin by computing a two-signed local field to distinguish the two sides of manifold patches, and then extend this to a multi-labeled global field capable of separating all sides of a non-manifold structure. By combining this multi-labeled field with the input UDF, we construct material interfaces that support non-manifold mesh extraction via a multi-labeled Marching Cubes algorithm. Extensive experiments on UDFs generated from diverse data sources, including point cloud reconstruction, multi-view reconstruction, and medial axis transforms, demonstrate that our approach robustly handles complex non-manifold surfaces and significantly outperforms existing methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/jjjkkyz/MIND.
arxiv_record.authors: Xuhui Chen, Fei Hou, Wencheng Wang, Hong Qin, Ying He
arxiv_record.title: MIND: Material Interface Generation from UDFs for Non-Manifold Surface Reconstruction

Appendix A explains how sampling and envelope choices cause holes, reconstruction failure, or incorrect merging. These materially qualify v1's robustness discussion.

E1.justification: The original benchmarks and reconstruction tasks remain. Appendix B substantially broadens qualitative coverage to indoor scenes, medical data, and additional detailed objects in Figure 16, while Appendix C explicitly tests a non-orientable surface. Additional examples within the existing point-cloud, multi-view, and medial-axis settings also appear.

Appendix A introduces sensitivity protocols varying downsampling voxel size from 0.002 to 0.01, r1 from 0.03 to 0.1, and r2 from 0.0025 to 0.02. These are additional experimental settings, not revisions to the original benchmark protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds a before-and-after refinement comparison in Figure 4, three parameter sensitivity studies in Appendix A, an erosion-induced missing-facet analysis in Figure 10, and a non-orientable failure case in Appendix C. These substantially expand diagnostic evidence beyond v1's comparisons and retained Laplacian illustration.

E5.justification: v1 Table 2 reports single scores; v2 Table 1 adds medians and standard deviations alongside the unchanged means. This introduces dispersion reporting, but no repeated-run counts, seeds, or explanation of the population summarized by the standard deviations is supplied. Additional runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: All six original benchmark scores and their ranking are retained as means, including MIND's 2.917 on ShapeNet-Car and 1.770 on DeepFashion3D. v2 substantially extends the findings with median/std entries, refinement outputs, sensitivity outcomes such as failure at r1 = 0.03, explicit failure cases, and additional qualitative reconstructions. These are added findings, not improved scores under the original settings.

M1.justification: The local side field, erosion and alpha-expansion labeling, region merging, modified M3C extraction, and UDF/Laplacian refinement remain unchanged. v2 clarifies existing envelope and background handling; blockwise labeling and dilation are suggested alternatives, not implemented method changes.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. Local corrections and expanded explanations accompany a new limitations paragraph, Appendices A–C, funding acknowledgments, and publication/corresponding-author updates. This extends the document without extensive rewriting of its existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 removes the conceptual representation table, restructures the numerical table into Mean/Median/Std columns, annotates introductory diagrams, and adds refinement, sensitivity, failure, and reconstruction figures. Original Figures 4–8 remain as Figures 5–9; some appendix views reuse existing cases with close-ups rather than supplying wholly new results.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Hu et al.'s local-shape UDF framework, Du et al.'s implicit surface networks, and Kong et al.'s Voronoi-assisted UDF diffusion. arxiv_record.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on object recognition achieve high task performance but continue to exhibit vulnerability under a range of visual perturbations and out-of-domain images, when compared with biological vision. Prior work has demonstrated that coupling a standard CNN with a front-end (VOneBlock) that mimics the primate primary visual cortex (V1) can improve overall model robustness. Expanding on this, we introduce Early Vision Networks (EVNets), a new class of hybrid CNNs that combine the VOneBlock with a novel SubcorticalBlock, whose architecture draws from computational models in neuroscience and is parameterized to maximize alignment with subcortical responses reported across multiple experimental studies. Without being optimized to do so, the assembly of the SubcorticalBlock with the VOneBlock improved V1 alignment across most standard V1 benchmarks, and better modeled extra-classical receptive field phenomena. In addition, EVNets exhibit stronger emergent shape bias and outperform the base CNN architecture by 9.3% on an aggregate benchmark of robustness evaluations, including adversarial perturbations, common corruptions, and domain shifts. Finally, we show that EVNets can be further improved when paired with a state-of-the-art data augmentation technique, surpassing the performance of the isolated data augmentation approach by 6.2% on our robustness benchmark. This result reveals complementary benefits between changes in architecture to better mimic biology and training-based machine learning approaches.
arxiv_record.authors: Lucas Piper, Arlindo L. Oliveira, Tiago Marques
arxiv_record.title: Explicitly Modeling Subcortical Vision with a Neuro-Inspired Front-End Improves CNN Robustness

native_events.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on object recognition achieve high task performance but continue to exhibit vulnerability under a range of visual perturbations and out-of-domain images, when compared with biological vision. Prior work has demonstrated that coupling a standard CNN with a front-end (VOneBlock) that mimics the primate primary visual cortex (V1) can improve overall model robustness. Expanding on this, we introduce Early Vision Networks (EVNets), a new class of hybrid CNNs that combine the VOneBlock with a novel SubcorticalBlock, whose architecture draws from computational models in neuroscience and is parameterized to maximize alignment with subcortical responses reported across multiple experimental studies. Without being optimized to do so, the assembly of the SubcorticalBlock with the VOneBlock improved V1 alignment across most standard V1 benchmarks, and  better modeled extra-classical receptive field phenomena. In addition, EVNets exhibit stronger emergent shape bias and outperform the base CNN architecture by 9.3\% on an aggregate benchmark of robustness evaluations, including adversarial perturbations, common corruptions, and domain shifts. Finally, we show that EVNets can be further improved when paired with a state-of-the-art data augmentation technique, surpassing the performance of the isolated data augmentation approach by 6.2\% on our robustness benchmark. This result reveals complementary benefits between changes in architecture to better mimic biology and training-based machine learning approaches.

arxiv_record.abstract: Adversarial input attacks can cause a significant shift of CLIP embeddings. This can affect the downstream robustness of models incorporating CLIP in the pipeline, such as text-to-image generative models or large vision language models. While some efforts have been done towards making the CLIP image encoders robust, the robustness of text encoders remains unexplored. In this work, we cover this gap in the literature. We propose LEAF: an efficient adversarial finetuning method for the text domain, with the ability to scale to large CLIP models. Our models significantly improve the zero-shot adversarial accuracy in the text domain, while maintaining the vision performance provided by robust image encoders. When combined with text-to-image diffusion models, we can improve the generation quality under adversarial noise. In multimodal retrieval tasks, LEAF improves the recall under adversarial noise over standard CLIP models. Finally, we show that robust text encoders facilitate better reconstruction of input text from its embedding via direct optimization. We open-source our code ( https://github.com/LIONS-EPFL/LEAF ) and models ( https://huggingface.co/LEAF-CLIP ).

arxiv_record.abstract:
Despite its empirical success, the theoretical foundations of self-supervised contrastive learning (CL) are not yet fully established. In this work, we address this gap by showing that standard CL objectives implicitly approximate a supervised variant we call the negatives-only supervised contrastive loss (NSCL), which excludes same-class contrasts. We prove that the gap between the CL and NSCL losses vanishes as the number of semantic classes increases, under a bound that is both label-agnostic and architecture-independent.
  We characterize the geometric structure of the global minimizers of the NSCL loss: the learned representations exhibit augmentation collapse, within-class collapse, and class centers that form a simplex equiangular tight frame. We further introduce a new bound on the few-shot error of linear-probing. This bound depends on two measures of feature variability--within-class dispersion and variation along the line between class centers. We show that directional variation dominates the bound and that the within-class dispersion's effect diminishes as the number of labeled samples increases. These properties enable CL and NSCL-trained representations to support accurate few-shot label recovery using simple linear probes.
  Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical findings: the gap between CL and NSCL losses decays at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\#\text{classes}})$; the two losses are highly correlated; minimizing the CL loss implicitly brings the NSCL loss close to the value achieved by direct minimization; and the proposed few-shot error bound provides a tight estimate of probing performance in practice. The code and project page of the paper are available at [\href{https://github.com/DLFundamentals/understanding-ssl}{code}, \href{https://dlfundamentals.github.io/ssl-is-approximately-sl/}{project page}].

arxiv_record.abstract: Protein structure prediction models are now capable of generating accurate 3D structural hypotheses from sequence alone. However, they routinely fail to capture the conformational diversity of dynamic biomolecular complexes, often requiring heuristic MSA subsampling approaches for generating alternative states. In parallel, cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has emerged as a powerful tool for imaging near-native structural heterogeneity, but is challenged by arduous pipelines to transform raw experimental data into atomic models. Here, we bridge the gap between these modalities, combining cryo-EM density maps with the rich sequence and biophysical priors learned by protein structure prediction models. Our method, CryoBoltz, guides the sampling trajectory of a pretrained biomolecular structure prediction model using both global and local structural constraints derived from density maps, driving predictions towards conformational states consistent with the experimental data. We demonstrate that this flexible yet powerful inference-time approach allows us to build atomic models into heterogeneous cryo-EM maps across a variety of dynamic biomolecular systems including transporters and antibodies. Code is available at https://github.com/ml-struct-bio/cryoboltz .
arxiv_record.authors: Rishwanth Raghu, Axel Levy, Gordon Wetzstein, Ellen D. Zhong
arxiv_record.title: Multiscale guidance of protein structure prediction with heterogeneous cryo-EM data

arxiv_record.abstract: Motivated by real-world settings where data collection and policy deployment -- whether for a single agent or across multiple agents -- are costly, we study the problem of on-policy single-agent reinforcement learning (RL) and federated RL (FRL) with a focus on minimizing burn-in costs (the sample sizes needed to reach near-optimal regret) and policy switching or communication costs. In parallel finite-horizon episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with $S$ states and $A$ actions, existing methods either require superlinear burn-in costs in $S$ and $A$ or fail to achieve logarithmic switching or communication costs. We propose two novel model-free RL algorithms -- Q-EarlySettled-LowCost and FedQ-EarlySettled-LowCost -- that are the first in the literature to simultaneously achieve: (i) the best near-optimal regret among all known model-free RL or FRL algorithms, (ii) low burn-in cost that scales linearly with $S$ and $A$, and (iii) logarithmic policy switching cost for single-agent RL or communication cost for FRL. Additionally, we establish gap-dependent theoretical guarantees for both regret and switching/communication costs, improving or matching the best-known gap-dependent bounds.
arxiv_record.authors: Haochen Zhang, Zhong Zheng, Lingzhou Xue

arxiv_record.abstract: Modern neural recording techniques such as two-photon imaging or Neuropixel probes allow to acquire vast time-series datasets with responses of hundreds or thousands of neurons. Contrastive learning is a powerful self-supervised framework for learning representations of complex datasets. Existing applications for neural time series rely on generic data augmentations and do not exploit the multi-trial data structure inherent in many neural datasets. Here we present TRACE, a new contrastive learning framework that averages across different subsets of trials to generate positive pairs. TRACE allows to directly learn a two-dimensional embedding, combining ideas from contrastive learning and neighbor embeddings. We show that TRACE outperforms other methods, resolving fine response differences in simulated data. Further, using in vivo recordings, we show that the representations learned by TRACE capture both biologically relevant continuous variation, cell-type-related cluster structure, and can assist data quality control.

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce Rectified Point Flow, a unified parameterization that formulates pairwise point cloud registration and multi-part shape assembly as a single conditional generative problem. Given unposed point clouds, our method learns a continuous point-wise velocity field that transports noisy points toward their target positions, from which part poses are recovered. In contrast to prior work that regresses part-wise poses with ad-hoc symmetry handling, our method intrinsically learns assembly symmetries without symmetry labels. Together with a self-supervised encoder focused on overlapping points, our method achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on six benchmarks spanning pairwise registration and shape assembly. Notably, our unified formulation enables effective joint training on diverse datasets, facilitating the learning of shared geometric priors and consequently boosting accuracy. Project page: https://rectified-pointflow.github.io/.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed in real-world settings increasingly face the need to unlearn sensitive, outdated, or proprietary information. Existing unlearning methods typically formulate forgetting and retention as a regularized trade-off, combining both objectives into a single scalarized loss. This often leads to unstable optimization and degraded performance on retained data, especially under aggressive forgetting. We propose a new formulation of LLM unlearning as a constrained optimization problem: forgetting is enforced via a novel logit-margin flattening loss that explicitly drives the output distribution toward uniformity on a designated forget set, while retention is preserved through a hard constraint on a separate retain set. Compared to entropy-based objectives, our loss is softmax-free, numerically stable, and maintains non-vanishing gradients, enabling more efficient and robust optimization. We solve the constrained problem using a scalable primal-dual algorithm that exposes the trade-off between forgetting and retention through the dynamics of the dual variable, all without any extra computational overhead. Evaluations on the TOFU and MUSE benchmarks across diverse LLM architectures demonstrate that our approach consistently matches or exceeds state-of-the-art baselines, effectively removing targeted information while preserving downstream utility.

arxiv_record.abstract: Real-time decoding of neural activity is central to neuroscience and neurotechnology applications, from closed-loop experiments to brain-computer interfaces, where models are subject to strict latency constraints. Traditional methods, including simple recurrent neural networks, are fast and lightweight but often struggle to generalize to unseen data. In contrast, recent Transformer-based approaches leverage large-scale pretraining for strong generalization performance, but typically have much larger computational requirements and are not always suitable for low-resource or real-time settings. To address these shortcomings, we present POSSM, a novel hybrid architecture that combines individual spike tokenization via a cross-attention module with a recurrent state-space model (SSM) backbone to enable (1) fast and causal online prediction on neural activity and (2) efficient generalization to new sessions, individuals, and tasks through multi-dataset pretraining. We evaluate POSSM's decoding performance and inference speed on intracortical decoding of monkey motor tasks, and show that it extends to clinical applications, namely handwriting and speech decoding in human subjects. Notably, we demonstrate that pretraining on monkey motor-cortical recordings improves decoding performance on the human handwriting task, highlighting the exciting potential for cross-species transfer. In all of these tasks, we find that POSSM achieves decoding accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art Transformers, at a fraction of the inference cost (up to 9x faster on GPU). These results suggest that hybrid SSMs are a promising approach to bridging the gap between accuracy, inference speed, and generalization when training neural decoders for real-time, closed-loop applications.

arxiv_record.abstract: Inference-time scaling trades efficiency for increased reasoning accuracy by generating longer or more parallel sequences. However, in Transformer LLMs, generation cost is bottlenecked by the size of the key-value (KV) cache, rather than the number of generated tokens. Hence, we explore inference-time hyper-scaling: by compressing the KV cache, we can generate more tokens within the same compute budget and further improve the accuracy of scaled inference. The success of this approach, however, hinges on the ability of compression methods to preserve accuracy even at high compression ratios. To make hyper-scaling practical, we introduce Dynamic Memory Sparsification (DMS), a novel method for sparsifying KV caches that only requires 1K training steps to achieve 8$\times$ compression, while maintaining better accuracy than training-free sparse attention. Instead of prematurely discarding cached tokens, DMS delays token eviction, implicitly merging representations and preserving critical information. We demonstrate the effectiveness of inference-time hyper-scaling with DMS on multiple families of LLMs, showing that it boosts accuracy for comparable inference latency and memory load. For instance, we enhance Qwen-R1 32B by 12.0 points on AIME 24, 8.6 on GPQA, and 9.7 on LiveCodeBench on average for an equivalent number of memory reads.
arxiv_record.authors: Adrian {\L}a\'ncucki, Konrad Staniszewski, Piotr Nawrot, Edoardo M. Ponti

C1.justification: The abstract strengthens the numerical Qwen-R1 32B gain claims and explicitly associates them with equivalent memory reads. The central contributions—hyper-scaling through cache compression and data-efficient DMS with delayed eviction—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting measured latency thresholds to model scale and batch size, and compression gains to query-serving throughput. It removes v1's speculation that long-context improvements arise from mitigating over-squashing and lost-in-the-middle effects. Most existing limitations and mechanism explanations remain.

D1.justification: V2 Table 3 newly supplies model-specific learning rates and GPU-hours per compression increment, while Sections 5.1 and H.2 document the added measurement and sampling implementations. The checklist clarifies proprietary-data and incomplete-code limitations. Conversely, v1's specific 32B parallelism, checkpoint-storage, and total-project compute disclosures are removed.

E1.justification: V2 retains the earlier benchmark coverage and adds MMLU-Pro, HumanEval, IFEval, and ArenaHard v0.1 in Table 2. This substantially broadens general-purpose evaluation, particularly by introducing instruction-following and conversation tasks.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain the same vanilla, H2O, TOVA, Quest, and DMC comparators. Quest remains the cache-read comparator and TOVA the peak-memory comparator; the added throughput and Qwen3 comparisons use the existing vanilla baseline strategy.

E3.justification: V2 introduces measured H100 latency and throughput protocols, including throughput at the maximum batch size fitting each configuration. Added Qwen3 experiments use 32K training contexts, a 512-token eviction window, and compression up to 12×. Its Table 2 evaluation specifies a 131072-token generation limit, temperature 0.6, and top-p 0.95; these are protocols for added experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds controlled latency analyses across context lengths, model sizes, and batch sizes in Figure 4, substantially extending v1's analytical treatment of memory bottlenecks with hardware measurements. Figure 6 also extends per-head compression analysis to CR8. The original eviction-policy, data-efficiency, and context-extrapolation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Table 4's unchanged uncertainty values are relabeled from standard deviations to standard errors in v2 Table 6. Appendix H.2 newly specifies averaging Qwen3 AIME results over 10 seeds and MATH-500 over three runs. This does not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial latency, throughput, Qwen3 benchmark, and 32B CR8 results. The reported 32B DMS-versus-vanilla cache-read Pareto margins change from 9.1 to 12.0 on AIME, 7.6 to 8.6 on GPQA, and 9.6 to 9.7 on LiveCodeBench (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 8). These are revised aggregate findings, not demonstrated method-only gains under fixed configurations. Table 1 also changes DMS CR4 MMLU from 40.2 to 40.3.

M1.justification: The operative DMS procedure retains learned eviction decisions, delayed removal, the distillation-plus-compression objective, and the same inference mechanism. Appendix C's separate-projection remark elaborates the already defined trainable projection rather than establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the original related-work section is split between Discussion and Appendix B, the self-attention primer is removed, and the results presentation is restructured. Detailed Llama discussion moves into the appendix, appendices are reorganized, and a conference checklist is appended.

P2.justification: The document changes from the largely two-column NVIDIA layout to a single-column NeurIPS format. Scaling plots are redesigned and redistributed between Figures 3 and 7, with compression-specific symbols and revised annotations. New latency, throughput, benchmark, and training-cost displays materially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for Qwen3, FlashAttention-2, and the four added benchmarks, while removing the over-squashing and lost-in-the-middle references with their associated speculation. The substantive positioning against DMC, training-free sparsification, and prior inference-time scaling remains stable.

T1.justification: The DMS mathematical construction, Pareto-margin definition, and latency derivation in Equations 2–6 remain substantively unchanged. Removing v1's standard multi-head-attention recap condenses background exposition rather than changing mathematical reasoning or theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V1 supports runtime advantages mainly through cache proxies and idealized latency analysis; v2 adds measured H100 latency and throughput, substantially strengthening evidence for the paper's central practical claim. Broader general-purpose evaluations further test applicability. The gains outweigh the loss of some resource-accounting details, although throughput benefits are not universal—Table 7 reports a negative AIME margin for the 1.5B model—and reproducibility remains incomplete.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same inference-time hyper-scaling and Dynamic Memory Sparsification work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds Qwen3 benchmark evaluations, measured latency, and throughput results.

before.justification: V1 reports original reasoning-benchmark evaluations, compression and eviction-policy ablations, and long-context experiments on Qwen and Llama models.

arxiv_record.abstract: Inverse folding models have proven to be highly effective zero-shot predictors of protein stability. Despite this success, the link between the amino acid preferences of an inverse folding model and the free-energy considerations underlying thermodynamic stability remains incompletely understood. A better understanding would be of interest not only from a theoretical perspective, but also potentially provide the basis for stronger zero-shot stability prediction. In this paper, we take steps to clarify the free-energy foundations of inverse folding models. Our derivation reveals the standard practice of likelihood ratios as a simplistic approximation and suggests several paths towards better estimates of the relative stability. We empirically assess these approaches and demonstrate that considerable gains in zero-shot performance can be achieved with fairly simple means.

C2.justification: Section 3.3.1 substantially narrows the justification for neglecting the unfolded term: it dominates for relatively stable variants, while folded-term dominance supports the approximation for strongly destabilizing mutations. V2 also interprets BioEmu as a scalable proxy and suggests structural information explains ESM2's disappointing corrections. However, its broad no-benefit wording overlooks VAMP-seq improvements from 0.51 to 0.59 for single-structure correction and 0.54 to 0.60 for ensemble correction.

D1.justification: V2 specifies 20 BioEmu samples for Figure 2 and discloses that autoregressive-order optimization was not implemented for the ProteinMPNN comparison. Conversely, it removes v1's exact ESM-IF checkpoint identifier and pretraining-source description. E1.justification: V2 adds a multi-protein subset of Tsuboyama et al.'s mega-scale stability dataset, accessed through ProteinGym and evaluated in Figure 2. This substantially broadens the represented proteins and high-throughput stability measurements beyond the retained Protein G, Guerois and VAMP-seq datasets.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds ProteinMPNN alongside ESM-IF on Protein G. Table 2 adds ESM2-based correction variants and sequence-only comparators using either amino-acid frequencies or ESM2, with several unfolded-state treatments. E3.justification: Added evaluations vary the inverse-folding model and ensemble generator on Protein G, and Figure 2 specifies 20 BioEmu samples for the new scaling experiment. E4.justification: V2 adds substantial tests of dependence on the inverse-folding model, replacement of MD by BioEmu, richer sequence corrections, and sequence-only versus structure-based scoring (Section 4.4, Tables 2–3 and Figure 6). arxiv_record.abstract: We study a relaxation of the problem of coupling probability distributions -- a list of samples is generated from one distribution and an accept is declared if any one of these samples is identical to the sample generated from the other distribution. We propose a novel method for generating samples, which extends the Gumbel-max sampling suggested in Daliri et al. (arXiv:2408.07978) for coupling probability distributions. We also establish a corresponding lower bound on the acceptance probability, which we call the list matching lemma. We next discuss two applications of our setup. First, we develop a new mechanism for multi-draft speculative sampling that is simple to implement and achieves performance competitive with baselines such as SpecTr and SpecInfer across a range of language tasks. Our method also guarantees a certain degree of drafter invariance with respect to the output tokens which is not supported by existing schemes. We also provide a theoretical lower bound on the token level acceptance probability. As our second application, we consider distributed lossy compression with side information in a setting where a source sample is compressed and available to multiple decoders, each with independent side information. We propose a compression technique that is based on our generalization of Gumbel-max sampling and show that it provides significant gains in experiments involving synthetic Gaussian sources and the MNIST image dataset.
arxiv_record.authors: Joseph Rowan, Buu Phan, Ashish Khisti
arxiv_record.title: List-Level Distribution Coupling with Applications to Speculative Decoding and Lossy Compression

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: GLS and its matching bound, competitive drafter-invariant multi-draft decoding, and improved multi-decoder compression. Additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability discussion through draft-count computation/memory tradeoffs, vocabulary and alignment limitations, and shared-randomness and floating-point requirements for distributed compression. Appendix D.2 also distinguishes output consistency from output quality and emphasizes that conditional invariance does not guarantee identical outputs.

D1.justification: v3 supplies an explicit code-repository URL, identifies Huggingface Transformers, and documents settings accompanying the Llama and CIFAR-10 additions, including patch dimensions and selected N and beta. Most existing implementation, hardware and training details are unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix D.4 adds CIFAR-10 compression, extending image coverage from handwritten digits to color natural images. Gaussian sources and all five language datasets are retained. The Llama additions change model configurations rather than language-task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the retained experiments. The Llama evaluations reuse the corresponding SpecInfer, SpecTr and Daliri comparisons, while CIFAR-10 reuses the compression baseline. The new consistency analysis also uses the existing SpecInfer comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama 2-68M/7B and Llama 3-1B/8B configurations, plus a paired consistency protocol using ROUGE, fixed randomness and drafter temperatures 1.0 versus 0.5. CIFAR-10 introduces 16-by-16 side-information patches. These substantially expand evaluation design. Section 4.4's full-vocabulary statement is not reconciled with Appendix D.1's retained top-50 setting, so a change to the original sampling protocol cannot be established.

E4.justification: New Tables 7-8 examine empirical matching probabilities and LML-bound tightness on actual LLM distributions across draft counts. Appendix D.2 adds quantitative output-consistency tests and a GSM8K case study under temperature changes. These directly investigate practical consequences of the theoretical properties beyond v1's existing efficiency analyses.

E5.justification: The new consistency study specifies paired runs sharing a seed and averaging over four seeds, with uncertainty values in Table 9. Existing five-seed LLM, ten-repeat Gaussian and five-repeat MNIST reporting is retained; no increase in repetitions of those experiments is documented.

E6.justification: Original numerical results remain unchanged, while v3 adds Llama performance, matching probabilities and bounds, ROUGE consistency, CIFAR-10 distortion, and absolute baseline throughput. For example, new Table 9 reports GSM8K ROUGE-L of 0.745 versus SpecInfer's 0.647; Tables 15-16 report CIFAR-10 MSE of 0.0788 versus 0.0956 at K=4 and Lmax=4. These are additional results under newly reported evaluations.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1-2, the strongly drafter-invariant variant, compression sampling procedures, and documented neural architectures and losses remain unchanged. The additional evaluations do not document a new method component.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and most existing prose are retained. Local expansions add practical guidance, two limitations subsections, Appendix A.7, Appendix D.2 and acknowledgements, alongside wording corrections and updated conference text.

P2.justification: Seven new tables substantially expand the displayed evidence: Llama comparisons, empirical matching/bound comparisons, ROUGE consistency and CIFAR-10 results. Existing compression tables are retained and renumbered. Figures remain largely unchanged, with Figure 4 gaining a Rate (bits) axis label and several displays repositioned.

R1.justification: New references support the added discussions and experiments, including recursive speculative decoding, Gumbel-top-k sampling, CIFAR-10, ROUGE, Transformers and a speculative-decoding survey. Core positioning relative to Daliri and the matching-lemma literature remains unchanged. DROP was already cited in a v1 footnote.

T1.justification: Remark 1 and Appendix A.7 add proofs that the LML bound is exact for point-mass proposals, a single proposal, and identical target/proposal distributions. This supplements the bound's characterization; the main theorems, drafter-invariance definitions and existing derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps: v1 did not directly measure practical output consistency or compare its bound with empirical matching on real LLM distributions. The new analyses, additional model and image evaluations, exactness proofs and deployment limitations substantially strengthen support for the retained contributions. Reporting flaws temper this gain: Appendix D.2 names NaturalReasoning where Table 9 labels MBPP, and the vocabulary-setting descriptions remain unreconciled. These limit reproducibility of parts of the evidence without outweighing the broader improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GLS research, with matching algorithms, theoretical results and original experiments. All 31 pages of v1 and 37 pages of v3, including appendices A-D, support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds Llama evaluations, empirical matching-probability measurements, decoding-consistency experiments and CIFAR-10 compression results.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy-distribution simulations, speculative-decoding experiments, and Gaussian-source and MNIST compression results in the main text and Appendix D.

arxiv_record.abstract: Virtual screening (VS) is a critical component of modern drug discovery, yet most existing methods--whether physics-based or deep learning-based--are developed around holo protein structures with known ligand-bound pockets. Consequently, their performance degrades significantly on apo or predicted structures such as those from AlphaFold2, which are more representative of real-world early-stage drug discovery, where pocket information is often missing. In this paper, we introduce an alignment-and-aggregation framework to enable accurate virtual screening under structural uncertainty. Our method comprises two core components: (1) a tri-modal contrastive learning module that aligns representations of the ligand, the holo pocket, and cavities detected from structures, thereby enhancing robustness to pocket localization error; and (2) a cross-attention based adapter for dynamically aggregating candidate binding sites, enabling the model to learn from activity data even without precise pocket annotations. We evaluated our method on a newly curated benchmark of apo structures, where it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in blind apo setting, improving the early enrichment factor (EF1%) from 11.75 to 37.19. Notably, it also maintains strong performance on holo structures. These results demonstrate the promise of our approach in advancing first-in-class drug discovery, particularly in scenarios lacking experimentally resolved protein-ligand complexes. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Wiley-Z/AANet.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about pocket-localization failures, alignment and aggregation, and near-holo screening under structural uncertainty. The headline EF1% comparison of 11.75 versus 37.19 is unchanged; additional experiments support the existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands qualifications and interpretation: structure-ID filtering may leave target redundancy, ECFP4 performance may exploit DUD-E topology bias, and larger pockets trade coverage against downsampling and irrelevant regions. Appendix D.3 explicitly acknowledges difficulties with flexible or disordered proteins and distinguishes pocket localization from full flexible-binding modeling.

D1.justification: V2 announces public implementation access and supplies an AANet code link absent from v1. New Appendix B.2 specifies ChEMBL molecule and activity filters, target mapping and masking of known positive pairs using UniProt IDs and InChI keys. Appendix D.1 also specifies uniform downsampling to at most 256 atoms, materially improving documentation of the existing pipeline.

E1.justification: V2 adds screening evaluation on 77 DEKOIS targets under holo, predicted-apo annotated and predicted-apo blind conditions (Appendix C.4, Table S10). This substantially extends the evaluated protein–compound data beyond the retained benchmarks; v1 mentioned DEKOIS only in baseline training exclusions.

E2.justification: V2 adds ECFP4 to the ligand-based comparison with AANet (Table S12), and GOLD appears as an additional docking comparator in Table S10. USR and PhaseShape were already evaluated in v1 Table S1. The main screening and pocket-identification comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.5 introduces a separate control excluding training proteins containing chains with at least 90% sequence identity to DUD-E targets, using MMseqs2 on PDBbind and ChEMBL. DEKOIS evaluation additionally reports EF0.5%, while the runtime comparison distinguishes 2.8M, 10M and 100M scoring workloads. These extend the evaluation design without establishing changes to the original main-table protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantial generalization check through homology removal (Table S11), runtime comparisons across workloads (Table S7), and quantitative coverage and atom-count analysis supporting the 10 Å radius (Appendix D.1). The original component ablations, detector-transfer tests, t-SNE analysis and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D.1 newly reports pocket atom counts using mean-plus/minus summaries, including 612.68 ± 240.75 and 199.32 ± 55.04, although the dispersion measure is unspecified. Both versions retain random seed 1 in Table S4; v2 does not add repeated-run uncertainty for screening performance.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for DEKOIS, homology filtering, ligand-based screening, runtime and pocket coverage. DEKOIS predicted-apo blind EF0.5% is 13.33 for AANet versus 0.92 for DrugCLIP. Under the same stated settings, Table 1 also revises Glide's DUD-E holo EF1% from 18.07 to 17.25 and TankBind's LIT-PCBA experimental-apo blind EF1% from 1.97 to 3.42; corresponding AUROC entries change too. AANet's original headline scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The tri-modal alignment, cavity negatives, enlarged pockets and cross-attention aggregation remain unchanged in Sections 3.3–3.4 and Algorithms 1–3. Newly documented activity-pair masking and atom downsampling provide implementation details without establishing a revision to the original procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order remain intact. V2 inserts ChEMBL-processing documentation, expands Appendix C, adds an Appendix D discussion, improves specific appendix references, and updates affiliations, acknowledgements and the conference footer. These are localized structural and editorial changes rather than a broad rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the appendix's tabular presentation with dedicated runtime, DEKOIS, homology-filtering and ligand-based comparison tables. Figure 3 is redrawn with revised phase labels and clearer training-data flow. Existing AUROC and full-holo tables are retained as Tables S8 and S9; Table S12 partly redisplays earlier USR and PhaseShape results alongside the new comparison.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to FlowDock, MMseqs2 and extended-connectivity fingerprints, and discusses PoseBusters when motivating physical plausibility. The ligand-based comparison broadens contextual positioning, but the main related-work narrative and novelty claims remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The pocket and IoU definitions, alignment and aggregation equations, and appendix metric formulas are retained. No theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is added or revised; the new appendix discussion motivates existing design choices.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens validation by addressing the target-redundancy concern left open by v1's structure-ID filtering: AANet retains its advantage under the added 90% sequence-identity exclusion control. DEKOIS evaluation and the ECFP4 comparison broaden scrutiny of generalization and benchmark bias. Detailed ChEMBL processing, implementation-access information and explicit flexible-protein limitations also improve reproducibility and scope. Screening uncertainty across training runs remains unreported, but the combined gains substantially improve the paper's evidential foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AANet study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and can be matched reliably, including material renumbered or relocated in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds DEKOIS evaluation, homology-filtered training comparisons, ligand-based comparisons and quantitative pocket-coverage analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original screening experiments on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA, pocket identification on COACH420, component ablations and additional empirical analyses in the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: A phenomenon known as ''Neural Collapse (NC)'' in deep classification tasks, in which the penultimate-layer features and the final classifiers exhibit an extremely simple geometric structure, has recently attracted considerable attention, with the expectation that it can deepen our understanding of how deep neural networks behave. The Unconstrained Feature Model (UFM) has been proposed to explain NC theoretically, and there emerges a growing body of work that extends NC to tasks other than classification and leverages it for practical applications. In this study, we investigate whether a similar phenomenon arises in deep Ordinal Regression (OR) tasks, via combining the cumulative link model for OR and UFM. We show that a phenomenon we call Ordinal Neural Collapse (ONC) indeed emerges and is characterized by the following three properties: (ONC1) all optimal features in the same class collapse to their within-class mean when regularization is applied; (ONC2) these class means align with the classifier, meaning that they collapse onto a one-dimensional subspace; (ONC3) the optimal latent variables (corresponding to logits or preactivations in classification tasks) are aligned according to the class order, and in particular, in the zero-regularization limit, a highly local and simple geometric relationship emerges between the latent variables and the threshold values. We prove these properties analytically within the UFM framework with fixed threshold values and corroborate them empirically across a variety of datasets. We also discuss how these insights can be leveraged in OR, highlighting the use of fixed thresholds.
arxiv_record.authors: Chuang Ma, Tomoyuki Obuchi, Toshiyuki Tanaka
arxiv_record.title: Neural Collapse in Cumulative Link Models for Ordinal Regression: An Analysis with Unconstrained Feature Model
