C1.justification: The abstract and central theoretical contributions remain essentially unchanged. The conclusion expands the demonstrated practical benefit of fixed thresholds from faster, more stable training to better classification accuracy, reflecting the new image experiments.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces the speculative minority-class benefit with an interpretation of UTKFace results and narrows its learnable-threshold discussion to ONC1–2. It newly acknowledges that the existing ONC3 metric requires uniformly spaced fixed thresholds. Appendix D.5 explicitly limits the theory's agreement with real networks to qualitative behavior in important respects.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds image preprocessing, pretrained-backbone adaptations, architecture-specific hyperparameters, distributed training details and runtime information; Table 3 adds clog-log settings. The new checklist also reports supplementary code and run instructions, specifically identifying tabular logit/probit code. Actual supplementary-code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds face-image age estimation on UTKFace, grouped into 20 ordinal classes, extending evaluation beyond the five retained tabular ordinal datasets. This introduces a substantially different input domain and prediction task.

E2.justification: Fixed and learnable thresholds remain the comparison pair in corresponding experiments. No external ordinal-regression baseline is added or removed; additional backbones and link functions are experimental configurations within the existing framework.

E3.justification: v2 adds accuracy, QWK, within-1 accuracy and minimum sensitivity, plus an adjusted ONC3 metric for fixed-threshold clog-log experiments. New UTKFace protocols specify an 80/20 stratified split, image preprocessing, three pretrained backbones and 300-epoch training. Appendix D.5 adds a 35-value regularization sweep. Existing tabular training settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D.3 newly tests whether ONC extends to an asymmetric link function. Appendix D.4 examines consistency across image backbones, and D.5 directly tests EOS predictions against trained networks across regularization strengths. The last analysis reveals quantitative discrepancies that v1's numerical EOS illustration did not examine.

E5.justification: v1 already uses 30-holdout averaging and shaded uncertainty bands. v2 adds three-seed repetitions for UTKFace, documents their averaged error bands, and reports error bars for the EOS–network comparison. The precise statistical definition of the bands remains unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for UTKFace, clog-log configurations and additional metrics on retained datasets. Figures 3, 35 and 36 report zero minimum sensitivity for learnable thresholds across all three image backbones, versus positive values for fixed thresholds. Figure 39 newly shows network weight-norm saturation and transition points differing from EOS predictions. These are new findings under added or modified settings.

M1.justification: The central CLM/UFM formulation and threshold parameterization remain unchanged. However, Appendix D.5 explicitly adds feature-norm regularization to the DNN training objective for the new theory-validation experiment; this is a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and main section sequence are retained, with much introductory and formulation prose unchanged. Editing concentrates on experimental descriptions, discussion, conclusion and the revised mathematical appendix. v2 also condenses affiliations and adds acknowledgments and a conference checklist.

P2.justification: Existing six-panel metric figures become ten-panel displays, with reordered panels and logarithmic MAE axes. v2 adds UTKFace, clog-log and theory-comparison figures, expands the hyperparameter table and adds two UTKFace tables. The old strict-log-concavity diagram is removed with its replaced proof.

R1.justification: v2 adds Leindler, Brøndsted and UTKFace/ResNet/DenseNet references, while removing the Barbato and Brascamp–Lieb proof sources. Section 2 revises its description of linguistic collapse, but the overall positioning within neural-collapse research remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 replaces v1's CDF-difference strict-log-concavity argument with a multidimensional translated-integral theorem, a geometric assumption and six supporting lemmas. Appendix D.3 also derives the asymmetric-link offset and defines an adjusted ONC3 metric. The main ONC and EOS theorem statements are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly could not evaluate the hypothesized minority-class benefit because its datasets yielded near-zero validation error. v2 addresses this limitation with a harder image task across three backbones and adds a direct theory–network comparison that exposes quantitative failures. These targeted checks substantially strengthen the empirical grounding and clarify applicability. The learnable-threshold ONC3 metric remains unresolved, and label-shift robustness is still not directly tested, but the expanded validation and more candid limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ONC study, with matching CLM/UFM formulations and core theorems. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds UTKFace experiments, clog-log experiments and a direct comparison between theoretical predictions and trained networks.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical solutions of the equations of state and neural-network experiments on five ordinal datasets, including training curves and feature visualizations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Graph-based learned simulators have emerged as a promising approach for simulating physical systems on unstructured meshes, offering speed and generalization across diverse geometries. However, they often struggle with capturing global phenomena, such as bending or long-range correlations usually occurring in solid mechanics, and suffer from error accumulation over long rollouts due to their reliance on local message passing and direct next-step prediction. We address these limitations by introducing the Rolling Diffusion-Batched Inference Network (ROBIN), a novel learned simulator that integrates two key innovations: (i) Rolling Diffusion-Batched Inference (ROBI), a parallelized inference scheme that amortizes the cost of diffusion-based refinement across physical time steps by overlapping denoising steps across a temporal window. (ii) A Hierarchical Graph Neural Network built on algebraic multigrid coarsening, enabling multiscale message passing across different mesh resolutions. This architecture, implemented via Algebraic-hierarchical Message Passing Networks, captures both fine-scale local dynamics and global structural effects critical for phenomena like beam bending or multi-body contact. We validate ROBIN on challenging 2D and 3D solid mechanics benchmarks involving geometric, material, and contact nonlinearities. ROBIN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on all tasks, substantially outperforming existing next-step learned simulators while reducing inference time by up to an order of magnitude compared to standard diffusion simulators.
arxiv_record.authors: Tobias W\"urth, Niklas Freymuth, Gerhard Neumann, Luise K\"arger
arxiv_record.title: Diffusion-Based Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks for Simulating Nonlinear Solid Mechanics

C1.justification: The core claims about diffusion refinement, hierarchical message passing, accuracy, and accelerated inference remain. v2's introduction additionally claims efficient transfer to much larger meshes while maintaining near-FEM accuracy, extending the claimed applicability beyond the original evaluations.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretation of truncation-induced mesh degradation and the IMPACTPLATE tradeoff between lower displacement error and higher gradient error, hypothesizing low-frequency stabilization versus high-frequency refinement. This qualifies the accuracy–speed interpretation beyond v1's global-error analysis. The SO(3) limitation also changes from restricted applicability to tensor fields and anisotropic materials to potential accuracy benefits for orientation-sensitive predictions.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the future code/data-release promise with reported availability and a project link. It adds BSMS implementation access and detailed training settings, mesh-size statistics, expanded compute accounting, and clearer AMG implementation instructions. Table 1 removes the simulator-name column. These are documentation and access-information changes; external availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The three original physical tasks remain. v2 adds BENDINGBEAMLARGE and a small-to-large mesh transfer scenario, with 8,897 average nodes versus 744 for BENDINGBEAM (Appendix B, Table 1). This extends coverage to substantially larger input meshes within the existing beam-bending task.

E2.justification: The principal comparison expands from MGN and HCMT to include BSMS on all three benchmarks, including qualitative rollout comparisons. BSMS was only cited in v1. v2 also evaluates an HCMT-backbone control retaining DDPMs and ROBI, materially strengthening comparisons with alternative hierarchical architectures.

E3.justification: v2 adds a truncation sweep on one trained model, displacement-gradient evaluation, and fine-tuning versus training from scratch on large meshes. Appendix C changes RMSE normalization from 1/N_i to 1/(N_i N_j) inside the square root. Appendix D swaps reported HCMT training budgets from 2M/3M to 3M/2M iterations for IMPACTPLATE/DEFORMINGPLATE. These are reported protocol revisions; they do not establish whether existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether AMPNs outperform an HCMT backbone under the same diffusion framework, how truncation affects displacement gradients and accumulated mesh damage, and whether pretraining aids larger-mesh learning. These appear in Figures 6–8 and 14–15. The K=5 and K=10 experiments already existed in v1 and are reorganized as ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: While Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) has become standard for improving sample fidelity in conditional diffusion models, it can harm diversity and induce memorization by applying constant guidance regardless of whether a particular sample needs correction. We propose FeedBack Guidance (FBG), which uses a state-dependent coefficient to self-regulate guidance amounts based on need. Our approach is derived from first principles by assuming the learned conditional distribution is linearly corrupted by the unconditional distribution, contrasting with CFG's implicit multiplicative assumption. Our scheme relies on feedback of its own predictions about the conditional signal informativeness to adapt guidance dynamically during inference, challenging the view of guidance as a fixed hyperparameter. The approach is benchmarked on ImageNet512x512, where it significantly outperforms Classifier-Free Guidance and is competitive to Limited Interval Guidance (LIG) while benefitting from a strong mathematical framework. On Text-To-Image generation, we demonstrate that, as anticipated, our approach automatically applies higher guidance scales for complex prompts than for simpler ones and that it can be easily combined with existing guidance schemes such as CFG or LIG.

arxiv_record.abstract: Predicting the 3D conformation of small molecules within protein binding sites is a key challenge in drug design. When a crystallized reference ligand (template) is available, it provides geometric priors that can guide 3D pose prediction. We present a two-stage method for ligand conformation generation guided by such templates. In the first stage, we introduce a molecular alignment approach based on flow-matching to generate 3D coordinates for the ligand, using the template structure as a reference. In the second stage, a differentiable pose optimization procedure refines this conformation based on shape and pharmacophore similarities, internal energy, and, optionally, the protein binding pocket. We introduce a new benchmark of ligand pairs co-crystallized with the same target to evaluate our approach and show that it outperforms standard docking tools and open-access alignment methods, especially in cases involving low similarity to the template or high ligand flexibility.
arxiv_record.authors: No\'emie Bergues, Arthur Carr\'e, Paul Join-Lambert, Brice Hoffmann, Arnaud Blondel and Hamza Tajmouati
arxiv_record.title: Template-Guided 3D Molecular Pose Generation via Flow Matching and Differentiable Optimization

arxiv_record.abstract: Synthetic time series generated by diffusion models enable sharing privacy-sensitive datasets, such as patients' functional MRI records. Key criteria for synthetic data include high data utility and traceability to verify the data source. Recent watermarking methods embed in homogeneous latent spaces, but state-of-the-art time series generators operate in data space, making latent-based watermarking incompatible. This creates the challenge of watermarking directly in data space while handling feature heterogeneity and temporal dependencies. We propose TimeWak, the first watermarking algorithm for multivariate time series diffusion models. To handle temporal dependence and spatial heterogeneity, TimeWak embeds a temporal chained-hashing watermark directly within the temporal-feature data space. The other unique feature is the $\epsilon$-exact inversion, which addresses the non-uniform reconstruction error distribution across features from inverting the diffusion process to detect watermarks. We derive the error bound of inverting multivariate time series while preserving robust watermark detectability. We extensively evaluate TimeWak on its impact on synthetic data quality, watermark detectability, and robustness under various post-editing attacks, against five datasets and baselines of different temporal lengths. Our results show that TimeWak achieves improvements of 61.96% in context-FID score, and 8.44% in correlational scores against the strongest state-of-the-art baseline, while remaining consistently detectable.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhi Wen Soi, Chaoyi Zhu, Fouad Abiad, Aditya Shankar, Jeroen M. Galjaard, Huijuan Wang, Lydia Y. Chen
arxiv_record.title: TimeWak: Temporal Chained-Hashing Watermark for Time Series Data

arxiv_record.abstract: The increasing capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have raised concerns about their misuse in AI-generated plagiarism and social engineering. While various AI-generated text detectors have been proposed to mitigate these risks, many remain vulnerable to simple evasion techniques such as paraphrasing. However, recent detectors have shown greater robustness against such basic attacks. In this work, we introduce Adversarial Paraphrasing, a training-free attack framework that universally humanizes any AI-generated text to evade detection more effectively. Our approach leverages an off-the-shelf instruction-following LLM to paraphrase AI-generated content under the guidance of an AI text detector, producing adversarial examples that are specifically optimized to bypass detection. Extensive experiments show that our attack is both broadly effective and highly transferable across several detection systems. For instance, compared to simple paraphrasing attack--which, ironically, increases the true positive at 1% false positive (T@1%F) by 8.57% on RADAR and 15.03% on Fast-DetectGPT--adversarial paraphrasing, guided by OpenAI-RoBERTa-Large, reduces T@1%F by 64.49% on RADAR and a striking 98.96% on Fast-DetectGPT. Across a diverse set of detectors--including neural network-based, watermark-based, and zero-shot approaches--our attack achieves an average T@1%F reduction of 87.88% under the guidance of OpenAI-RoBERTa-Large. We also analyze the tradeoff between text quality and attack success to find that our method can significantly reduce detection rates, with mostly a slight degradation in text quality. Our adversarial setup highlights the need for more robust and resilient detection strategies in the light of increasingly sophisticated evasion techniques.

arxiv_record.abstract: State entropy regularization has empirically shown better exploration and sample complexity in reinforcement learning (RL). However, its theoretical guarantees have not been studied. In this paper, we show that state entropy regularization improves robustness to structured and spatially correlated perturbations. These types of variation are common in transfer learning but often overlooked by standard robust RL methods, which typically focus on small, uncorrelated changes. We provide a comprehensive characterization of these robustness properties, including formal guarantees under reward and transition uncertainty, as well as settings where the method performs poorly. Much of our analysis contrasts state entropy with the widely used policy entropy regularization, highlighting their different benefits. Finally, from a practical standpoint, we illustrate that compared with policy entropy, the robustness advantages of state entropy are more sensitive to the number of rollouts used for policy evaluation.

E5.justification: Both versions report 96% confidence bounds across 25 seeds and 200 evaluation episodes for the main experiments. E6.justification: Figures 5–6 add substantial results for Pusher reward shifts, Ant obstacles, and action-robust comparators. Retained experiments preserve their qualitative conclusions.

M1.justification: Appendix B.1 retains the same k-nearest-neighbor entropy bonus, intrinsic-reward discounting, and cosine temperature schedule. Joint state/policy-entropy training is also retained. The additional environments apply the existing procedure.

P1.justification: Edits are localized: clarified uncertainty-set wording and spatial-perturbation terminology, expanded experimental descriptions, relocation of the CVaR definition to Appendix A.6, and added acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist. arxiv_record.abstract: Characterizing a large language model's (LLM's) knowledge of a given question is challenging. As a result, prior work has primarily examined LLM behavior under knowledge conflicts, where the model's internal parametric memory contradicts information in the external context. However, this does not fully reflect how well the model knows the answer to the question. In this paper, we first introduce a taxonomy of five knowledge statuses based on the consistency and correctness of LLM knowledge modes. We then propose KScope, a hierarchical framework of statistical tests that progressively refines hypotheses about knowledge modes and characterizes LLM knowledge into one of these five statuses. We apply KScope to nine LLMs across four datasets and systematically establish: (1) Supporting context narrows knowledge gaps across models. (2) Context features related to difficulty, relevance, and familiarity drive successful knowledge updates. (3) LLMs exhibit similar feature preferences when partially correct or conflicted, but diverge sharply when consistently wrong. (4) Context summarization constrained by our feature analysis, together with enhanced credibility, further improves update effectiveness and generalizes across LLMs.
arxiv_record.authors: Yuxin Xiao, Shan Chen, Jack Gallifant, Danielle Bitterman, Thomas Hartvigsen, Marzyeh Ghassemi
arxiv_record.title: KScope: A Framework for Characterizing the Knowledge Status of Language Models

C1.justification: The introduction adds a principal finding that noisy retrieval and open-ended questions reduce knowledge-update effectiveness, and qualifies existing domain/model comparisons as multiple-choice results. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion otherwise retain the taxonomy, KScope, feature-analysis, and augmentation claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving refusals and misleading context, including Gemma's increased absent knowledge without answer options. It explicitly confines the feature and augmentation analyses to gold-context multiple choice and revises the limitations after testing noisy retrieval and open-ended questions. Existing feature-based interpretations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the top-ten-paragraph input and gemma-2-9b-it clustering model for its added experiments. Existing hardware, sampling settings, regression details, appendix prompts, and code-access information are retained; the code link is relocated. Retrieval and clustering implementation details remain brief.

E1.justification: The four datasets remain unchanged, but v2 substantially extends HotpotQA coverage to noisy retrieved context and open-ended answering without predefined options. V1 evaluated three-option questions, using gold supporting evidence for contextual knowledge. These additions change both input conditions and task requirements.

E2.justification: The context-augmentation comparisons retain original context, credibility enhancement, naive summarization, constrained summarization, and their combined strategy. Appendix C retains the majority-class dummy comparator for logistic regression. The additional HotpotQA evaluations reuse the existing nine target LLMs without introducing a competing characterization method.

E3.justification: Sections 5.2–5.3 introduce substantial additional evaluation protocols: supplying the top ten retrieved Wikipedia paragraphs and evaluating free-form responses through semantic clustering with gemma-2-9b-it. Existing experiments retain their settings, including temperature 1, 100 responses, 20 question paraphrases, and the original regression evaluation procedure.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic tests of sensitivity to retrieval quality and answer format across nine LLMs. Figure 5 compares these conditions, while Appendix B Figures 18–19 examine transitions from each initial knowledge status. These analyses test robustness beyond v1's gold-context multiple-choice setting; existing sensitivity and augmentation analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version introduces a different repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or uncertainty-reporting practice. The KScope significance threshold, Bonferroni procedures, correlation significance annotations, and response-sampling counts are retained. The additional experiments do not introduce a new statistical reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Matched original results are unchanged, but v2 adds extensive status distributions and transition results. For Llama-8B on HotpotQA, Figure 5 newly reports 66.6% consistent-correct knowledge with noisy multiple-choice context and 88.6% with open-ended gold context, alongside the retained 95.2% for multiple-choice gold context. These are different experimental conditions, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The four-stage KScope procedure, response sampling, and context-augmentation methods are unchanged. Semantic clustering for open-ended responses was already specified in v1 Section 3.2; v2 evaluates that existing capability and identifies its clustering model rather than introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: V2 consolidates the original distribution and transition discussion into Section 5.1 and organizes new Sections 5.2–5.3 around evaluation settings. It adds scope qualifications, revises limitations, and updates the publication footer. Most prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure 5, combining two retained HotpotQA distributions with three new distributions, and adds appendix transition plots in Figures 18–19. Existing plots receive explicit setting labels and revised captions, with subsequent renumbering and reflow. The established visual designs are largely retained.

R1.justification: The reference list is identical, and the central novelty positioning is retained. Section 2 makes a limited substantive positioning change: the work now examines knowledge updates under both gold and noisy retrieval, whereas v1 described a gold-retrieval setting.

T1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Figure 2 retain the same knowledge-mode definition, five status conditions, empirical distribution estimator, statistical hypotheses, and hierarchical testing logic. No new mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs accompany the added evaluations.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly left open-ended evaluation and noisy retrieval untested despite claiming broader applicability. V2 addresses both gaps across nine LLMs in Sections 5.2–5.3 and Appendix B, providing evidence of applicability and revealing important failure conditions beyond idealized evaluation. This substantially strengthens the paper's empirical support. The gains remain bounded by the HotpotQA-only extensions, brief retrieval/clustering documentation, and unchanged gold-context scope of the feature and augmentation analyses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KScope research work. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching across the revisions.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and adds noisy-context and open-ended HotpotQA evaluations, including detailed knowledge-status transitions in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments characterizing nine LLMs across four datasets, feature-importance analyses, context-augmentation experiments, and supplementary results in the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Generating high fidelity, differentially private (DP) synthetic images offers a promising route to share and analyze sensitive visual data without compromising individual privacy. However, existing DP image synthesis methods struggle to produce high resolution outputs that faithfully capture the structure of the original data. In this paper, we introduce a novel method, referred to as Synthesis via Private Textual Intermediaries (SPTI), that can generate high resolution DP images with easy adoption. The key idea is to shift the challenge of DP image synthesis from the image domain to the text domain by leveraging state of the art DP text generation methods. SPTI first summarizes each private image into a concise textual description using image to text models, then applies a modified Private Evolution algorithm to generate DP text, and finally reconstructs images using text to image models. Notably, SPTI requires no model training, only inference with off the shelf models. Given a private dataset, SPTI produces synthetic images of substantially higher quality than prior DP approaches. On the LSUN Bedroom dataset, SPTI attains an FID equal to 26.71 under epsilon equal to 1.0, improving over Private Evolution FID of 40.36. Similarly, on MM CelebA HQ, SPTI achieves an FID equal to 33.27 at epsilon equal to 1.0, compared to 57.01 from DP fine tuning baselines. Overall, our results demonstrate that Synthesis via Private Textual Intermediaries provides a resource efficient and proprietary model compatible framework for generating high resolution DP synthetic images, greatly expanding access to private visual datasets.
arxiv_record.authors: Haoxiang Wang, Zinan Lin, Da Yu, Huishuai Zhang
arxiv_record.title: Synthesize Privacy-Preserving High-Resolution Images via Private Textual Intermediaries

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of training-free, API-compatible DP image synthesis through textual intermediaries and image-space voting. The new evaluations support these existing contributions rather than redefine them. Changing headline FID inequalities to equalities does not alter the central scientific claim.

C2.justification: Appendix D newly attributes poor Cat/bird performance to low diversity rather than small sample size alone, adding a substantive applicability boundary. Section 4.3 links downstream gains to synthetic-data diversity. Section 7 explicitly acknowledges higher computational demands than PE and argues that diversity and generalization benefits justify the cost.

D1.justification: v3 newly supplies a code-release link and substantially expands resource disclosures. Section 7 replaces the brief 80 GB hardware statement with approximately 70 GB peak memory, 19 hours on an A800 or 15.5 hours on two A100s, PE resource comparisons, and token budgets. It also documents the new classifier and bird-subset construction; most existing hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: The original six synthesis datasets remain. v3 adds CelebA Wearing_Lipstick classification, extending evaluation to downstream predictive utility, and ImageNet100-derived bird populations with different class diversity in Appendix D.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds DP-finetune comparisons on LSUN Bedroom, Cat, European Art, Wave-ui-25k, and Sprite Fright; v1 compares only SPTI and PE there, although DP-finetune already appears on MM-CelebA-HQ. The new classification evaluation also includes a classifier trained on real data as a reference alongside PE-generated data.

E3.justification: The new downstream protocol trains WRN-40-4 on 2,000–10,000 synthetic or real samples and evaluates classification accuracy. Appendix D introduces a controlled design crossing two versus twenty bird classes with 200 versus 2,000 images. For retained Cat experiments, the reported lookahead degree changes from 8 to 4 for both SPTI and PE; this does not itself establish rerunning.

E4.justification: New Appendix D investigates whether the Cat failure reflects limited diversity or small dataset size through controlled bird experiments. Appendix B.3 adds training/test learning curves and comparative generated-face examples. The retained API-choice ablation also gains an Infinity backend in Table 4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for the empirical results. Added training curves and experimental conditions do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Numerous FID values and trajectories are revised. At epsilon=1, Table 1 changes LSUN Bedroom from 26.71 to 26.39 and European Art from 50.78 to 57.64. Table 2 reverses the SPTI backbone ranking: LDM versus SDXL changes from 37.96 versus 33.27 to 33.41 versus 34.17. New baseline, classification, bird, and Infinity results substantially expand the evidence. Cat changes cannot be treated as same-setting gains because its reported lookahead changes.

M1.justification: The central SPTI pipeline is retained. Algorithm 2 makes limited computational corrections: lookahead variations take the current caption population instead of N, embeddings are averaged without the extra Phi operation, and population expansion uses L-1 instead of K-1. These establish corrections to the specified algorithm, without establishing an implementation change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained. v3 inserts a downstream-task subsection and new appendix analyses, expands the computational-overhead discussion, and makes local wording, citation, affiliation, and venue edits. Existing configuration and dataset appendices move from D/E to E/F.

P2.justification: Figure 1 redraws the SPTI flow to show private images as references for evolving random captions. Appendix FID plots are redrawn and reorganized into paired layouts. v3 adds classification and learning-curve figures, comparative face panels, and the bird-results table, while expanding Table 1 with baseline rows and Table 4 with an Infinity column.

R1.justification: v3 adds Kong and Syed's concurrent caption-based private photo-album synthesis and explicitly distinguishes its hierarchical fine-tuning from SPTI's API-based image voting. It also adds a Struct-Bench citation. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal DP definition, Wasserstein formulation, histogram-sensitivity argument, Gaussian calibration and composition equation, and postprocessing guarantee are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive revision to the privacy reasoning appears.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily validated utility through FID and left the Cat failure unexplained. v3 adds direct downstream-utility evidence, a controlled diversity-versus-size investigation, broader DP-finetuning comparisons, and explicit computational costs, substantially improving empirical support and applicability assessment. arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, leveraging pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) for building vision-language-action (VLA) models has emerged as a promising approach to effective robot manipulation learning. However, only few methods incorporate 3D signals into VLMs for action prediction, and they do not fully leverage the spatial structure inherent in 3D data, leading to low sample efficiency. In this paper, we introduce BridgeVLA, a novel 3D VLA model that (1) projects 3D inputs to multiple 2D images, ensuring input alignment with the VLM backbone, and (2) utilizes 2D heatmaps for action prediction, unifying the input and output spaces within a consistent 2D image space. In addition, we propose a scalable pre-training method that equips the VLM backbone with the capability to predict 2D heatmaps before downstream policy learning. Extensive experiments show the proposed method is able to learn 3D manipulation efficiently and effectively. BridgeVLA outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods across three simulation benchmarks. In RLBench, it improves the average success rate from 81.4% to 88.2%. In COLOSSEUM, it demonstrates significantly better performance in challenging generalization settings, boosting the average success rate from 56.7% to 64.0%. In GemBench, it surpasses all the comparing baseline methods in terms of average success rate. In real-robot experiments, BridgeVLA outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline method by 32% on average. It generalizes robustly in multiple out-of-distribution settings, including visual disturbances and unseen instructions. Remarkably, it is able to achieve a success rate of 96.8% on 10+ tasks with only 3 trajectories per task, highlighting its extraordinary sample efficiency. arxiv_record.abstract: Recent studies empirically reveal that large reasoning models (LRMs) can automatically allocate more reasoning strengths (i.e., the number of reasoning tokens) for harder problems, exhibiting difficulty-awareness for better task performance. While this automatic reasoning strength allocation phenomenon has been widely observed, its underlying mechanism remains largely unexplored. To this end, we provide explanations for this phenomenon from the perspective of model activations. We find evidence that LRMs pre-plan the reasoning strengths in their activations even before generation, with this reasoning strength causally controlled by the magnitude of a pre-allocated directional vector. Specifically, we show that the number of reasoning tokens is predictable solely based on the question activations using linear probes, indicating that LRMs estimate the required reasoning strength in advance. We then uncover that LRMs encode this reasoning strength through a pre-allocated directional vector embedded in the activations of the model, where the vector's magnitude modulates the reasoning strength. Subtracting this vector can lead to reduced reasoning token number and performance, while adding this vector can lead to increased reasoning token number and even improved performance. We further reveal that this direction vector consistently yields positive reasoning length prediction, and it modifies the logits of end-of-reasoning token </think> to affect the reasoning length. Finally, we demonstrate two potential applications of our findings: overthinking behavior detection and enabling efficient reasoning on simple problems. Our work provides new insights into the internal mechanisms of reasoning in LRMs and offers practical tools for controlling their reasoning behaviors. Our code is available at https://github.com/AlphaLab-USTC/LRM-plans-CoT.
arxiv_record.authors: Leheng Sheng and An Zhang and Zijian Wu and Weixiang Zhao and Changshuo Shen and Yi Zhang and Xiang Wang and Tat-Seng Chua

arxiv_record.abstract: State-of-the-art embeddings often capture distinct yet complementary discriminative features: For instance, one image embedding model may excel at distinguishing fine-grained textures, while another focuses on object-level structure. Motivated by this observation, we propose a principled approach to fuse such complementary representations through kernel multiplication. Multiplying the kernel similarity functions of two embeddings allows their discriminative structures to interact, producing a fused representation whose kernel encodes the union of the clusters identified by each parent embedding. This formulation also provides a natural way to construct joint kernels for paired multi-modal data (e.g., image-text tuples), where the product of modality-specific kernels inherits structure from both domains. We highlight that this kernel product is mathematically realized via the Kronecker product of the embedding feature maps, yielding our proposed KrossFuse framework for embedding fusion. To address the computational cost of the resulting high-dimensional Kronecker space, we further develop RP-KrossFuse, a scalable variant that leverages random projections for efficient approximation. As a key application, we use this framework to bridge the performance gap between cross-modal embeddings (e.g., CLIP, BLIP) and unimodal experts (e.g., DINOv2, E5). Experiments show that RP-KrossFuse effectively integrates these models, enhancing modality-specific performance while preserving cross-modal alignment. The project code is available at https://github.com/yokiwuuu/KrossFuse.
arxiv_record.authors: Youqi Wu, Jingwei Zhang, Farzan Farnia
arxiv_record.title: When Kernels Multiply, Clusters Unify: Fusing Embeddings with the Kronecker Product

Multiplying the kernel similarity functions of two embeddings allows their discriminative structures to interact, producing a fused representation whose kernel encodes the union of the clusters identified by each parent embedding. This formulation also provides a natural way to construct joint kernels for paired multi-modal data (e.g., image-text tuples), where the product of modality-specific kernels inherits structure from both domains. We highlight that this kernel product is mathematically realized via the Kronecker product of the embedding feature maps, yielding our proposed KrossFuse framework for embedding fusion. To address the computational cost of the resulting high-dimensional Kronecker space, we further develop RP-KrossFuse, a scalable variant that leverages random projections for efficient approximation. As a key application, we use this framework to bridge the performance gap between cross-modal embeddings (e.g., CLIP, BLIP) and unimodal experts (e.g., DINOv2, E5). Experiments show that RP-KrossFuse effectively integrates these models, enhancing modality-specific performance while preserving cross-modal alignment. The project code is available at https://github.com/yokiwuuu/KrossFuse.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on combining cross-modal embeddings with unimodal experts while preserving alignment. V2's abstract, introduction, and contribution list broaden this to a general framework for unifying complementary cluster structures and constructing joint kernels for paired multimodal data. Cross-modal/unimodal fusion becomes a key application of that broader claim.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about signed kernels, hyperparameter dependence, larger fused dimensions, and dimensional comparability, with PCA suggested when compactness is required. It explicitly confines learned unitary alignment to cross-modal clustering. New discussion also explains where concatenation remains competitive and conditions the parallel-inference argument on sufficient memory.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-code access link, explicit projection dimensions in experimental descriptions and table captions, separate profiling hardware and batch-size details, and unimodal-fusion pseudocode. These are incremental reproducibility disclosures; the original encoder choices, C-search range, and general two-RTX-4090 setup remain. Newly specified dimensions do not establish changes to earlier runs.

E1.justification: V2 adds multimodal classification on MVSA-Single and MVSA-Multiple, class-conditional ImageNet generation using DiT-XL/2, and a six-group profession/gender image-text clustering example using SD-XL Turbo outputs. These extend the represented data and task requirements beyond v1's retained classification, clustering, retrieval, and few-shot coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds plain concatenation comparisons across classification and clustering in C.8, MobileCLIP and OpenVision comparison rows in Table 9, and CLIP-based c-VSG as the diffusion comparator in Table 12. COMM is not new: its results in v1's appendix Table 3 are incorporated into v2's main Table 1.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include diffusion assessment using precision, recall, density, and coverage, plus runtime and peak-memory benchmarking with batch size 128 on two RTX 3090 GPUs, including parallel RP-KrossFuse with projection dimension 5000. ImageNet testing also adds backbone configurations. These are additional protocols; the PDFs do not establish changes to the retained experiments' settings.

E4.justification: V2 expands backbone generalization analysis in C.6, adds inference and fusion efficiency profiling in C.7, and investigates when concatenation versus product fusion helps across supervised classification and unsupervised clustering in C.8. Figure 2 adds a complementary image-text clustering case study. The original expert, kernel, projection-dimension, and hyperparameter-C ablations remain.

E5.justification: The new checklist states that results average multiple runs and asserts small observed variance, while explicitly acknowledging absent error bars and significance tests. V1 already reports five-fold cross-validation for text experiments but lacks this general repeated-run disclosure. V2 supplies neither run counts nor seeds, and does not establish that more runs were performed.

E6.justification: Matched earlier benchmark tables retain their numerical values, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 9–12 and C.8. Examples include MVSA-Single accuracy of 74.3% versus concatenation's 71.3%, and diffusion recall of 0.484 versus CLIP-based c-VSG's 0.413. Figure 1 also gains clustering scores. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Appendix C.9 adds an inference adaptation that replaces CLIP embeddings inside contextualized Vendi Score Guidance with fused CLIP and DINOv2 representations. The core product-kernel, symmetrization, random-projection, and Fourier-feature constructions remain unchanged. The new unimodal pseudocode documents an existing case; the earlier cross-modal algorithm moves to Appendix A.5.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution framing, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 adds a limitations discussion, a related-work subsection, Appendix C.7–C.9, acknowledgments, and a conference checklist. It also moves cross-modal pseudocode to the appendix and foregrounds unimodal fusion, substantially changing the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V2 adds the generated image-text comparison in Figure 2, redraws the fusion schematic as Figure 3, and annotates Figure 1 with clustering scores. It brings existing appendix comparisons into the main text, expands Table 9, adds Tables 10–12, and adopts a different conference layout. Most earlier appendix visualizations are retained and reformatted.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly attributes the kernel-product/Kronecker identity to established kernel literature and adds a related-work subsection connecting the framework to generative-model evaluation and guidance, including KID and Vendi-based approaches. This substantially broadens research positioning beyond v1's emphasis on representation fusion and cross-modal alignment.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 changes its error bound from sqrt(B log(4n/delta)/l) to sqrt(2 B^2 log(2n^2/delta)/l). Appendix A.3 correspondingly revises the Hoeffding exponent and union-bound algebra. This is a localized mathematical revision; the propositions, feature-map constructions, and Theorem 2 remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses two important gaps in v1: comparison against plain concatenation and measured computational evidence for scalability (C.7–C.8). These strengthen the justification for the fusion operation and clarify its practical value. Broader backbone checks and explicit applicability limitations further improve the paper. New application experiments remain sparsely documented and uncertainty is unquantified, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KrossFuse/RP-KrossFuse research despite the changed title and broader framing in v2. The methods, equations, results, figures, and appendices support reliable matching and comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds backbone comparisons, computational benchmarks, MVSA classification, and diffusion-guidance experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original clustering, classification, image-text retrieval, few-shot learning, and ablation results in Section 6 and Appendix C.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent deep reinforcement learning methods have achieved remarkable success in solving multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems (MOCOPs) by decomposing them into multiple subproblems, each associated with a specific weight vector. However, these methods typically treat all subproblems equally and solve them using a single model, hindering the effective exploration of the solution space and thus leading to suboptimal performance. To overcome the limitation, we propose POCCO, a novel plug-and-play framework that enables adaptive selection of model structures for subproblems, which are subsequently optimized based on preference signals rather than explicit reward values. Specifically, we design a conditional computation block that routes subproblems to specialized neural architectures. Moreover, we propose a preference-driven optimization algorithm that learns pairwise preferences between winning and losing solutions. We evaluate the efficacy and versatility of POCCO by applying it to two state-of-the-art neural methods for MOCOPs. Experimental results across four classic MOCOP benchmarks demonstrate its significant superiority and strong generalization.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: adaptive conditional computation, preference-driven training, plug-and-play integration, superior performance, and generalization. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations linking PL to lower gradient variance, attributing the failure of neutralized pairs to lost supervision, and discussing expert capacity versus data volume. It also interprets the DPO and scalarization comparisons and explicitly acknowledges higher GPU memory consumption. The original limitations concerning complex constraints and large problems remain.

D1.justification: V3 replaces v1's future-release promise with a code/data repository link and an MIT release statement, documents the DPO reference-model procedure and training times, and reports GPU memory requirements. Table 17 revises three baseline licenses to 'No license' and adds PMOCO. However, the checklist still promises future release, leaving availability statements internally inconsistent.

E1.justification: V3 Appendix J extends evaluation to Bi-TSP and Bi-KP instances with 300, 500, and 1,000 nodes or items. This adds larger input-scale scenarios within retained task families; the original routing, knapsack, and KroAB coverage remains.

E2.justification: DPO, cited but not evaluated in v1, becomes an actual comparator in v3 Appendix K and Table 10 on Bi-TSP sizes 20–200. The comparator sets in the original benchmark tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: V3 adds substantive experimental controls: DPO with a previous-epoch reference model, different expert counts including a variant trained on twice the data, WS-versus-Tchebycheff training, and initial-batch gradient and size-50 memory measurements. These expand the evaluation design; the original benchmark training budget, metrics, and augmentation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether zeroing preference signals for mutually non-dominated pairs harms learning, how expert count interacts with training-data volume, whether scalarization choice matters, and how PL affects gradient variance. GPU memory comparisons also expose resource costs. These substantially extend v1's retained component and hyperparameter ablations.

E5.justification: V3 adds gradient-variance estimates for the first five training batches in Appendix B and Table 3. This is new variability reporting, not evidence of additional independent training runs. The 1% Wilcoxon testing practice remains unchanged; neither version supplies seed counts or confidence intervals, and v3 explicitly acknowledges omitting error bars.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and matched appendix tables retain their numerical results, but v3 adds substantial new findings. For example, Table 9 reports Bi-KP1000 HV of 0.8408 for POCCO-W versus 0.2439 for WE-CA, while Bi-KP300 favors WE-CA, 0.6000 versus 0.5947. V3 also corrects the worst Bi-TSP200 ablation variant from POCCO-MED to POCCO-ME, matching Figure 4.

M1.justification: The CCO architecture, top-k routing, length-normalized Bradley–Terry preference loss, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V3 clarifies the original four-FF-plus-one-ID expert configuration. DPO, neutralized preferences, and alternative scalarization are experimental comparisons or ablations, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Related Works moves from Appendix A to Section 2, the gating explanation expands, terminology and grammatical errors are corrected, and acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist are added. The scientific appendix additions do not entail extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the tabulated presentation with new displays for gradient variance, neutralized pairs, larger instances, DPO, expert counts, scalarization, and memory use. Existing figures and benchmark tables are largely retained and repositioned. The asset table gains a PMOCO row and expanded license entries.

R1.justification: V3 removes the cited work 'Preference optimization for combinatorial optimization problems' by Guanquan Lin and colleagues. BOPO and ORPO remain the same cited works despite publication-detail updates. The new DPO comparison sharpens positioning within preference optimization, while the broader literature framing remains stable.

T1.justification: New Appendix B explicitly derives the gradient of the existing preference loss and contrasts it with REINFORCE. This adds mathematical reasoning, while the original definitions and method equations remain intact. The variance-reduction discussion supplies no formal variance bound or theorem.

improvement.justification: V3 fills important validation gaps in v1's argument for preference learning and computational efficiency: it directly compares DPO, tests preference-pair handling and expert capacity, and quantifies memory and training-time costs. These additions make the central design choices and tradeoffs substantially more assessable while preserving the original results. The gains are qualified by an unproved variance-reduction argument, absent error bars, and inconsistent release statements, but the added controlled evidence provides a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same POCCO framework and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Shared content can be matched reliably despite section moves and expanded supplementary material in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds results on gradient variance, larger instances, DPO, preference-pair handling, expert counts, scalarization, and GPU memory.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, generalization experiments, component ablations, and hyperparameter studies for POCCO, including Tables 1–7 and Figures 3–6.

arxiv_record.abstract: Safe deployment of machine learning (ML) models in safety-critical domains such as medical imaging requires detecting inputs with characteristics not seen during training, known as out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, to prevent unreliable predictions. Effective OOD detection after deployment could benefit from access to the training data, enabling direct comparison between test samples and the training data distribution to identify differences. State-of-the-art OOD detection methods, however, either discard the training data after deployment or assume that test samples and training data are centrally stored together, an assumption that rarely holds in real-world settings. This is because shipping the training data with the deployed model is usually impossible due to the size of training databases, as well as proprietary or privacy constraints. We introduce the Isolation Network, an OOD detection framework that quantifies the difficulty of separating a target test sample from the training data by solving a binary classification task. We then propose Decentralized Isolation Networks (DIsoN), which enables the comparison of training and test data when data-sharing is impossible, by exchanging only model parameters between the remote computational nodes of training and deployment. We further extend DIsoN with class-conditioning, comparing a target sample solely with training data of its predicted class. We evaluate DIsoN on four medical imaging datasets (dermatology, chest X-ray, breast ultrasound, histopathology) across 12 OOD detection tasks. DIsoN performs favorably against existing methods while respecting data-privacy. This decentralized OOD detection framework opens the way for a new type of service that ML developers could provide along with their models: providing remote, secure utilization of their training data for OOD detection services. Code: https://github.com/FelixWag/DIsoN
arxiv_record.authors: Felix Wagner, Pramit Saha, Harry Anthony, J. Alison Noble, Konstantinos Kamnitsas
arxiv_record.title: DIsoN: Decentralized Isolation Networks for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Medical Imaging

native_events.abstract: Safe deployment of machine learning (ML) models in safety-critical domains such as medical imaging requires detecting inputs with characteristics not seen during training, known as out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, to prevent unreliable predictions. Effective OOD detection after deployment could benefit from access to the training data, enabling direct comparison between test samples and the training data distribution to identify differences. State-of-the-art OOD detection methods, however, either discard the training data after deployment or assume that test samples and training data are centrally stored together, an assumption that rarely holds in real-world settings. This is because shipping the training data with the deployed model is usually impossible due to the size of training databases, as well as proprietary or privacy constraints. We introduce the Isolation Network, an OOD detection framework that quantifies the difficulty of separating a target test sample from the training data by solving a binary classification task. We then propose Decentralized Isolation Networks (DIsoN), which enables the comparison of training and test data when data-sharing is impossible, by exchanging only model parameters between the remote computational nodes of training and deployment. We further extend DIsoN with class-conditioning, comparing a target sample solely with training data of its predicted class. We evaluate DIsoN on four medical imaging datasets (dermatology, chest X-ray, breast ultrasound, histopathology) across 12 OOD detection tasks. DIsoN performs favorably against existing methods while respecting data-privacy. This decentralized OOD detection framework opens the way for a new type of service that ML developers could provide along with their models: providing remote, secure utilization of their training data for OOD detection services. Code available at: https://github.com/FelixWag/DIsoN

arxiv_record.abstract: Though safety alignment has been applied to most large language models (LLMs), LLM service providers generally deploy a subsequent moderation as the external safety guardrail in real-world products. Existing moderators mainly practice a conventional full detection, which determines the harmfulness based on the complete LLM output, causing high service latency. Recent works pay more attention to partial detection where moderators oversee the generation midway and early stop the output if harmfulness is detected, but they directly apply moderators trained with the full detection paradigm to incomplete outputs, introducing a training-inference gap that lowers the performance. In this paper, we explore how to form a data-and-model solution that natively supports partial detection. For the data, we construct FineHarm, a dataset consisting of 29K prompt-response pairs with fine-grained annotations to provide reasonable supervision for token-level training. Then, we propose the streaming content monitor, which is trained with dual supervision of response- and token-level labels and can follow the output stream of LLM to make a timely judgment of harmfulness. Experiments show that SCM gains 0.95+ in macro F1 score that is comparable to full detection, by only seeing the first 18% of tokens in responses on average. Moreover, the SCM can serve as a pseudo-harmfulness annotator for improving safety alignment and lead to a higher harmlessness score than DPO.
arxiv_record.authors: Yang Li, Qiang Sheng, Yehan Yang, Xueyao Zhang, Juan Cao
arxiv_record.title: From Judgment to Interference: Early Stopping LLM Harmful Outputs via Streaming Content Monitoring

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful but static; they lack mechanisms to adapt their weights in response to new tasks, knowledge, or examples. We introduce Self-Adapting LLMs (SEAL), a framework that enables LLMs to self-adapt by generating their own finetuning data and update directives. Given a new input, the model produces a self-edit-a generation that may restructure the information in different ways, specify optimization hyperparameters, or invoke tools for data augmentation and gradient-based updates. Through supervised finetuning (SFT), these self-edits result in persistent weight updates, enabling lasting adaptation. To train the model to produce effective self-edits, we use a reinforcement learning loop with the downstream performance of the updated model as the reward signal. Unlike prior approaches that rely on separate adaptation modules or auxiliary networks, SEAL directly uses the model's own generation to control its adaptation process. Experiments on knowledge incorporation and few-shot generalization show that SEAL is a promising step toward language models capable of self-directed adaptation. Our website and code is available at https://jyopari.github.io/posts/seal.
arxiv_record.authors: Adam Zweiger, Jyothish Pari, Han Guo, Ekin Aky\"urek, Yoon Kim, Pulkit Agrawal

arxiv_record.abstract:
The recent advent of reasoning models like OpenAI's o1 was met with excited speculation by the AI community about the mechanisms underlying these capabilities in closed models, followed by a rush of replication efforts, particularly from the open source community. These speculations were largely settled by the demonstration from DeepSeek-R1 that chains-of-thought and reinforcement learning (RL) can effectively replicate reasoning on top of base LLMs. However, it remains valuable to explore alternative methods for theoretically eliciting reasoning that could help elucidate the underlying mechanisms, as well as providing additional methods that may offer complementary benefits.
  Here, we build on the long-standing literature in cognitive psychology and cognitive architectures, which postulates that reasoning arises from the orchestrated, sequential execution of a set of modular, predetermined cognitive operations. Crucially, we implement this key idea within a modern agentic tool-calling framework. In particular, we endow an LLM with a small set of "cognitive tools" encapsulating specific reasoning operations, each executed by the LLM itself. Surprisingly, this simple strategy results in considerable gains in performance on standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks compared to base LLMs, for both closed and open-weight models. For instance, providing our "cognitive tools" to GPT-4.1 increases its pass@1 performance on AIME2024 from 32% to 53%, even surpassing the performance of o1-preview.
  In addition to its practical implications, this demonstration contributes to the debate regarding the role of post-training methods in eliciting reasoning in LLMs versus the role of inherent capabilities acquired during pre-training, and whether post-training merely uncovers these latent abilities.
arxiv_record.authors: Brown Ebouky, Andrea Bartezzaghi, Mattia Rigotti
arxiv_record.title: Eliciting Reasoning in Language Models with Cognitive Tools

arxiv_record.abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) at the wrists could enable natural, keyboard-free text entry, yet the state-of-the-art emg2qwerty baseline still misrecognizes $51.8\%$ of characters in the zero-shot setting on unseen users and $7.0\%$ after user-specific fine-tuning. We trace many of these errors to mismatched cross-user signal statistics, fragile reliance on high-order feature dependencies, and the absence of architectural inductive biases aligned with the bilateral nature of typing. To address these issues, we introduce three simple modifications: (i) Rolling Time Normalization, which adaptively aligns input distributions across users; (ii) Aggressive Channel Masking, which encourages reliance on low-order feature combinations more likely to generalize across users; and (iii) a Split-and-Share encoder that processes each hand independently with weight-shared streams to reflect the bilateral symmetry of the neuromuscular system. Combined with a five-fold reduction in spectral resolution ($33\!\rightarrow\!6$ frequency bands), these components yield a compact Split-and-Share model, SplashNet-mini, which uses only $\tfrac14$ the parameters and $0.6\times$ the FLOPs of the baseline while reducing character-error rate (CER) to $36.4\%$ zero-shot and $5.9\%$ after fine-tuning. An upscaled variant, SplashNet ($\tfrac12$ the parameters, $1.15\times$ the FLOPs of the baseline), further lowers error to $35.7\%$ and $5.5\%$, representing relative improvements of $31\%$ and $21\%$ in the zero-shot and fine-tuned settings, respectively. SplashNet therefore establishes a new state of the art without requiring additional data.
arxiv_record.authors: Nima Hadidi, Jason Chan, Ebrahim Feghhi, Jonathan C. Kao
arxiv_record.title: SplashNet: Split-and-Share Encoders for Accurate and Efficient Typing with Surface Electromyography

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding claims retain the same three principal contributions, compact-model efficiency claims, and approximately 31% zero-shot and 21% finetuned error reductions. The added experiments do not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly qualifies low-order feature similarity as a working hypothesis (Section 2). New analyses develop interpretations concerning masking-value stability, matched normalization context, and the masking explanation for poorer greedy decoding. Appendix A.9 also identifies limited transfer to pose tracking and proposes early electrode mixing as a possible boundary, substantially extending the mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 documents implementation details for the added variants, including inverse spectral-mask mapping, mean imputation, and feature masking after the first emg2pose convolution. Figure 5 specifies activation sampling every 100th timestep from one session per test user. The original optimizer, schedule, hardware, runtime, and repository disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only emg2qwerty typing; emg2pose is merely cited. v2 adds actual hand-pose tracking experiments under user, stage, and combined generalization regimes (Appendix A.9, Table 10), substantially extending the evaluated task coverage.

E2.justification: The original typing comparisons retain Sivakumar et al. and the same model variants. v2 additionally evaluates the Salter et al. emg2pose baseline against adaptations using RTN, ACM, and their combination (Table 10).

E3.justification: v2 adds an 18-user training-domain beam-search evaluation and a separate 78/18 training/validation experiment retaining the original eight test users (Section 4.6, Appendix A.8). Added protocols also vary masking order, mask width, and normalization windows, and evaluate pose tracking with angular-error and landmark-distance metrics. These are additional experimental designs, not replacements of the original typing protocol.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component and decoding comparisons, v2 tests pre-aggregation masking, ACM widths, RSG removal, RTN window matching, and mean-imputation masking (Tables 5–8). It also adds UMAP representations and alternative-split analyses (Figure 5, Table 9), substantially expanding evidence about mechanisms and robustness.

E5.justification: Appendix A.5 introduces two-tailed paired tests for the new sensitivity analyses, while the main comparisons retain one-tailed tests. Tables 5 and 6 newly provide standard deviations for some previously reported greedy and other-domain results. Neither version discloses seed or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Original typing CERs remain unchanged, including SplashNet's 35.67% zero-shot and 5.51% finetuned results. However, Table 1 revises baseline/mini/full-model GFLOPs from 201.325/118.346/229.384 to 61.61/36.84/71.38 under the same stated 30-second measurement description. v2 also adds extensive validation, ablation, representation, and pose-tracking results; these are new results under specified conditions, not same-setting accuracy improvements.

M1.justification: The principal SplashNet architecture and preprocessing remain unchanged. Appendix A.9 adds an adaptation for emg2pose: RTN and ACM operate on first-convolution outputs, with ACM zeroing 50% or 75% of features in specified training samples. This changes the procedure for the added task.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted wording corrections and explanatory additions, moves the beam-search description from Appendix A.5 into Section 4.5, and adds acknowledgments and a conference checklist. The main narrative and most existing prose remain intact; the scientific appendix additions do not constitute wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with Tables 5–10 and the four-panel UMAP Figure 5. Tables 1 and 3 gain training-domain columns and explanatory captions, with gray text distinguishing those results. Original Figures 1–4 are retained.

R1.justification: Section 3, the 22 cited works, and the Split-and-Share novelty positioning are unchanged. Salter et al. and emg2pose were already discussed in v1; their additional experimental use does not introduce a new literature positioning claim.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and equations for spectral aggregation, RTN, masking, and encoder operations are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added analyses are empirical.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantive evidential gaps in v1 through the masking-order control, normalization and masking sensitivity tests, and the alternative participant split (Tables 5–9). These strengthen assessment of the proposed mechanisms and generalization. Explicitly qualifying the low-order hypothesis and reporting weak pose-transfer gains also clarify applicability. Although the substantial FLOPs revision remains insufficiently explained, the added controls and more careful interpretation provide a substantial net quality improvement.

arxiv_record.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique in which a compact "student" network is trained to replicate the predictive behavior of a larger "teacher" network. In logit-based knowledge distillation, it has become the de facto approach to augment cross-entropy with a distillation term. Typically, this term is either a KL divergence that matches marginal probabilities or a correlation-based loss that captures intra- and inter-class relationships. In every case, it acts as an additional term to cross-entropy. This term has its own weight, which must be carefully tuned. In this paper, we adopt a choice-theoretic perspective and recast knowledge distillation under the Plackett-Luce model by interpreting teacher logits as "worth" scores. We introduce "Plackett-Luce Distillation (PLD)", a weighted list-wise ranking loss. In PLD, the teacher model transfers knowledge of its full ranking of classes, weighting each ranked choice by its own confidence. PLD directly optimizes a single "teacher-optimal" ranking. The true label is placed first, followed by the remaining classes in descending teacher confidence. This process yields a convex and translation-invariant surrogate that subsumes weighted cross-entropy. Empirically, across CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and MS-COCO, PLD achieves consistent gains across diverse architectures and distillation objectives, including divergence-based, correlation-based, and feature-based methods, in both homogeneous and heterogeneous teacher-student pairs.

arxiv_record.abstract: Randomness is an unavoidable part of training deep learning models, yet something that traditional training data attribution algorithms fail to rigorously account for. They ignore the fact that, due to stochasticity in the initialisation and batching, training on the same dataset can yield different models. In this paper, we address this shortcoming through introducing distributional training data attribution (d-TDA), the goal of which is to predict how the distribution of model outputs (over training runs) depends upon the dataset. Intriguingly, we find that influence functions (IFs), a popular data attribution tool, are 'secretly distributional': they emerge from our framework as the limit to unrolled differentiation, without requiring restrictive convexity assumptions. This provides a new perspective on the effectiveness of IFs in deep learning. We demonstrate the practical utility of d-TDA in experiments, including improving data pruning for vision transformers and identifying influential examples with diffusion models.
arxiv_record.authors: Bruno Mlodozeniec, Isaac Reid, Sam Power, David Krueger, Murat Erdogdu, Richard E. Turner, Roger Grosse
arxiv_record.title: Distributional Training Data Attribution: What do Influence Functions Sample?

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models are advancing autonomous driving by enabling realistic data synthesis, predictive end-to-end planning, and closed-loop simulation, with a primary focus on temporally consistent generation. However, large-scale 3D scene generation requiring spatial coherence remains underexplored. In this paper, we present X-Scene, a novel framework for large-scale driving scene generation that achieves geometric intricacy, appearance fidelity, and flexible controllability. Specifically, X-Scene supports multi-granular control, including low-level layout conditioning driven by user input or text for detailed scene composition, and high-level semantic guidance informed by user intent and LLM-enriched prompts for efficient customization. To enhance geometric and visual fidelity, we introduce a unified pipeline that sequentially generates 3D semantic occupancy and corresponding multi-view images and videos, ensuring alignment and temporal consistency across modalities. We further extend local regions into large-scale scenes via consistency-aware outpainting, which extrapolates occupancy and images from previously generated areas to maintain spatial and visual coherence. The resulting scenes are lifted into high-quality 3DGS representations, supporting diverse applications such as simulation and scene exploration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that X-Scene substantially advances controllability and fidelity in large-scale scene generation, empowering data generation and simulation for autonomous driving.

arxiv_record.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) perform well in video understanding but degrade on long videos due to fixed-length context and weak long-term dependency modeling. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can expand knowledge dynamically, yet existing video RAG schemes adopt fixed retrieval paradigms that ignore query difficulty. This uniform design causes redundant computation and latency for simple queries, while coarse retrieval for complex, multi-hop reasoning can miss key information. Such single-step retrieval severely limits the trade-off between efficiency and cognitive depth. We propose AdaVideoRAG, an adaptive RAG framework for long-video understanding. A lightweight intent classifier dynamically selects suitable retrieval schemes according to query complexity from the simplest to the most sophisticated. We design an Omni-Knowledge Indexing module that extracts and organizes multi-modal information into three databases: (1) a text base built from clip captions, ASR, and OCR; (2) a visual base; and (3) a knowledge graph for deep semantic understanding. This supports hierarchical knowledge access, from naive retrieval to graph-based retrieval, balancing resource cost and reasoning ability. To evaluate deep understanding, we further construct the HiVU benchmark. Experiments show that AdaVideoRAG significantly improves both efficiency and accuracy on long-video QA tasks and can be seamlessly plugged into existing MLLMs through lightweight APIs, establishing a new paradigm for adaptive retrieval-augmented video analysis.

metadata.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated excellent performance in video understanding but suffer from degraded effectiveness when processing long videos due to fixed-length contexts and weaknesses in modeling long-term dependencies. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) technology can mitigate these limitations through dynamic knowledge expansion, but existing RAG schemes for video understanding employ fixed retrieval paradigms that use uniform structures regardless of input query difficulty. This introduces redundant computational overhead and latency (*e.g.*, complex graph traversal operations) for simple queries (*e.g.*, frame-level object recognition) while potentially causing critical information loss due to insufficient retrieval granularity for multi-hop reasoning. Such single-step retrieval mechanisms severely constrain the model's balance between resource efficiency and cognitive depth.  To address this, we first propose a novel AdaVideoRAG framework for long-video understanding, which uses a lightweight intent classifier to dynamically and adaptively allocate appropriate retrieval schemes, ranging from the simplest to the most sophisticated, for different video understanding tasks based on query complexity. We introduce an Omni-Knowledge Indexing module to extract valuable information from multi-modal signals for context modeling and build corresponding databases, *i.e.*, a text base from clip captions, ASR, and OCR; a visual base; and a graph for deep semantic understanding. This enables hierarchical knowledge access, integration, and generation from naive retrieval to graph retrieval, achieving an optimal balance between resource consumption and video understanding capabilities.   Finally, we construct the HiVU benchmark for deep understanding evaluation. Extensive experiments show that our framework enhances the overall efficiency and accuracy of Video-QA for long videos and can be seamlessly integrated with existing MLLMs via lightweight API calls, establishing a new paradigm for adaptive retrieval augmentation in video analysis.

arxiv_record.abstract: Training Transformers on algorithmic tasks frequently demonstrates an intriguing abrupt learning phenomenon: an extended performance plateau followed by a sudden, sharp improvement. This work investigates the underlying mechanisms for such dynamics, primarily in shallow Transformers. We reveal that during the plateau, the model often develops an interpretable partial solution while simultaneously exhibiting a strong repetition bias in their outputs. This output degeneracy is accompanied by internal representation collapse, where hidden states across different tokens become nearly parallel. We further identify the slow learning of optimal attention maps as a key bottleneck. Hidden progress in attention configuration during the plateau precedes the eventual rapid convergence, and directly intervening on attention significantly alters plateau duration and the severity of repetition bias and representational collapse. We validate that these identified phenomena-repetition bias and representation collapse-are not artifacts of toy setups but also manifest in the early pre-training stage of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.
arxiv_record.authors: Pulkit Gopalani, Wei Hu
arxiv_record.title: What Happens During the Loss Plateau? Understanding Abrupt Learning in Transformers
