arxiv_record.abstract: Deploying large, complex policies in the real world requires the ability to steer them to fit the needs of a situation. Most common steering approaches, like goal-conditioning, require training the robot policy with a distribution of test-time objectives in mind. To overcome this limitation, we present DynaGuide, a steering method for diffusion policies using guidance from an external dynamics model during the diffusion denoising process. DynaGuide separates the dynamics model from the base policy, which gives it multiple advantages, including the ability to steer towards multiple objectives, enhance underrepresented base policy behaviors, and maintain robustness on low-quality objectives. The separate guidance signal also allows DynaGuide to work with off-the-shelf pretrained diffusion policies. We demonstrate the performance and features of DynaGuide against other steering approaches in a series of simulated and real experiments, showing an average steering success of 70% on a set of articulated CALVIN tasks and outperforming goal-conditioning by 5.4x when steered with low-quality objectives. We also successfully steer an off-the-shelf real robot policy to express preference for particular objects and even create novel behavior. Videos and more can be found on the project website: https://dynaguide.github.io

arxiv_record.abstract: Previous methods for image geo-localization have typically treated the task as either classification or retrieval, often relying on black-box decisions that lack interpretability. The rise of large vision-language models (LVLMs) has enabled a rethinking of geo-localization as a reasoning-driven task grounded in visual cues. However, two major challenges persist. On the data side, existing reasoning-focused datasets are primarily based on street-view imagery, offering limited scene diversity and constrained viewpoints. On the modeling side, current approaches predominantly rely on supervised fine-tuning, which yields only marginal improvements in reasoning capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose a novel pipeline that constructs a reasoning-oriented geo-localization dataset, MP16-Reason, using diverse social media images. We introduce GLOBE, Group-relative policy optimization for Localizability assessment and Optimized visual-cue reasoning, yielding Bi-objective geo-Enhancement for the VLM in recognition and reasoning. GLOBE incorporates task-specific rewards that jointly enhance localizability assessment, visual-cue reasoning, and geolocation accuracy. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that GLOBE outperforms state-of-the-art open-source LVLMs on geo-localization tasks, particularly in diverse visual scenes, while also generating more insightful and interpretable reasoning trajectories. The data and code are available at https://github.com/lingli1996/GLOBE.
arxiv_record.authors: Ling Li, Yao Zhou, Yuxuan Liang, Fugee Tsung, Jiaheng Wei
arxiv_record.title: Recognition through Reasoning: Reinforcing Image Geo-localization with Large Vision-Language Models

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper establishes a continuous time approximation, a piece-wise continuous differential equation, for the discrete Heavy-Ball (HB) momentum method with explicit discretization error. Investigating continuous differential equations has been a promising approach for studying the discrete optimization methods. Despite the crucial role of momentum in gradient-based optimization methods, the gap between the original discrete dynamics and the continuous time approximations due to the discretization error has not been comprehensively bridged yet. In this work, we study the HB momentum method in continuous time while putting more focus on the discretization error to provide additional theoretical tools to this area. In particular, we design a first-order piece-wise continuous differential equation, where we add a number of counter terms to account for the discretization error explicitly. arxiv_record.abstract: LLM-based agent applications have shown increasingly remarkable capabilities in complex workflows but incur substantial costs and latency due to extensive planning and reasoning requirements. Existing LLM caching techniques (like context caching and semantic caching), primarily designed for serving chatbots, are insufficient for agent applications where outputs depend on external data and environmental contexts. We propose Agentic Plan Caching (APC), a novel test-time memory that extracts, stores, adapts, and reuses structured plan templates from planning stages of agent applications across semantically similar tasks to reduce the cost and latency of serving. Unlike traditional semantic caching, our system extracts plan templates from completed agent executions at test-time, employs keyword extraction to match new requests against cached plans, and utilizes lightweight models to adapt these templates to task-specific plans with contexts. Evaluation across multiple real-world agent applications shows that our system can reduce costs by 50.31% and latency by 27.28% on average while maintaining performance, offering a more efficient solution for serving LLM-based agents that complements existing LLM serving infrastructures.
arxiv_record.authors: Qizheng Zhang, Michael Wornow, Gerry Wan, Kunle Olukotun
arxiv_record.title: Agentic Plan Caching: Test-Time Memory for Fast and Cost-Efficient LLM Agents

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning GAIA's limited initial keyword reuse but useful replanning reuse, cache saturation near the number of unique task keywords, fuzzy matching's relevance/efficiency tradeoff, and cold-start overhead with possible offline prewarming. The earlier limitations and societal-impact discussion are retained in Appendix E rather than removed.

D1.justification: v2 specifies Python dictionary lookup, the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 fuzzy matcher and semantic-caching thresholds of 80%, 85% and 90%. Main-text Llama-3.2-8B references become Llama-3.1-8B, matching v1's appendices rather than establishing a model change. E1.justification: Beyond the retained FinanceBench and TabMWP coverage, v2 evaluates QASPER scientific-document questions, AIME 2024/2025 mathematics and GAIA tasks involving multi-step reasoning and tool use. This substantially broadens the evaluated domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: The four original named baselines and their participation in the retained benchmark comparisons are unchanged. Tables 5–6 add a fuzzy keyword-retrieval alternative evaluated against default exact matching. The added benchmark and latency comparisons otherwise use the existing accuracy-optimal and cost-optimal controls.

E3.justification: v2 adds a wall-clock benchmark using 100 randomly sampled FinanceBench queries, LRU cache-capacity sweeps, lookup timing up to one million entries, fuzzy-threshold experiments and cold-start tracking. GAIA uses Open Deep Research with GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini. The original 200-question FinanceBench and TabMWP evaluation settings remain documented unchanged.

E4.justification: New Sections 4.3–4.5 analyze latency by component, cache-capacity saturation, exact versus fuzzy lookup scalability, fuzzy-matching accuracy tradeoffs and cache warm-up. These substantially extend the operational sensitivity analysis. Existing cache-hit/miss comparisons and Appendix C model-sensitivity studies are retained.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports averaging cache-lookup measurements over 100 trials in Section 4.4 and Table 5; v1 provides no corresponding repeated-trial reporting. Neither version supplies defined error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests for the main cost/accuracy results, despite v2's affirmative checklist statement.

E6.justification: The original benchmark plots, cost breakdown and Appendix C numerical results are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results: Table 1 reports GAIA APC cost/accuracy of $16.27/36.97%, versus $69.02/37.58% for the accuracy-optimal baseline; Table 3 reports FinanceBench latency of 1424.82 versus 1959.24 seconds. Tables 4–7 add cache-management findings. Revised headline aggregates cover expanded experiments rather than demonstrating a same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The core workflow, Algorithms 1–3 and appendix prompts remain unchanged. However, v2 implements optional fuzzy keyword retrieval and LRU eviction, previously left for future work, and reports automatic caching disablement when hit rates remain low.

P1.justification: The title and terminology adopt APC and test-time memory, and the abstract and concluding summary are updated. The Discussion becomes a Conclusion, with most discussion text moved verbatim to Appendix E; acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist are added. Most existing explanatory prose and appendix content remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds six experimental tables, retains but rescales and relocates Figures 1–5, and reformats the document in NeurIPS style. The appendix algorithms and model-sensitivity tables are consolidated into denser layouts. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond table renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 adds a focused comparison with classic case-based planning, distinguishing automatic LLM template extraction from symbolic planning. v2 also adds benchmark, agent-memory, context-caching and social-simulation references and removes Mind2Web. The existing positioning around serving efficiency rather than enhanced agent capability largely remains.

T1.justification: Neither version contains substantive theoretical results, proofs or formal derivations. The appendix algorithms and worked-example mathematics are unchanged; v2's standard dictionary lookup complexity statement does not introduce a new theoretical contribution.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation and untested deployment behavior through additional domains, a second agent architecture, measured latency, and cache-capacity, retrieval and cold-start analyses. These strengthen evidence for practical applicability and expose operating tradeoffs. These weaknesses qualify, but do not outweigh, the substantial evidential gains.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper presents improved native unified multimodal models, \emph{i.e.,} Show-o2, that leverage autoregressive modeling and flow matching. Built upon a 3D causal variational autoencoder space, unified visual representations are constructed through a dual-path of spatial (-temporal) fusion, enabling scalability across image and video modalities while ensuring effective multimodal understanding and generation. Based on a language model, autoregressive modeling and flow matching are natively applied to the language head and flow head, respectively, to facilitate text token prediction and image/video generation. A two-stage training recipe is designed to effectively learn and scale to larger models. The resulting Show-o2 models demonstrate versatility in handling a wide range of multimodal understanding and generation tasks across diverse modalities, including text, images, and videos. Code and models are released at https://github.com/showlab/Show-o.

arxiv_record.comments: NeurIPS 2025. (v3: update to include video understanding, OneIG, and more ablation study results)

arxiv_record.abstract: Test-Time Scaling (TTS) improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by using additional inference-time computation to explore multiple reasoning paths through search. Yet how to allocate a fixed rollout budget most effectively during search remains underexplored, often resulting in inefficient use of compute at test time. To bridge this gap, we formulate test-time search as a resource allocation problem and derive the optimal allocation strategy that maximizes the probability of obtaining a correct solution under a fixed rollout budget. Within this formulation, we reveal a core limitation of existing search methods: solution-level allocation tends to favor reasoning directions with more candidates, leading to theoretically suboptimal and inefficient use of compute. To address this, we propose Direction-Oriented Resource Allocation (DORA), a provably optimal method that mitigates this bias by decoupling direction quality from candidate count and allocating resources at the direction level. To demonstrate DORA's effectiveness, we conduct extensive experiments on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks including MATH500, AIME2024, and AIME2025. The empirical results show that DORA consistently outperforms strong baselines with comparable computational cost, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy. We hope our findings contribute to a broader understanding of optimal TTS for LLMs.

arxiv_record.abstract: Heterogeneous Large Language Model (LLM) fusion integrates the strengths of multiple source LLMs with different architectures into a target LLM with low computational overhead. While promising, existing methods suffer from two major limitations: 1) reliance on real data from limited domain for knowledge fusion, preventing the target LLM from fully acquiring knowledge across diverse domains, and 2) fixed data allocation proportions across domains, failing to dynamically adjust according to the target LLM's varying capabilities across domains, leading to a capability imbalance. To overcome these limitations, we propose Bohdi, a synthetic-data-only heterogeneous LLM fusion framework. Through the organization of knowledge domains into a hierarchical tree structure, Bohdi enables automatic domain exploration and multi-domain data generation through multi-model collaboration, thereby comprehensively extracting knowledge from source LLMs. By formalizing domain expansion and data sampling proportion allocation on the knowledge tree as a Hierarchical Multi-Armed Bandit problem, Bohdi leverages the designed DynaBranches mechanism to adaptively adjust sampling proportions based on the target LLM's performance feedback across domains. Integrated with our proposed Introspection-Rebirth (IR) mechanism, DynaBranches dynamically tracks capability shifts during target LLM's updates via Sliding Window Binomial Likelihood Ratio Testing (SWBLRT), further enhancing its online adaptation capability. Comparative experimental results on a comprehensive suite of benchmarks demonstrate that Bohdi significantly outperforms existing baselines on multiple target LLMs, exhibits higher data efficiency, and virtually eliminates the imbalance in the target LLM's capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/gjq100/Bohdi.git.
arxiv_record.authors: Junqi Gao, Zhichang Guo, Dazhi Zhang, Dong Li, Runze Liu, Pengfei Li, Kai Tian, Biqing Qi

D1.justification: v3 documents subsampling for the new controlled experiment, including 594 examples from each of three domains for applicable baselines, and supplies five generated question-answer examples. Existing training and generation settings, hardware disclosures, prompt templates, and code-access information remain unchanged.

Appendix G explicitly presents generated samples from the existing main experiments rather than introducing additional training or evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: FuseChat, SFT, FuseChat-3.0, and Condor remain the main baselines, including in the new budget-controlled comparison. Table 5 additionally evaluates three fixed-leader comparison variants, using Mistral, phi-4, or Qwen, against Bohdi's random-leader policy.

E3.justification: Table 6 adds a controlled comparison with approximately 1,782 training examples per method, supplementing the original comparison of 90K–95K baseline examples against roughly 1.7K Bohdi examples. Tables 2–3 also change the reported BBH setting from 0-shot CoT to 3-shot CoT while retaining scores; the PDFs do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds a targeted leader-selection ablation: Table 5 tests whether fixing each source model as leader changes performance relative to random selection. Existing component, SWBLRT-parameter, sampling-ratio, and source-count analyses remain. Appendix G adds illustrative generated examples without a systematic quality analysis.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v3's Table 6 explicitly reports three independent runs and mean ± standard deviation for benchmark scores, overall scores, and Bohdi's generated-data count. arxiv_record.abstract: Generative models of graphs based on discrete Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) offer a principled approach to molecular generation by systematically removing structural noise through iterative atom and bond adjustments. However, existing formulations are fundamentally limited by their inability to adapt the graph size (that is, the number of atoms) during the diffusion process, severely restricting their effectiveness in conditional generation scenarios such as property-driven molecular design, where the targeted property often correlates with the molecular size. In this paper, we reformulate the noising and denoising processes to support monotonic insertion and deletion of nodes. The resulting model, which we call GrIDDD, dynamically grows or shrinks the chemical graph during generation. GrIDDD matches or exceeds the performance of existing graph diffusion models on molecular property targeting despite being trained on a more difficult problem. Furthermore, when applied to molecular optimization, GrIDDD exhibits competitive performance compared to specialized optimization models. This work paves the way for size-adaptive molecular generation with graph diffusion.

arxiv_record.abstract: Modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reason over hour-long video, yet their key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with time-quickly exceeding the fixed memory of phones, AR glasses, and edge robots. Prior compression schemes either assume the whole video and user query are available offline or must first build the full cache, so memory still scales with stream length. InfiniPot-V is the first training-free, query-agnostic framework that enforces a hard, length-independent memory cap for streaming video understanding. During video encoding it monitors the cache and, once a user-set threshold is reached, runs a lightweight compression pass that (i) removes temporally redundant tokens via Temporal-axis Redundancy (TaR) metric and (ii) keeps semantically significant tokens via Value-Norm (VaN) ranking. Across four open-source MLLMs and four long-video and streaming-video benchmarks, InfiniPot-V cuts peak GPU memory by up to 94%, sustains real-time generation, and matches or surpasses full-cache accuracy-even in multi-turn dialogues. By dissolving the KV cache bottleneck without retraining or query knowledge, InfiniPot-V closes the gap for on-device streaming video assistants.
arxiv_record.authors: Minsoo Kim, Kyuhong Shim, Jungwook Choi, Simyung Chang
arxiv_record.title: InfiniPot-V: Memory-Constrained KV Cache Compression for Streaming Video Understanding

arxiv_record.abstract: Sign Language Video Generation (SLVG) seeks to generate identity-preserving sign language videos from spoken language texts. Existing methods primarily rely on the single coarse condition (\eg, skeleton sequences) as the intermediary to bridge the translation model and the video generation model, which limits both the naturalness and expressiveness of the generated videos. To overcome these limitations, we propose SignViP, a novel SLVG framework that incorporates multiple fine-grained conditions for improved generation fidelity. Rather than directly translating error-prone high-dimensional conditions, SignViP adopts a discrete tokenization paradigm to integrate and represent fine-grained conditions (\ie, fine-grained poses and 3D hands). SignViP contains three core components. (1) Sign Video Diffusion Model is jointly trained with a multi-condition encoder to learn continuous embeddings that encapsulate fine-grained motion and appearance. (2) Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) Autoencoder is further trained to compress and quantize these embeddings into discrete tokens for compact representation of the conditions. (3) Multi-Condition Token Translator is trained to translate spoken language text to discrete multi-condition tokens. During inference, Multi-Condition Token Translator first translates the spoken language text into discrete multi-condition tokens. These tokens are then decoded to continuous embeddings by FSQ Autoencoder, which are subsequently injected into Sign Video Diffusion Model to guide video generation. Experimental results show that SignViP achieves state-of-the-art performance across metrics, including video quality, temporal coherence, and semantic fidelity. The code is available at https://github.com/umnooob/signvip/.
arxiv_record.authors: Cong Wang, Zexuan Deng, Zhiwei Jiang, Yafeng Yin, Fei Shen, Zifeng Cheng, Shiping Ge, Shiwei Gan, Qing Gu

These tokens are then decoded to continuous embeddings by FSQ Autoencoder, which are subsequently injected into Sign Video Diffusion Model to guide video generation. Experimental results show that SignViP achieves state-of-the-art performance across metrics, including video quality, temporal coherence, and semantic fidelity. The code is available at https://github.com/umnooob/signvip/.

arxiv_record.abstract: Sampling efficiently from a target unnormalized probability density remains a core challenge, with relevance across countless high-impact scientific applications. A promising approach towards this challenge is the design of amortized samplers that borrow key ideas, such as probability path design, from state-of-the-art generative diffusion models. However, all existing diffusion-based samplers remain unable to draw samples from distributions at the scale of even simple molecular systems. In this paper, we propose Progressive Inference-Time Annealing (PITA), a novel framework to learn diffusion-based samplers that combines two complementary interpolation techniques: I.) Annealing of the Boltzmann distribution and II.) Diffusion smoothing. PITA trains a sequence of diffusion models from high to low temperatures by sequentially training each model at progressively higher temperatures, leveraging engineered easy access to samples of the temperature-annealed target density. In the subsequent step, PITA enables simulating the trained diffusion model to procure training samples at a lower temperature for the next diffusion model through inference-time annealing using a novel Feynman-Kac PDE combined with Sequential Monte Carlo. Empirically, PITA enables, for the first time, equilibrium sampling of N-body particle systems, Alanine Dipeptide, and tripeptides in Cartesian coordinates with dramatically lower energy function evaluations. Code available at: https://github.com/taraak/pita

C1.justification: The central claims remain progressive diffusion-based Boltzmann sampling, Cartesian peptide sampling, and reduced energy-evaluation requirements. Correcting 'progressively higher' to 'progressively lower' temperatures in the abstract aligns its wording with the procedure already described in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of amortization break-even points and inference-time ESS, including motivation for resampling and future drift modifications. It also extends the stated benefit of AL3 relaxation to TA-BG. Existing limitations concerning energy-model training, resource costs, and imperfect mode weights remain.

D1.justification: Appendices E, I, and J add SMC/PT settings, MD-NF parameterization details, explicit score-scaling equations, a 564.3-minute ALDP training time, and inference pseudocode. Existing PITA hyperparameters and the code link remain. The new listing contains inconsistencies, including div(xt) instead of the score divergence in Equation 12 and an undefined dU_dt variable.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Cartesian-coordinate sampling on LJ-13, Alanine Dipeptide, and Alanine Tripeptide. Added comparisons and diagnostics use the existing systems and tasks.

E2.justification: The ALDP comparison adds MD-NF, FKC, and Score Scaling in Table 2, plus PT and SMC in new Table 4. Score scaling already appeared in the earlier CFG ablation, which remains, but now participates in the main comparison. Table 3 additionally evaluates relaxed TA-BG; the LJ-13 comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Table 1 separates interatomic Distance-W2 from Geometric-W2. Table 3 changes MD-Diff's AL3 energy budget from 5 × 10^7 to 8 × 10^7 and adds TA-BG relaxation at the larger budget. New experiments specify SMC/PT schedules and 30k-sample timing and ESS evaluations. The reported OpenMM temperature changes from 310 K to 300 K, without establishing whether simulations were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix F examines ESS during PITA inference without resampling, across temperature transitions and integration time. Table 3 adds a TA-BG relaxation comparison. Existing temperature-jump, schedule, loss, resampling, and MD-mixing analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 2 and 3 retain standard deviations over three seeds, with no reported increase in runs or new significance-testing procedure. ESS was already defined and reported in Appendix D.2; its new applications extend diagnostics rather than introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 relocates the iDEM/Adjoint values 1.61/1.67 from Distance-W2 to Geometric-W2, reports iDEM Distance-W2 as 0.127, and leaves Adjoint Distance-W2 unavailable. Table 3 replaces MD-Diff results under the larger budget and adds relaxed TA-BG, whose Energy-W2 is 4.863 versus 178.558 without relaxation. Other additions include baseline scores, ESS results, and inference times of 4.7/139.2/59.5 minutes for PITA/SMC/PT per 30k samples. These are corrected, additional, or changed-setting results.

M1.justification: PITA's inference equations, training losses, network architectures, and progressive annealing procedure remain unchanged. Appendix J adds pseudocode describing existing inference; it does not establish a revised method.

P1.justification: There are localized language corrections, updated author/contact and conference information, a moved Boltzmann-generator paragraph, and new appendix sections. Most existing prose and the overall argument remain intact.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is substantially expanded: Figure 1 is redrawn, Tables 1–3 gain metric columns or comparison rows, and Figures 3 and 5 incorporate revised AL3 comparisons. New Tables 4–6 and Figure 10 present classical baselines, timings, and ESS diagnostics. Other appendix plots are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds Noble et al. on sampling with known modes and Klein–Noé and Tan et al. on transferable sampling. The Boltzmann-generator discussion largely moves from the appendix into Section 4. Numerous other reference changes are publication-metadata updates, with the main positioning retained.

T1.justification: Propositions 1–3, their proofs, endpoint corrections, and network-preconditioning mathematics are retained. The added score-scaling equations explain an operation already described in v1's CFG ablation rather than introduce a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: Separating the conflated LJ-13 metrics and adding equal-budget AL3 baseline comparisons address important weaknesses in v1's empirical support. Classical SMC/PT comparisons and amortization timings substantially strengthen evaluation of the efficiency claim. The gains outweigh localized problems: broad superiority wording remains insufficiently qualified, Appendix F's stabilization claim conflicts with Figure 10's rising curve, and the new pseudocode contains errors.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PITA and share the same principal experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, proofs, and experimental appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons, timing measurements, and effective-sample-size diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original sampling experiments on LJ-13, Alanine Dipeptide, and Alanine Tripeptide, together with ablations and molecular-dynamics analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Synthetic video generation is progressing very rapidly. The latest models can produce very realistic high-resolution videos that are virtually indistinguishable from real ones. Although several video forensic detectors have been recently proposed, they often exhibit poor generalization, which limits their applicability in a real-world scenario. Our key insight to overcome this issue is to guide the detector towards *seeing what really matters*. In fact, a well-designed forensic classifier should focus on identifying intrinsic low-level artifacts introduced by a generative architecture rather than relying on high-level semantic flaws that characterize a specific model. In this work, first, we study different generative architectures, searching and identifying discriminative features that are unbiased, robust to impairments, and shared across models. Then, we introduce a novel forensic-oriented data augmentation strategy based on the wavelet decomposition and replace specific frequency-related bands to drive the model to exploit more relevant forensic cues. Our novel training paradigm improves the generalizability of AI-generated video detectors, without the need for complex algorithms and large datasets that include multiple synthetic generators. To evaluate our approach, we train the detector using data from a single generative model and test it against videos produced by a wide range of other models. Despite its simplicity, our method achieves a significant accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art detectors and obtains excellent results even on very recent generative models, such as NOVA and FLUX.
arxiv_record.authors: Riccardo Corvi and Davide Cozzolino and Ekta Prashnani and Shalini De Mello and Koki Nagano and Luisa Verdoliva

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: diagonal frequency cues support generalization, WaveRep encourages their use, and strong detection is possible with single-generator training. The added experiments support these claims without redefining their core scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets frequency injection as evidence that the detector uses the intended cues and links the new frequency-baseline comparisons to codec-aware design. It also identifies severe-compression threshold failure and discusses calibration recovery. The existing limitations concerning temporal artifacts and future synthesis paradigms remain.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the future code/data-release promise with a project-repository address. It specifies framewise denoising and selection of the first 64 inference frames, while removing v1's explicit 64-frame training statement. Most implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware and timing information are unchanged.

E1.justification: The original Panda70M, GenVideo and recent-generator coverage is retained. v2 adds the SAFE challenge setting with unknown test generators and variable video properties, plus controlled recompression and frequency-transplant input scenarios. Additional training settings use generator families already represented in v1's evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 adds FreqNet and FIRE as directly relevant frequency-based comparators, evaluating both their original models and Pyramid Flow retraining in Tables 1–2 and supplementary Tables 7–10. These substantially expand the comparison supporting the frequency-based approach; all six previous baselines remain.

E3.justification: New protocols vary training across one, two and four generators, compare 20% versus full training data, and substitute CogVideo X1.5 for Pyramid Flow. Additional tests measure TNR after frequency injection and evaluate CRF 20–32 across wavelet depths, including threshold calibration with ten validation videos. The original benchmark splits and principal metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the original augmentation, backbone and wavelet-depth ablations, v2 tests dependence on training-generator number, generator identity and dataset size. arxiv_record.abstract: Latent stochastic differential equation (SDE) models are important tools for the unsupervised discovery of dynamical systems from data, with applications ranging from engineering to neuroscience. In these complex domains, exact posterior inference of the latent state path is typically intractable, motivating the use of approximate methods such as variational inference (VI). However, existing VI methods for inference in latent SDEs often suffer from slow convergence and numerical instability. We propose SDE Inference via Natural Gradients (SING), a method that leverages natural gradient VI to efficiently exploit the underlying geometry of the model and variational posterior. SING enables fast and reliable inference in latent SDE models by approximating intractable integrals and parallelizing computations in time. We provide theoretical guarantees that SING approximately optimizes the intractable, continuous-time objective of interest. Moreover, we demonstrate that better state inference enables more accurate estimation of nonlinear drift functions using, for example, Gaussian process SDE models. SING outperforms prior methods in state inference and drift estimation on a variety of datasets, including a challenging application to modeling neural dynamics in freely behaving animals. Altogether, our results illustrate the potential of SING as a tool for accurate inference in complex dynamical systems, especially those characterized by limited prior knowledge and non-conjugate structure.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, there has been significant progress in learning-based diffusion samplers, which aim to sample from a given unnormalized density. Many of these approaches formulate the sampling task as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem using a canonical uninformative reference process, which limits their ability to efficiently guide trajectories toward the target distribution. In this work, we propose the Non-Equilibrium Annealed Adjoint Sampler (NAAS), a novel SOC-based diffusion framework that employs annealed reference dynamics as a non-stationary base SDE. This annealing structure provides a natural progression toward the target distribution and generates informative reference trajectories, thereby enhancing the stability and efficiency of learning the control. Owing to our SOC formulation, our framework can incorporate a variety of SOC solvers, thereby offering high flexibility in algorithmic design. As one instantiation, we employ a lean adjoint system inspired by adjoint matching, enabling efficient and scalable training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NAAS across a range of tasks, including sampling from classical energy landscapes and molecular Boltzmann distributions.
arxiv_record.authors: Jaemoo Choi, Yongxin Chen, Molei Tao, Guan-Horng Liu

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper presents a computational model for universal video temporal grounding, which accurately localizes temporal moments in videos based on natural language queries (e.g., questions or descriptions). Unlike existing methods that are often limited to specific video domains or durations, we propose UniTime, a robust and universal video grounding model leveraging the strong vision-language understanding capabilities of generative Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Our model effectively handles videos of diverse views, genres, and lengths while comprehending complex language queries. The key contributions include: (i) We consider steering strong MLLMs for temporal grounding in videos. To enable precise timestamp outputs, we incorporate temporal information by interleaving timestamp tokens with video tokens. (ii) By training the model to handle videos with different input granularities through adaptive frame scaling, our approach achieves robust temporal grounding for both short and long videos. (iii) Comprehensive experiments show that UniTime outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both zero-shot and dataset-specific finetuned settings across five public temporal grounding benchmarks. (iv) When employed as a preliminary moment retriever for long-form video question-answering (VideoQA), UniTime significantly improves VideoQA accuracy, highlighting its value for complex video understanding tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: Zeqian Li, Shangzhe Di, Zhonghua Zhai, Weilin Huang, Yanfeng Wang, Weidi Xie
arxiv_record.title: Universal Video Temporal Grounding with Generative Multi-modal Large Language Models

Unlike existing methods that are often limited to specific video domains or durations, we propose **UniTime**, a robust and universal video grounding model leveraging the strong vision-language understanding capabilities of generative Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Our model effectively handles videos of diverse views, genres, and lengths while comprehending complex language queries. The key contributions include: (i) We consider steering strong MLLMs for temporal grounding in videos. To enable precise timestamp outputs, we incorporate temporal information by interleaving timestamp tokens with video tokens. (ii) By training the model to handle videos with different input granularities through adaptive frame scaling, our approach achieves robust temporal grounding for both short and long videos. (iii) Comprehensive experiments show that UniTime outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both zero-shot and dataset-specific finetuned settings across five public temporal grounding benchmarks. (iv) When employed as a preliminary moment retriever for long-form video question-answering (VideoQA), UniTime significantly improves VideoQA accuracy, highlighting its value for complex video understanding tasks.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: universal grounding through timestamp interleaving and adaptive scaling, hierarchical inference, efficient training, benchmark performance and downstream VideoQA benefits. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning balanced short/long-video performance against closed models, consistency relative to VTune, and accuracy-versus-computation tradeoffs for processing strategies and thresholds. The existing limitations concerning task specialization, reasoning capabilities and fixed segment lengths remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds training-cost information: Table 11 reports 21, 12 and 24.5 hours for processing alternatives, and the text reports five additional days for short-video token compression in UniTime-Full. It also explains threshold routing and the hardware-imposed token ceiling. Existing optimization details, prompts and project link are retained.

E1.justification: The training datasets, five main grounding benchmarks and four VideoQA benchmarks remain unchanged. Appendix D adds Charades-CON and ActivityNet-CON evaluations involving paraphrased queries and shifted moments, extending test conditions within existing video domains.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Qwen2-VL-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B baselines. New Table 5 compares Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4o and Seed1.5-VL. Tables 6 and 10 further add InternVL2.5 baselines and consistency comparisons involving Gemini 1.5 Flash, Video-LLaMA and TimeChat with and without VTune.

E3.justification: V2 introduces random-subset closed-model evaluation that excludes outputs without timestamps, consistency evaluation across three paraphrases and shifted moments, and controlled processing, threshold and token-budget sweeps. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original training defaults and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds consistency testing, resizing-versus-compression controls, timestamp-versus-position-encoding ablations, and sensitivity analyses for both frame thresholds and token budget. Backbone analysis expands to InternVL2.5. The earlier Qwen size/type studies are partly incorporated into Section 3.4, rather than being entirely new experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Table 10's bracketed values are relative consistency scores; averaging across three paraphrases defines an evaluation metric rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Shared main benchmark, module-ablation, robustness and VideoQA scores remain unchanged. Tables 5–6 and 10–15 add substantial results, including Charades-STA mIoU of 63.15 versus 44.85 for timestamp insertion versus dense position encodings. V1 Table 9's Qwen2.5-VL UniTime results on ANet-Captions, QVHighlights and TaCoS are omitted. New subset results do not establish improvements over earlier full-benchmark scores.

M1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.3 retain adaptive frame scaling, timestamp interleaving, hierarchical inference, the autoregressive objective and video-centric training. Additional backbone experiments and explanations do not document a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: V2 inserts closed-model and flexibility subsections, moves and reworks model ablations, reorganizes the later appendices, and adds cross-references, acknowledgements and the conference designation. Most existing introduction, method, related-work and conclusion prose is retained.

P2.justification: The table presentation expands substantially with closed-model, consistency, processing, encoding and hyperparameter displays. The separate model-size/type tables are recast into Table 6's baseline-versus-UniTime layout, Table 3 gains rows, and several displays move. The eight existing figures retain their substantive content.

R1.justification: Eight references are added, covering newly evaluated models and grounding-consistency research. Section 3.6 and Appendix D explicitly position UniTime against VTune's consistency-oriented training. The broader related-work taxonomy and earlier citations remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds a mathematical specification of rephrased grounding consistency using IoU between predictions for original and paraphrased queries, averaged over three variants. The original task formulation, scaling equations, sequence construction and training loss remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked direct controls isolating timestamp encoding and resizing versus token compression. V2 supplies these controls and sensitivity/cost evidence in Tables 11–15, while Table 6 extends validation beyond Qwen and Appendix D adds consistency testing. This substantially strengthens support for central design and generality claims. Benefits are tempered by omitted cross-dataset backbone results and weaknesses in the new closed-model comparison: unspecified subset sizes, exclusion of untimestamped outputs, and a Seed1.5-VL prose score of 72.2 conflicting with Table 5's 73.69. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniTime research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds closed-model comparisons, broader backbone evaluations, grounding-consistency tests and additional ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original temporal-grounding and VideoQA experiments, module and robustness analyses, and additional model-size and architecture experiments in Appendix D.

arxiv_record.abstract: This work establishes that sparse Bayesian neural networks achieve optimal posterior contraction rates over anisotropic Besov spaces and their hierarchical compositions. These structures reflect the intrinsic dimensionality of the underlying function, thereby mitigating the curse of dimensionality. Our analysis shows that Bayesian neural networks equipped with either sparse or continuous shrinkage priors attain the optimal rates which are dependent on the intrinsic dimension of the true structures. Moreover, we show that these priors enable rate adaptation, allowing the posterior to contract at the optimal rate even when the smoothness level of the true function is unknown. The proposed framework accommodates a broad class of functions, including additive and multiplicative Besov functions as special cases. These results advance the theoretical foundations of Bayesian neural networks and provide rigorous justification for their practical effectiveness in high-dimensional, structured estimation problems.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain near-minimax contraction and adaptation over anisotropic and composite Besov spaces. v2 makes the composite-Besov novelty more explicit, but v1's Table 1 footnote already distinguished earlier composite Hölder results. No new principal contribution is introduced.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds practical guidance favoring sparse architectures and sparsity-inducing priors, and explicitly extends the interpretation toward neural-network performance more broadly. Appendix A.2 explains why the scaled sigmoid accompanies unit-bounded functions. The existing computational and horseshoe-prior limitations remain.

D1.justification: The explicit prior hyperparameter recipe and approximating-network specifications are revised. v2 additionally details layerwise rescaling coefficients in C.5 and the exact network parameter count in C.8. These concern the theoretical construction; no implementation, hardware, runtime or code/data release is introduced.

E1.justification: Neither version trains or evaluates on datasets or test scenarios. Added discussion of images motivates the theory and does not establish additional evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods experimentally. Table 1 compares theoretical literature; its revision does not add or remove evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an empirical evaluation protocol. Changes to theoretical network constructions, classification risk and norm inequalities belong to the model and theory assessments.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, sensitivity experiments, robustness tests or empirical case studies. The additive, multiplicative, rotated and piecewise mathematical examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repetitions, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Revised probability bounds are theoretical derivations, not changes in empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: No empirical result entries are added, removed or updated. The illustrative functions and principal contraction-rate orders remain the same; corrections to mathematical bounds and definitions are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The network and prior families remain, but their specifications receive meaningful refinements. Example 3.5 changes the continuous prior's slab weight from 1/T to exp[-2 C_A(log n)^2] and revises its spike scale. Appendix A.2 replaces the ordinary sigmoid with a scaled sigmoid. These change the specified models without introducing a new inference framework.

P1.justification: The main organization remains. v2 polishes prose, expands motivation and discussion, adds acknowledgments and proof pointers, and consolidates selected appendix statements. The heavy-tail proof moves from v1 C.16 to v2 C.9, and classification inequalities are integrated into surrounding text or proofs.

P2.justification: Table 1 is reorganized into single-function and composite-function columns, and a new Table 2 summarizes assumptions and theorems. Figure 1 adds panel labels and color scales; Figure 2 gains color styling. These revise existing displays and add a summary without changing the overall layout substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds Donoho–Johnstone (1995), Pope et al. (2021), and four references on CNN and transformer theory. Section 1.1 clarifies that Egels and Castillo's composite results concern Hölder classes, resolving misleading v1 prose while retaining its earlier table-footnote distinction. Publication updates concern already cited works.

T1.justification: Assumption (C3) now requires exponentially smaller tail mass in (log n)^2 and uses a smaller threshold. v2 C.12 replaces v1 C.10's binomial-tail argument, while C.13 adds missing weight-tail control and an explicit adaptive-shrinkage argument. Lemma B.4 revises approximation tolerance, depth and sparsity, supported by an expanded rescaling construction. Appendix A also corrects excess classification risk by subtracting Bayes risk and changes the empirical-norm upper-bound coefficient from 1/2 to 3/2. These substantially revise the mathematical support.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper's mathematical support by correcting the shrinkage tail-bound argument, supplying missing adaptive sieve control, expanding the bounded-weight approximation construction, and repairing the classification-risk definition. These address central deficiencies in a theoretical paper. The stronger shrinkage assumption narrows applicability, and new Table 2 incorrectly associates Theorem 3.14(i)/(ii) with prior families rather than assumptions (A4)/(A5). Those limitations do not outweigh the substantial proof corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of posterior contraction for sparse Bayesian neural networks. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–C are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 remains a theoretical paper. Neither its main text nor appendices report original empirical outcomes; the figures illustrate specified functions and compositional structures.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical results and proofs, without original experiments, simulations or data analyses. Its function plots are mathematical illustrations; Appendix A's empirical-norm results are theoretical.

arxiv_record.abstract: Training and inference of Large Language Models (LLMs) with tensor-parallelism requires substantial communication to synchronize activations. Our findings suggest that with a few minor adjustments to current practices, LLMs can be trained without fully synchronizing activations, reducing bandwidth demands. We name this "Communication-Aware Architecture for Tensor-parallelism" (CAAT-Net). We train a 7B parameter CAAT-Net model and show that tensor-parallel communication can be reduced by up to 50% with no significant drop in pretraining accuracy across nearly all evaluated benchmarks. We also experiment with smaller 130M and 1.1B models to show the robustness and scalability of our method. We find that, in some scenarios, validation loss can even improve when reducing communication. Finally, we demonstrate how CAAT-Net accelerates both training and inference workloads across various settings and model sizes.
arxiv_record.authors: Itay Lamprecht, Asaf Karnieli, Yair Hanani, Niv Giladi, Daniel Soudry
arxiv_record.title: Tensor-Parallelism with Partially Synchronized Activations

C1.justification: The central communication-reduction and acceleration claims remain. V2 qualifies the abstract's accuracy claim with 'across nearly all evaluated benchmarks' and describes accuracy as 'largely on par' in the contributions, while elevating possible validation-loss improvements into the abstract.

C2.justification: V2 adds the ensemble interpretation at zero synchronization, explains the computation-graph distinction, and discusses optional scaling and hardware-buffer alignment as accuracy/speed considerations. It removes v1's explicit caution about generalizing small-model trends and treating validation loss as a proxy. The training-speed projection limitation remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code link, NVIDIA device and NVLink specifications, the gpt-fast implementation reference, and GPT-XL configuration details. It also specifies training-speed micro-batches of 4 for TP4 and 8 for TP8/16; these disclosures alone do not establish changes to the corresponding earlier settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use RedPajama and the same seven evaluation benchmarks, alongside validation loss, training throughput and inference latency. Added experiments vary model architectures, synchronization, precision and hardware within these retained tasks; they introduce no new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: Fully synchronized models remain the accuracy and speed comparators, and Top-K and random masking remain the compression comparators. The added NVIDIA experiments use a different implementation framework but retain the full-all-reduce reference method.

E3.justification: Llama2-7B training increases from 90B to 160B tokens. V2 introduces a TinyLlama synchronization sweep, GPT3-XL training over 50B tokens, NVIDIA inference experiments using gpt-fast, and controlled precision/scaling experiments. These substantially expand experimental configurations and protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct bfloat16-versus-fp32 accumulation experiments showing instability after approximately 15K steps (Appendix E.1), private-channel scaling ablations (E.3), and synchronization sensitivity across TinyLlama configurations. GPT-XL and NVIDIA experiments additionally test architecture and hardware robustness beyond v1's evidence.

E5.justification: Accuracy uncertainty margins appear in both versions. V2 additionally reports Welch's t-test, identifying the 7B BoolQ difference as marginally significant with p-value 0.046 and describing other accuracy differences as nonsignificant. Neither version specifies additional repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the 7B results after longer training: baseline/CAAT-Net BoolQ changes from 62.75/62.29 to 64.89/62.51. TinyLlama scores and 130M curves are revised; GPT-XL, expanded synchronization and NVIDIA results are added. Training throughput values also change, including TP16 at p=0.25 from 110190 to 112456 tokens/s. These are revised or newly reported results, not established same-setting gains. Existing 34B/70B inference measurements are retained.

M1.justification: Private-channel correction changes from scaling weights at initialization in v1 Section 3.2 to multiplying activations by the corrective factor in v2 Section 4. V2 also introduces sequential logical-device inference with local summation when using fewer physical devices. The central partial-reduction and backward-synchronization procedures remain.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: attention equations move to Appendix A, channel scaling moves into implementation, large-scale and synchronization experiments are combined, and compression accounting moves to Appendix D. The abstract, architectural explanation, inference discussion and experimental narrative are also rewritten.

P2.justification: Figures 3 and 4 become expanded multipanel displays, the compression table becomes Figure 5, and new diagnostic Figures 6–7 and evaluation tables are introduced. Architecture diagrams and captions are revised. The earlier 34B/70B speedup plots disappear, while their numerical tables remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for context parallelism, LayerNorm and RMSNorm. It expands discussion of the already-cited Ladder Residual method and explains how competing communication demands motivate complementarity with overlap methods. The overall research positioning remains.

T1.justification: V2 generalizes the stated backward-pass derivation from RMSNorm to arbitrary normalization functions, including LayerNorm, and removes v1's Top-K MMSE-optimality assertion. The MLP/attention definitions, residual-gradient reasoning and Appendix C speedup derivation are otherwise retained, despite relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support for important implementation requirements through direct precision and scaling ablations, and tests robustness across synchronization levels, architectures and hardware. The code link and explicit BoolQ significance qualification improve reproducibility information and claim calibration. Training-speed evidence remains a 16-bit projection, and the retained 14% speedup statement conflicts with the approximately 16.4% implied by the revised Table 6. These reporting limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CAAT-Net. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including material relocated between sections.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E retain original experiments and add GPT-XL evaluations, numerical-precision and scaling ablations, TinyLlama synchronization sweeps, and NVIDIA timing measurements.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original model-training results, zero-shot evaluations, synchronization and compression experiments, and training/inference timing measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Multi-compartment Hodgkin-Huxley models are biophysical models of how electrical signals propagate throughout a neuron, and they form the basis of our knowledge of neural computation at the cellular level. However, these models have many free parameters that must be estimated for each cell, and existing fitting methods rely on intracellular voltage measurements that are highly challenging to obtain in vivo. Recent advances in neural recording technology with high-density probes and arrays enable dense sampling of extracellular voltage from many sites surrounding a neuron, allowing indirect measurement of many compartments of a cell simultaneously. Here, we propose a method for inferring the underlying membrane voltage, biophysical parameters, and the neuron's position relative to the probe, using extracellular measurements alone. We use an Extended Kalman Filter to infer membrane voltage and channel states using efficient, differentiable simulators. Then, we learn the model parameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood using gradient-based methods. We demonstrate the performance of this approach using simulated data and real neuron morphologies.

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about extracellular-only biophysical inference, robustness to misspecification, and applicability to reconstructed morphologies remain substantially unchanged. The introduction expands the claimed scalable-inference contribution from diagonal covariance approximation to both diagonal and block-diagonal approximations.

C2.justification: V1 mainly gives generic warnings about approximation bias. V2 identifies concrete validity conditions involving integration steps, gating sensitivities, firing frequency, and electrode–compartment geometry. It explains RGC diagonal-EKF failure through measurement coupling, motivates preserving voltage correlations, and discusses reducing gating variances as a mitigation. These substantially qualify the method's applicability.

D1.justification: V2 newly states the multi-branch axial resistivity, but omits previously specified current-injection amplitudes for misspecification, RGC, and CA1 experiments. Software versions, hardware, and code-access information remain. Reproducibility also suffers from an unresolved discrepancy: Table 1 retains leak conductance 0.003 S/cm² while the revised single-branch plots mark approximately 0.0003 as the true value.

E1.justification: The simulated extracellular-inference tasks and RGC/CA1 morphology coverage remain. V2 adds explicit high- versus low-frequency spiking scenarios in a 100-compartment cable analysis (Figure B.2), extending the tested dynamical regimes. Changes in compartment counts within existing validation tasks are principally experimental-setting changes.

E2.justification: The simple-model comparison expands from EKF versus MSE fitting to full EKF, diagonal EKF, block-diagonal EKF, and MSE (Figure 2C). V2 also adds diagonal-versus-full EKF comparisons for the multi-branch model and diagonal-versus-block-diagonal comparisons for RGC, substantially broadening the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes from one compartment, 10 µm electrode distance, and 3 µV baseline noise to ten compartments, 5 µm, and 1 µV. Multi-branch injected current changes from 0.5 to 2 nA. RGC uses 10 rather than 169 electrodes and replaces the 0.1/10 µV sweep with low-noise experiments. CA1 noise changes from 1 to 0.1 µV and fitting switches from full to block-diagonal EKF.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantial approximation-validity analyses: firing-regime Jacobian heatmaps, measurement-coupling heatmaps, and diagonal-EKF parameter, voltage, and localization diagnostics (Appendix B; Figures E.2 and E.6–E.9). RGC becomes an explicit approximation-failure comparison. V1's RGC noise-sensitivity sweep is removed; the channel-misspecification tests and runtime analysis remain, with the former using revised setups.

E5.justification: V2 no longer reports the RGC ten-dataset replication and associated mean/standard-deviation summaries shown in v1's Appendix D. It reports over 100 RGC initializations instead of 100. Forty-dataset uncertainty reporting for simpler models remains. Missing replication reporting does not establish that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: V2 adds results showing block-diagonal EKF matching full EKF/MSE while diagonal EKF exhibits bias (Figure 2C). RGC results change from successful diagonal-EKF recovery to diagonal failure and block-diagonal success (Figure 4). CA1 recovery traces are replaced, with remaining errors emphasized for leak conductances. These involve changed formulations or settings, so they do not establish same-setting performance gains; the approximately twofold diagonal-EKF runtime result is retained.

M1.justification: V2 revises the stated observation model: transmembrane current includes surface area and capacitive current, yielding a voltage-only linear observation mapping (Section 2). It also introduces a block-diagonal EKF with dense voltage covariance and diagonal gating covariance, substantially extending v1's full and diagonal EKF procedures.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially reorganized: Section 3.2 separates diagonal approximation, validity, and block-diagonal approximation; experimental passages are rewritten around approximation comparisons; and appendices place validity theory and geometric identifiability before experimental details. The abstract and broad six-section main-text outline remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different conference layout and substantially redesigns the visual presentation. Figure 2 introduces boxplots and rearranged panels; Figure 4 replaces noise/conductance panels with approximation comparisons and a heatmap. Multiple diagnostic figures are added, and RGC noise-sweep displays disappear. Existing localization and runtime figures are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gold, Henze, and Koch (2007), 'Using extracellular action potential recordings to constrain compartmental models,' when defining transmembrane current. The broader literature coverage and first-to-fit positioning remain largely unchanged. Conversion to numbered references is stylistic.

T1.justification: V2 revises the transmembrane-current definition and derives the linear observation mapping. New Appendices B and C analyze Jacobian sensitivities and electrode coupling, define the BD(K) covariance family, and prove its closure under stated assumptions, with block update and complexity derivations. The earlier geometric unidentifiability argument is retained in Appendix D.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the scientific foundation by correcting the main-text current formulation and replacing broadly favorable diagonal-EKF evidence with explicit validity conditions, a demonstrated failure case, and an evaluated block-diagonal alternative. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulation results for these neuron models, including comparisons of covariance approximations, reconstruction results, and analyses of approximation failure.

arxiv_record.abstract: State-of-the-art text-to-image models generate photorealistic images at an unprecedented speed. This work focuses on models that operate in a bitwise autoregressive manner over a discrete set of tokens that is practically infinite in size. However, their impressive generative power comes with a growing risk: as their outputs increasingly populate the Internet, they are likely to be scraped and reused as training data-potentially by the very same models. This phenomenon has been shown to lead to model collapse, where repeated training on generated content, especially from the models' own previous versions, causes a gradual degradation in performance. A promising mitigation strategy is watermarking, which embeds human-imperceptible yet detectable signals into generated images-enabling the identification of generated content. In this work, we introduce BitMark, a robust bitwise watermarking framework. Our method embeds a watermark directly at the bit level of the token stream during the image generation process. Our bitwise watermark subtly influences the bits to preserve visual fidelity and generation speed while remaining robust against a spectrum of removal techniques. Furthermore, it exhibits high radioactivity, i.e., when watermarked generated images are used to train another image generative model, this second model's outputs will also carry the watermark. The radioactive traces remain detectable even when only fine-tuning diffusion or image autoregressive models on images watermarked with our BitMark. Overall, our approach provides a principled step toward preventing model collapse in image generative models by enabling reliable detection of generated outputs. The code is available at https://github.com/sprintml/BitMark.

C1.justification: The abstract and first contribution broaden the Infinity-focused scope to bitwise image generators, explicitly including Instella. The conclusion additionally claims a significant radioactivity-induced distributional shift with only 5% watermarked training data, substantially extending the stated applicability conditions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking Instella/BiGR robustness limitations to their smaller token counts, hypothesizes that Infinity-8B's lower bias reduces robustness, and interprets weak radioactivity through distribution-level significance. Existing rotation, image-quality, and large-scale false-positive limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a BitMark repository link, single-scale pseudocode, baseline message lengths, and generation settings for the added models. Existing hardware and fine-tuning details remain. Some specificity is lost from the interpolation and convolution descriptions, while BiGR's added preprocessing noise is not quantified.

E1.justification: MS-COCO and ImageNet coverage is retained. v2 adds LAION POP for false-positive evaluation (Table 19), horizontal and vertical flipping, and combined rotation-plus-center-crop inputs, modestly extending the existing image-watermarking scenarios.

E2.justification: v1 reports BitMark's robustness without direct numerical comparisons against other watermarking methods. v2 evaluates RivaGAN, StegaStamp, and TrustMark on Infinity-2B images alongside BitMark in Table 2, substantially expanding the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Infinity-8B and Instella configurations with delta=1.5, and BiGR configurations at two resolutions with delta=3 and 5,000 prompts. New protocols vary watermarked fine-tuning fractions, apply rotation correction with optional 50% center cropping, and transfer an MS-COCO-calibrated threshold across datasets. The original fine-tuning hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test radioactivity under clean/watermarked training mixtures (Table 6), rotation correction with and without cropping (Tables 13–14), and false-positive calibration across datasets (Table 19). Existing bit-sequence, scale, watermark-strength, and Bit-Flipper analyses are retained under reorganized appendices.

E5.justification: v2 adds a one-tailed Mann–Whitney U test and p-value reporting for the radioactivity dilution experiment (Section 4.3, Table 6). Existing mean/standard-deviation reporting continues; neither version specifies repeated-training run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: Substantial new results cover baselines, additional models, and supplementary analyses. Examples include 22.7% TPR at 1% FPR after fine-tuning with 10% watermarked data, and newly measured rotation-correction TPRs of 18.4% without correction versus 98.3% with correction. Table 5 also changes Infinity-2B radioactivity from 99.7% to 100.0%, although v2's prose still says 99.7%.

M1.justification: The core bit-pattern logit bias and z-score detector remain unchanged. v2 adds single-scale embedding and detection procedures without multiscale residual processing (Algorithms 3–4), and introduces noise before encoding for BiGR detection (Appendix G). These are limited procedural adaptations.

P1.justification: The appendices are extensively reorganized: limitations and related work move forward, natural-image evaluation becomes an experimental subsection, and attack material is consolidated. The title and framing are revised, and a NeurIPS checklist is appended, although much existing prose remains.

P2.justification: v2 introduces a main comparison table with baseline/model rows and flipping columns, adds several experimental tables, and relocates the original watermark-strength table to the appendix. Existing figures are resized or repositioned, and the timing table is transposed. The original qualitative image content is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Instella, BiGR, TrustMark, StegaStamp, and RivaGAN, with corresponding model background and comparison positioning. The underlying discussion of LLM watermarking, diffusion watermarking, and model collapse is largely retained.

T1.justification: The bit-bias equation, z-score definition and null model, and green/red-list combinatorial reasoning are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the new significance test is an empirical statistical procedure.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 through direct watermark-baseline comparisons and mixed-data radioactivity controls. Measured rotation correction and explicit model-specific weaknesses further strengthen evidence about practical applicability. These gains outweigh the new Table 5 table/prose inconsistency and incomplete specification of BiGR's noise preprocessing.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BitMark research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renaming and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds watermark-baseline comparisons, mixed-data radioactivity, rotation correction, additional model evaluations, and cross-dataset false-positive measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Finetuning large pretrained neural networks is known to be resource-intensive, both in terms of memory and computational cost. To mitigate this, a common approach is to restrict training to a subset of the model parameters. By analyzing the relationship between gradients and weights during finetuning, we observe a notable pattern: large gradients are often associated with small-magnitude weights. This correlation is more pronounced in finetuning settings than in training from scratch. Motivated by this observation, we propose NANOADAM, which dynamically updates only the small-magnitude weights during finetuning and offers several practical advantages: first, this criterion is gradient-free -- the parameter subset can be determined without gradient computation; second, it preserves large-magnitude weights, which are likely to encode critical features learned during pretraining, thereby reducing the risk of catastrophic forgetting; thirdly, it permits the use of larger learning rates and consistently leads to better generalization performance in experiments. We demonstrate this for both NLP and vision tasks.

arxiv_record.abstract: Greedy Equivalence Search (GES) is a classic score-based algorithm for causal discovery from observational data. In the sample limit, it recovers the Markov equivalence class of graphs that describe the data. Still, it faces two challenges in practice: computational cost and finite-sample accuracy. In this paper, we develop Less Greedy Equivalence Search (LGES), a variant of GES that retains its theoretical guarantees while partially addressing these limitations. LGES modifies the greedy step; rather than always applying the highest-scoring insertion, it avoids edge insertions between variables for which the score implies some conditional independence. This more targeted search yields up to a \(10\)-fold speed-up and a substantial reduction in structural error relative to GES. Moreover, LGES can guide the search using prior knowledge, and can correct this knowledge when contradicted by data. Finally, LGES can use interventional data to refine the learned observational equivalence class. We prove that LGES recovers the true equivalence class in the sample limit, even with misspecified knowledge. Experiments demonstrate that LGES outperforms GES and other baselines in speed, accuracy, and robustness to misspecified knowledge. Our code is available at https://github.com/CausalAILab/lges.

arxiv_record.journal-ref: Forthcoming in Proceedings of the 39th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (2025)
